subject: GK
question: Which architectural style is the Brihadeeswarar Temple in Tamil Nadu known for?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Dravidian**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Brihadeeswarar Temple**, located in **Thanjavur**, **Tamil Nadu**, is one of the most celebrated examples of **Dravidian Architecture**. This style is characterized by its pyramid-shaped towers, known as **Vimanas**, and large temple complexes. **Dravidian** architecture is the correct answer because the temple exhibits all the classic features of this South Indian style, such as the **Vimana**, **Mandapa**, and **Gopurams**.

• The temple was built by the **Chola Emperor Raja Raja Chola I** between **1003 AD** and **1010 AD**. It was a symbol of the **Chola Dynasty's** power and their devotion to **Lord Shiva**.

• A unique feature of this temple is its **Vimana** (the tower over the sanctum), which stands at a height of **216 feet** (approximately **66 meters**). At the time of its construction, it was one of the tallest structures in the world.

• The temple is constructed entirely out of **granite**. This is a remarkable feat because there are no granite sources within a **60-kilometer** radius of **Thanjavur**, implying a massive logistical effort during the **11th century**.

• The temple is part of the **UNESCO World Heritage Site** known as the **Great Living Chola Temples**, which also includes the **Brihadisvara Temple** at **Gangaikonda Cholapuram** and the **Airavatesvara Temple** at **Darasuram**.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Nagara Style**: This architectural style is predominant in **Northern India**. Unlike the **Dravidian** style, the **Nagara** style features a beehive-shaped tower called a **Shikhara**. It typically does not have the massive **Gopurams** (gateways) or the large water tanks that are common in South Indian temples. Examples include the **Kandariya Mahadeva Temple** in **Khajuraho** and the **Sun Temple** in **Konark**.

• **Vesara Style**: This is a hybrid style that combines elements of both **Nagara** and **Dravidian** architecture. It flourished in the **Deccan** region of India, particularly under the **Chalukya** and **Hoysala** dynasties. The **Chennakesava Temple** at **Belur** is a famous example of this style.

• **Indo-Saracenic Style**: This is a **revivalist** architectural style used by **British architects** in India during the late **19th century**. It blends **Indo-Islamic**, **Hindu**, and **Gothic** elements. Notable examples include the **Victoria Memorial** in **Kolkata** and the **Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus** in **Mumbai**.

• **Chola Art and Culture**: The **Chola** period is known as the **Golden Age** of **Tamil** culture. Apart from architecture, the **Cholas** were famous for their **bronze sculptures**, particularly the **Nataraja** (the dancing Shiva), and their extensive maritime trade across **Southeast Asia**.

**Important Points__**

• The **Kumbam** (the apex or the bulbous structure at the top of the tower) of the **Brihadeeswarar Temple** is carved out of a **single rock** and is estimated to weigh about **80 tons**.

• The temple is also known as **Dakshina Meru** (the Meru of the South). The **Shiva Linga** inside the sanctum is one of the largest in India, standing **3.7 meters** tall.

• The temple complex features a massive statue of **Nandi** (the sacred bull), which is also carved from a **single stone**. It measures about **13 feet** in height and **16 feet** in length.

• The walls of the temple are covered with **Chola-era frescoes** and **inscriptions** in **Tamil** and **Sanskrit**, which provide valuable historical data about the **Chola** administration, social life, and economy.

• In **2010**, the temple celebrated its **1000th anniversary**, an event marked by significant cultural celebrations and the release of a commemorative **1000-rupee coin** by the **Reserve Bank of India**.
</ul

question: Which metal casting technique was mastered by ancient Indian sculptors?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Cire-perdue (lost-wax casting)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Cire-perdue**, also known as the **lost-wax casting technique**, was widely practiced by ancient Indian sculptors. This method involves creating a duplicate metal sculpture from an original wax model.
 
• The process begins by sculpting the desired object in wax, which is then coated with clay or other refractory materials to create a mold. The mold is then heated to melt the wax, which is "lost" or drained away, leaving a cavity in its place.
 
• Molten metal (usually bronze or copper alloys) is poured into the cavity, allowed to cool, and then the outer mold is broken away to reveal the final sculpture. This method is highly precise and allows for intricate detailing. *Hence, this is the correct technique mastered by ancient Indian sculptors.*
 
• Ancient Indian artisans, particularly during the **Chola dynasty** (9th–13th centuries CE), were renowned for producing exquisite bronze statues using this technique. Examples include the famous **Nataraja (Lord of Dance) sculptures**.
 
• This technique was not limited to religious or spiritual sculptures but was also used for crafting utilitarian objects and decorations. *Hence, the mastery of Cire-perdue by Indian sculptors is historically significant.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Hammer forging:**

 
 
• Hammer forging is a technique where metal is shaped by hammering it into the desired form, usually while it is hot. This method is not suitable for intricate sculptures but is primarily used for tools, weapons, and other functional items.
 
• It does not offer the precision and detailing achievable with the lost-wax casting technique. Hence, this was not the primary technique mastered by ancient Indian sculptors.
 
 
 
• **Die-casting:**
 
 
• Die-casting is a modern industrial process where molten metal is forced into a mold cavity under high pressure. It is used for mass production of parts and components in industries such as automotive and electronics.
 
• This technique was not used in ancient India, as it requires advanced technology and equipment that were unavailable during that time.
 
 
 
• **Sand casting:**
 
 
• Sand casting involves creating a mold from sand and pouring molten metal into it. While it is a traditional technique, it does not allow for the fine detailing that Cire-perdue provides.
 
• This method is more suited for larger, less intricate objects, such as industrial components or simple sculptures.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Cire-perdue:**
 
 
• This technique has been used to create statues, jewelry, and other intricate artifacts worldwide, including in regions like Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Greece, in addition to India.
 
• In modern times, lost-wax casting is still used in art and jewelry making, demonstrating its enduring significance.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Historical Significance:**

 
 
• The Cire-perdue technique has been a hallmark of ancient Indian craftsmanship, particularly in regions such as Tamil Nadu and Odisha.
 
• The Chola bronze sculptures are UNESCO-recognized cultural artifacts and are considered masterpieces of world art.
 
 
 
• **Modern Adaptations:**
 
 
• Today, the technique is used with advanced materials and tools, but the core principles remain unchanged from ancient practices.
 
• Lost-wax casting continues to inspire artists and is integral to the production of fine art and jewelry globally.

question: The rock-cut caves of Ajanta and Ellora, famous for their murals and sculptures, are located in which present-day state of India?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Maharashtra**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Ajanta and Ellora caves** are located in the **Aurangabad district** of the state of **Maharashtra**, India.
 
• **Ajanta Caves**: These caves are a group of **29 rock-cut Buddhist caves**, dating from the **2nd century BCE to about 480 CE**. They are famous for their **murals**, which depict stories from the life of Buddha and the Jataka tales. *Hence, the statement about murals is correct.*
 
• **Ellora Caves**: Located around **100 km away from Ajanta**, the Ellora caves consist of **34 rock-cut temples and monasteries**, dating from the **6th to 11th century CE**. These caves include **Buddhist, Hindu, and Jain monuments**. They are known for their intricate **sculptures**, notably the magnificent **Kailasa temple** (Cave 16), a monolithic structure dedicated to Lord Shiva.
 
• Both **Ajanta** and **Ellora caves** are recognized as **UNESCO World Heritage Sites** for their **historical**, **artistic**, and **cultural importance**.
 
• These caves are renowned for their architectural brilliance and artistic heritage, representing the **religious and cultural diversity of ancient India.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Ajanta Caves:**

 
 
• The **Ajanta caves** are carved into a **horseshoe-shaped rock face** overlooking the **Waghur River**.
 
• They are famous for their **frescoes and paintings**, which use a technique of mixing natural pigments with a plaster base. The paintings depict scenes from the **Jataka tales**, which narrate the previous births and lives of Buddha.
 
• The caves were rediscovered in **1819** by a British officer named **John Smith**, during a tiger hunt.
 
 
 
• **Ellora Caves:**
 
 
• These caves represent **three major religions** of India: **Buddhism**, **Hinduism**, and **Jainism**.
 
• The **Kailasa temple**, one of the largest monolithic rock-cut structures in the world, was commissioned by the **Rashtrakuta king Krishna I** in the 8th century CE.
 
• The Buddhist caves include monasteries and prayer halls, while the Jain caves are known for their intricate carvings and attention to detail.
 
 
 
• **Historical Significance:**
 
 
• Both Ajanta and Ellora caves reflect the **religious tolerance** and **artistic achievements** of ancient India.
 
• They showcase the **fusion of art, religion, and architecture**, serving as testimony to the skill and dedication of ancient Indian craftsmen.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Tourism:**

 
 
• The Ajanta and Ellora caves are popular **tourist destinations**, attracting visitors from all over the world.
 
• They are well-connected to major cities like **Aurangabad**, which serves as the nearest city for accommodation and transportation.
 
 
 
• **Preservation:**
 
 
• The caves are protected and maintained by the **Archaeological Survey of India (ASI)** and are part of India's rich cultural heritage.
 
• Efforts are ongoing to preserve the **delicate paintings** and carvings from environmental and human-induced damage.

subject: GK
question: Read the below statements marked as Assertion (A) and Reason (R). Mark the correct options:**Assertion (A):** Victorian Gothic buildings near Mumbai's Oval Maidan include Indian features like sloping tiled roofs and verandas.**Reason (R):** They were built using local basalt and Porbandar limestone, allowing integration of climate-suited features with Gothic style.

options.text: Both A and R are correct, and R explains A
Both A and R are correct, but R does not explain A
A is correct, R is incorrect
A is incorrect, R is correct

solution:
The correct answer is __**Both A and R are correct, and R explains A**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Assertion (A)** states that **Victorian Gothic** buildings near **Mumbai's Oval Maidan** include Indian features like **sloping tiled roofs** and **verandas**. This is correct because the **Gothic Revival** style, imported from **Europe** in the **19th century**, had to be adapted to the **tropical climate** of **India**. The **sloping roofs** were essential to drain the heavy **monsoon** rainwater, while **verandas** and **balconies** provided necessary shade and cross-ventilation. *Hence, statement A is correct.*

• **Reason (R)** explains that these buildings were constructed using local materials like **basalt** (specifically **Kurla basalt**) and **Porbandar limestone**. The availability of these local stones allowed architects to integrate **climate-suited features** into the **Gothic** framework. The **basalt** provided a sturdy, dark foundation, while the **limestone** allowed for intricate carvings and the creation of open galleries and **verandas** that are characteristic of Indian domestic architecture. *Hence, statement R is correct.*

• The **Reason (R)** directly explains **Assertion (A)** because the choice of **local materials** and the technical flexibility they offered enabled the **British architects** and **Indian craftsmen** to modify the rigid **European Gothic** designs. This synthesis created a unique architectural language known as **Bombay Gothic** or **Indo-Gothic**, where the structural logic of the **Gothic** style was successfully merged with **Indian** environmental needs. *Therefore, R is the correct explanation of A.*

• The buildings facing the **Oval Maidan**, such as the **Bombay High Court** and the **University of Mumbai**, serve as primary examples of this adaptation. They represent a period of **urban expansion** in the **1860s** and **1870s** following the demolition of the **Fort walls**.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **UNESCO World Heritage Status**: The **Victorian Gothic and Art Deco Ensembles of Mumbai** were officially inscribed as a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** in **July 2018**. This ensemble includes **19th-century Victorian Gothic** public buildings and **20th-century Art Deco** residential buildings around the **Oval Maidan**.

• **Architectural Features**: The **Victorian Gothic** style in **Mumbai** is characterized by **pointed arches**, **ribbed vaults**, and **flying buttresses**. However, the **Indian** influence added **carvings** of local flora and fauna, **wooden shutters**, and **deep eaves** to protect against the **sun** and **rain**.

• **Key Architects**: Prominent architects like **Sir George Gilbert Scott** (who designed the **University Library** and **Rajabai Clock Tower**) and **Colonel James Fuller** (who designed the **High Court**) were instrumental in shaping this skyline. The **Rajabai Tower**, standing at **280 feet**, was modeled after **Big Ben** in **London** but incorporated **oriental** motifs.

• **Materials Used**: The use of **Kurla basalt** (a dark grey stone) and **Malad stone** (a buff-colored stone) created a distinctive **polychromatic** effect. **Porbandar limestone** from **Gujarat** was frequently used for decorative elements due to its relative softness and ease of carving.

• **Historical Context**: This architectural movement flourished under the governorship of **Sir Bartle Frere** (**1862–1867**), who envisioned **Bombay** as a **Urbs Prima in Indis** (The First City in India). The wealth generated from the **Cotton Trade** during the **American Civil War** provided the **funding** for these grand projects.

**Important Points__**

• **Indo-Saracenic Influence**: While the buildings near the **Oval Maidan** are predominantly **Victorian Gothic**, they laid the groundwork for the **Indo-Saracenic** style, which further integrated **Islamic** and **Hindu** architectural elements like **domes**, **chhatris**, and **minarets** (e.g., the **Gateway of India** and **Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Vastu Sangrahalaya**).

• **Urban Planning**: The **Oval Maidan** acts as a **green buffer** between two distinct architectural eras: the **Victorian Gothic** buildings to its **east** and the **Art Deco** buildings to its **west** (built on the **Backbay Reclamation** in the **1930s**).

• **Climate Adaptation**: The **verandas** were not just aesthetic; they served as **buffer zones** that prevented the interior rooms from heating up, a crucial feature before the advent of **air conditioning**. The **sloping tiled roofs** typically used **Mangalore tiles**, which were highly effective for **heavy rainfall**.

question: Which year marked the completion of Rashtrapati Bhavan?
solution:
The correct answer is __**1929**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The construction of the **Rashtrapati Bhavan**, originally known as the **Viceroy's House**, was completed in the year **1929**. The project was a massive undertaking that spanned nearly **17 years** from its inception to its final completion. **Hence, this option is correct.**

• The year **1912** marked the **commencement** of the construction work on **Raisina Hill**. This followed the **1911** announcement by **King George V** during the **Delhi Durbar** that the capital of **British India** would be shifted from **Calcutta** to **Delhi**. Hence, this option is incorrect as it refers to the start, not the completion.

• The year **1921** is significant in the history of **New Delhi** as the **foundation stone** of the **Council House** (now known as the **Old Parliament House** or **Sansad Bhavan**) was laid by the **Duke of Connaught**, but the **Viceroy's House** was still in the middle of its construction phase during this time. Hence, this option is incorrect.

• The year **1935** is historically important for the **Government of India Act 1935**, which introduced significant constitutional reforms. However, the **Rashtrapati Bhavan** had already been completed and occupied by the **Viceroy** for several years by then. Hence, this option is incorrect.

• The primary architect responsible for the design was **Sir Edwin Lutyens**, who worked alongside **Herbert Baker**. Lutyens was tasked with creating a residence that would symbolize the permanence of **British rule** in India, resulting in a structure that covers a floor area of **200,000 square feet**.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Rashtrapati Bhavan** is the official residence of the **President of India** and is located at the Western end of **Rajpath** (now renamed **Kartavya Path**) in **New Delhi**. It is situated on **Raisina Hill**, which was leveled specifically for this project.

• The building comprises **four floors** and **340 rooms**, including the **Durbar Hall**, **Ashoka Hall**, and various guest suites. It is surrounded by a massive estate of **330 acres**, which includes the famous **Amrit Udyan** (formerly **Mughal Gardens**).

• The architectural style is a unique blend of **Mughal**, **Hindu**, and **Western Classical** influences. Notable Indian features include **chhatris** (dome-shaped pavilions), **jaalis** (perforated stone screens), and **chajjas** (overhanging eaves).

• The first resident of the building was **Lord Irwin**, the **Viceroy of India**, who moved into the house on **January 23, 1931**. After India gained independence, **C. Rajagopalachari** became the first Indian to reside there as the **Governor-General** in **1948**.

• On **January 26, 1950**, when India became a **Republic**, the building was officially renamed **Rashtrapati Bhavan**, and **Dr. Rajendra Prasad** became its first occupant in the capacity of the **President of India**.

**Important Points__**

• The central **dome** of the **Rashtrapati Bhavan** is one of its most striking features. It was inspired by the **Great Stupa at Sanchi**, showcasing the integration of **Buddhist architectural** elements into the design.

• The construction involved the use of approximately **700 million bricks** and **3 million cubic feet of stone**. The exterior is primarily made of **red and cream sandstone**, which was sourced from **Bharatpur** and **Dholpur**.

• The **Jaipur Column**, which stands in the center of the **Forecourt**, was a gift from the **Maharaja of Jaipur**, **Sawai Madho Singh**, to commemorate the building of the new capital city.

• The **Durbar Hall** is the most significant room within the building, located directly under the main dome. It is used for high-profile state ceremonies, such as the presentation of **Civilian and Military Awards** (like the **Bharat Ratna** and **Padma Awards**) and the **swearing-in** of the **Prime Minister** and the **Council of Ministers**.

• The **Ashoka Hall**, known for its magnificent **ceiling painting** and Persian-style carpets, serves as the venue for formal **State Banquets** and the credential ceremonies of **Foreign Ambassadors**.

subject: GK
question: The Mathura style of sculpture is distinguished by:

options.text: Indian indigenous themes with some Hellenistic influence
Purely Indian styles with no outside influence

solution:
The correct answer is __**Indian indigenous themes with some Hellenistic influence**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Mathura School of Art** flourished during the **Kushana Empire**, primarily between the **1st Century AD** and the **3rd Century AD**. This school developed concurrently with the **Gandhara School** but remained rooted in local traditions. ***Hence, the statement regarding its historical age is correct.***
 
• Unlike the Gandhara school, which was heavily influenced by **Greco-Roman** aesthetics, the **Mathura style** was largely an **indigenous** development that evolved from the earlier **Yaksha** and **Yakshini** figures of the **Maurya** and **Sunga** periods. ***Hence, the statement about its indigenous themes is correct.***
 
• The primary material used in the **Mathura School** was **spotted red sandstone**, sourced from nearby quarries like **Sikri** and **Kankali Tila**. This is a distinguishing feature from the **Grey Schist** used in **Gandhara**. ***Hence, the statement regarding the material used is correct.***
 
• While the school is celebrated for its **Indian** character, it was not entirely isolated; as the **Kushana** rulers controlled both **Mathura** and **Gandhara**, a cross-cultural exchange occurred, leading to **Hellenistic influences** appearing in later Mathura works, such as the treatment of **folds in drapery** and certain **iconographic** elements. ***Hence, the statement about Hellenistic influence is correct.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Themes and Religious Diversity:**
 
 
• The **Mathura School** was unique because it catered to three major religions: **Buddhism**, **Jainism**, and **Hinduism**.
 
• In **Buddhism**, it is credited with creating the first human representations of the **Buddha**, who was previously represented only through symbols like the **Bodhi tree** or **footprints**.
 
• In **Jainism**, the school produced numerous **Ayagapattas** (tablet of homage) and statues of **Tirthankaras** characterized by the **Srivatsa** mark on the chest.
 
• In **Hinduism**, early representations of **Shiva** (in **Lingam** and human form), **Vishnu**, and **Surya** were carved during this period.
 
 
 
• **Geographical Location:**
 
 
• The center of this art form was **Mathura**, situated on the banks of the **Yamuna River** in present-day **Uttar Pradesh**, **India**.
 
• Its location at the junction of major trade routes like the **Uttarapath** facilitated the spread of these sculptures to far-off places like **Sarnath** and **Shravasti**.
 
 
 
• **Physical Characteristics of Sculptures:**
 
 
• Sculptures often displayed **fleshy bodies** with a sense of **voluptuousness**, reflecting **Indian** notions of beauty and vitality (**Prana**).
 
• The **Buddha** figures typically featured a **shaven head** (later curly hair), a **large halo** decorated with geometric patterns, and the **Abhaya Mudra** (gesture of fearlessness).
 
• The drapery was usually **transparent** and clung closely to the body, often covering only the left shoulder (**Ekanshika**).
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Royal Statuary:** A famous example of the **Mathura School** is the **headless statue of Kanishka**, which shows him in **central Asian** attire—heavy boots and a long coat—demonstrating the **Kushana** identity.
 
• **Evolution into Gupta Art:** The **Mathura School** served as the foundation for the **Golden Age** of **Gupta Art** in the **4th and 5th centuries**. The **Gupta** artists refined the **Mathura** style, adding spiritual depth and more intricate decoration to the **haloes**.
 
• **Key Difference from Gandhara:** While **Gandhara** Buddha looked like **Apollo** (Greco-Roman features, wavy hair, muscular), the **Mathura** Buddha was modeled after the **Indian Yakshas** (smiling face, rounder features).

question: Which style of architecture was used in Lakshmi Vilas Palace in Vadodara, Gujarat?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Indo-arabic**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Indo-Arabic architecture** was used in **Lakshmi Vilas Palace in Vadodara**, Gujarat.
 
• Constructed in **1890 by Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad III,** the Lakshmi Vilas Palace in Vadodara, Gujarat, showcases the Indo-Saracenic architectural style.
 
• This fusion style harmonizes Indian, Islamic, and European architectural elements, such as Mughal, Gothic, and Hindu influences.
 
• Spanning 500 acres, the palace boasts exquisite Belgian stained glass and authentic teak woodwork.
 
• Its interior evokes the grandeur of a sprawling European country estate, complete with modern amenities like elevators.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Indo-Islamic architecture** embodies the architectural style of the Indian subcontinent, crafted by and for Islamic patrons and purposes. 
 
• Its roots trace back to the establishment of Delhi as the capital of the Ghurid dynasty in 1193, marking the inception of significant developments in this architectural tradition. 
 
• The subsequent Delhi Sultanate, comprising various Central Asian dynasties, and later the Mughal Empire from the 15th century onward, further advanced Indo-Islamic architecture. 
 
• These dynasties facilitated the integration of Islamic architectural and artistic styles from West Asia into the fabric of the Indian subcontinent.

question: Which of the following terms is NOT related to the structure of a stupa?
solution:
correct answer is__** ​Vimana.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• Vimana is the structure over the** garbhagriha or inner sanctum in the Hindu temples of South India and Odisha in East India**.
 
• In typical temples of Odisha using the **Kalinga style** of architecture, the vimana is the **tallest structure of the temple**, as it is in the shikhara towers of temples in West and North India.
 
• By contrast, **in large South Indian temples**, it is typically** smaller than the great gatehouses or gopuram**, which are the most immediately striking architectural elements in a temple complex.
 
• A vimana is usually shaped as a** pyramid, consisting of several stories or tala**.
 
• Vimana are divided in two groups: **jati vimanas** that have up to four tala and **mukhya vimana** that have five tala and more.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The stupa has **three special features **found in every stupa across the world.

 
 
• They are** A hemispherical mound (anda)**: The anda’s domed shape **(green highlights**) recalls a mound of dirt that was used to cover the Buddha’s remains.
 
• A **square railing (harmika)**: The harmika **(red highlights)** is inspired by a square railing or fence that surrounded the mound of dirt, marking it as a sacred burial site.
 
• A** central pillar** supporting a triple-umbrella form** (chattra)**: It was derived from umbrellas that were placed over the mound to protect it from the elements (purple highlights).

 The Indian gateway, usually of stone, marking the entrance to a Buddhist shrine or stupa or to a Hindu temple is known as "**Torana**".

 
 
•

•

•

• A **vedika** is a wooden fence that surrounds a sacred place that can be free-standing at ground level.
 
• In Buddhism and Hinduism, the **Chhatra** is an auspicious symbol representing royalty and protection. It is in the form of a stone disk typically decorated at the apex of a Buddhist stupa.

subject: GK
question: The basic notes in Indian classical music are called ________
solution:
The correct answer is __**Swaras**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Swaras** are the fundamental musical notes in **Indian classical music**. They represent the basic pitch and are the primary units from which melodies are constructed. ***Hence, the correct answer is Swaras.***

• There are **seven** basic notes in the Indian musical scale, collectively referred to as the **Sapta Swara**. These are **Shadja (Sa)**, **Rishabha (Re)**, **Gandhara (Ga)**, **Madhyama (Ma)**, **Panchama (Pa)**, **Dhaivata (Dha)**, and **Nishada (Ni)**.

• **Ragas** are melodic frameworks or modes used for composition and improvisation. A **Raga** is not a single note but a specific combination of **swaras** that evokes a particular emotion or mood. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***

• **Talas** refer to the rhythmic cycles or time measures in **Indian music**. They provide the beat and tempo for a performance, ensuring rhythmic consistency and structure. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***

• **Alankars** are musical ornaments or sequential patterns of **swaras**. They are used to decorate a melody and demonstrate a musician's technical skill through various permutations and combinations of notes. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Indian Classical Music** is categorized into two major systems: **Hindustani Classical Music** of **North India** and **Carnatic Classical Music** of **South India**. Both systems use the same **seven** basic **swaras**.

• The **Sama Veda** is considered the source of **Indian music**, as it consists of verses from the **Rig Veda** set to musical notes, forming the earliest known musical tradition in **India**.

• The **Natyashastra**, an ancient encyclopedic treatise on the performing arts by **Bharata Muni** (composed between **200 BCE** and **200 CE**), provides the earliest detailed description of **swaras** and **shrutis**.

• An octave in **Indian music** is divided into **22 Shrutis** (microtones). The **seven** main **swaras** are placed at specific intervals within these **22 shrutis** to create a scale.

• The **12 notes** in a full scale consist of **7 Shuddha Swaras** (natural notes) and **5 Vikrit Swaras** (modified notes). The **Vikrit Swaras** include **4 Komal** (flat) notes and **1 Teevra** (sharp) note.

**Important Points__**

• **Achala Swaras**: These are 'immovable' or fixed notes. **Shadja (Sa)** and **Panchama (Pa)** are the only two notes that do not have **Komal** or **Teevra** variations in the **Indian musical scale**.

• **Chala Swaras**: These are 'movable' notes that can be altered from their natural positions. **Re, Ga, Ma, Dha,** and **Ni** fall into this category and can be shifted to become **Komal** or **Teevra**.

• **Vadi and Samvadi**: The **Vadi** is the most prominent note in a **Raga**, often called the 'king' of the raga, while the **Samvadi** is the second most important note, acting as the 'minister' to support the melody.

• **Aroha and Avroha**: **Aroha** is the ascending sequence of **swaras** (e.g., **Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Dha Ni Sa**), and **Avroha** is the descending sequence (e.g., **Sa Ni Dha Pa Ma Ga Re Sa**).

subject: GK
question: Who composed the famous Carnatic music work 'Pancharatna Kritis'?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Tyagaraja**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Tyagaraja** (**1767–1847**) was a legendary composer and a saint of **Carnatic music** who lived in **Thiruvaiyaru**, **Tamil Nadu**. He is the composer of the **Pancharatna Kritis**, which are considered the most significant and masterful of his works. **Hence, the correct answer is Tyagaraja.**

• The **Pancharatna Kritis**, meaning **Five Gems**, are a set of five musical compositions dedicated to **Lord Rama**. They are composed in the **Ghanaraga Panchaka**, which refers to five traditional **heavy ragas**: **Nata**, **Gaula**, **Arabhi**, **Varali**, and **Sri**.

• **Purandara Dasa** (**1484–1564**) is revered as the **Pitamaha** (Grandfather) of **Carnatic music** for codifying the basic lessons and structure of the art form. However, he did not compose the **Pancharatna Kritis**. **Hence, option 2 is incorrect.**

• **Muthuswami Dikshitar** (**1775–1835**) was a contemporary of **Tyagaraja** and a member of the **Trinity of Carnatic Music**. He is famous for his **Sanskrit** compositions and the **Navagraha Kritis**, but not the **Pancharatna Kritis**. **Hence, option 3 is incorrect.**

• **Shyama Shastri** (**1762–1827**) is the oldest member of the **Trinity**. He is renowned for his mastery over **Tala** (rhythm) and his famous **Swarajatis** dedicated to **Goddess Kamakshi**. **Hence, option 4 is incorrect.**

**Additional Information__**
__

• **The Trinity of Carnatic Music**: This refers to the three most influential composers of the **18th** and **19th centuries**—**Tyagaraja**, **Muthuswami Dikshitar**, and **Shyama Shastri**. All three were born in **Tiruvarur** and revolutionized **South Indian classical music**.

• **Tyagaraja Aradhana**: This is a world-famous **annual music festival** held in **Thiruvaiyaru** to honor the **samadhi** (passing) of **Saint Tyagaraja**. During this festival, hundreds of musicians gather to sing the **Pancharatna Kritis** in unison as a tribute.

• **Language of Compositions**: **Tyagaraja** primarily composed in **Telugu**, which was the court language of the **Thanjavur Maratha kingdom** at the time. He also composed several pieces in **Sanskrit**.

• **Musical Contribution of Purandara Dasa**: He is credited with creating the **Sarali Varisai**, **Jantai Varisai**, and **Alankaras**, which are the foundational exercises for every student of **Carnatic music**. He composed in **Kannada**.

• **Muthuswami Dikshitar's Style**: His compositions are known for their **slow tempo** (**Chowka kala**) and the use of the signature **Guruguha**. He traveled extensively across **India**, incorporating elements of **Hindustani music** into his works.

**Important Points__**

• The five specific **Pancharatna Kritis** are: **Jagadananda Karaka** (Raga Nata), **Dudukugala** (Raga Gaula), **Sadhinchene** (Raga Arabhi), **Kanakanaruchira** (Raga Varali), and **Endaro Mahanubhavulu** (Raga Sri).

• **Jagadananda Karaka** is unique among the five as it is the only one composed entirely in **Sanskrit**, listing **108** names and attributes of **Lord Rama**.

• The **Pancharatna Kritis** are set to **Adi Tala**, which is an **8-beat cycle**. They follow a **Charanam** structure where each stanza is followed by a **Swara-Sahitya** (rhythmic syllables followed by lyrics).

• **Tyagaraja** is said to have composed over **24,000** songs in his lifetime, though only about **700** to **800** are available to us today. His works are characterized by **Bhakti** (devotion) and **Sringara** (beauty).

subject: GK
question: Carnatic music is mainly practiced in which part of India?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Southern India**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• **Carnatic music** is one of the two main sub-genres of **Indian classical music**, the other being **Hindustani music**. It is primarily practiced in the **southern part of India**, encompassing the states of **Andhra Pradesh**, **Telangana**, **Karnataka**, **Kerala**, and **Tamil Nadu**. ***Hence, the correct answer is Southern India.***

• The system is fundamentally based on **Hindu traditions** and is relatively free from the **Persian** and **Islamic** influences that shaped **Hindustani music** in **Northern India** after the **12th century**.

• The foundation of modern **Carnatic music** was laid by **Purandara Dasa** (**1484–1564**), who is revered as the **Pitamaha** (Grandfather) of the genre. He codified the basic lessons, such as **Sarali Varisai** and **Alankaram**, which are still used by students today.

• The music is predominantly **vocal-oriented**. Even when played on instruments, the performance style aims to replicate the nuances of the human voice, a characteristic known as the **Gayaki** style.

• The core components of this musical system are **Raga** (the melodic framework) and **Tala** (the rhythmic cycle). There are **72 Melakarta ragas**, which serve as the parent scales from which thousands of other ragas are derived.

**Additional Information__**

__

• **The Trinity of Carnatic Music**: This refers to three legendary composers of the **18th and 19th centuries**—**Tyagaraja**, **Muthuswami Dikshitar**, and **Syama Sastri**. They all lived in the **Tanjore** region of **Tamil Nadu** and their compositions form the backbone of the modern concert repertoire.

• **Musical Instruments**: Common instruments used in **Southern Indian** classical recitals include the **Veena**, **Mridangam** (the primary percussion instrument), **Violin** (adapted into the system in the **19th century**), **Ghatam** (an earthen pot), **Kanjira**, and the **Venu** (bamboo flute).

• **Madras Music Season**: Held annually in **Chennai** during **December and January**, this is one of the largest cultural festivals in the world. It features thousands of performances by both established maestros and upcoming artists, drawing audiences from across the globe.

• **Composition Structure**: A typical **Carnatic** composition, known as a **Kriti**, is divided into three sections: the **Pallavi** (the thematic line), the **Anupallavi** (the second part), and the **Charanam** (the final stanza).

• **Geographical Divide**: The **Vindhya Mountains** are traditionally considered the boundary separating the **Hindustani** music of **Northern India** from the **Carnatic** music of **Southern India**.

**Important Points__**

• **Linguistic Diversity**: While the music is practiced across **Southern India**, the lyrics of the compositions are primarily in **Sanskrit**, **Telugu**, **Kannada**, and **Tamil**. **Telugu** is particularly prominent due to the prolific contributions of **Tyagaraja**.

• **Comparison with Hindustani Music**: While **Northern India's** classical music places a heavy emphasis on **improvisation** and the exploration of a raga's mood, **Southern India's** **Carnatic music** is more structured, with a greater focus on **fixed compositions** and intricate **mathematical rhythmic patterns**.

• **Sruthi and Laya**: In **Carnatic music**, it is often said that **Sruthi** (pitch/intonation) is the mother and **Laya** (rhythm) is the father, emphasizing the balance required between melody and time.

subject: GK
question: The Baul music tradition belongs to which state?
solution:
The correct answer is __**West Bengal**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Baul** music is a unique and highly celebrated folk tradition that belongs to the state of **West Bengal** in **India** and the country of **Bangladesh**. It is not just a musical genre but a spiritual way of life practiced by a group of mystic minstrels known as **Bauls**.

• The tradition was recognized by **UNESCO** in **2005** when it was proclaimed a **Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity**, and it was later inscribed on the **Representative List** in **2008**.

• **Rajasthan** is incorrect because its folk music is primarily characterized by the **Manganiyar** and **Langa** traditions, which use instruments like the **Kamaicha** and **Khartal**.

• **Gujarat** is incorrect because it is famous for folk forms like **Garba**, **Dandiya Raas**, and **Siddhi Dhamal**, which are distinct from the mystic wandering tradition of the **Bauls**.

• **Tamil Nadu** is incorrect as it is the primary seat of **Carnatic Music** and folk forms such as **Karakattam** and **Villu Paatu**, which have different rhythmic and melodic structures compared to **Bengali** folk music.

• The **Baul** philosophy emphasizes the search for the divine within the human body, a concept known as **Moner Manush** (the Man of the Heart). They reject the caste system and formal religious rituals of both **Hinduism** and **Islam**.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Lalon Shah** (also known as **Lalon Fakir**), who lived in the **19th century**, is the most iconic figure in the **Baul** tradition. His songs, which number in the thousands, form the core of the **Baul** repertoire and focus on social equality and spiritual liberation.

• The **Baul** tradition is a syncretic blend of **Sufism**, **Vaishnavism**, and **Sahajiya Buddhism**. This fusion allows **Bauls** to bridge the gap between different religious communities in **West Bengal**.

• **Rabindranath Tagore**, the **Nobel Prize** winner for Literature, was deeply influenced by **Baul** music. He incorporated its simple yet profound melodies and philosophical themes into his own compositions, known as **Rabindra Sangeet**.

• The **Poush Mela**, held annually in **Shantiniketan** in the **Birbhum** district of **West Bengal**, is a major cultural event where **Baul** singers from across the region gather to perform. Another significant gathering is the **Joydev Kenduli Mela**, held during **Makar Sankranti**.

• The instruments used in **Baul** music are simple and portable, reflecting their nomadic lifestyle. These include the **Ektara** (one-stringed lute), **Duggi** (a small hand drum), **Khol** (terracotta drum), and **Ghungur** (ankle bells worn by the singer while dancing).

**Important Points__**

• The word **Baul** is believed to be derived from the **Sanskrit** words **Vatula** (meaning mad or possessed by the wind) or **Vyakula** (meaning restless or impatient), signifying their intense spiritual longing.

• **Bauls** are easily identified by their distinctive attire, which often consists of a long, saffron or multi-colored patchwork robe called an **Alkhalla**, and they often keep long, matted hair.

• The lyrics of **Baul** songs are composed in the **Bengali** language and are famous for their use of **Sandhya Bhasha** (twilight language), which uses metaphors related to daily life, such as fishing or farming, to explain complex spiritual truths.

• Geographically, the heartland of the **Baul** tradition in **India** includes districts like **Birbhum**, **Nadia**, **Bankura**, and **Murshidabad** in **West Bengal**.

__
 
• **Every year, from early January to early February, the Mamallapuram Dance Festival **takes place for four weeks in **Tamil Nadu**.
 
• **Exponents of Bharatnatyam, Kuchipudi, Kathakali, Mohiniattam, Odissi, and Kathak **gather in this town for this major festival to perform spellbinding performances in **Bharatnatyam, Kuchipudi, Kathakali, Mohini Attam, Odissi, and Kathak**.

These are dated to the 7th and 8th centuries: rathas (temples in the form of chariots), mandapas (cave sanctuaries), the giant open-air rock relief the Descent of the Ganges, and the** Shore Temple **dedicated to **Shiva**.

subject: GK
question: Which year is considered the approximate composition period of the Natya Shastra, the earliest known treatise on Indian music and dance?
solution:
The correct answer is __**200 BCE**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The **Natya Shastra** is the most ancient and comprehensive treatise on the performing arts, including **dance**, **music**, and **drama**. It is traditionally attributed to the legendary sage **Bharata Muni**.

• The approximate period of its composition is widely accepted by historians and scholars to be between **200 BCE and 200 CE**. The year **200 BCE** represents the beginning of this classical period of compilation. ***Hence, the correct answer is 200 BCE.***

• The text is written in **Sanskrit** and is composed of approximately **6000 poetic verses** (shlokas) spread across **36 chapters**. It provides a detailed framework for everything from stage design to the emotional states of actors.

• It is often referred to as the **Pancham Veda** or the **Fifth Veda**. This designation signifies its importance as a sacred text that was intended to be accessible to all sections of society, unlike the four primary Vedas.

• The other options, such as **1000 BCE**, **500 CE**, and **1500 CE**, are historically inaccurate. **1000 BCE** corresponds to the early **Vedic period**, while **500 CE** and **1500 CE** belong to the **Gupta** and **Medieval** periods respectively, which are much later than the linguistic and cultural context of the **Natya Shastra**.

**Additional Information__**

__

• **Rasa Theory**: The **Natya Shastra** is famous for introducing the concept of **Rasa** (aesthetic essence or sentiment). It lists **eight primary Rasas**: **Shringara** (Love), **Hasya** (Mirth), **Karuna** (Compassion), **Raudra** (Anger), **Veera** (Heroism), **Bhayanaka** (Fear), **Bibhatsa** (Disgust), and **Adbhuta** (Wonder).

• **Classification of Music**: The treatise classifies musical instruments into four distinct categories: **Tata Vadya** (stringed instruments), **Avanaddha Vadya** (percussion instruments like **drums**), **Ghana Vadya** (solid instruments like **cymbals**), and **Sushira Vadya** (wind instruments like **flutes**).

• **Dance Elements**: It describes **108 Karanas** (basic dance movements) and various **Mudras** (hand gestures). These elements form the technical foundation for all **Indian Classical Dance** forms such as **Bharatanatyam**, **Odissi**, and **Kathakali**.

• **Theatrical Architecture**: The text provides specific guidelines for the construction of playhouses (**Natyamandapa**), describing three shapes: **Vikrishta** (rectangular), **Chaturasra** (square), and **Tryasra** (triangular).

**Important Points__**

• **Abhinavagupta**: The most influential commentary on the **Natya Shastra** is the **Abhinavabharati**, written by the **Kashmiri** philosopher **Abhinavagupta** in the **10th-11th century CE**. This commentary is essential for modern interpretations of the text.

• **Gandharva Veda**: The musical science described in the **Natya Shastra** is known as **Gandharva**, which is considered an **Upaveda** of the **Sama Veda**. It focuses on the ritualistic and spiritual power of sound.

• **Shrutis and Swaras**: The text establishes the system of **22 Shrutis** (microtones) and the **seven Swaras** (notes: **Sa, Re, Ga, Ma, Pa, Dha, Ni**), which remain the bedrock of **Hindustani** and **Carnatic** classical music.

• **Tandava and Lasya**: It distinguishes between **Tandava** (the vigorous, masculine dance attributed to **Lord Shiva**) and **Lasya** (the graceful, feminine dance attributed to **Goddess Parvati**).
</ul

• **Shahid Parvez Khan and Budhaditya Mukherjee **are renowned players of the sitar, while **Anushka Shankar,** daughter of legendary sitar maestro Ravi Shankar, also plays the sitar. **Hara Shankar Bhattacharya** is a notable player of the sarod.

question: Which musical instrument is commonly associated with Indian classical music?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Sitar**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Sitar** is a plucked stringed instrument that is synonymous with **Hindustani classical music** of **Northern India**. It is recognized globally as an icon of Indian musical heritage. ***Hence, the Sitar is the correct option.***
 
• It evolved into its current form during the **18th century** in **Mughal India**, though its precursors dates back much further. It is believed to have been influenced by the **Veena** and the Persian **Sehtar**.
 
• The instrument features a long **hollow neck** and a **gourd resonance chamber** known as a **Tumba**. It typically possesses **18 to 21 strings**, including **sympathetic strings** (Tarabdar) that vibrate to produce a distinct shimmering sound.
 
• Renowned maestros like **Pandit Ravi Shankar** and **Ustad Vilayat Khan** played a pivotal role in popularizing the **Sitar** in the **Western world** during the **1960s**, notably influencing artists like the **Beatles**.
 
• The **Sitar** is used to perform **Ragas**, which are the melodic frameworks of Indian music. The player uses a wire plectrum called a **Mizrab** on the index finger to pluck the strings.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Guitar:**

 
 
• The **Guitar** is traditionally a **Western** musical instrument. However, in the context of Indian classical music, it has been modified into the **Mohan Veena** by **Pandit Vishwa Mohan Bhatt**.
 
• Despite these adaptations, the standard acoustic or electric **Guitar** is not considered a primary traditional instrument of Indian classical systems.
 
 
 
• **Violin:**
 
 
• While the **Violin** is of **European origin**, it has been completely integrated into **Carnatic classical music** (South India) since the **19th century**.
 
• Legendary musicians like **Baluswami Dikshitar** and **Lalgudi Jayaraman** adapted its playing technique to suit Indian **Gamaka** (ornamentation). While commonly used, the **Sitar** remains the more iconic "Indian" string instrument in global general knowledge.
 
 
 
• **Piano:**
 
 
• The **Piano** is a keyboard instrument rooted in **Western Classical** and **Jazz** traditions.
 
• Due to its **tempered scale** (fixed notes), it is historically difficult to perform the continuous slides (**Meend**) essential to Indian classical music, making it rare in traditional performances.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Classification of Instruments:** In Indian musicology, instruments are classified into four categories: **Tata Vadya** (Chordophones/Strings), **Sushira Vadya** (Aerophones/Wind), **Avanaddha Vadya** (Membranophones/Drums), and **Ghana Vadya** (Idiophones/Solid). The **Sitar** belongs to the **Tata Vadya** group.
 
• **Gharanas:** The playing of the **Sitar** is divided into various **Gharanas** (schools of music) such as the **Imdadkhani Gharana** (Etawah) and the **Maihar Gharana**, each with unique stylistic features.
 
• **Construction Materials:** A traditional **Sitar** is made using **Teak wood** or **Tun wood** for the neck and bridges made of **ebony** or **camel bone**. The **Tumba** is crafted from a specially seasoned **dried gourd**.
 
• **Techniques:** The **Sitar** allows for a technique called **Meend**, where the player pulls the main melody string across the **fret** to change the pitch by as much as a **fifth interval**, mimicking the human voice.

question: The Gandhara art style is primarily associated with which religion?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Buddhism**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Gandhara art** is a style of visual art that developed in the **northwestern part** of ancient India, centered around the **Gandhara region**, which encompasses parts of modern-day **Pakistan** and eastern **Afghanistan**.
 
• It is primarily associated with **Buddhism** and is famous for being the first school of art to represent **Lord Buddha** in **human form** (anthropomorphic representation) rather than through symbols like footprints or an empty throne.
 
• The style is often referred to as **Greco-Buddhist art** because it represents a unique fusion of **Greek** and **Roman** artistic techniques with **Indian Buddhist** iconographic themes.
 
• This art form flourished between the **1st century BC** and the **7th century AD**, reaching its zenith during the reign of the **Kushana Empire**, particularly under **King Kanishka** in the **1st and 2nd centuries AD**.
 
• The primary subject matter of Gandhara art is the **life of Buddha** and the stories of **Bodhisattvas**, depicting various stages from his birth to his **Mahaparinirvana** (death).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Artistic Features**: The Buddha in Gandhara art is depicted with **Hellenistic features**, including **wavy hair**, a **sharp nose**, **muscular physique**, and **heavy robes** resembling a **Roman toga** with realistic folds.
 
• **Materials Used**: Early sculptures (1st and 2nd century) were carved from **bluish-grey schist stone**. In the later periods (3rd to 7th century), artists shifted towards using **stucco** (a type of plaster) and **terracotta** for creating large-scale figures.
 
• **Geographical Spread**: From the Gandhara region, this artistic style spread along the **Silk Road** to **Central Asia** and eventually influenced **Buddhist art** in **China**, **Korea**, and **Japan**.
 
• **Comparison with Mathura School**: While the Gandhara school was heavily influenced by **foreign elements**, the **Mathura School of Art**, which developed simultaneously, was entirely **indigenous**. question:
Read the below statements marked as Assertion (A) and Reason (R). Mark the correct options:
Assertion (A): Ajanta is the only surviving site that contains paintings from both the first century BCE and the fifth century CE.
Reason (R): Ajanta has chaitya caves from the early phase and only vihara-chaitya caves from the later phase

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

solution:
The correct answer is __**A is true, but R is false.**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• **Assertion (A)** states that **Ajanta** is the only surviving site that contains paintings from both the **first century BCE** and the **fifth century CE**. This is accurate because the **Ajanta Caves** were developed in two distinct phases: the **Satavahana phase** (Hinayana) and the **Vakataka phase** (Mahayana). The earlier paintings, found in **Caves 9 and 10**, date back to the **1st and 2nd centuries BCE**, while the later, more famous murals date to the **5th and 6th centuries CE**. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***

• **Reason (R)** claims that **Ajanta** has **chaitya caves** from the early phase and only **vihara-chaitya caves** from the later phase. This is factually incorrect because the later phase (Mahayana) also contains magnificent, independent **Chaitya caves**, such as **Cave 19** and **Cave 26**, which are distinct from the **Viharas** (monasteries). The early phase also included both **Chaityas** (Caves 9 and 10) and **Viharas** (Caves 12, 13, and 15A). ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***

• The core logic of the question rests on the chronological development of **Buddhist rock-cut architecture**. While the site is unique for its chronological span of surviving mural art, the classification of cave types in the later phase is not limited to a hybrid **vihara-chaitya** form; rather, both traditional forms continued to evolve with more elaborate ornamentation.

• The **Assertion** is a recognized historical fact regarding the preservation of **Indian mural paintings**, whereas the **Reason** misrepresents the architectural typology of the **Mahayana phase** at the site.

**Additional Information__**

__

• **Location and Geography:** The **Ajanta Caves** are situated in the **Aurangabad** district (now **Chhatrapati Sambhaji Nagar**) of **Maharashtra**. They are carved into a **horseshoe-shaped** basaltic cliff overlooking the **Waghur River**.

• **Discovery:** The caves were forgotten for centuries until they were accidentally rediscovered in **1819** by a British officer named **John Smith** during a hunting expedition.

• **UNESCO Recognition:** Due to their immense historical and artistic value, the **Ajanta Caves** were declared a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** in the year **1983**.

• **Artistic Themes:** The paintings primarily depict the **Jataka tales**, which describe the previous births of **Lord Buddha**, and various scenes from the life of **Gautama Buddha**. Famous murals include the **Padmapani** and **Vajrapani** Bodhisattvas in **Cave 1**.

• **Technique:** The artists used a technique known as **Fresco-secco**. This involved applying a thick layer of mud, lime, and straw plaster to the rock wall, followed by a thin coat of lime wash, upon which pigments were applied once the surface was dry.

**Important Points__**

• **Architectural Types:** A **Chaitya** is a prayer or assembly hall with a **stupa** at the end, while a **Vihara** is a residential monastery consisting of a central hall with small cells for monks to live in.

• **Patronage:** The second phase of construction (approx. **460–480 CE**) occurred during the reign of the **Vakataka King Harishena**. This period saw a transition from the **aniconic** (symbolic) representation of Buddha to **iconic** (human form) representation.

• **Number of Caves:** There are approximately **30 caves** at the site, including those that remained unfinished. **Caves 1, 2, 16, and 17** contain some of the best-preserved and most sophisticated ancient paintings in the world.

• **Linguistic and Cultural Impact:** The **Ajanta** style of painting influenced art across **Asia**, spreading along the **Silk Road** to places like **Sigiriya** in **Sri Lanka** and various sites in **Central Asia** and **China**.

__

• The **Bodhisattva** statues of the **Gandhara School of Art** are a prime example of **Graeco-Buddhist art**, which combined **Indian** religious themes with **Greek** and **Roman** artistic techniques.

• The **Greek** influence is clearly visible in the **physiognomy** of the statues, featuring **wavy hair**, **sharp facial features**, **muscular bodies**, and **realistic anatomy**, which were inspired by **Hellenistic** sculptures of gods like **Apollo**. ***Hence, the correct answer is Greek.***

• The **drapery** or clothing depicted on these **Bodhisattva** figures resembles the **Roman toga**, characterized by **heavy, thick folds** and a realistic flow that follows the contours of the body.

• The **Gandhara** artists used **anthropomorphic** representations, depicting the **Buddha** and **Bodhisattvas** in human form with **idealized beauty**, a concept central to **Greek** art.

• Other options like **Mughal**, **Persian**, and **Rajput** are incorrect because they belong to different **chronological periods** or **cultural contexts**; for example, **Mughal** and **Rajput** styles emerged in the **medieval period**, long after the peak of **Gandhara** art.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Geographical Location and Period:** The **Gandhara School** flourished in the **northwestern** part of the **Indian subcontinent** (modern-day **Pakistan** and **Afghanistan**) from the **1st century BCE** to the **4th century CE**.

• **Patronage:** This artistic style received significant support from the **Kushan Empire**, particularly under the reign of **King Kanishka**, who was a great promoter of **Mahayana Buddhism**.

• **Materials Used:** Early **Gandhara** sculptures were primarily made of **grey schist** (a type of stone), while later works frequently utilized **stucco** (plaster) for finer detailing.

• **Depiction of Bodhisattvas:** Unlike the **Buddha**, who was often shown in simple robes, **Bodhisattvas** like **Maitreya** and **Avalokiteshvara** were depicted as **princes** wearing elaborate **jewelry**, **turbans**, **sandals**, and sometimes even **mustaches**.

**Important Points__**

• **Cultural Syncretism:** The **Greek** influence reached the region following the conquests of **Alexander the Great** in **326 BCE** and the subsequent establishment of **Indo-Greek** kingdoms.

• **Artistic Features:** Key **Hellenistic** features include the **halo** (prabhamandala) which was initially plain in **Gandhara**, the **ushnisha** (cranial bump) styled like a **Greek topknot**, and the **meditative** yet **human-like** facial expressions.

• **Major Centers:** The prominent centers of **Gandhara** art were **Taxila**, **Peshawar** (Purushapura), **Bagram**, and **Bamiyan**.

• **Legacy:** This school played a crucial role in the spread of **Buddhist imagery** along the **Silk Road** to **Central Asia**, **China**, and **Japan**.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The **Mathura school of sculpture** flourished primarily during the **Kushana period** between the **1st century AD** and the **3rd century AD**. It is celebrated for being an **indigenous style** of art that developed without significant foreign influence.

• A primary feature of this school is the **Iconography of Buddha and Hindu deities**. It was one of the earliest schools to create **anthropomorphic** (human) representations of the **Buddha**, alongside **Jain Tirthankaras** and **Hindu gods** like **Vishnu**, **Shiva**, **Surya**, and **Kubera**. ***Hence, the correct answer is option 4.***

• The material used in the **Mathura school** was **Spotted Red Sandstone**, which was locally sourced. This is a major distinguishing factor from the **Gandhara school**, which utilized **Grey Schist** or **Blue-grey Schist**. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***

• The feature of **Highly polished sandstone** is a characteristic of **Mauryan Art** (e.g., **Ashokan Pillars**), not the **Mathura school**. The **Mathura** artists focused more on **voluptuousness** and **anatomical details** rather than a mirror-like polish. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***

• The **Mathura school** was purely **Indian** in its inspiration and execution. In contrast, the **Gandhara school** exhibited **Heavy Greek influence** (Hellenistic style), often referred to as **Greco-Buddhist art**. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**

__

• **Geographical Location**: The school was centered around **Mathura** in **Uttar Pradesh**, which served as a major junction for trade and culture during the **Kushana Empire**.

• **Patronage**: The development of this school was heavily supported by the **Kushana rulers**, most notably **King Kanishka**, who was a great patron of **Buddhism** and the arts.

• **Artistic Characteristics**: Sculptures from this school are known for their **fleshy bodies**, **smiling expressions**, and **transparent drapery**. The **Buddha** is often depicted with a **shaved head** or a **protuberance** (Ushnisha) and is frequently shown in the **Abhaya Mudra** (gesture of fearlessness).

• **Secular Art**: Beyond religious icons, the school produced **secular sculptures**, including portraits of kings. A famous example is the **headless statue of Kanishka**, which showcases the **Central Asian** dress style including long tunics and heavy boots.

• **Evolution of Buddha**: In the early stages, **Buddha** was represented through symbols like the **Dharmachakra** or **Bodhi tree**, but the **Mathura school** played a pivotal role in transitioning these into **full-scale human idols**.

**Important Points__**

• **Religious Synthesis**: The **Mathura school** is unique because it simultaneously catered to **Buddhism**, **Jainism**, and **Brahmanism** (Hinduism), reflecting the **religious pluralism** of ancient India.

• **Influence on Later Art**: The techniques and iconographic standards established in **Mathura** laid the foundation for the **Gupta school of art** (4th-6th century AD), which is often described as the **Golden Age** of Indian sculpture.

• **Yakshas and Yakshinis**: The school continued the ancient Indian tradition of carving **Yakshas** and **Yakshinis**, which were fertility deities. These figures were carved with **sensuality** and **elaborate jewelry**, representing the **idealized human form**.

• **Comparison with Gandhara**: While **Gandhara** art focused on **realism** and **muscularity** (similar to **Apollo**), **Mathura art** focused on **inner spirituality** and **grace**.

subject: GK
question: The Mathura school of art flourished mainly during which period?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Gupta period**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Mathura school of art** is one of the most significant schools of ancient Indian sculpture that flourished prominently during the **Kushan period** and reached its artistic zenith during the **Gupta period** (from the **4th to 6th century AD**). Hence, among the given options, the **Gupta period** is the correct answer.
 
• During the **Gupta period**, the **Mathura school** evolved from the bold and masculine styles of the earlier **Kushan** era into a more refined, elegant, and spiritual form. This era is often referred to as the **"Golden Age"** of Indian art.
 
• The primary material used by the artists of the **Mathura school** throughout its existence was **spotted red sandstone**, which was locally available in **Mathura** and surrounding regions like **Sikri**.
 
• The **Gupta** influence added a sense of **inner serenity** and **grace** to the sculptures, particularly in the depiction of the **Buddha**. The "wet drapery" style, where the clothing appears transparent and clings to the body, became a hallmark of this period.
 
• **Mathura** served as a major manufacturing hub for idols, and its products were exported to various parts of **Northern India**, including **Sarnath** and **Prayagraj**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Distinction from Gandhara School:**
 
 
• The **Gandhara school** (flourished **1st century BC to 4th century AD**) was heavily influenced by **Greco-Roman** styles and used **bluish-grey schist** or **stucco**.
 
• In contrast, the **Mathura school** was purely **indigenous** and did not exhibit foreign influence, focusing on local traditions and physical mass.
 
 
 
• **Religious Diversity:**
 
 
• The **Mathura school** was unique because it produced images for three major religions: **Buddhism**, **Jainism**, and **Hinduism**.
 
• It is credited with the first anthropomorphic (human form) representations of the **Buddha**, often shown in the **Abhaya Mudra** (gesture of fearlessness).
 
• It also created statues of **Jain Tirthankaras** and **Hindu deities** like **Shiva**, **Vishnu**, and **Surya**.
 
 
 
• **Maurya Period (322–185 BC):**
 
 
• This period is known for **court art** like the **Lion Capital of Ashoka** and **monolithic pillars**. While **Mathura** was an important city, the specific "Mathura school" of sculpture had not yet developed into its characteristic form. Hence, this option is incorrect.
 
 
 
• **Mughal Period (1526–1857):**
 
 
• The **Mughal** era focused largely on **Indo-Islamic architecture** (like the **Taj Mahal**) and **miniature paintings**. Stone sculpture of deities was not a primary feature of this period due to religious practices. Hence, this option is incorrect.
 
 
 
• **British Period (1858–1947):**
 
 
• Art during the **British Raj** was dominated by **Indo-Saracenic architecture** and **Western academic realism** in painting. The ancient schools of stone sculpture like **Mathura** were no longer active in their traditional sense. Hence, this option is incorrect.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Location:** The school was centered around **Mathura** in **Uttar Pradesh**, which was a strategic junction of trade routes.
 
• **Key Features:** The **Gupta-era Mathura** sculptures are characterized by the **halo (Prabhamandala)**, which became elaborately decorated with floral and geometric patterns, unlike the plain halos of the **Kushan** period.
 
• **Historical Impact:** The **Mathura school** laid the foundation for the **Medieval** styles of Indian sculpture, influencing the development of art across **South Asia**.
 
• **Archaeological Findings:** Thousands of fragments and statues have been recovered from sites like **Kankali Tila** (Jain) and **Katra Keshavdev** in **Mathura**, now housed in the **Mathura Museum**.

72:T

question: The art of Mathura influenced which other ancient Indian art style?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Gandhara art**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Mathura School of Art** flourished during the **1st Century AD** to the **3rd Century AD** under the patronage of the **Kushana Empire**, specifically under **King Kanishka**. It is considered a purely **indigenous style** of art that developed in **Mathura**, **Uttar Pradesh**.
 
• During the **Kushana period**, the **Mathura** and **Gandhara** schools of art co-existed and significantly influenced each other. While **Gandhara art** had strong **Greco-Roman** influences, the **Mathura school** provided the **iconographic models** and indigenous spiritual features for the depiction of the **Buddha**.
 
• The **Mathura art** style influenced **Gandhara art** in the representation of the **Buddha**'s physical form, such as the **Ushnisha** (cranial bump) and the **Urna** (mark on the forehead), which were integrated into the **Graeco-Buddhist** style.
 
• The primary material used in **Mathura art** was **Red Spotted Sandstone**, which was sourced locally. This style was not limited to **Buddhism**; it also produced images related to **Jainism** (Tirthankaras) and **Hinduism** (Vishnu, Shiva, and Surya).
 
• The **Mathura school** is credited with creating the first **anthropomorphic** (human form) representations of the **Buddha** in **India**, moving away from the purely symbolic representations (like the Bodhi tree or footprints) seen in earlier traditions like **Sanchi** and **Bharhut**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Gandhara Art:**
 
 
• Located in the **Northwest Frontier** (modern-day **Pakistan** and **Afghanistan**), this style is often called the **Graeco-Buddhist School of Art**.
 
• It utilized **Blue-grey Schist** stone and was characterized by realistic human figures with **Hellenistic** features, such as wavy hair and muscular bodies.
 
• While it absorbed **Mathura**'s spiritual iconography, it retained **Roman** artistic techniques in its drapery and facial expressions.
 
 
 
• **Mughal Art:**
 
 
• This style emerged much later, during the **16th Century** to the **18th Century**, blending **Persian**, **Indian**, and **Islamic** influences.
 
• It is primarily known for its **miniature paintings** and monumental architecture like the **Taj Mahal**. It did not have a direct contemporary relationship with **Mathura art** of the **ancient period**.
 
 
 
• **Chola Art:**
 
 
• Originating in **South India** during the **9th Century** to the **13th Century AD**, this style is famous for **Dravidian architecture** and **Bronze sculptures**.
 
• The **Nataraja** (Dancing Shiva) is the most iconic example of **Chola** craftsmanship. This style developed independently of the **Northern Mathura** influence.
 
 
 
• **Rajput Art:**
 
 
• Flourishing between the **16th and 19th Centuries** in **Rajasthan**, this style is renowned for **miniature paintings** depicting **Radha-Krishna** themes and **epic stories**.
 
• It evolved from the **Western Indian** school and **Mughal** influences, belonging to the **Medieval** rather than the **Ancient** period.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **Kushana Dynasty**, under **Kanishka**, served as a bridge between **India** and **Central Asia**, allowing for a unique cultural synthesis that defined the **Gandhara-Mathura** interaction.
 
• **Mathura** remained a major center for religious art for over **1,200 years**, and its stylistic elements eventually paved the way for the **Gupta Art** of the **4th Century AD**, often referred to as the **"Golden Age"** of **Indian Art**.
 
• The **Mathura Buddha** is characterized by a **smiling face**, **shaven head**, and **Abhaya Mudra** (gesture of fearlessness), whereas the **Gandhara Buddha** often appears more **meditative** and **solemn**.

question: Which ruler greatly supported Gandhara art?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Kanishka**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Kanishka**, the most powerful ruler of the **Kushan Dynasty**, was the greatest patron of **Gandhara Art**. Under his reign in the **1st and 2nd centuries CE**, this school of art reached its zenith. ***Hence, the statement regarding Kanishka is correct.***

• **Gandhara Art** is a unique style of **Buddhist visual art** that developed in the **North-Western** part of the Indian subcontinent, primarily in regions like **Peshawar** and **Taxila** (modern-day **Pakistan** and **Afghanistan**).

• It is famously known as **Greco-Buddhist Art** because it combined **Hellenistic (Greek)** and **Roman** artistic techniques with **Indian Buddhist** themes. The **Buddha** was often depicted with features resembling the Greek god **Apollo**, including wavy hair and muscular anatomy.

• The emergence of **Mahayana Buddhism** during **Kanishka’s** time encouraged the creation of **Buddha** images in human form, replacing the earlier symbolic representations like the **Wheel** or **Footprints**.

• While **Ashoka** was a great promoter of **Buddhism** in the **3rd century BCE**, his artistic contributions were mainly **Stupas** and **Pillars** (Mauryan Art) rather than the specific **Gandhara** style. ***Hence, the option involving Ashoka is incorrect.***

• **Samudragupta** belonged to the **Gupta Dynasty** (the **Golden Age** of India), which patronized the **Mathura** and **Sarnath** schools of art, focusing on indigenous styles rather than the **Gandhara** style. ***Hence, the option involving Samudragupta is incorrect.***

• **Harsha** (Harshavardhana) ruled in the **7th century CE** and was a patron of **Buddhism** and **Nalanda University**, but by his time, the **Gandhara** school had already declined following the **Huna** invasions. ***Hence, the option involving Harsha is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Features of Gandhara Art:** The primary material used in the early phase was **Blue-grey Schist stone**, which was later replaced by **Stucco** (lime plaster). The sculptures are characterized by **realistic anatomy**, **wavy hair**, **large foreheads**, and **heavy drapery** resembling a Roman **Toga**.

• **Kanishka I:** He ascended the throne in approximately **78 CE**, a date that marks the beginning of the **Saka Era**, which is still used by the **Government of India**. He organized the **Fourth Buddhist Council** in **Kundalvana, Kashmir**, where **Buddhism** was formally split into **Hinayana** and **Mahayana** sects.

• **Comparison with Mathura School:** Unlike the **Gandhara School**, which was foreign-influenced, the **Mathura School of Art** was entirely **indigenous**. It used **Spotted Red Sandstone** and produced images of **Buddha**, **Jain Tirthankaras**, and **Hindu Deities**.

• **Geographical Spread:** The **Gandhara** style spread along the **Silk Road** into **Central Asia** and **China**, significantly influencing the **Buddhist art** of those regions. Major archaeological sites include **Bamiyan**, **Hadda**, and **Begram**.

• **Decline:** The school began to decline after the **3rd century CE** and was severely damaged during the **5th century CE** by the invasion of the **White Hunas** (Hephthalites), who destroyed many monasteries and workshops in the **Gandhara** region.

**Important Points__**

• **Kushan Empire:** At its peak under **Kanishka**, the empire extended from **Central Asia** to the **Gangetic Plain**, with capitals at **Purushapura** (Peshawar) and **Mathura**. This vast territory facilitated the exchange of ideas between the **East** and the **West**.

• **The Buddha Image:** The **Gandhara School** is credited with being one of the first to depict **Buddha** in human form. These statues often show the **Buddha** in various **Mudras** (gestures), such as the **Abhaya Mudra** (fearlessness) and **Dhyana Mudra** (meditation).

• **Patronage:** Besides **Kanishka**, other **Kushan** rulers like **Huvishka** also supported the arts, but **Kanishka’s** contribution remains the most significant due to his religious zeal and the economic prosperity of his **reign**.

question: Which of the following pair of dances belongs to Kerala?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Kathakali and Mohiniyattam**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Kathakali and Mohiniyattam** pair of dances **belongs to Kerala**.
 
• Kathakali and Mohiniyattam are classical dance forms originating from Kerala, India.
 
• **Kathakali **is renowned for its **theatrical elements,** including elaborate costumes, intricate makeup, expressive face masks, and ornate ornaments.
 
• **Mohiniyattam **is characterized by its graceful movements, predominantly performed by women.
 
• It is often described as a blend of **Kathakali and Bharatanatyam styles.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Kathakali **remains popular in India, preserving its traditional practices. With over 500 Attakatha plays, many dating back to before the 20th century, Kathakali has a rich repertoire.
 
• Recent productions have expanded its horizons by incorporating stories from various cultures and mythologies, including those of Miguel de Cervantes, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, and William Shakespeare.
 
• **Mohiniyattam** is celebrated for its elegance, typically performed as solo recitals by female dancers.
 
• The name "Mohiniyattam" derives from "Mohini," the feminine aspect of Lord Vishnu, signifying the "dance of Mohini."
 
• The dance narrates the tale of Mohini, an enchantress avatar of the divine in Vaishnavism.
