question: Which of the following is a new offense defined under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Terrorist act**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
__ 
 
• The **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023** is a significant reform in Indian criminal law, aimed at replacing the British-era Indian Penal Code (IPC) 1860 with more modern and relevant provisions. 
 
• One of the new offenses defined under this law is a **Terrorist act**, which addresses acts of terrorism that threaten India's sovereignty, unity, integrity, and security. 
 
• The definition of a **Terrorist act** under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, includes provisions that cover acts of violence, disruption of public order, and damage to critical infrastructure, intending to create fear or coerce the government. 
 
• This reform expands the legal framework to combat terrorism more effectively, ensuring stricter penalties and enhanced investigation mechanisms for terrorist activities. 
 
• Other offenses like **criminal intimidation, adultery, and sedition** were already covered under the repealed IPC, but terrorism has been elaborated upon as a distinct and critical offense in the updated legislation. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
 
 
• **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023:** 
 
 
• The **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita Bill, 2023**, was introduced in Parliament as part of a broader effort to modernize India’s criminal justice system. 
 
• This law aims to replace the **Indian Penal Code (IPC), 1860**, which was drafted during British colonial rule. 
 
• It incorporates provisions for **modern crimes** such as cybercrime, terrorism, and organized crime. 
 
• The bill emphasizes the principles of justice and equality, ensuring that the laws are in sync with the **21st-century challenges**. 
 
 
 
• **Key features of the Terrorist Act under Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023:** 
 
 
• Defines terrorism comprehensively, including acts causing **terror, fear, or coercion**. 
 
• Addresses activities that disrupt **sovereignty, integrity, and public order** in India. 
 
• Includes provisions for **stringent punishments**, such as life imprisonment and death penalties for severe offenses. 
 
• Provisions for **seizure of properties** and financial assets linked to terrorism. 
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Sedition:** 
 
 
• The offense of **sedition** under Section 124A of the IPC has been **repealed** in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. 
 
• However, provisions dealing with acts threatening **sovereignty and integrity** have been incorporated under the new law. 
 
• This reflects a shift in focus from suppressing dissent to addressing **real and tangible threats** to national security. 
 
 
 
• **Criminal Intimidation and Adultery:** 
 
 
• **Criminal Intimidation** continues to be a punishable offense under the new law, but it is not a newly defined offense. 
 
• **Adultery** was decriminalized by the **Supreme Court of India in 2018** through its verdict in the **Joseph Shine case**. 
 
 
 
• **Modern Challenges Addressed:** 
 
 
• The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, aims to strengthen the legal framework against crimes such as **terrorism, cybercrime, and organized crime**. 
 
• It aligns India's criminal justice system with global standards, ensuring **timely justice** for victims and effective deterrence for offenders.

question: Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which of the following has been emphasized for the first time in criminal law regarding sexual offences?

options.text: Marital rape as a punishable offense
Consent must be explicitly defined and recorded
Death penalty for all rape cases
Gender neutrality in sexual assault definitions

solution:
The correct answer is __**Gender neutrality in sexual assault definitions**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023**, which replaced the **Indian Penal Code (IPC)** of **1860**, has introduced a significant shift by emphasizing **gender neutrality** in several definitions related to sexual assault and victims. While the core definition of rape under **Section 63** remains largely gender-specific (perpetrated by a man), the BNS 2023 moves toward recognizing **transgender persons** and uses more inclusive language in various sections related to sexual offenses. ***Hence, statement D is correct.***
 
• One of the most notable additions is **Section 69**, which specifically criminalizes sexual intercourse through **deceitful means** or a **false promise to marry**. This is the first time such an offense has been codified with a distinct punishment of up to **10 years** of **imprisonment**, moving away from the previous ambiguity in the **IPC**.
 
• The **BNS 2023** prioritizes offenses against **women and children** by placing them in **Chapter 5** of the code. This structural change signifies the legislature's intent to give paramount importance to these crimes compared to the **IPC**, where such offenses were placed much later in the document.
 
• Regarding **marital rape**, the **BNS 2023** retains the **exception** (Exception 2 to Section 63) which states that sexual intercourse by a man with his own wife, the wife not being under **18 years** of age, is not rape. Therefore, marital rape has not been made a punishable offense under this new Sanhita. ***Hence, statement A is incorrect.***
 
• While the **death penalty** is a possible punishment under **Section 70(2)** for the **gang rape** of a girl under **18 years** of age, it is not prescribed for "all" rape cases. The law maintains a hierarchy of punishments based on the severity and age of the victim. ***Hence, statement C is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Implementation and Timeline:** The **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS)** received the assent of the **President of India** on **December 25, 2023**. It officially came into force on **July 1, 2024**, marking a new era in the Indian criminal justice system by repealing the **British-era IPC**.
 
• **Definition of Consent:** Under the **BNS**, **consent** is defined as an unequivocal voluntary agreement when the woman by words, gestures, or any form of verbal or non-verbal communication, communicates willingness to participate in the specific sexual act. However, this definition was already evolved through the **Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013**; thus, it is not a "first time" inclusion in **2023**. ***Hence, statement B is incorrect.***
 
• **Aggravated Punishment:** The **BNS 2023** increases the minimum punishment for **rape** from **7 years** to **10 years** of **rigorous imprisonment**. For the **gang rape** of a woman, the punishment is **imprisonment for life** (which means the remainder of that person's natural life) or **rigorous imprisonment** for a term not less than **20 years**.
 
• **Protection of Minors:** The new code emphasizes the protection of **children** (defined as anyone under **18 years**). Crimes against children carry much more stringent penalties, including the **death penalty** or **life imprisonment** without the possibility of remission in specific aggravated cases.
 
• **Community Service:** For the first time in Indian criminal law, the **BNS 2023** introduces **Community Service** as a form of **punishment** for petty offenses, aiming at a more **reformative** approach to justice rather than purely **retributive**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Section 63 (Rape):** Replaces **Section 375** of the **IPC**. It maintains the **four-step** definition of the act but adds clarity to the **punitive measures** in subsequent sections.
 
• **Section 70 (Gang Rape):** Specifically deals with **gang rape**, providing a minimum of **20 years** of imprisonment or **life imprisonment**.
 
• **Rights of the Victim:** The **BNS**, alongside the **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS)**, emphasizes that the **victim’s statement** must be recorded through **audio-video means** in sexual offense cases to ensure transparency and prevent tampering.
 
• **Deceitful Means (Section 69):** This includes the use of **false promises** regarding **employment**, **promotion**, or **marriage** while concealing one's **identity**. It addresses a long-standing gap where such cases were previously litigated under general rape or cheating provisions.

question: Which of the following has been decriminalized as per the BNS, 2023?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Attempt to suicide**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023**, which replaced the **Indian Penal Code (IPC), 1860**, has effectively **decriminalized** the general act of **attempting suicide**.

• Under the old **IPC**, **Section 309** categorized the attempt to commit suicide as a criminal offense punishable with imprisonment or a fine.

• The **BNS, 2023** has omitted the equivalent of Section 309, acknowledging that individuals attempting suicide often require **medical and psychological support** rather than criminal prosecution.

• However, the BNS introduces **Section 226**, which specifically penalizes an attempt to commit suicide only if it is done with the intent to **compel or restrain a public servant** from discharging their official duty.

• Other options like **Voyeurism** (Section 77), **Domestic Violence** (Section 85 and 86), and **Cyberstalking** (Section 78) remain serious criminal offenses under the new legal framework.

**Additional Information__**

• The **Mental Healthcare Act, 2017**, through **Section 115**, had already significantly reduced the impact of Section 309 IPC by creating a presumption of **severe stress** for anyone attempting suicide.

• The **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita** received the President's assent on **December 25, 2023**, and came into force on **July 1, 2024**.

• The shift in law reflects a **humanitarian approach** toward mental health issues in India's criminal justice system.

• The BNS also introduced **Community Service** as a form of punishment for the first time for petty offenses.
</ul

question: Which of the following statement is TRUE about the Bharatiya Sakshya Sanhita?

options.text: It allows digital evidence as primary evidence.
It replaces the Code of Criminal Procedure.
It limits the use of electronic records.
It only applies to civil cases.

solution:
The correct answer is __**It allows digital evidence as primary evidence.**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Bharatiya Sakshya Sanhita (BSS)** was enacted to replace the colonial-era **Indian Evidence Act, 1872**.

• One of the most transformative features of the BSS is that it treats **electronic or digital records** as **primary evidence**. This means that information stored in digital form is legally equivalent to a physical paper document.

• The scope of **documentary evidence** has been widened to include **emails, server logs, computer output, messages, and location data** stored on digital devices like smartphones and laptops.

• **Option 2 is incorrect** because the **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS)** is the law that replaces the **Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC)**, not the BSS.

• **Option 3 is incorrect** because the BSS **expands** the use of electronic records to keep pace with modern technology, rather than limiting them.

• **Option 4 is incorrect** because the BSS applies to **all judicial proceedings**, which encompasses both **civil and criminal** cases.

**Additional Information__**

• The **Bharatiya Sakshya Sanhita, 2023** received the **President's assent** on **December 25, 2023**, and officially came into effect on **July 1, 2024**.

• The new Act contains **170 sections**, which is a slight increase from the 167 sections in the original 1872 Act.

• It introduces updated provisions for the **admissibility of electronic records**, requiring a specific **certificate** to verify the authenticity and integrity of the digital source.

• The primary objective of the BSS is to **modernize the rules of evidence** and ensure that the legal system can effectively handle **cybercrimes** and digital footprints in the 21st century.

• The **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS)** is the third major law in this overhaul, replacing the **Indian Penal Code (IPC)**.
</ul

question: Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which of the following is correct regarding the punishment for mob lynching?

options.text: Only imprisonment up to 5 years is allowed
Punishable with up to 7 years, life imprisonment, or death
Mob lynching is treated as a bailable offence with a fine
Only life imprisonment is prescribed regardless of severity

solution:
The correct answer is __**Punishable with up to 7 years, life imprisonment, or death**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023**, which replaces the **Indian Penal Code (IPC)**, has introduced specific provisions to deal with the offence of **mob lynching**.

• Under **Section 103(2)** of the BNS, when a group of **five or more persons** acting in concert commits murder on the ground of **race, caste or community, sex, place of birth, language, personal belief** or any other similar ground, each member of such group shall be punished.

• The prescribed punishment for this offence includes **death**, **imprisonment for life**, or **imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than seven years**, and the offenders shall also be liable to a **fine**.

• This provision was specifically added to provide a legal framework to penalize **hate-motivated killings** by mobs, which was not explicitly defined as a separate category under the old IPC.

• Other options are incorrect because the law provides for a range of punishments depending on the severity, including the **death penalty**, and it is categorized as a **heinous, non-bailable offence**.

**Additional Information__**

• The **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS)** received the President's assent on **December 25, 2023**, and officially came into force on **July 1, 2024**.

• Along with the BNS, two other major laws were enacted: the **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS)**, replacing the CrPC, and the **Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA)**, replacing the Indian Evidence Act.

• The introduction of **Section 103(2)** follows various directives from the **Supreme Court of India** (notably in the **Tehseen Poonawalla case**) urging the government to create a special law to tackle lynching.

• The BNS also introduces other new categories of offences such as **organized crime** and **terrorist acts** within the general penal code.
</ul

subject: GK
question: As per the Forest (Conservation) Amendment Act, 2023, which of the following categories of land is not covered under the provisions of the Act?

options.text: Land notified as forest under the Indian Forest Act, 1927
Forest land near international borders for defence projects up to 5 hectares in LWE areas
Land recorded as forest in government records as of October 25, 1980
Land proposed for silvicultural operations in reserved forests

solution:
The correct answer is __**Forest land near international borders for defence projects up to 5 hectares in LWE areas**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Forest (Conservation) Amendment Act, 2023**, was enacted to clarify and amend the scope of the original **Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980**. It specifies which categories of land fall under the purview of the law and which are exempted to facilitate national security and public utility.
 
• According to the **2023 Amendment**, the Act applies to land **notified as forest** under the **Indian Forest Act, 1927**, or any other law for the time being in force. This ensures that legally recognized forest tracts remain protected. *Hence, statement 1 is incorrect as this land is covered under the Act.*
 
• The Act also covers land that has been **recorded as forest** in **government records** on or after **October 25, 1980**. This provision was included to align with the **Supreme Court's** **1996** **Godavarman judgement**, which expanded the definition of forests. *Hence, statement 3 is incorrect as this land is also covered under the Act.*
 
• The **Amendment** introduced specific exemptions for **strategic projects** and **security infrastructure**. It states that the Act shall **not apply** to forest land up to **5 hectares** in **Left Wing Extremism (LWE)** affected areas as notified by the **Central Government**, intended for **public utility projects**. It also exempts strategic linear projects within **100 km** of **international borders**. ***Hence, statement 2 is the correct answer as this category of land is explicitly not covered under the provisions of the Act.***
 
• Reserved forests are the most protected category of forests under the **Indian Forest Act, 1927**, and are strictly covered under the **Forest (Conservation) Act**. While certain activities like **silvicultural operations** are not treated as "non-forest purposes," the land itself remains fully covered by the Act's regulatory framework. *Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **The Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980:** This **Act** was enacted by the **Parliament of India** to provide for the conservation of forests and for matters connected therewith. It prohibits the use of forest land for **non-forest purposes** without the prior approval of the **Central Government**.
 
• **Left Wing Extremism (LWE):** Certain districts in **India** (often referred to as the **Red Corridor**) are affected by **Naxalite-Maoist insurgency**. The **2023 Amendment** seeks to speed up **infrastructure development** (like roads and communication) in these **LWE areas** by exempting small patches of land (up to **5 hectares**) from the lengthy forest clearance process.
 
• **Indian Forest Act, 1927:** This is the colonial-era law that provides the framework for declaring **Reserved Forests**, **Protected Forests**, and **Village Forests**. The **2023 Amendment** uses this **Act** as a primary reference to define "notified" forest land.
 
• **Strategic Linear Projects:** These include **National Highways**, **Railway lines**, and **communication lines** of **national importance**. The exemption for projects within **100 km** of the **Line of Control (LoC)** or **Line of Actual Control (LAC)** is aimed at enhancing **India’s** **border security** and **defence readiness**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad Case (1996):** Before the **2023 Amendment**, the **Supreme Court of India** interpreted the **1980 Act** to apply to all areas that resembled the "dictionary meaning" of forests, regardless of ownership or notification. The **2023 Act** clarifies that it only applies to lands notified or recorded as forests after **1980**, effectively narrowing the scope back to documented forests.
 
• **Exemption Limits:** Apart from the **5 hectares** for **LWE areas**, the **Amendment** also allows for up to **10 hectares** of forest land to be used for **security-related infrastructure** and up to **0.10 hectares** alongside roads or rail lines for providing access to habitations.
 
• **Non-Forest Purpose:** The **Amendment** clarifies that **silvicultural operations**, **establishment of check-posts**, **fire lines**, **wireless communications**, and **eco-tourism facilities** included in the **Working Plan** are not considered "non-forest purposes" and thus do not require the standard diversion approval.

question: In the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, which of the following provisions has been introduced for the first time concerning crimes against women?

options.text: Inclusion of community service as a punishment for domestic violence.
Provision for capital punishment in cases of gang rape of a woman under 18 years.
Reduction of the age of consent for sexual activities to 16 years.

solution:
The correct answer is __**Provision for capital punishment in cases of gang rape of a woman under 18 years.**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023**, is a proposed replacement for the Indian Penal Code (IPC). It introduces several new provisions aimed at modernizing India's criminal justice system.
 
• One of the key provisions introduced in the **BNS, 2023**, is the **provision for capital punishment** in cases of the **gang rape of a woman under the age of 18 years**, which was not explicitly included in the earlier IPC framework. *Hence, this statement is correct.*
 
• The inclusion of this provision reflects a stronger stance towards crimes against women, particularly minors, ensuring stricter penalties for heinous crimes.
 
• Other options like community service for domestic violence, legalization of marital rape, or lowering the age of consent to 16 years are not part of the provisions in **BNS, 2023**. Hence, these statements are incorrect.

**Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Provisions Related to Crimes Against Women in BNS, 2023:**

 
 
• **Capital Punishment:** The introduction of capital punishment in cases of gang rape of a woman under 18 years reflects the government’s commitment to addressing sexual violence with the highest degree of seriousness.
 
• **Focus on Women’s Safety:** The **BNS, 2023**, emphasizes stricter laws for crimes against women to deter offenders and ensure faster delivery of justice.
 
 
 
• **Details of Other Options:**
 
 
• **Inclusion of community service as a punishment for domestic violence:** No such provision has been included in the **BNS, 2023**. Domestic violence laws in India are primarily governed by the **Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005**, which focuses on protective orders rather than community service.
 
• **Legalization of marital rape:** Marital rape is not legalized under **BNS, 2023**. The debate around criminalizing marital rape continues, and it remains a complex socio-legal issue in India.
 
• **Reduction of the age of consent for sexual activities to 16 years:** The age of consent in India remains **18 years** under the **Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012**. The **BNS, 2023**, does not propose any changes to this.
 
 
 
• **Background of BNS, 2023:**
 
 
• The **BNS, 2023**, was introduced to replace colonial-era laws like the **Indian Penal Code (1860)**, aiming to modernize the criminal justice system in alignment with contemporary needs.
 
• It seeks to address gaps in the existing legal framework, particularly concerning crimes against women, children, and vulnerable groups.
 
 

**Important Points__**

 
• **Key Features of BNS, 2023:**

 
 
• The **BNS, 2023**, introduces provisions for faster trials and stricter punishments for specific crimes, including sexual offenses.
 
• It aims to decolonize the Indian legal system by replacing laws introduced during British rule, focusing on a more victim-centric approach.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Capital Punishment Provision:**
 
 
• The inclusion of capital punishment for gang rape cases involving minors under 18 years serves as a strong deterrent against such heinous crimes.
 
• It aligns with public demand for stricter laws to safeguard women and children, particularly in light of high-profile cases of sexual violence in India.
 
 
 
• **Legal and Social Implications:**
 
 
• The **BNS, 2023**, aims to balance retributive justice with preventive measures, ensuring better protection for vulnerable groups.
 
• The provision also reflects India’s commitment to international conventions on women’s and children’s rights, such as the **Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW)**.

• Other options like **Civil laws**, **Consumer laws**, and **Tax laws** are incorrect because they refer to substantive or procedural laws governed by different statutes like the Code of Civil Procedure, Consumer Protection Act, and Income Tax Act, rather than the rules of evidence.

**Additional Information__**

• The **Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam** is one of the three major criminal law reforms passed by the Indian Parliament in **December 2023**.

• The other two laws in this reform package are the **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita** (replacing the Indian Penal Code) and the **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita** (replacing the Code of Criminal Procedure).

• The act received **Presidential assent** on **December 25, 2023**, and aims to remove colonial-era terminology and align the justice system with contemporary technological realities.

• It allows for the **oral evidence** to be given electronically, enabling witnesses, accused persons, and victims to appear via **audio-video means**.

__

• The **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS)**, 2023, which replaced the **Indian Penal Code (IPC)** of 1860, contains a dedicated chapter for crimes against vulnerable groups.

• **Chapter V** of the BNS is titled **'Of Offences against Women and Children'**. It consolidates and streamlines various provisions related to sexual offences, marriage-related crimes, and offences against minors.

• This chapter includes sections on **rape** (Section 63), **sexual harassment** (Section 74), **voyeurism** (Section 77), **stalking** (Section 78), and **crimes against children** such as abandonment and trafficking.

• **Chapter III** of the BNS deals with **General Exceptions** (acts which are not considered offences under specific circumstances).

• **Chapter VII** of the BNS focuses on **Offences against the State**, such as treason or waging war against the Government of India.

• **Chapter IX** of the BNS pertains to **Offences relating to Elections**.

**Additional Information__**

• The **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita** received the **Presidential assent** on **December 25, 2023**, and officially came into force on **July 1, 2024**.

• The BNS has reduced the number of sections from 511 (in the IPC) to **358**, aiming to modernize the criminal justice system and remove colonial-era terminology.

• One significant addition in Chapter V is the introduction of **Section 69**, which criminalizes sexual intercourse by **deceitful means** or making false promises to marry.

• The act also introduces **Community Service** as a form of punishment for petty offences for the first time in Indian criminal law.
</ul

question: Who is appointed as the 26th 'Chief Election Commissioner of India'?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Rajiv Kumar**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Rajiv Kumar** assumed charge as the **25th Chief Election Commissioner (CEC)** of **India** on **May 15, 2022**. He succeeded **Sushil Chandra**, who demitted office on **May 14, 2022**.
 
• Before his appointment as the **CEC**, he had been serving as an **Election Commissioner** since **September 1, 2020**. His tenure is marked by overseeing significant **electoral reforms** and the conduct of several **State Assembly elections** and the **2024 General Elections**.
 
• The **Chief Election Commissioner** is the head of the **Election Commission of India (ECI)**, a **constitutional body** responsible for conducting free and fair **elections** in the **country**.
 
• As per the **Indian Constitution**, the **CEC** and other **Election Commissioners** hold office for a **term** of **six years** or until they attain the **age** of **65 years**, whichever is earlier.
 
• **Rajiv Kumar** is a **1984-batch** Indian Administrative Service (**IAS**) officer of the **Bihar/Jharkhand** cadre and has previously served as the **Finance Secretary** to the **Government of India**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Structure of ECI**: Originally, the commission had only one **Chief Election Commissioner**. Following the **Election Commissioner Amendment Act, 1989**, it was made a multi-member body. Currently, it consists of **one CEC** and **two Election Commissioners**.
 
• **Constitutional Basis**: **Article 324** to **Article 329** in **Part XV** of the **Constitution of India** provide the **legal framework** for the **electoral system** and the establishment of the **Commission**.
 
• **Recent Appointments**: In **March 2024**, **Gyanesh Kumar** and **Sukhbir Singh Sandhu** were appointed as **Election Commissioners** to fill the vacancies in the three-member panel under the new **Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners Act, 2023**.
 
• **Historical Context**: **Sukumar Sen** was the **first Chief Election Commissioner** of **India**, serving from **March 21, 1950**, to **December 19, 1958**. He managed the first two **General Elections** of independent **India** in **1951-52** and **1957**.
 
• **Functions**: The **Election Commission** prepares **electoral rolls**, notifies **election dates** and schedules, grants **recognition** to **political parties**, and enforces the **Model Code of Conduct (MCC)** during **elections**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Appointment Process**: The **CEC** is appointed by the **President of India**. Following a **Supreme Court** ruling and subsequent **legislation** in **2023**, the **selection committee** consists of the **Prime Minister**, a **Union Cabinet Minister**, and the **Leader of the Opposition** in the **Lok Sabha**.
 
• **Removal Mechanism**: To ensure **independence**, the **CEC** can only be **removed** from office through a process of **impeachment** by **Parliament**, similar to a **Judge** of the **Supreme Court of India**, on grounds of **proved misbehaviour** or **incapacity**.
 
• **Salary and Status**: The **CEC** and **Election Commissioners** enjoy the same **status** and receive the same **salary** and **perks** as available to **Judges** of the **Supreme Court** of **India**.
 
• **Voter Awareness**: The **ECI** operates the **Systematic Voters' Education and Electoral Participation (SVEEP)** program to increase **voter turnout** and **awareness** across **India**.
</ul

question: In India, the Chairperson of the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) appointed in 2025 is ___________.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Shri Justice V. Ramasubramanian**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
__

• **Shri Justice V. Ramasubramanian**, a former judge of the **Supreme Court of India**, was appointed as the **Chairperson** of the **National Human Rights Commission (NHRC)** in **2025**.

• The **Chairperson** and members of the NHRC are appointed by the **President of India** on the recommendations of a high-powered committee chaired by the **Prime Minister**.

• He succeeded **Shri Justice Arun Kumar Mishra**, who had been serving as the Chairperson since June 2021.

• The **Protection of Human Rights (Amendment) Act, 2019**, stipulates that a person who has been a **Judge of the Supreme Court** (in addition to a retired Chief Justice of India) is eligible to be appointed as the Chairperson of the NHRC.

• **Shri Justice H.L. Dattu** and **Shri Justice K.G. Balakrishnan** are former Chairpersons who served their respective terms prior to Justice Arun Kumar Mishra.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• The **National Human Rights Commission (NHRC)** of India is a **Statutory public body** constituted on **12 October 1993** under the **Protection of Human Rights Ordinance**.

• It was given a statutory basis by the **Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA)**.

• The headquarters of the NHRC is located in **New Delhi**.

• The **Selection Committee** for the NHRC includes the **Prime Minister** (Chairperson), the **Speaker of the Lok Sabha**, the **Union Home Minister**, the **Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha**, and the **Leaders of the Opposition** in both Houses of Parliament.

• The term of office for the Chairperson and members is **three years** or until they attain the age of **70 years**, whichever is earlier.

• **Justice Ranganath Misra** was the **first Chairperson** of the National Human Rights Commission.
</ul

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] Additional Information__

• The appointment of GC Murmu as the external auditor is a significant achievement for India, reflecting the country's growing influence in international organizations.
 
• The role of the external auditor involves auditing the financial statements of the ILO and ensuring that the organization’s funds are used efficiently and effectively.

question:
Fill in the blank:
In 2022, _______ was appointed as India's second 'Chief of Defence Staff.'
solution:
The correct answer is __**General Anil Chauhan**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• **General Anil Chauhan** was appointed as India's second **Chief of Defence Staff (CDS)** on **September 28, 2022**.

• The post of CDS had been vacant for nine months following the tragic death of the first CDS, **General Bipin Rawat**, in a helicopter crash in **December 2021**.

• General Chauhan is a retired officer of the **Indian Army** and had previously served as the **Eastern Army Commander** before his retirement in May 2021.

• As the CDS, he also functions as the **Secretary to the Government of India**, Department of Military Affairs, and the **Permanent Chairman of the Chiefs of Staff Committee**.

• The other options are incorrect because **Air Marshal Padma Bandopadhyay** was the first woman to be promoted to the rank of Air Marshal, **Lt. Gen. Madhuri Kanitkar** is a high-ranking officer in the Army Medical Corps, and **Admiral Sunil Lanba** is a former Chief of the Naval Staff.

**Additional Information__**

• The **Chief of Defence Staff (CDS)** is a **four-star General** rank officer who acts as the **Principal Military Adviser** to the Minister of Defence on all tri-service matters.

• The creation of the CDS post was recommended by the **Kargil Review Committee** in 2001 to improve **jointness** and **integration** between the Army, Navy, and Air Force.

• The CDS does not exercise any military command, including over the three Service Chiefs, but coordinates the functioning of the three services to ensure **synergy** in operations and procurement.

• The age limit for the post of CDS is **65 years**, and there is no fixed tenure specified like the three service chiefs (who serve for 3 years or until age 62).
</ul

question: Who succeeded M. Venkaiah Naidu as the Vice President of India in 2022?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Jagdeep Dhankhar**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Jagdeep Dhankhar** succeeded **M. Venkaiah Naidu** as the **Vice President of India** on **August 11, 2022**, following the completion of Naidu's term.
 
• He was elected as the **14th Vice President of India** and is also the **Chairman of the Rajya Sabha**, as per the constitutional provision of the Vice President's role.
 
• Jagdeep Dhankhar is a seasoned politician and lawyer, having previously served as the **Governor of West Bengal** from **July 2019 to July 2022**.
 
• The election for the Vice President was held on **August 6, 2022**, and Dhankhar emerged victorious by securing a significant majority of votes, defeating the opposition candidate **Margaret Alva**.
 
• The Vice President of India is elected by an electoral college consisting of the **Members of Parliament (MPs) from both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha**. This election is conducted by secret ballot, following the system of proportional representation by a single transferable vote.
 
• Jagdeep Dhankhar's leadership and extensive experience in politics, law, and governance played a crucial role in his selection for this esteemed position.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Jagdeep Dhankhar:**

 
 
• **Born:** May 18, 1951, in **Kithana, Rajasthan**, Jagdeep Dhankhar is known for his distinguished career in both politics and law.
 
• He served as a Member of Parliament (MP) from **Jhunjhunu constituency** in Rajasthan during 1989-1991 and has been associated with the **Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)**.
 
• He has also served as the Minister of State for Parliamentary Affairs in the **Chandra Shekhar government** (1990-1991).
 
 
 
• **Role of the Vice President of India:**
 
 
• The Vice President is the **second-highest constitutional office** in India after the President. The primary responsibility is to act as the **Chairperson of the Rajya Sabha**.
 
• In the event of the President's absence, resignation, or removal, the Vice President may act as the **President of India** temporarily.
 
 
 
• **M. Venkaiah Naidu:**
 
 
• **M. Venkaiah Naidu** served as the **13th Vice President of India** from **August 11, 2017, to August 10, 2022**.
 
• He is a prominent leader from the BJP and is well-known for his contributions to policy-making and governance during his tenure.
 
 
 
• **Other Candidates for Vice President in 2022:**
 
 
• **Margaret Alva**, the opposition candidate, contested against Dhankhar but lost the election with a significant margin.
 
• The election showcased the importance of strong political alliances, as Dhankhar secured the backing of the **NDA (National Democratic Alliance)**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Election Process:**

 
 
• The Vice President is elected through an electoral college comprising **Members of Parliament** (MPs) from both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha.
 
• The election is conducted using a **single transferable vote** system through a secret ballot.
 
 
 
• **Vice President's Tenure:**
 
 
• The Vice President serves a term of **five years** but can be re-elected for subsequent terms.
 
• In case of resignation or removal, the Vice President can vacate the office before completing the term.

question: In 2024, Smt. Vijaya Kishore Rahatkar was appointed as the 9th Chairperson of the National Commission for Women (NCW). Which of the following is **correct** regarding her role and responsibilities?

options.text: Designing fiscal and tax policies for women's entrepreneurship
Framing monetary policies for women's economic development
Reviewing legal safeguards for women and recommending remedial measures
Conducting national elections and preparing voter lists

solution:
The correct answer is __**Reviewing legal safeguards for women and recommending remedial measures**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• Smt. **Vijaya Kishore Rahatkar** was appointed as the **9th Chairperson** of the **National Commission for Women (NCW)** in **October 2024**.

• The **National Commission for Women** is a **statutory body** formed under the **National Commission for Women Act, 1990**, to protect and promote the interests of women in India.

• The core responsibility of the NCW and its Chairperson is to **review the constitutional and legal safeguards** provided for women and recommend **remedial legislative measures** to address any gaps or inadequacies.

• The Commission is empowered to **investigate and examine** all matters relating to the safeguards provided for women under the Constitution and other laws.

• It also takes **suo motu notice** of matters involving the deprivation of women's rights and non-implementation of laws enacted to provide protection to women.

• **Option 1 and 2** are incorrect because **fiscal, tax, and monetary policies** fall under the jurisdiction of the **Ministry of Finance** and the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)**.

• **Option 4** is incorrect as the **Election Commission of India** is responsible for conducting national elections and preparing voter lists.

**Additional Information__**

• The **NCW** was established on **31st January 1992**. The first Chairperson of the commission was **Jayanti Patnaik**.

• Smt. **Vijaya Rahatkar** has a significant background in public service, having served as the Chairperson of the **Maharashtra State Commission for Women** (2016-2021) and the Mayor of **Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (Aurangabad)**.

• The Commission consists of a **Chairperson**, five members (with at least one member each from **Scheduled Castes** and **Scheduled Tribes**), and a **Member Secretary**.

• The NCW also participates and advises on the **planning process** of socio-economic development of women and evaluates the progress of the development of women under the Union and any State.
</ul

question: What is the primary reason for Afghanistan's low ranking in the World Happiness Report 2025?

options.text: Economic instability and lack of social support.
High levels of corruption and poor governance.
Worsening conditions for women and societal unrest.

solution:
The correct answer is __**Worsening conditions for women and societal unrest.**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Afghanistan** has been ranked as the **least happy country** in the world in the **World Happiness Report 2025**, a position it has held since the **Taliban** regained power in **August 2021**.

• The primary reason for this record-low ranking is the **drastic restriction of human rights**, particularly the **worsening conditions for women and girls**. The ban on **female education** beyond primary school and the exclusion of women from most **employment sectors** have led to a collapse in societal well-being.

• The report highlights that the **freedom to make life choices** has reached an all-time low in the country, contributing significantly to the overall sense of **societal unrest** and despair.

• While **economic instability** and **poverty** are severe, the systemic **gender-based oppression** and the lack of **social support** systems are the most distinctive factors cited for Afghanistan's unique position at the bottom of the index.

**Additional Information__**

• The **World Happiness Report** is a publication of the **United Nations Sustainable Development Solutions Network (SDSN)** and uses data primarily from the **Gallup World Poll**.

• The rankings are based on a three-year average of life evaluations. For the 2025 report, data from **2022 to 2024** was analyzed.

• **Finland** continues to hold the title of the **happiest country in the world** for the eighth consecutive year in 2025, followed by other Nordic nations like **Denmark** and **Iceland**.

• The report evaluates countries based on six key variables: **GDP per capita**, **social support**, **healthy life expectancy**, **freedom to make life choices**, **generosity**, and **freedom from corruption**.

• The **International Day of Happiness** is celebrated annually on **March 20th**, the day the report is typically released.
</ul

question: What is the function of the "Speak Up!" portal launched by NADA (National Anti Doping Agency)?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Report Anti-Doping Rule Violations confidentially**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **National Anti-Doping Agency (NADA)** India launched the **"Speak Up!"** portal as a secure and confidential digital platform dedicated to reporting **Anti-Doping Rule Violations (ADRV)**. This function allows individuals to report suspicious activities without fear of repercussions. ***Hence, the statement regarding reporting violations is correct.***
 
• The primary **use** of this portal is to protect the **integrity** of sports in **India** by encouraging **whistleblowers**, including **athletes**, **coaches**, and **support personnel**, to share sensitive information about doping.
 
• The **"Speak Up!"** portal ensures **anonymity**, meaning the identity of the informant is strictly protected under the guidelines of the **World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA)**. This **feature** is critical for gathering intelligence that may not be available through routine testing.
 
• The portal is a key component of **NADA's** **Intelligence and Investigations** framework. It focuses on catching not just the athletes who use **banned substances**, but also the wider network of **suppliers** and **facilitators** involved in doping rings.
 
• By providing a dedicated **online platform**, **NADA** aims to foster a **clean sports culture** where stakeholders feel empowered to contribute to a **dope-free environment**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **National Anti-Doping Agency (NADA):** It was established as a registered society under the **Societies Registration Act** on **November 24, 2005**. It functions under the **Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports**, Government of **India**.
 
• **WADA (World Anti-Doping Agency):** Founded on **November 10, 1999**, in **Lausanne, Switzerland**, and now headquartered in **Montreal, Canada**. **WADA** sets the **Global Anti-Doping Code**, which **NADA** India follows to maintain international standards in **drug testing** and **adjudication**.
 
• **Therapeutic Use Exemptions (TUE):** This is a process where an **athlete** can request permission to use a **prohibited substance** for legitimate **medical reasons**. Applications are reviewed by a **TUE Committee** consisting of **medical experts** to ensure no unfair advantage is gained.
 
• **Banned Substances:** These are listed annually by **WADA** in the **Prohibited List**. Categories include **Anabolic Agents**, **Peptide Hormones**, **Stimulants**, and **Glucocorticoids**. The list is updated every **year**, effective from **January 1st**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Anti-Doping Rule Violations (ADRV):** Under the **2021 WADA Code**, there are **11** distinct violations. These include the **presence** of a substance, **attempted use**, **refusing** a sample collection, **whereabouts failures**, and **trafficking**.
 
• **Dope Testing Process:** **NADA** conducts both **In-Competition** and **Out-of-Competition** testing. Samples (blood or urine) are analyzed at **WADA-accredited laboratories**. In **India**, the **National Dope Testing Laboratory (NDTL)** is the primary facility for analysis.
 
• **Consequences of Doping:** Athletes found guilty of an **ADRV** face sanctions including **disqualification** of results, **forfeiture** of medals, and **period of ineligibility** (bans) ranging from a **few months** to a **lifetime ban** for repeat offenders.
 
• **The Registered Testing Pool (RTP):** High-level athletes must provide their **location** and **contact details** for **one hour** every **day** to allow for **unannounced testing**. Failure to provide this **data** three times in **12 months** constitutes an **ADRV**.
</ul

question: How does the BRICS Vaccine R&D Center support vaccine affordability?

options.text: By reducing production costs through joint research
By focusing only on high-income countries

solution:
The correct answer is __**By reducing production costs through joint research**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **BRICS Vaccine R&D Center** was formally launched on **22 March 2022** through a virtual ceremony hosted by **China**, with the participation of health ministers from **Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa**.
 
• The center serves as a collaborative platform for **joint research, development, and commercialization** of vaccines. By pooling resources and expertise, the member nations aim to **reduce production costs** and minimize the financial burden of individual research efforts. *Hence, the statement regarding reducing costs through joint research is correct.*
 
• A primary goal of this initiative is to ensure **vaccine affordability** and **equitable access**, especially for developing nations and **low-income countries**, treating vaccines as a **global public good**.
 
• The center facilitates **technology transfer** and **information sharing** among national vaccine centers. This prevents the duplication of efforts and speeds up the transition from **laboratory research** to **mass production**.
 
• The collaboration leverages the unique strengths of each member, such as **India's** massive **manufacturing capacity** and **Russia's** advancements in **vector-based vaccines**, to provide **cost-effective healthcare solutions** globally.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **BRICS Partnership:** The **BRICS** group (**Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa**) represents about **42%** of the **global population** and over **23%** of the **global GDP**. The group focuses on **multilateral cooperation** in fields like trade, health, and security.
 
• **Health Cooperation:** During the **13th BRICS Summit** in **2021**, chaired by **India**, member nations emphasized the need for a **BRICS Integrated Early Warning System** for preventing mass infectious disease risks.
 
• **Countering Restrictions:** Unlike the suggestion of increasing **patent restrictions**, **India** and **South Africa** have been leading voices at the **World Trade Organization (WTO)** for a **TRIPS waiver** (Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights) to allow easier and cheaper production of **COVID-19 vaccines**.
 
• **Role of India:** Known as the **Pharmacy of the World**, **India** supplies over **60%** of the world's vaccine demand. Through the **Vaccine Maitri** initiative, **India** supplied millions of doses to various **nations**, reinforcing the **BRICS** commitment to global health.
 
• **Future Pandemic Preparedness:** The **Vaccine R&D Center** is designed to act as a **networked center** to respond rapidly to future outbreaks by establishing a **standardized framework** for **clinical trials** and **emergency use authorizations**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Launch Date:** The official launch took place on **March 22, 2022**, during the tenure of **Dr. Mansukh Mandaviya** as the **Union Minister of Health and Family Welfare** of **India**.
 
• **Eliminating Barriers:** The center actively works against **vaccine nationalism** and **export limits**, promoting the idea that **global recovery** is only possible when **vaccines** are accessible to all, regardless of a **country's** economic status.
 
• **Technical Network:** It involves key institutions like the **Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR)** from **India** and similar premier health bodies from other **member states** to ensure **scientific excellence** and **data transparency**.
 
• **Expansion:** The **BRICS** bloc recently expanded in **2024** to include **Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, and the United Arab Emirates**, which is expected to further broaden the scope and impact of the **Vaccine R&D Center**.

question: Which of the following best characterizes the structural focus areas of BRICS cooperation in recent years?

options.text: Economic integration, regional military defense, and cultural exchange
Politics and security, economy and finance, and people-to-people engagement
Free trade agreements, military alliances, and counter-terrorism
Monetary policy, green energy, and space collaboration

solution:
The correct answer is __**Politics and security, economy and finance, and people-to-people engagement**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• The cooperation among **BRICS** nations (Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa) is structurally organized around **three main pillars** that have been consistently emphasized in recent summits and declarations.

• **Politics and Security**: This pillar focuses on promoting a more **multipolar world order**, reforming **global governance** institutions like the UN and IMF, and cooperating on **counter-terrorism** and regional stability.

• **Economy and Finance**: This is a core area involving the **New Development Bank (NDB)**, the **Contingent Reserve Arrangement (CRA)**, and initiatives to enhance **intra-BRICS trade** and investment.

• **People-to-People Engagement**: This pillar aims to strengthen ties through **cultural exchanges**, sports, youth forums, and academic collaborations to build mutual trust and understanding among the citizens of member countries.

• The other options are incorrect because **BRICS** is not a **military alliance** or a **regional defense** organization, nor is it currently a formal **Free Trade Agreement (FTA)** zone, although trade facilitation is a major goal.

**Additional Information__**

• The term **BRIC** was originally coined by **Jim O'Neill** of Goldman Sachs in 2001 to highlight the economic potential of Brazil, Russia, India, and China.

• The first formal summit took place in **Yekaterinburg, Russia**, in 2009. **South Africa** joined the group in 2010, changing the acronym to **BRICS**.

• In a historic expansion during the **15th BRICS Summit** in **Johannesburg (2023)**, the group invited several new members, including **Egypt**, **Ethiopia**, **Iran**, and the **United Arab Emirates**, to join effective January 1, 2024.

• The **New Development Bank (NDB)**, headquartered in **Shanghai**, was established to mobilize resources for infrastructure and sustainable development projects in BRICS and other emerging economies.

question: According to the 2024 GHI, what is India's child wasting rate, and how does it compare globally ?
solution:
The correct answer is __**18.7%**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **India's child wasting rate** as per the **2024 Global Hunger Index (GHI)** is **18.7%**. This refers to the proportion of children under the age of five who have a low weight-for-height, indicating acute undernutrition.
 
• Child wasting is one of the four key indicators used in calculating the **Global Hunger Index**, alongside child stunting, child mortality, and undernourishment.
 
• The rate of **18.7%** places India among the worst-performing countries globally in terms of child wasting, highlighting a significant challenge in addressing acute child malnutrition. Hence, option 3 is correct.
 
• **Child wasting** is a critical health indicator as it represents a child's immediate nutritional status and their vulnerability to illness and mortality.
 
• Globally, the average child wasting rate is much lower than India's, emphasizing the country's lagging position in this area. *Hence, the correct answer is 18.7%.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Global Hunger Index (GHI):**

 
 
• The **Global Hunger Index** is an annual report that tracks hunger and malnutrition across countries. It is jointly published by **Concern Worldwide** and **Welthungerhilfe**.
 
• The index uses four indicators: **undernourishment, child stunting, child wasting, and child mortality** to measure and rank hunger levels globally.
 
• A higher GHI score reflects worse hunger conditions in a country.
 
 
 
• **Child Wasting:**
 
 
• Wasting is defined as low weight-for-height. It usually indicates **acute malnutrition**, often caused by insufficient food intake or illnesses like diarrhea.
 
• Wasted children are at a higher risk of mortality and long-term developmental issues.
 
• The **World Health Organization (WHO)** considers child wasting rates above 15% as a critical public health emergency.
 
 
 
• **India's Position:**
 
 
• India has consistently reported high levels of child wasting in recent GHI reports, reflecting persistent challenges in public health and nutrition.
 
• Contributing factors include **poverty, food insecurity, lack of healthcare access, and poor sanitation.**
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Other GHI Indicators:**

 
 
• **Child Stunting:** Refers to low height-for-age and indicates chronic malnutrition.
 
• **Child Mortality:** Measures the mortality rate of children under five, often linked to malnutrition and poor health services.
 
• **Undernourishment:** Refers to the proportion of the population with insufficient caloric intake.
 
 
 
• **Government Initiatives:**
 
 
• India has implemented programs like **POSHAN Abhiyaan** to combat malnutrition and improve child health indicators.
 
• Efforts such as the **Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS)** and **Mid-Day Meal Scheme** aim to address child hunger and malnutrition.

question: Which of the following authorities are empowered to investigate cybercrimes under the new law?

options.text: Cybercrime investigation cells set up by the government

solution:
The correct answer is __**Cybercrime investigation cells set up by the government**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• Under the legal framework for digital security, specifically the **Information Technology (IT) Act, 2000** and the newer **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS)**, the authority to investigate cybercrimes is primarily vested in specialized **Cybercrime investigation cells** and designated police officers.

• **Cybercrime investigation cells** are specialized units established by the government (at both state and central levels) equipped with the technical expertise and forensic tools necessary to track digital footprints, handle **electronic evidence**, and deal with complex crimes like hacking, phishing, and data breaches.

• While **local police stations** can register a First Information Report (FIR) regarding cybercrimes, the actual investigation of complex cases is usually transferred to these specialized cells because local officers may lack the high-level technical training required.

• **Private investigators** do not have the legal authority to conduct criminal investigations or exercise police powers such as search and seizure.

• **Internet Service Providers (ISPs)** are considered **intermediaries** under the law; they are required to cooperate with law enforcement agencies by providing data and logs but do not have the power to investigate crimes themselves.

**Additional Information__**

• The **Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C)** was established by the **Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA)** to provide a framework and eco-system for Law Enforcement Agencies (LEAs) to deal with cybercrimes in a comprehensive and coordinated manner.

• The **National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal** (www.cybercrime.gov.in) allows citizens to report cybercrimes online, which are then routed to the relevant state/UT law enforcement agencies.

• **Section 78** of the **Information Technology Act, 2000**, stipulates that a police officer not below the rank of **Inspector** shall investigate any offence under this Act.

• **CERT-In (Indian Computer Emergency Response Team)** serves as the national nodal agency for responding to computer security incidents and strengthening the security-related defense of the Indian internet domain.
</ul

question: Which Asian country ranked as the happiest in the World Happiness Report 2025?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Taiwan**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
__ 

• **Taiwan** emerged as the happiest country in Asia in the **World Happiness Report 2025**, which evaluates global happiness levels based on various criteria such as **social support, life expectancy, freedom, and corruption levels**. 

• The **World Happiness Report** is a landmark survey published annually by the **United Nations Sustainable Development Solutions Network**. It ranks countries based on surveys and data from sources like the **Gallup World Poll**. 

• **Taiwan's high ranking** is attributed to its strong social infrastructure, high-quality healthcare system, effective governance, and emphasis on community support. 

• In recent years, Taiwan has focused on improving **mental health awareness**, environmental sustainability, and quality of life, contributing significantly to its happiness ranking. 

• Countries are rated on parameters such as **GDP per capita, social support, healthy life expectancy, freedom to make life choices, generosity, and perceptions of corruption**, where Taiwan excelled among its Asian counterparts. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
__ 

• **World Happiness Report:** 
 

• The **World Happiness Report** is an annual publication that ranks countries based on their levels of happiness, using data from surveys conducted by organizations such as the **Gallup World Poll**. 

• Key indicators include **economic performance**, social support, life expectancy, freedom, generosity, and perceptions of corruption. 

• This report serves as a **benchmark** for governments and organizations to measure and improve societal well-being. 
 
 

• **Taiwan's Key Characteristics:** 
 

• Taiwan has a highly developed healthcare system that ensures **universal health coverage** for its citizens, contributing to high life expectancy and overall happiness. 

• The country emphasizes **community engagement**, environmental sustainability, and mental health programs, which align with the metrics of happiness. 

• Taiwan's citizens benefit from **strong economic stability**, with high GDP per capita and robust government initiatives to promote well-being. 
 
 

• **Comparison with Other Asian Countries:** 
 

• **Singapore:** Known for its high economic stability and healthcare standards, but lower rankings in social freedom and perceptions of corruption impacted its happiness score. 

• **Japan:** Despite its advanced economy and healthcare, lower social engagement and perceptions of isolation affected its ranking. 

• **South Korea:** Faced challenges like high-pressure lifestyles and mental health issues, which contributed to relatively lower happiness scores. 
 
 

• **Global Context:** 
 

• Globally, countries like **Finland**, **Denmark**, and **Switzerland** frequently top the happiness rankings due to their strong focus on social support, governance, and quality of life. 

• The **World Happiness Report** serves as an important tool for analyzing the correlation between governance, economic policies, and societal well-being. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 

• **Happiness Metrics:** 
 

• The **Gallup World Poll** collects data on various happiness indicators, which include social freedom, perceptions of corruption, and economic stability. 

• Countries are ranked based on a score derived from these metrics, making comparisons across regions possible. 
 
 

• **Significance of the Report:**

question: What is the ranking of India in the World Happiness Report 2025?
solution:
The correct answer is __**118th**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• In the **World Happiness Report 2025**, India has been ranked **118th** among 143 countries surveyed globally.

• India showed an improvement of **8 positions** compared to the previous year, where it was ranked **126th** in the **2024** report.

• The report is an annual publication of the **United Nations Sustainable Development Solutions Network (SDSN)** and is released to mark the **International Day of Happiness** on **March 20th**.

• The rankings are determined based on self-reported life evaluations from the **Gallup World Poll**, averaged over a three-year period (2022-2024 for the 2025 report).

• The report considers six primary factors to explain the variation in happiness levels: **GDP per capita**, **social support**, **healthy life expectancy**, **freedom to make life choices**, **generosity**, and **perception of corruption**.

**Additional Information__**

• **Finland** has secured the **1st rank** for the **8th consecutive year**, maintaining its status as the happiest country in the world.

• The top five happiest nations in the 2025 list include **Finland**, **Denmark**, **Iceland**, **Sweden**, and **Israel**.

• **Afghanistan** continues to be ranked at the bottom of the index (**143rd**), followed by **Lebanon** and **Lesotho**.

• The 2025 report also focused on the **well-being of different age groups**, noting that happiness levels among the **youth** have seen a decline in several Western nations.

• Among India's neighbors, countries like **Nepal**, **China**, and **Bhutan** typically rank higher than India in this index.
</ul

question: BIMSTEC stands for?

options.text: Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation
Bangladesh India Maritime Security and Trade Economic Council
Bhutan India Myanmar South Asia Trade Economic Cooperation
Bay of Bengal International Maritime and Security Treaty

solution:
The correct answer is __**Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **BIMSTEC** stands for the **Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation**. It is a regional multilateral organization comprising seven Member States in the littoral and adjacent areas of the **Bay of Bengal**. Hence, the statement in option 1 is correct.

• The organization was established on **6 June 1997** through the signing of the **Bangkok Declaration**. It was initially formed with four member states and was known as **BIST-EC** (**Bangladesh, India, Sri Lanka, and Thailand Economic Cooperation**).

• The **Permanent Secretariat** of **BIMSTEC** is located in **Dhaka, Bangladesh**. It was inaugurated in **2014** to provide institutionalized support for the activities of the group and to coordinate the implementation of various projects.

• The membership of the organization currently includes five countries from **South Asia** (**Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Nepal, and Sri Lanka**) and two countries from **Southeast Asia** (**Myanmar and Thailand**).

• The other options provided, such as **Bangladesh India Maritime Security and Trade Economic Council**, **Bhutan India Myanmar South Asia Trade Economic Cooperation**, and **Bay of Bengal International Maritime and Security Treaty**, are incorrect expansions and do not represent any official international body. Hence, statements 2, 3, and 4 are incorrect.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Evolution of Membership**: After its inception in **1997**, the group expanded to include **Myanmar** on **22 December 1997**, changing the name to **BIMST-EC**. In **February 2004**, **Nepal** and **Bhutan** became full members, leading to the current name.

• **Economic Significance**: The **BIMSTEC** region is home to approximately **1.5 billion people**, which constitutes around **22%** of the total global population. The member states have a combined **Gross Domestic Product (GDP)** of over **3.5 trillion USD**.

• **Institutional Structure**: The **Chairmanship** of **BIMSTEC** rotates among the member states in alphabetical order. **Thailand** took over the chairmanship from **Sri Lanka** for the **2022-2023** period.

• **Sectors of Cooperation**: Cooperation within **BIMSTEC** was initially divided into **14 sectors**, including **Trade, Technology, Energy, Transport, Tourism, and Fisheries**. Recently, these were reorganized into **7 pillars**, with each member state leading one pillar. **India** is the lead country for the **Security** pillar.

**Important Points__**

• **BIMSTEC Charter**: A significant milestone was achieved during the **Fifth BIMSTEC Summit** held in **Colombo, Sri Lanka**, on **30 March 2022**, where the **BIMSTEC Charter** was signed. This charter provides the organization with a formal legal personality.

• **Connectivity Projects**: The organization emphasizes regional integration through projects like the **BIMSTEC Master Plan for Transport Connectivity**. Key initiatives include the **Kaladan Multi-modal Transit Transport Project** and the **Asian Highway Network**, aimed at linking **India** with **Southeast Asia**.

• **Strategic Importance for India**: For **India**, **BIMSTEC** serves as a crucial platform to fulfill its **Neighborhood First** and **Act East** policies. It provides a functional alternative to **SAARC**, which has been stagnant due to regional tensions.

• **Free Trade Agreement (FTA)**: The member nations signed the **BIMSTEC Free Trade Area Framework Agreement** in **2004** to stimulate trade and investment. Negotiations are ongoing to finalize the **BIMSTEC FTA** to further reduce tariffs and non-tariff barriers.
</ul

question: Which Indian state hosts the world's largest floating solar power plant, operational since 2023?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Madhya Pradesh**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
__ 
 
• **Madhya Pradesh** is home to the **world's largest floating solar power plant**, which became operational in **2023**. 
 
• The solar power plant is located at the **Omkareshwar Dam reservoir** on the Narmada River in Khandwa district, Madhya Pradesh. 
 
• It has a total capacity of **600 MW**, making it the largest floating solar project globally. 
 
• The project aims to increase the use of **renewable energy** in India and reduce dependence on fossil fuels. 
 
• This plant is expected to help Madhya Pradesh meet its **renewable energy targets** and contribute significantly to India's clean energy initiatives. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
__ 
 
• **Floating Solar Power Plants:** 
 
 
• Floating solar power plants are built on water bodies like reservoirs, lakes, and dams, utilizing unused water surfaces. 
 
• These plants help conserve land, which is particularly beneficial in densely populated areas. 
 
• They also reduce water evaporation, helping conserve water in reservoirs. 
 
• Floating solar panels operate more efficiently due to the cooling effect of water. 
 
 
 
• **Omkareshwar Dam:** 
 
 
• The Omkareshwar Dam is located on the **Narmada River** and is a key infrastructure supporting agriculture and electricity generation. 
 
• The reservoir created by the dam is now being utilized for the floating solar project. 
 
 
 
• **Renewable Energy in India:** 
 
 
• India is aggressively working to achieve its renewable energy target of **500 GW** by 2030 under the Paris Agreement. 
 
• Solar energy is a significant contributor, with India ranking among the leading nations in solar power capacity globally. 
 
• The floating solar plant in Madhya Pradesh is part of this larger effort to transition toward sustainable energy. 
 
 
 
• **Global Context:** 
 
 
• Floating solar plants are becoming popular globally in countries like **China, Japan, and South Korea** due to their land conservation benefits. 
 
• India's Omkareshwar project sets a global benchmark in capacity and technology. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 
 
• **Advantages of Floating Solar Plants:** 
 
 
• Efficient land usage: No need for vast land areas like traditional solar farms. 
 
• Reduced water evaporation: The panels protect the water surface from sunlight exposure. 
 
• Improved efficiency: Panels remain cooler, enhancing energy generation. 
 
• Eco-friendly: Helps reduce carbon emissions and promotes clean energy. 
 
 
 
• **Madhya Pradesh's Renewable Energy Goals:** 
 
 
• The state aims to become a renewable energy hub, focusing on solar, wind, and hydropower. 
 
• The floating solar plant aligns with India's larger commitment to achieving net-zero emissions by **2070**.

question: Which state became the first to pass a Uniform Civil Code (UCC) bill in 2024?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Uttarakhand**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Uttarakhand** became the first state in independent India to pass a **Uniform Civil Code (UCC) Bill** on **February 7, 2024**.

• The bill was passed by the **Uttarakhand Legislative Assembly** following a detailed report submitted by a five-member committee headed by retired Supreme Court Judge **Ranjana Prakash Desai**.

• The primary objective of the **UCC Bill 2024** is to establish a common legal framework for **marriage, divorce, land, property, and inheritance** for all citizens, irrespective of their religion.

• A significant feature of the bill is the mandatory registration of **live-in relationships**, with failure to do so potentially leading to imprisonment or fines.

• The bill specifically excludes **Scheduled Tribes (STs)** from its application, respecting the unique traditions and customary rights of tribal communities in the state.

**Additional Information__**

• **Article 44** of the **Indian Constitution**, which is part of the **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)**, states that the State shall endeavor to secure for the citizens a **Uniform Civil Code** throughout the territory of India.

• While **Goa** has followed a Uniform Civil Code (the **Portuguese Civil Code of 1867**) since its liberation, **Uttarakhand** is the first state to draft and pass its own UCC legislation after India's independence.

• The **President of India**, Droupadi Murmu, gave her official assent to the **Uttarakhand Uniform Civil Code Bill** in **March 2024**, making it an Act.

• The bill prohibits **polygamy** and sets a uniform age for marriage (18 for women and 21 for men) across all communities.
</ul

question: The natural aging of a lake by nutrient enrichment of its water is called ______.
solution:
The correct answer is __**eutrophication**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• When a body of water becomes **highly mineralized and nutrient-rich, **planktonic algae develop rapidly as a result of this.
 
• **Eutrophication** is the process of excessive growth of planktonic algae in nutrient-rich water.
 
• Hypoxia is formed as a result of excessive planktonic algae development, which leads to the death of aquatic animals due to low oxygen levels and the gradual disappearance of the lake.
 
• **Excess phosphorus** is usually always the source of eutrophication in freshwater ecosystems, but nitrogen and phosphorus may play diverse roles in marine habitats.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Plankton** is a varied group of organisms that live in water and are unable to swim against the stream. 
 
• **Biomagnification** is the accumulation of a chemical by an organism as a result of water and food exposure, resulting in a concentration that is higher than would have been expected from equilibrium if the chemical had only been exposed to water.

question: Each step or level of a food chain forms a trophic level. Which of the following is at the first trophic level of the said food chain?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Autotrophs or the producers.**__ 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The first trophic level of the said food chain is Autotrophs or the producers.**
 
• A food chain shows the feeding relationship between different organisms in a particular environment and/or habitat.
 
• A food chain shows how energy is passed from the sun to producers, from producers to consumers, and from consumers to decomposes such as fungi.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Based on the source of their nutrition or food, organisms occupy a specific place in the food chain that is known as their trophic level.
 
• Producers belong to the first trophic level, herbivores (primary consumer) to the second and carnivores (secondary consumer) to the third. The important point to note is that the amount of energy decreases at successive trophic levels.

question: What is the primary purpose of the 2024 Environmental Performance Index (EPI)?

options.text: To evaluate GDP growth across developing nations
To offer a global ranking of environmental NGOs
To rank countries on environmental and climate performance
To list the most polluted cities across continents

solution:
The correct answer is __**To rank countries on environmental and climate performance**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Environmental Performance Index (EPI)** is a biennial report that provides a data-driven summary of the state of sustainability around the world.

• Its primary purpose is to **rank countries** based on their performance across various **environmental health** and **ecosystem vitality** indicators.

• The **2024 EPI** evaluates 180 countries on their progress toward mitigating **climate change**, improving **environmental health**, and protecting **ecosystems**.

• The index uses **58 performance indicators** across 11 issue categories to provide a scorecard that highlights leaders and laggards in environmental performance.

• It is developed by researchers at **Yale University** and **Columbia University** in collaboration with the **World Economic Forum**.

**Additional Information__**

• In the **2024 EPI**, **Estonia** secured the top rank, followed by **Luxembourg** and **Germany**.

• The index helps policymakers identify **environmental threats**, track the effectiveness of policies, and move toward **UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)**.

• The 2024 report emphasizes the urgent need for countries to accelerate their efforts to reach **net-zero emissions** by 2050 to meet **Paris Agreement** targets.

• The rankings are often used by **civil society** and **international organizations** to hold governments accountable for their environmental commitments.
