question: Biotic potential can be defined as:

options.text: the minimum number of individuals of a species that can survive but cannot reproduce
the minimum number of individuals a species can produce
the maximum number of individuals a species can produce
the maximum number of individuals of a species that cannot survive after birth

solution:
The correct answer is __**the maximum number of individuals a species can produce**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Biotic potential** refers to the **maximum reproductive capacity** of an organism under optimum environmental conditions.
 
• This concept is significant in population ecology as it helps to understand the growth potential of a species.
 
• The **biotic potential** is influenced by factors such as the organism's rate of reproduction and the duration of its reproductive life.
 
• It is an idealized concept assuming no limiting factors like food scarcity, predation, or disease, which in reality always exist to some extent.
 
• The actual population size is often lower than the biotic potential due to these environmental resistance factors.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Understanding biotic potential is crucial for **conservation efforts** and managing species that are endangered or overpopulated.
 
• **Environmental resistance** includes all factors that limit the biotic potential of an organism, such as food availability, predation, disease, and habitat destruction.
 
• In practical terms, the biotic potential is rarely achieved in natural environments due to these limiting factors.
 
• Ecologists use the concept to model population growth and to predict how populations will respond to changes in environmental conditions.
 
• The study of biotic potential is part of **population ecology**, which examines the dynamics of species populations and how they interact with the environment.

question: What is the basic requirement for an ecosystem to function and sustain?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Input of solar energy**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• **Solar energy** forms the **foundation **of the **food chain**.

 
 
• Plants, through the process of **photosynthesis**,** use solar energy** to **convert water and carbon dioxide into organic matter** (food).
 
 
 
• It is the** basic requirement** for an **ecosystem **to **function **and sustain itself.
 
• This organic matter serves as the primary energy source for all other organisms in the ecosystem, either directly through herbivory or indirectly through other **trophic levels (predation and decomposition)**.
 
• **Without **a constant** input of solar energy,** this **energy flow would cease**, leading to the **collapse of the ecosystem.**
 
• **Soil structure**, **organisms **(including plants and animals), and **micro-organisms** are all **crucial components of an ecosystem**, playing significant roles in nutrient cycling, decomposition, and maintaining the overall balance.
 
• However, **their existence and function ultimately depend on the continuous input of solar energy**.

question: The ______ is the primary layer of the rainforest and forms a roof over the two remaining layers.
solution:
The correct answer is __**canopy layer.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• The **overlapping branches and leaves **of rainforest trees make up the canopy layer**.**
 
• This layer can reach heights of over **100 feet (30 meters) **above the ground.
 
• The rainforest is the richest home for plant and animal life, with scientists estimating that between** 60 and 90 per cent **of it may be found in the **treetops**.
 
• The canopy is home to a wide variety of well-known species, such as **sloths, tiny cats, frogs, lizards, birds, snakes, and monkeys.**
 
• During the** day**, the** canopy is drier and hotter** than other parts of the forest, and the plants and animals that live there are specially adapted for life in the trees.

 
• Canopy layer plants** absorb the light** that penetrates through from the top layer, which is known as the **emergent layer.**
 
• The canopy layer absorbs an estimated** 75-98% of light,** blocking this light from reaching the layers below.
 
• Most of the** rainfall **is captured by the **canopy layer** and very little gets to the plants at the **lower levels. ​**
 
• [IMAGE: https://animalcorner.org/wp-content/img/strata.jpg] ** **

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Understory layer:**

 
 
• The understory, a stratum made up of** young trees, short species of trees, shrubs, and soft-stemmed plants**, can be found many** meters below** the bottom of the canopy.
 
• From rainforest to rainforest, the understory** differs greatly**.
 
 
 
• **Forest floor:**
 
 
• The forest floor, also known as **detritus, duff, and the O horizon**, is one of the forest ecosystem's most recognizable characteristics.
 
• It mostly comprises **vegetative elements** that have been** shed, such as leaves, branches, bark, and stems,** which are present above the soil surface in varying states of decomposition.
 
 
 
• **Emergent layer: **
 
 
• The emergent layer is the** uppermost layer **of a rainforest.
 
• This layer experiences** intense sunlight, copious amounts of rain, and strong winds**.
 
• The **tallest trees tower 230 fee**t **(70 m) **above all other plants.

__
 
• **James Hansen** is best known for his** testimony on climate change to congressional committees in the 1980s**.
 
• His testimony helped raise wider awareness of the global warming issue.
 
• Hansen's work has been crucial in understanding the impact of human activities on the climate.
 
• He emphasized the importance of reducing greenhouse gas emissions to mitigate the effects of climate change.
 
• Hansen's efforts have influenced both public policy and scientific research on climate change.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

question: Which Indian River has received the most national attention for severe ecological damage caused by illegal sand mining, particularly in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Ganga**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Ganga** river, spanning approximately **2,525 km**, is the most significant river in India, but it has faced severe ecological degradation due to **illegal sand mining**, particularly in the states of **Uttar Pradesh** and **Bihar**.
 
• Illegal extraction of sand from the riverbed of the **Ganga** has led to the depletion of **groundwater** levels, alteration of the river's natural course, and massive **soil erosion** along the banks.
 
• The **National Green Tribunal (NGT)** has frequently intervened, issuing several bans and strict guidelines to regulate mining activities in **Uttar Pradesh** and **Bihar** to prevent further damage to the **Ganga** ecosystem.
 
• This activity poses a direct threat to endangered species such as the **Gangetic Dolphin** (India's national aquatic animal) and the **Gharial**, as their nesting and breeding grounds are destroyed by heavy machinery used in mining.
 
• The **Namami Gange Programme**, an Integrated Conservation Mission launched in **June 2014**, recognizes the control of illegal mining as a vital component for the **rejuvenation** and **pollution abatement** of the river.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Krishna River**:

 
 
• It originates at **Mahabaleshwar** in **Maharashtra** and flows through **Karnataka**, **Telangana**, and **Andhra Pradesh**.
 
• While it also faces sand mining issues, it is more frequently in the news for **inter-state water sharing disputes** between the riparian states.
 
 
 
• **Palar River**:
 
 
• This is an **ephemeral river** flowing through **Karnataka**, **Andhra Pradesh**, and **Tamil Nadu**.
 
• It has suffered extreme ecological damage and **groundwater depletion** due to rampant sand mining in the **Vellore** and **Kanchipuram** districts of **Tamil Nadu**, though it receives less "national" attention compared to the **Ganga**.
 
 
 
• **Narmada River**:
 
 
• Known as the "**Life Line of Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat**," it is the largest west-flowing river in India, flowing through a **rift valley**.
 
• Sand mining occurs in the **Narmada** basin, but the river is globally recognized more for the **Narmada Bachao Andolan** and the construction of the **Sardar Sarovar Dam**.
 
 
 
• **Legal Status of Sand**:
 
 
• In India, sand is classified as a "**minor mineral**" under the **Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957**.
 
• The **State Governments** have the power to frame rules for the grant of quarry leases and the regulation of mining for minor minerals.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Ecological Impact**: Excessive sand mining causes the riverbed to deepen (**incising**), which can lead to the collapse of **bridge foundations** and other infrastructure.
 
• **Sustainable Sand Mining Management Guidelines (2016)**: These were released by the **Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC)** to promote scientific mining and monitoring through **Remote Sensing** and **GIS**.
 
• **Data Fact**: India is the second-largest consumer of **sand** in the world after **China**, driven largely by the booming **construction** and **infrastructure** sectors.

question: Medha Patkar led a movement to protest against a large dam's construction? What was the name of the movement?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Narmada Bachao Andolan**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Medha Patkar** is a prominent Indian social activist who led the **Narmada Bachao Andolan (NBA)**, a movement protesting the construction of large dams on the **Narmada River**, including the Sardar Sarovar Dam.
 
• The **Narmada Bachao Andolan** (Save the Narmada Movement) began in **1985** and primarily opposed the displacement of local communities and environmental damage caused by the dam's construction.
 
• The primary concern of the movement was the displacement of thousands of **tribal people, farmers, and villagers** whose homes and lands were submerged due to the dam projects.
 
• The NBA also highlighted the lack of proper **rehabilitation and resettlement** policies for the affected people and raised concerns about the ecological impact, including deforestation and loss of biodiversity.
 
• The movement gained international attention and raised significant debates on the costs and benefits of large-scale development projects, questioning their impact on marginalized communities.
 
• Despite its opposition, the **Sardar Sarovar Dam** was completed, but the NBA succeeded in bringing attention to the plight of displaced people and the importance of sustainable development.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Medha Patkar:**

 
 
• Medha Patkar, born on **1 December 1954**, is a renowned social reformer and environmental activist.
 
• She founded the **Narmada Bachao Andolan** and has worked extensively for the rights of displaced people, particularly in tribal and rural areas.
 
• Her activism has also extended to other issues, including urban slum redevelopment and women’s rights.
 
• She has received several awards, including the **Right Livelihood Award** in 1991 for her efforts in environmental and social justice.
 
 
 
• **Sardar Sarovar Dam:**
 
 
• The **Sardar Sarovar Dam** is a major dam on the **Narmada River** in Gujarat, India.
 
• It is part of the Narmada Valley Project, which includes the construction of several dams and canals aimed at providing **irrigation, drinking water, and hydroelectric power**.
 
• The dam is one of the largest infrastructure projects in India and has been a subject of both praise and criticism due to its economic benefits and social/environmental costs.
 
 
 
• **Environmental Concerns:**
 
 
• Large dams like the Sardar Sarovar cause significant environmental impacts, including **deforestation, loss of wildlife habitats, and changes to river ecosystems**.
 
• Such projects also lead to the submersion of fertile agricultural lands and displacement of local communities.
 
 
 
• **Other Movements Led by Medha Patkar:**
 
 
• She has also been part of the **Right to Information (RTI) movement** and the **National Alliance of People's Movements (NAPM)**, which advocates for various social justice causes.
 
• Patkar has been vocal about issues related to urban displacement, particularly in Mumbai, where she campaigned against the demolition of slums.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Chipko Movement:**

 
 
• The **Chipko Movement**, initiated in the 1970s in Uttarakhand (then part of Uttar Pradesh), was an environmental movement to **protect trees and forests** from being cut down.
 
• It involved villagers, particularly women, hugging trees to prevent their felling, hence the name "Chipko" (meaning "to hug").
 
 
 
• **Save Ganga Movement:**
 
 
• This movement focuses on cleaning and conserving the **Ganga River**, which is considered sacred in India but is heavily polluted.
 
• Initiatives under this movement include the **Namami Gange Programme**, launched by the Indian government to rejuvenate the river.
 
 
 
• **Project Tiger:**
 
 
• Launched in **1973**, this project aims to conserve the tiger population in India and its natural habitats.
 
• It has led to the establishment of several **tiger reserves** across the country.

subject: GK
question:
Fill in the blank:
AQI values above ______ indicate unhealthy air quality for sensitive groups.
solution:
The correct answer is __**100**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Air Quality Index (AQI)** is a standardized system used to report daily air quality and its potential health effects. It focuses on health effects individuals might experience within a few hours or days after breathing polluted air.

• The **AQI** scale typically ranges from **0 to 500**. An **AQI value of 100** generally corresponds to the **National Ambient Air Quality Standard** for the pollutant, which is the level set by regulatory bodies like the **Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)** or the **Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB)** to protect public health.

• When **AQI** values are between **101 and 150**, the air quality is classified as **Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups**. This means that while the general public may not be immediately affected, people with **lung disease**, **asthma**, **children**, and **older adults** are at a greater risk from exposure to ozone or particle pollution. ***Hence, the statement that values above 100 indicate unhealthy air for sensitive groups is correct.***

• An **AQI** value of **50** or below represents **Good** air quality with little to no health risk. ***Hence, the option 50 is incorrect as it is within the safe range.***

• An **AQI** value of **75** falls within the **Moderate** or **Satisfactory** range (**51 to 100**), where air quality is acceptable but may pose a slight risk for a very small number of people who are unusually sensitive to air pollution. ***Hence, the option 75 is incorrect.***

• An **AQI** value of **25** is well within the **Good** category, indicating very clean air. ***Hence, the option 25 is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• In **India**, the **National Air Quality Index (NAQI)** was launched by the **Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change** on **17 September 2014**. It was developed as part of the **Swachh Bharat Abhiyan** to provide a **One Color-One Number-One Description** for the common man to judge air quality.

• The **Indian AQI** system categorizes air quality into **six levels**: **Good (0-50)**, **Satisfactory (51-100)**, **Moderately Polluted (101-200)**, **Poor (201-300)**, **Very Poor (301-400)**, and **Severe (401-500)**.

• The **NAQI** monitors **eight major pollutants** to calculate the index: **Particulate Matter (PM10)**, **Particulate Matter (PM2.5)**, **Nitrogen Dioxide (NO2)**, **Sulphur Dioxide (SO2)**, **Carbon Monoxide (CO)**, **Ozone (O3)**, **Ammonia (NH3)**, and **Lead (Pb)**.

• The **sub-index** for each pollutant is calculated based on its **24-hour average** concentration (except for **CO** and **O3**, which use **8-hour** averages), and the overall **AQI** is determined by the highest sub-index among the pollutants.

• **Sensitive groups** include individuals with pre-existing **respiratory conditions** like **COPD** or **bronchitis**, **cardiovascular diseases**, **pregnant women**, and **infants** whose lungs are still developing.

**Important Points__**

• **PM2.5** (particles smaller than **2.5 micrometers**) is considered the most dangerous pollutant because its small size allows it to penetrate deep into the **lungs** and enter the **bloodstream**, causing long-term health issues.

• The **World Health Organization (WHO)** updated its **Global Air Quality Guidelines** in **2021**, significantly lowering the recommended limits for key pollutants, reflecting the increased evidence of health impacts even at lower concentrations.

• During **winter months** in **North India**, the **AQI** often enters the **Severe** category (above **400**) due to factors like **stubble burning**, **vehicular emissions**, and **meteorological conditions** such as **temperature inversion**.

• The **Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB)**, a statutory organization under the **Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974**, is responsible for maintaining the **National Air Quality Monitoring Programme (NAMP)** across **India**.
</ul

__
 
• Mahatma Gandhi **Marine National Park** is a national park of India near **Wandoor** on the** Andaman Islands**.
 
• It belongs to the **South Andaman** administrative **district,** part of the **Indian union territory** of Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
 
• The park was created on **24 May 1983** under the **Wildlife Protection Act** of **1972** to protect marine life such as the corals and nesting sea turtles prevalent in the area.

• The Only **6 Marine National Park** and **Water Sanctuarie**s of **India.**

 
 
 

 **Gulf of Kutch Marine National Park.**
 
 
Marine National Park in **Gulf** of **Kutch** is situated on the **southern** shore of the **Gulf** of **Kutch** in **Jamnagar**, **Gujarat**.

 
It is the **first national marine** **park **of **India** with **42** islands on **Jamnagar coast** in the Marine National Park.

 
Some popular islands **Poshitra**, **Pirotan**, **Karubhar **and **Narara.**

 
 
 

 **Gahirmatha Marine Wildlife Sanctuary.**
 
 
Gahirmatha is the **first** and the only marine sanctuary of **Orissa**, number of marvellous creatures including Olive **Ridley** sea **turtles** migrate here in **huge numbers**.

 
Gahirmatha Beach separates the **Bhitarkanika** Mangroves from the **Bay of Bengal** and is the **world’s most** important **nesting** beach for **Olive Ridley** Sea Turtles.

 
In **1997** Govt declared Gahirmatha as marine sanctuary to **save turtles**.

question: Which of the following is NOT considered a method of conservation of natural resources?

__
 
• **Extraction** is not considered a method of conservation of natural resources.
 
• Conservation methods typically include practices that help preserve and protect natural resources, such as **afforestation, recycling, and terrace farming**.
 
• **Afforestation** refers to planting trees to create forests, which helps in maintaining ecological balance.
 
• **Recycling** involves converting waste materials into reusable materials, thereby reducing the need for new raw materials.
 
• **Terrace farming** is an agricultural practice that prevents soil erosion and conserves water.

• Methods such as **afforestation** and **recycling** help in reducing the environmental impact and preserving biodiversity.
 
• **Extraction**, on the other hand, often depletes natural resources and can cause significant environmental damage if not managed sustainably.
 
• Conservation efforts focus on sustainable practices to maintain the health of ecosystems and the availability of resources.

question: The Vienna Convention is related to ____________.
solution:
The correct answer is __**protection of ozone layer.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The** Vienna Convention**, formally known as the Vienna Convention for the** Protection of the Ozone Layer**, was adopted in **1985** to address the depletion of the ozone layer.
 
• The convention is a **legally binding agreement** that aims to promote international cooperation to protect the ozone layer. It encourages countries to: 
 
 
• Exchange information and conduct research on the ozone layer 
 
• Adopt laws and regulations to protect the ozone layer 
 
• Develop controls for ozone layer development.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Montreal Protocol:**

 
 
• Adopted in** 1987**, this protocol aims to **phase out the production and consumption of ozone-depleting substances,** such as chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs).
 
• It is considered one of the most successful environmental treaties, leading to significant recovery of the ozone layer.
 
 
 
• **Kyoto Protocol:**
 
 
• Adopted in **1997**, this international agreement commits its parties to **reduce greenhouse gas emissions**, based on the premise that global warming exists and human-made CO2 emissions have caused it.
 
• The protocol emphasizes binding commitments for developed countries to mitigate climate change.
 
 
 
• **Paris Agreement:**
 
 
• Adopted in **2015,** this landmark accord aims to** limit global warming** to well below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels.
 
• It encourages countries to set their emission reduction targets and report on their progress.
 
 
 
• **Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD):**
 
 
• Established in** 1992**, this convention aims to conserve biological diversity, promote sustainable use of its components, and ensure fair sharing of benefits arising from genetic resources.
 
• It emphasizes the importance of preserving ecosystems and species.
 
 
 
• **UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC):**
 
 
• Adopted in **1992**, this treaty sets the framework for international efforts to combat climate change, with periodic Conferences of the Parties (COP) to assess progress and set binding commitments.

Consider the following statements regarding India's Green Credit Programme:
1. It provides credits for verified voluntary environmental actions like afforestation and water harvesting.
2. It operates under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
3. Credits are tradable and recognized by financial institutions.
solution:
The correct answer is __**All 1, 2, and 3 are correct**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
__ 

• **India's Green Credit Programme** is designed to incentivize individuals, institutions, and industries to undertake **voluntary environmental actions** such as afforestation, water harvesting, waste management, and energy efficiency measures. *Hence, statement 1 is correct.* 

• The programme operates under the **Environment (Protection) Act, 1986**, which is a key legislation for environmental protection in India. It provides the legal framework for the programme's implementation. *Hence, statement 2 is correct.* 

• Credits earned through the programme are **tradable**, meaning they can be bought and sold in the market. These credits are recognized by **financial institutions**, enabling participants to monetize their environmental efforts. *Hence, statement 3 is correct.* 

• The Green Credit Programme represents a significant step towards **sustainable development** by aligning economic incentives with environmental conservation. 

• **Tradable credits** allow industries and businesses to offset their environmental footprints by investing in green initiatives. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
__ 

• **Environment (Protection) Act, 1986:** 

• This act was enacted in **1986** following the Bhopal gas tragedy to provide measures for the protection and improvement of the environment. 

• It empowers the central government to take all necessary measures to protect the environment and prevent pollution. 

• The act is comprehensive, covering aspects such as emissions, hazardous waste management, and environmental standards. 
 
 

• **Green Credit Trading Mechanism:** 

• Trading allows entities that perform better environmentally to sell their **credits** to those that fall short, thus encouraging widespread adoption of green practices. 

• Examples include **carbon credits**, which are similar in concept but focus specifically on reducing greenhouse gas emissions. 
 
 

• **Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs):** 

• The Green Credit Programme aligns with several SDGs, including **SDG 13 (Climate Action)** and **SDG 15 (Life on Land)**, by promoting afforestation and reducing environmental degradation. 

• It also indirectly supports **SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth)** by creating economic opportunities through green initiatives. 
 
 

• **Global Examples of Green Credit Systems:** 

• Countries like **China** have implemented similar programmes, such as the **China Certified Emissions Reduction (CCER)** system. 

• The European Union operates the **Emissions Trading System (EU ETS)**, which is one of the largest carbon trading platforms globally. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 

• **Afforestation:** 

• Afforestation involves planting trees in areas that were not previously forested, helping mitigate climate change by sequestering **carbon dioxide**. 

• India's Green Credit Programme promotes afforestation as a key activity for earning credits. 
 
 

• **Water Harvesting:** 

• Water harvesting techniques help conserve water resources, reduce dependence on groundwater, and ensure sustainable water management. 

• Such initiatives are crucial for addressing water scarcity in drought-prone regions. 
 
 

• **Waste Management:** 

• Efficient waste management practices, such as recycling and composting, reduce landfill waste and promote a circular economy. 

• India's Green Credit Programme encourages industries to adopt sustainable waste management systems. 
 
 

• **Energy Efficiency:** 

• Improving energy efficiency reduces energy consumption and emissions, contributing to sustainable industrial growth. 

• Participants in the Green Credit Programme can earn credits by implementing energy-efficient technologies and practices. 
 
 
</ul

question:
Consider the following statements regarding the GIB (Great Indian Bustard):
1. It is listed as Critically Endangered under the IUCN Red List.
2. It is found in the grasslands of Gujarat, Maharashtra, and Rajasthan.
3. The species is protected under Schedule II of the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Only 1 and 2 are correct**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Great Indian Bustard** (Ardeotis nigriceps) is a large bird that is among the heaviest flying birds in the world. It is currently categorized as **Critically Endangered** on the **IUCN Red List** due to a drastic decline in its population, which is estimated to be fewer than **150 individuals** left in the wild. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***

• This species is primarily found in the **grassland** and **arid ecosystems** of India. Its distribution is largely restricted to the states of **Rajasthan**, **Gujarat**, and **Maharashtra**. The **Desert National Park** in **Jaisalmer**, **Rajasthan**, serves as the most significant stronghold for the species. Small populations also exist in **Karnataka** and **Andhra Pradesh**. ***Hence, statement 2 is correct.***

• The **Great Indian Bustard** is granted the highest level of legal protection under the **Wildlife Protection Act, 1972**. It is listed under **Schedule I** of the act, which provides it with the same level of protection as the **Tiger** and the **Elephant**. It is not listed under Schedule II. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***

• ***Hence, the correct answer is Only 1 and 2 are correct.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Physical Characteristics:** The **Great Indian Bustard** is easily identifiable by its large size, **black crown** on the forehead, and a pale neck and underparts. Males are generally larger and possess a **gular pouch** which they inflate during the **breeding season** to produce a deep resonant call.

• **Habitat and Ecology:** It is considered an **indicator species** for the health of **grassland habitats**. It prefers open landscapes with short grass and avoids areas with dense trees or intensive agriculture. It is an **omnivore**, consuming a diet of **grass seeds**, **insects** like grasshoppers and beetles, and occasionally small **rodents** or **reptiles**.

• **Conservation Status and International Agreements:**

• **IUCN Red List:** **Critically Endangered**.

• **CITES:** **Appendix I**, which strictly regulates international trade.

• **CMS (Convention on Migratory Species):** **Appendix I**, following its inclusion during **COP13** held in **Gandhinagar** in **2020**.

• **Major Threats:**

• **Power Lines:** The most immediate threat is the collision with **high-voltage overhead power lines** in the **Thar Desert** region. Due to their poor frontal vision and heavy weight, they cannot maneuver quickly to avoid these wires.

• **Habitat Loss:** The conversion of **grasslands** into **agricultural land**, **renewable energy plants** (solar and wind farms), and **industrial areas** has fragmented their habitat.

• **Predation:** Eggs laid on the ground are highly vulnerable to **feral dogs**, **pigs**, and **crows**.

• **Conservation Efforts:**

• **Project Great Indian Bustard:** Initiated by the **Rajasthan Government** to protect the breeding grounds and improve the habitat.

• **Conservation Breeding:** A **breeding center** has been established in **Sam**, **Jaisalmer**, as a collaborative effort between the **Wildlife Institute of India (WII)** and the **Rajasthan Forest Department** to raise a captive population for future reintroduction.

• **Legal Intervention:** The **Supreme Court of India** has passed orders to convert **overhead power lines** to **underground cables** in critical GIB habitats to prevent fatalities.

**Important Points__**

• The **Great Indian Bustard** is the **State Bird of Rajasthan**, where it is locally known as **Godawan**.

• It was once widely distributed across the **Deccan Plateau** and the **Indo-Gangetic plains**, but its range has shrunk by over **90 percent** in the last few decades.

• The **Desert National Park** (DNP) remains the only place in the world where a **breeding population** of GIB exists in the wild.
</ul

question:
Consider the following statements about India's Biosphere Reserves:
1. All biosphere reserves are notified as UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
2. Gulf of Mannar and Great Nicobar are included in the World Network of Biosphere Reserves.
3. Biosphere reserves often include core, buffer, and transition zones.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Only 2 and 3 are correct**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Biosphere Reserves** are designated by the **national government** and must meet a minimal set of criteria to be included in the **World Network of Biosphere Reserves (WNBR)** under **UNESCO’s Man and the Biosphere (MAB) Programme**. While some **Biosphere Reserves** like the **Sundarbans** or **Nanda Devi** are also **UNESCO World Heritage Sites**, these are two separate programs with different legal frameworks and objectives. Not every biosphere reserve is a **World Heritage Site**. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• The **World Network of Biosphere Reserves (WNBR)** is a global network of sites that excel in biodiversity conservation and sustainable development. In **India**, out of **18** notified biosphere reserves, **12** are part of the **WNBR**. Both the **Gulf of Mannar** (located in **Tamil Nadu**) and the **Great Nicobar** (located in the **Andaman and Nicobar Islands**) are included in this prestigious international list. ***Hence, statement 2 is correct.***
 
• A **Biosphere Reserve** is structured into three specific zones to manage conservation and human activity effectively. The **Core Area** is a strictly protected ecosystem that contributes to the conservation of landscapes, ecosystems, and species. The **Buffer Zone** surrounds the core and is used for activities compatible with sound ecological practices, such as **environmental education** and **research**. The **Transition Area** is the outermost part where **sustainable development** practices and human settlements are permitted. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***

**Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Biosphere Reserves in India:**
 
 
• There are currently **18** notified **Biosphere Reserves** in **India**, established to protect larger areas of natural habitat than a typical **National Park** or **Animal Sanctuary**.
 
• The **Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve**, established in **1986**, was the first biosphere reserve in **India**. It spans across the states of **Tamil Nadu**, **Karnataka**, and **Kerala**.
 
• The **Panna Biosphere Reserve** in **Madhya Pradesh** became the **12th** Indian reserve to be included in the **UNESCO WNBR** in **2020**.
 
• The **Gulf of Kachchh** in **Gujarat** is the **largest** biosphere reserve in **India** by area, while **Dibru-Saikhowa** in **Assam** is considered one of the **smallest**.
 
 
 
• **UNESCO Man and the Biosphere (MAB) Programme:**
 
 
• Launched in **1971**, the **MAB Programme** is an intergovernmental scientific program that aims to establish a scientific basis for the improvement of relationships between people and their environments.
 
• It promotes innovative approaches to **economic development** that are socially and culturally appropriate and environmentally sustainable.
 
 

**Important Points__**

 
• **Functions of Biosphere Reserves:**
 
 
• **Conservation:** To ensure the conservation of **landscapes**, **ecosystems**, **species**, and **genetic variation**.
 
• **Development:** To foster **economic** and **human development** which is socio-culturally and ecologically sustainable.
 
• **Logistic Support:** To provide support for **research**, **monitoring**, **education**, and **information exchange** related to local, national, and global issues of conservation and development.
 
 
 
• **Zoning Details:**
 
 
• The **Core Zone** is often a **National Park** or a **Sanctuary** protected under the **Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972**. It is kept free from **human interference**.
 
• In the **Buffer Zone**, limited **tourism**, **grazing**, and **fishing** might be allowed to reduce the pressure on the core area.
 
• The **Transition Zone** is the area of **cooperation** where conservation goals and sustainable development are balanced with the help of **local communities**.

• The primary objective of this scheme is to promote the **conservation** and **optimal use of wetlands**, specifically focusing on the **75 Ramsar sites** identified in India at the time of its launch.

• India has significantly increased its number of **Ramsar sites** in recent years, reaching a total of **85 sites** as of 2024, the highest in South Asia.

• The **Amrit Dharohar** scheme works in synergy with other environmental programs like **MISHTI** (Mangrove Initiative for Shoreline Habitats & Tangible Incomes), which focuses on mangrove plantation along the coastline.

question:
Read the following statements regarding the Chipko Movement:

Statement 1: The Chipko Movement originated in the 18th century by the Bishnoi community in Rajasthan.

Statement 2: The 2023 celebrations marked 50 years since its modern revival in Chamoli, Uttarakhand.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Both statements 1 and 2 are correct**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Statement 1:** The **Chipko Movement originated in the 18th century** by the **Bishnoi community in Rajasthan**. This is correct. It was a precursor to environmental conservation movements and is often credited for its success in protecting trees. In 1730, under the leadership of **Amrita Devi**, the Bishnoi community sacrificed their lives to protect Khejri trees from being cut down by royal orders.
 
• **Statement 2:** The **modern revival of the Chipko Movement in Chamoli, Uttarakhand**, began in 1973. **The 2023 celebrations** marked **50 years** since this revival. This statement is also correct. The movement gained momentum when villagers, led by **Sunderlal Bahuguna**, hugged trees to prevent deforestation by contractors in the Himalayan region.
 
• The **Chipko Movement** is a milestone in India’s environmental activism history and has inspired countless other conservation efforts globally. *Hence, both statements are correct.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **18th Century Origin of Chipko Movement:**

 
 
• The Bishnoi community of Rajasthan initiated the first known tree-hugging movement to protect the environment. Amrita Devi and more than 300 Bishnois sacrificed their lives in 1730 to protect Khejri trees.
 
• The Bishnoi practice of preserving flora and fauna was rooted in their religious beliefs, emphasizing harmony with nature.
 
 
 
• **Modern Chipko Movement (1973):**
 
 
• The modern Chipko Movement began in the **Chamoli district of Uttarakhand** when villagers opposed commercial deforestation in the Himalayas.
 
• **Leaders:** Prominent leaders like **Sunderlal Bahuguna**, **Chandi Prasad Bhatt**, and **Gaura Devi** played key roles in organizing protests.
 
• The movement's slogan, **“Ecology is permanent economy,”** highlighted the importance of sustainable development.
 
 
 
• **Impact and Legacy:**
 
 
• The Chipko Movement led to a 15-year ban on cutting trees in the Himalayan forests by the Indian government.
 
• It inspired environmental movements worldwide, including the **Appiko Movement in Karnataka**.
 
• The movement emphasized the role of **women** in environmental conservation, as they were often at the forefront of protests.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Amrita Devi’s Sacrifice:** Her famous quote, **"If a tree is saved even at the cost of one's head, it is worth it,"** symbolizes the Bishnoi commitment to environmental conservation.
 
• **Role of Women:** Women played a critical role in the Chipko Movement, as they were directly affected by deforestation due to their reliance on forests for fuel, fodder, and water.
 
• **Global Recognition:** The Chipko Movement has been recognized as a pioneering environmental conservation effort and is often cited in global forums discussing climate change and sustainable development.

__
 
• The** gradual thinning of the Earth's ozone layer** in the upper atmosphere caused by the** discharge of chemical compounds** containing gaseous **chlorine or bromine** from industry and other human activities is referred to as **ozone depletion.**
 
• The thinning is mainly noticeable **over Antarctica** and in the **polar regions.**
 
• Depletion raises the **quantity of ultraviolet (UV) radiation** reaching the Earth's surface, raising the risk of **skin cancer, cataracts, and genetic and immune system damage.**
 
• The **Montreal Protocol **was the first of several international agreements to prohibit the production and use of **ozone-depleting chemicals**, and it was ratified in **1987.**

• **Heart stroke:**

 
 
• When** blood supply **to the heart is** obstructed**, the heart muscle is severely damaged, resulting in a** heart attack.**
 
• **Coronary artery disease**, which happens when** plaque builds up** in the arteries, is the leading cause of heart attacks.
 
• Over time, the plaque restricts blood flow, forcing the heart to work harder – and potentially leading to **damaged or failing heart muscles.**
 
 
 
• **Brain stroke:**
 
 
• A stroke occurs when the **blood flow** to any area of the brain is **cut off**. It's also known as a** brain stroke.**
 
• If blood supply to the brain is interrupted for more than a few seconds and the brain is** deprived of oxygen and blood**, **brain cells die **and the abilities regulated by that portion of the brain are lost.
 
 
 
• **Tuberculosis:**
 
 
• Tuberculosis (TB) is a potentially **fatal infectious illness** affecting mostly the **lungs.**
 
• Tuberculosis bacteria are communicated from person to person via **minute droplets **discharged into the air by **coughs and sneezes.**

2. India's per capita emissions are higher than the global average.
3. The report ranks India among top 10 countries in Environmental Performance Index.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Only 1**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Energy sector** is the largest contributor to India's **Greenhouse Gas (GHG)** emissions, accounting for approximately **75%** of the total emissions due to the nation's high dependence on **coal** for electricity and the growth of the **transportation** sector. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• India's **per capita emissions** are significantly lower than the **global average**; while the global average stands at approximately **6.3 tonnes of CO2 equivalent (tCO2e)**, India's average is only about **2.4 tCO2e**, reflecting a vast disparity in consumption patterns compared to developed nations. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• The **Environmental Performance Index (EPI)**, which measures various sustainability indicators, has historically ranked India at the bottom of the table (e.g., **180th** out of 180 countries in the **2022 report**), primarily due to poor **air quality** and high **carbon growth rates**. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***

 **Additional Information__**

 
• **State of India's Environment Report 2024**:
 
 
• This comprehensive report is published annually by the **Centre for Science and Environment (CSE)** and the magazine **Down To Earth**.
 
• It provides data-driven insights into **climate change**, **biodiversity loss**, **urbanization**, **water management**, and **public health** within the Indian context.
 
 
 
• **Environmental Indices and Rankings**:
 
 
• While India ranks poorly in the **EPI**, it consistently ranks among the top performers in the **Climate Change Performance Index (CCPI)**, often placing in the top 10 (ranked **7th** in **CCPI 2024**) due to its ambitious **Renewable Energy** targets and low **per capita emissions**.
 
• The **Energy sector** breakdown includes **Electricity generation** (the largest sub-component), followed by **Manufacturing**, **Construction**, and **Transport**.
 
• Other significant emission sources in India include the **Agriculture sector** (methane from livestock and rice cultivation) and **Industrial Processes and Product Use (IPPU)**.

• **UNESCO designated the Sundarbans Biosphere Reserve as a World Heritage Site** in **1987**, recognizing its ecological significance and the role it plays in supporting biodiversity.
 
• It is home to the **Royal Bengal Tiger**, along with other species such as estuarine crocodiles, Indian python, and spotted deer. The mangroves also serve as a breeding ground for diverse fish species and aquatic life. *Hence, it is globally significant for biodiversity conservation.*
 
• The Sundarbans Biosphere Reserve plays a crucial role in regulating the climatic conditions of the region and mitigating the effects of **climate change** and rising sea levels.

• **Biosphere Reserves in India:**

• They play a significant role in **conservation, research, and sustainable development** of ecosystems and communities.

question: Which Indian satellite provides high-resolution images for monitoring agriculture, forestry, and coastal resources?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Cartosat-3** is a third-generation agile satellite with very high-resolution imaging capabilities, designed to meet the increasing demands for **large-scale mapping**, **urban planning**, and **infrastructure development**. It is specifically optimized for monitoring **agriculture, forestry, and coastal resources**. *Hence, the correct answer is **Cartosat-3**.*
 
• Launched on **November 27, 2019**, by the **Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)**, it was carried by the **PSLV-C47** rocket from the **Satish Dhawan Space Centre** in **Sriharikota**, **Andhra Pradesh**.
 
• The satellite boasts a **Panchromatic resolution** of **0.25 meters**, which was the highest for any civilian satellite at its launch, and a **Multispectral resolution** of **1.13 meters**.
 
• **RISAT-2** (Radar Imaging Satellite-2) was launched in **2009** and uses **Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR)** technology. It is primarily used for **defense surveillance** and disaster management as it can provide images in all weather conditions, including through clouds and at night. *Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.*
 
• **GSAT-6** is a **multimedia communication satellite** launched in **2015**. It features a large **6-meter S-band unfurlable antenna** and is used for **strategic communication** and mobile satellite services. *Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.*
 
• **INSAT-4B** was launched in **2007** as part of the **INSAT-4** series. It is a **communication satellite** equipped with **Ku-band** and **C-band** transponders, primarily serving **Direct-to-Home (DTH)** television and broadcasting needs. *Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• The **Cartosat series** is a significant part of the **Indian Remote Sensing (IRS)** satellite program. These satellites are placed in **Sun-synchronous polar orbits** to ensure consistent lighting conditions for imaging.
 
• **Remote Sensing** technology in India is used for diverse applications such as **groundwater prospecting**, **crop acreage estimation**, **flood mapping**, and **potential fishing zone (PFZ)** identification.
 
• The **National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC)**, located in **Hyderabad**, is responsible for the acquisition, processing, and distribution of data from these satellites.
 
• **ISRO**, established on **August 15, 1969**, is the primary space agency of India, headquartered in **Bengaluru**. It operates under the **Department of Space**.
 
• The **Bhuvan** geoportal is an **ISRO** initiative that provides 2D and 3D visualization of the **Indian terrain** using high-resolution data from the **Cartosat** and **Resourcesat** series.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Cartosat-3** has a mission life of **5 years** and carries advanced sensors that operate in the **visible and near-infrared** regions of the electromagnetic spectrum.
 
• The **PSLV (Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle)** is known as the **Workhorse of ISRO** due to its high success rate in launching remote sensing satellites into polar orbits.
 
• During the **PSLV-C47** mission, **Cartosat-3** was launched along with **13 commercial nanosatellites** from the **United States of America**, highlighting India's growing role in the **global space market**.
 
• The data provided by **Cartosat-3** is crucial for **cadastral mapping**, which involves the detailed recording of property boundaries and land ownership for **governance** and **taxation**.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Polaris Dawn Mission and Van Allen Radiation Belts:**1. The Van Allen Belts consist of charged particles originating exclusively from the Sun.
2. The Polaris Dawn Mission studied the biological effects of space radiation by traveling through high-radiation zones around Earth.
3. Spacecraft passing through the Van Allen Belts must limit their transit time to reduce radiation exposure.
Which of the above statements is/are correct**?
solution:
The correct answer is __**2 and 3 only**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Statement 1 is incorrect:** The **Van Allen Radiation Belts** are two donut-shaped regions of energetic charged particles (protons and electrons) trapped by Earth's magnetic field. While a significant portion of these particles originates from the **Solar Wind** (the Sun), they also come from **Cosmic Rays** originating from outside the solar system. Therefore, they do not originate exclusively from the Sun.

• **Statement 2 is correct:** The **Polaris Dawn Mission**, a private spaceflight mission operated by **SpaceX**, was specifically designed to reach a high-altitude orbit (with an apogee of approximately 1,400 kilometers). This trajectory allowed the crew to pass through portions of the **Van Allen belts** to conduct research on the **biological effects of space radiation** on the human body, which is crucial for future long-duration missions to the Moon and Mars.

• **Statement 3 is correct:** Due to the high intensity of ionizing radiation within the **Van Allen Belts**, spacecraft and their crews are at risk of radiation sickness and electronic failure. To mitigate these risks, mission planners ensure that spacecraft pass through these zones as **quickly as possible** to minimize the total **cumulative radiation dose**.

**Additional Information__**

• The **Polaris Dawn** mission featured the first-ever **commercial spacewalk** (Extravehicular Activity or EVA) conducted by private citizens.

• The mission utilized the **SpaceX Crew Dragon** spacecraft and reached the highest Earth orbit for a crewed mission since the **Apollo program**.

• The **Van Allen belts** were discovered in 1958 by **James Van Allen** using data from the **Explorer 1** satellite, which was the first U.S. satellite.

• The **Inner Belt** mostly contains high-energy protons, while the **Outer Belt** is primarily composed of high-energy electrons.
</ul

question: One of the key objectives of India's Venus Orbiter Mission (VOM) is to study the ________ and surface topography of Venus.

The correct answer is __**airglow and atmospheric dust**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Venus Orbiter Mission (VOM)**, colloquially known as **Shukrayaan-1**, was officially approved by the **Union Cabinet** of India, chaired by Prime Minister **Narendra Modi**, on **September 18, 2024**.
 
• One of the primary scientific objectives of the mission is to study the **Venusian atmosphere**, specifically focusing on the **airglow** and **atmospheric dust**. This study helps in understanding the chemical processes and the dynamics of the **upper atmosphere** of the planet.
 
• The mission also aims to investigate the **surface topography** and **stratigraphy** of Venus using **high-resolution synthetic aperture radar (SAR)**. This will allow scientists to see through the thick cloud cover that permanently shrouds the planet. ***Hence, the statement regarding airglow and atmospheric dust is correct.***
 
• The **Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)** is the lead agency responsible for the development and execution of the **Venus Orbiter Mission**. The mission is scheduled for a launch window in **March 2028**, taking advantage of the planetary alignment that occurs roughly every **19 months**.
 
• The total approved budget for the **Venus Orbiter Mission** is approximately **₹1,236 crore**, which includes the cost of the spacecraft, payloads, and the launch vehicle.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Venus (The Planet):**
 
 
• **Venus** is often called **Earth’s Twin** due to its similar size and density, but it has a vastly different environment. It is the **hottest planet** in the solar system, with surface temperatures reaching **467°C (872°F)**.
 
• The atmosphere of **Venus** consists of **96.5% Carbon Dioxide** and **3.5% Nitrogen**, leading to a runaway **greenhouse effect**. The atmospheric pressure at the surface is **92 times** that of Earth.
 
 
 
• **VOM Payload and Technology:**
 
 
• The mission will carry several scientific instruments, including **Spectrometers** and **Radars**. These will measure **Solar Wind interactions** with the Venusian **ionosphere** and examine the **shallow subsurface** features.
 
• The mission will use the **LVM3 (Launch Vehicle Mark-3)**, India's most powerful rocket, to propel the orbiter into space.
 
 
 
• **Planetary Orbit:**
 
 
• **Venus** exhibits **retrograde rotation**, meaning it rotates on its axis in the opposite direction to most planets in the solar system, including Earth. A day on **Venus** (one rotation) is longer than its year (one revolution around the **Sun**).
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Scientific Significance:** By studying **airglow and atmospheric dust**, **ISRO** aims to find clues about why **Venus** evolved so differently from Earth, despite having a similar origin. The study of **dust particles** in the atmosphere provides insights into the **volcanic activity** and **meteoritic impacts** on the planet.
 
• **International Context:** **India** joins a select group of nations, including the **USA (NASA)**, **Europe (ESA)**, and **Russia (Roscosmos)**, that have successfully sent or planned missions to **Venus**.
 
• **Future Outlook:** The data collected by **VOM** will contribute to global scientific knowledge about **exoplanets** and the evolution of **planetary atmospheres**, which is critical for understanding climate change on Earth.

49:T

question: The Bharatiya Antariksh Station (BAS), India's planned space station, is proposed to orbit at what approximate altitude above the Earth's surface ?
solution:
The correct answer is __**400-450 km**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The Bharatiya Antariksh Station (BAS):**

 
 
• The **Bharatiya Antariksh Station** (BAS) is a proposed space station by **India**, under the guidance of the **Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO).**
 
• It aims to serve as a platform for **scientific research, space exploration, and technological experiments**.
 
 
 
• **Proposed Altitude:**
 
 
• The BAS is planned to orbit the Earth at an approximate altitude of **400-450 km**, which is within the **Low Earth Orbit (LEO).**
 
• This altitude is optimal for **human spaceflight missions** and scientific experiments due to **easy accessibility and reduced radiation exposure** compared to higher altitudes.
 
 
 
• **Low Earth Orbit (LEO):**
 
 
• LEO typically ranges from an altitude of **160 km to 1,000 km** above the Earth’s surface.
 
• It is widely used for **satellites, space stations, and human spaceflight missions** due to its proximity to the Earth's surface.
 
 
 
• **ISRO's Vision:**
 
 
• The development of BAS aligns with ISRO's vision of **strengthening India's space capabilities** and achieving **self-reliance in space exploration.**
 
• It is expected to be a significant step forward after the **Gaganyaan mission**, India’s first human spaceflight program.
 
 

**Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Features of Low Earth Orbit (LEO):**

 
 
• LEO is preferred for space stations like the **International Space Station (ISS)** due to its **moderate orbital speed** and **low energy requirements** for launching payloads.
 
• Satellites in LEO are used for **Earth observation, communication, and research**.
 
• The orbital period of LEO satellites is approximately **90 minutes to 2 hours**.
 
 
 
• **Space Stations Around the World:**
 
 
• The most notable space station currently in orbit is the **International Space Station (ISS)**, orbiting at an altitude of around **408 km**.
 
• China has developed its own space station, **Tiangong**, which also orbits within LEO.
 
• India’s BAS will add to the growing list of **national space stations**, showcasing its advancements in space technology.
 
 
 
• **Gaganyaan Mission:**
 
 
• India’s **Gaganyaan mission**, planned for launch in the near future, will be the country’s first crewed spaceflight mission.
 
• It is a precursor to the establishment of the **Bharatiya Antariksh Station**, as it will test technologies critical for human space exploration.
 
 

**Important Points__**

 
• **Altitude Comparison:**

 
 
• **200-250 km:** This is a lower range of LEO, but it is not ideal for long-term space station missions due to **higher atmospheric drag**.
 
• **400-450 km:** This range is suitable for stable orbits and long-term missions, as planned for BAS. *Correct answer.*
 
• **600-650 km:** Higher altitudes face increased **radiation exposure**, making it less suitable for human habitation.
 
• **850-900 km:** This range is used for specialized satellites, not for space stations, due to high energy requirements for reaching and maintaining the orbit.
 
 
 
• **Significance of BAS:**
 
 
• It will enable **advanced scientific research**, including microgravity experiments and space technology testing.
 
• BAS will place India among the few nations capable of operating their own **human spaceflight programs**.

question: The ISRO satellite series, used mainly for meteorological and weather forecasting purposes, is:
solution:
The correct answer is __**INSAT**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• **INSAT (Indian National Satellite System)** is a series of multipurpose geostationary satellites launched by **ISRO** to satisfy the telecommunications, broadcasting, **meteorology**, and search and rescue needs of **India**. It is the primary satellite series used for **weather forecasting** and monitoring atmospheric conditions. ***Hence, option 1 is correct.***

• The **INSAT** system was established in **1983** with the commissioning of **INSAT-1B**. It is a joint venture of the **Department of Space (DOS)**, **Department of Telecommunications**, **India Meteorological Department (IMD)**, **All India Radio (AIR)**, and **Doordarshan**.

• Specific satellites like **INSAT-3D** and **INSAT-3DR** are currently operational and carry advanced **multi-spectral imagers** and **sounders**. These instruments provide vertical profiles of temperature and humidity, which are crucial for accurate **weather forecasting** and **cyclone tracking**.

• **RISAT (Radar Imaging Satellite)** is a series of **Indian remote sensing satellites** that use **Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR)** to provide all-weather surveillance. While it can see through clouds, its primary use is for **agriculture**, **forestry**, and **disaster management** imaging rather than general meteorological forecasting. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***

• **Cartosat** is a series of **Earth observation satellites** used specifically for **cartography** (mapping). They provide high-resolution images used for **urban planning**, **coastal land use**, and **Land Information Systems (LIS)**. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***

• **IRNSS (Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System)**, commercially known as **NavIC**, is an independent regional navigation satellite system designed to provide accurate position information services to users in **India**. It functions similarly to the **Global Positioning System (GPS)**. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**

__

• **ISRO (Indian Space Research Organisation)**: Founded by **Dr. Vikram Sarabhai** on **15 August 1969**, it is headquartered in **Bengaluru**. It is the primary agency in **India** for space research and planetary exploration.

• **Kalpana-1**: This was the first exclusive **meteorological satellite** launched by **ISRO** on **September 12, 2002**. Originally named **METSAT-1**, it was renamed in honor of the **Indian-American** astronaut **Kalpana Chawla**, who perished in the **Columbia Space Shuttle** disaster.

• **NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation)**: This system consists of a constellation of **7 satellites**. It provides two types of services: **Standard Positioning Service (SPS)** for civilian users and **Restricted Service (RS)** for authorized users like the **Indian Armed Forces**.

• **Remote Sensing**: **India** has one of the largest constellations of remote sensing satellites in operation today, including the **Resourcesat**, **Oceansat**, and **Scatsat** series, which help in monitoring **natural resources** and **oceanic winds**.

**Important Points__**

• The **India Meteorological Department (IMD)** utilizes data from the **INSAT** series at its **Meteorological Data Utilization Centre (MDUC)** located in **New Delhi**. This data is vital for issuing **early warnings** for **tsunamis**, **floods**, and **heavy rainfall**.

• **INSAT-3DR**, launched in **2016**, carries a **Data Relay Transponder (DRT)**. This component is used to receive **meteorological**, **hydrological**, and **oceanographic** data from remote and uninhabited locations through **Automatic Data Collection Platforms (ADCPs)**.

• The **GSAT** series is another important satellite family from **ISRO**, which focuses primarily on **digital audio**, **data**, and **video broadcasting**, complementing the communication capabilities of the **INSAT** series.
</ul

subject: GK
question: Where will India's Aditya-L1 mission be placed?

options.text: At the Sun-Earth L1 point in a halo orbit

solution:
The correct answer is __**At the Sun-Earth L1 point in a halo orbit**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Aditya-L1** mission is **India’s first dedicated space mission** to study the **Sun**. It is designed to be placed in a **halo orbit** around the **Lagrangian point 1 (L1)** of the **Sun-Earth system**.
 
• The **Sun-Earth L1 point** is located approximately **1.5 million kilometers** away from the **Earth**, which is about **1%** of the total distance between the **Earth** and the **Sun**.
 
• A satellite placed in the **halo orbit** around the **L1 point** has the major advantage of continuously viewing the **Sun** without any **occultation** or **eclipses**. This allows for uninterrupted monitoring of **solar activities** and their impact on **space weather**.
 
• The **Lagrange points** are positions in space where the **gravitational forces** of a **two-body system** (like the Sun and Earth) produce enhanced regions of attraction and repulsion. These can be used by spacecraft to reduce **fuel consumption** needed to remain in position.
 
• Option 1 is incorrect because the **Sun-Earth L2 point** is located on the opposite side of the Earth from the Sun and is typically used for **space telescopes** like the **James Webb Space Telescope (JWST)** to observe the deep universe.
 
• Option 3 is incorrect because the **Earth-Moon L1 point** is located between the Earth and the Moon, which is not suitable for a mission dedicated to **solar observation**.
 
• Option 4 is incorrect because the **Mars-Sun L1 point** would be located near **Mars**, which is far beyond the scope of a mission intended to monitor the Sun from the vicinity of **Earth**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Launch Details:** The **Aditya-L1** spacecraft was successfully launched on **September 2, 2023**, by the **Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)** using the **PSLV-C57** launch vehicle from the **Satish Dhawan Space Centre** in **Sriharikota**.
 
• **Mission Payloads:** The spacecraft carries **seven scientific payloads**. These include the **Visible Emission Line Coronagraph (VELC)**, **Solar Ultraviolet Imaging Telescope (SUIT)**, **Solar Low Energy X-ray Spectrometer (SoLEXS)**, **High Energy L1 Orbiting X-ray Spectrometer (HEL1OS)**, **Aditya Solar wind Particle Experiment (ASPEX)**, **Plasma Analyser Package For Aditya (PAPA)**, and **Advanced Tri-axial High Resolution Digital Magnetometers**.
 
• **Scientific Objectives:** The mission aims to study the **solar corona** (the outermost layer), **photosphere**, and **chromosphere**. It also investigates **Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs)**, **solar flares**, and the **solar wind** to understand the dynamics of the **solar atmosphere** and **coronal heating**.
 
• **Mission Duration:** The mission has a planned life of approximately **5.2 years**, during which it will provide crucial data to predict **space weather** events that can affect **satellite communications** and **power grids** on Earth.
 
• **Lagrange Points:** There are five such points in the **Sun-Earth system**, labeled **L1 to L5**. **L1**, **L2**, and **L3** are unstable, while **L4** and **L5** are stable points.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Halo Orbit:** Unlike a simple circular orbit, a **halo orbit** is a three-dimensional, periodic orbit near the **L1 point**. It allows the spacecraft to stay out of the **Earth's shadow** and maintain a constant line of sight with both the **Sun** and **Earth** ground stations.
 
• **Distance Comparison:** The distance to **L1** (**1.5 million km**) is much greater than the distance to the **International Space Station (ISS)**, which orbits at about **400 km**, but it is much less than the distance to the **Sun** (about **150 million km**).
 
• **Global Context:** With the success of **Aditya-L1**, **India** joins a select group of nations and agencies, such as **NASA** and the **ESA**, that have placed observatories at the **L1 point** for solar research, following missions like **SOHO (Solar and Heliospheric Observatory)**.

question: India recently became the fourth country to successfully demonstrate space docking. Which of the following countries had achieved this feat before India?
solution:
The correct answer is __**USA, Russia, China**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• **India** has achieved a major milestone in its space exploration journey by becoming the **fourth country** in the world to successfully demonstrate **space docking** technology.

• **Space docking** is a complex maneuver where two independently launched spacecraft are joined together in orbit to form a single unit. This is essential for transferring crew, fuel, or cargo.

• Before India, only the **United States (USA)**, **Russia** (formerly the Soviet Union), and **China** had mastered this critical technology.

• The **Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)** conducted this demonstration through the **SPADEX** (Space Docking Experiment) mission, which involved two satellites (a Chaser and a Target) meeting and joining in space.

• This capability is a prerequisite for India's future ambitious projects, including the **Bharatiya Antariksh Station** (India's own space station) and the **Gaganyaan** mission's advanced phases.

**Additional Information__**

• The first-ever manual space docking was performed by the **USA** in **1966** during the **Gemini 8** mission, piloted by **Neil Armstrong** and **David Scott**.

• The **Soviet Union** achieved the first fully automated docking in **1967** using the **Cosmos 186** and **Cosmos 188** spacecraft.

• **China** became the third nation to achieve independent docking capability in **2011** with the **Shenzhou 8** and **Tiangong-1** mission.

• Mastering docking technology allows for **satellite servicing**, **refueling in orbit**, and **deep-space exploration** missions where multiple components must be assembled in space.

• India aims to establish its own space station by the year **2035** and land an Indian on the **Moon** by **2040**.
</ul

question:
Instructions: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully. Choose the correct option:
Assertion (A): India launched the South Asian Satellite (SAS) in 2017 for use by SAARC nations.
Reason (R): The SAS was launched from the Sriharikota spaceport, and its terminals were installed in all SAARC countries.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

solution:
The correct answer is __**A is true, but R is false**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Assertion (A)** states that **India** launched the **South Asian Satellite (SAS)** in **2017** for use by **SAARC** nations. This statement is **correct**. The satellite, also known as **GSAT-9**, was launched on **May 5, 2017**, as a gift from **India** to its neighboring countries to bolster communication and regional cooperation.

• The **South Asian Satellite** was a brainchild of Prime Minister **Narendra Modi**, who proposed the idea during the **18th SAARC Summit** held in **Nepal** in **2014**. The project aimed to provide various communication applications to **South Asian** countries.

• **Reason (R)** states that the **SAS** was launched from the **Sriharikota** spaceport, and its terminals were installed in all **SAARC** countries. This statement is **incorrect**. While the satellite was indeed launched from the **Satish Dhawan Space Centre** in **Sriharikota** using the **GSLV-F09** rocket, it does not serve all **SAARC** nations.

• **Pakistan**, a key member of **SAARC**, decided to opt out of the project, claiming it had its own space program and technical capabilities. Consequently, the satellite benefits only seven out of the eight **SAARC** members: **India**, **Afghanistan**, **Bangladesh**, **Bhutan**, **Maldives**, **Nepal**, and **Sri Lanka**. Therefore, terminals were not installed in **Pakistan**. ***Hence, statement A is true, but statement R is false.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Technical Specifications:** The **GSAT-9** is a **Geostationary Communication Satellite** developed by the **Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)**. It weighs approximately **2,230 kg** and is equipped with **12 Ku-band transponders**.

• **Mission Life:** The satellite has an intended mission life of more than **12 years**. It is positioned at **48 degrees East** longitude in the geostationary orbit.

• **Applications:** The **South Asian Satellite** provides a wide range of services, including **Tele-education**, **Tele-medicine**, **Disaster Management Support**, **Broadcasting** (DTH), and **VSAT** (Very Small Aperture Terminal) connectivity for banking and government networks.

• **Regional Cooperation:** The project is a significant part of **India**'s **'Neighborhood First'** policy. By providing the satellite services free of charge to participating nations, **India** aimed to strengthen diplomatic ties and aid the socio-economic development of the **South Asian** region.

• **SAARC Overview:** The **South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC)** was established in **1985**. Its secretariat is located in **Kathmandu, Nepal**. The member states include **Afghanistan**, **Bangladesh**, **Bhutan**, **India**, **Maldives**, **Nepal**, **Pakistan**, and **Sri Lanka**.

**Important Points__**

• **Cost of Project:** The total cost of the **South Asian Satellite** project was approximately **₹235 crore** (around **USD 36 million**), which was entirely funded by the **Government of India**. The participating nations only had to bear the cost of ground station infrastructure and maintenance.

• **Launch Vehicle:** The **GSLV-F09** (Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle) used for this mission featured the indigenous **Cryogenic Upper Stage (CUS)**, marking another milestone for **ISRO**'s heavy-lift capabilities.

• **Ground Terminals:** **India** assisted participating countries like **Bhutan** and **Afghanistan** in setting up the necessary ground stations and terminals to receive and transmit data via the **GSAT-9** satellite.

• **Strategic Importance:** Beyond its functional uses, the satellite serves as a strategic tool for **India** to counter the growing influence of other global powers in the **Indian Ocean** and **South Asian** region by providing essential space-based infrastructure.

question:
Match the ISRO mission with its primary objective:
1. Chandrayaan-2
2. Aditya-L1
3. Mangalyaan
solution:
The correct answer is __**1-Lunar Orbiter, 2-Sun Study, 3-Mars Orbit**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Chandrayaan-2**:
 
 
• Launched on **July 22, 2019**, from the **Satish Dhawan Space Centre**, this mission was India's second lunar exploration.
 
• It consisted of a **Lunar Orbiter**, the **Vikram** lander, and the **Pragyan** rover. While the lander failed to make a soft landing, the **Orbiter** remains operational in **Lunar Orbit**, collecting data on the Moon's topography and mineralogy. ***Hence, 1 matches with Lunar Orbiter.***
 
 
 
• **Aditya-L1**:
 
 
• This is **India's first solar mission**, launched on **September 2, 2023**, using the **PSLV-C57** rocket.
 
• The spacecraft is placed in a halo orbit around the **Lagrange point 1 (L1)** of the Sun-Earth system. Its primary objective is **Sun Study**, specifically observing the **Solar Corona**, **Chromosphere**, and solar winds. ***Hence, 2 matches with Sun Study.***
 
 
 
• **Mangalyaan (Mars Orbiter Mission)**:
 
 
• Launched on **November 5, 2013**, by **ISRO**, it was India's first interplanetary mission.
 
• The spacecraft successfully entered **Mars Orbit** on **September 24, 2014**, making India the **first nation** to reach Mars on its **maiden attempt**. The mission studied the Martian atmosphere and surface. ***Hence, 3 matches with Mars Orbit.***
 
 
 
• ***Hence, the correct match is A - 2, B - 1, C - 4, D - 3 is not applicable here as per the specific options, but the direct pairing is 1-Lunar Orbiter, 2-Sun Study, 3-Mars Orbit.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **ISRO (Indian Space Research Organisation)**:
 
 
• The national space agency of **India**, headquartered in **Bengaluru**. It was founded by **Dr. Vikram Sarabhai** on **August 15, 1969**.
 
• **ISRO** is under the **Department of Space**, which is directly overseen by the **Prime Minister of India**.
 
 
 
• **Chandrayaan-3**:
 
 
• Launched in **July 2023**, this mission successfully achieved a soft landing on the **Lunar South Pole** on **August 23, 2023**.
 
• With this, India became the **fourth country** to soft-land on the Moon and the **first** to reach the **South Polar region**.
 
 
 
• **Space Science Terminologies**:
 
 
• **Lagrange Point (L1)**: A location in space where the gravitational forces of two large bodies (like the **Sun** and **Earth**) produce enhanced regions of attraction and repulsion, allowing a spacecraft to stay in a **fixed position** relative to them.
 
• **Orbiter**: A spacecraft designed to go into orbit around a celestial body without landing on its surface.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Launch Vehicles**:
 
 
• **PSLV (Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle)**: Known as the **"Workhorse of ISRO"**, it was used for **Mangalyaan** and **Aditya-L1**.
 
• **LVM3 (Launch Vehicle Mark-III)**: Previously known as **GSLV Mk-III**, it is the heaviest rocket of **ISRO** used for the **Chandrayaan-2** and **Chandrayaan-3** missions.
 
 
 
• **Global Milestones**:
 
 
• India's **Mangalyaan** mission was one of the **cheapest** Mars missions in the world, costing approximately **$74 million**.

question: Which of the following is the CORRECT objective of ISRO's Gaganyaan mission scheduled for launch in 2025?
