• **Non-polar bonds do not have any type of net dipole moment** and are generally formed in compounds where there is a presence of symmetry. 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• In chemistry, a dipole refers to **the separation of charges within a molecule between two covalently bonded types of atoms or atoms that share an ionic bond**.
 
• The main difference between polar and dipolar molecules is **polar molecules have two opposite ends with opposite electrical charges, whereas dipolar molecules have only two poles**.

question: Identify the statement that is true for London forces.

options.text: These forces are always attractive, and the interaction energy is directly proportional to the sixth power of the distance between two interacting particles.
These forces are always attractive, and the interaction energy is inversely proportional to the second power of the distance between two interacting particles.
These forces are always attractive, and the interaction energy is inversely proportional to the sixth power of the distance between two interacting particles.

solution:
The correct answer is "__**These forces are always attractive, and the interaction energy is inversely proportional to the sixth power of the distance between two interacting particles".**__

• The attractive forces cause nonpolar substances to condense to liquids and to freeze into solids when the temperature is lowered sufficiently.
 
• **Larger** the molecules, **higher** is the magnitude of London forces because larger electron clouds are polarised. So, their magnitude depends on the polarisability of the particle.

• London forces are important only at short distances (~500pm) and their magnitude depends on the polarisability of the particle.
 
• The larger, the molecular size, the more the polarisability and more would be the strength of dispersion.
 
• Potential energy is negative when the forces are attractive in nature. Therefore, potential energy is inversely proportional to intermolecular force of attraction.

question: What remains constant during the melting process of a pure substance?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Temperature**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• During the melting process of a **pure substance**, the **Temperature** remains constant until the entire solid has transitioned into the liquid state. This constant temperature value is defined as the **melting point** of the substance.
 
• When heat is applied to a solid at its **melting point**, the energy is not used to increase the **average kinetic energy** of the molecules, which would normally result in a temperature rise. Instead, the energy is consumed to break the **intermolecular forces** and **chemical bonds** holding the solid lattice together.
 
• The heat absorbed by the substance during this phase change without a change in temperature is known as the **Latent Heat of Fusion**. For **water**, this value is approximately **334 Joules per gram** or **80 calories per gram** at **0 degrees Celsius**.
 
• Since **temperature** is a macroscopic measure of the **average kinetic energy** of particles, and this energy remains static during the phase transition (as the energy becomes **potential energy**), the thermometer reading does not change.
 
• The **purity** of a substance is often determined by how constant the temperature remains during melting; a **pure substance** has a **sharp melting point**, whereas a mixture melts over a **range of temperatures**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Mass**: In any physical or chemical change occurring in a closed system, the **Mass** of the substance remains constant due to the **Law of Conservation of Mass**. However, mass is a general property of matter and not a specific thermodynamic variable that characterizes the phase change of melting itself.
 
• **Volume**: Most substances experience a change in **Volume** during the melting process. Generally, substances expand upon melting (volume increases), but **water** is a notable exception; **ice** is less dense than **liquid water**, meaning the **volume decreases** when ice melts.
 
• **Pressure**: While **Pressure** is often kept constant during a laboratory experiment to measure a boiling or melting point, it is an **intensive variable** that can be manipulated externally. An increase in pressure typically raises the **melting point** of most solids, but for **water**, increasing the pressure actually lowers the melting point.
 
• **States of Matter**: Melting is one of the primary **phase transitions**. Other transitions include **freezing** (liquid to solid), **vaporization** (liquid to gas), **condensation** (gas to liquid), **sublimation** (solid to gas), and **deposition** (gas to solid).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Thermal Equilibrium**: During the melting process, the solid phase and the liquid phase of the **pure substance** coexist in a state of **thermal equilibrium**. As long as both phases are present, the system stays at the **equilibrium temperature**.
 
• **Kinetic Theory of Matter**: According to this theory, the internal energy of a substance consists of both **kinetic energy** and **potential energy**. During melting, all added heat goes into increasing the **potential energy** associated with the arrangement of molecules, leaving the **kinetic energy** (and thus the **temperature**) unchanged.
 
• **Standard Conditions**: The **Normal Melting Point** is defined as the temperature at which a substance melts at **1 atmosphere (101.325 kPa)** of pressure. For **pure water**, this is exactly **273.15 Kelvin** or **0 degrees Celsius**.
 
• **Impact of Impurities**: The presence of a solute or impurity in a **pure substance** causes **Melting Point Depression**. This is a **colligative property**, meaning the substance will begin to melt at a **lower temperature** than its standard pure state.

question: How is the molecular composition of water represented in chemical terms?
solution:
The correct answer is __**H₂O**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Water** is composed of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom, which is chemically represented as **H₂O**.
 
• The molecular composition of water is a result of covalent bonding, where the hydrogen atoms share electrons with the oxygen atom.
 
• The structure of the **H₂O molecule** is bent or angular due to the electron repulsion in the oxygen atom, forming a bond angle of approximately **104.5°**.
 
• Water is a universal solvent due to its **polar nature**. The oxygen atom has a partial negative charge, and the hydrogen atoms have a partial positive charge.
 
• This polarity allows water to dissolve many substances, making it essential for **biological and chemical processes.**
 
• The molecular formula of water is distinct from other compounds like **CO₂** (carbon dioxide), **O₂** (oxygen gas), or **NaCl** (sodium chloride).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Characteristics of Water (H₂O):**

 
 
• **Chemical Formula:** The formula **H₂O** indicates two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
 
• **Bond Type:** The bonds between hydrogen and oxygen in water are **covalent bonds.**
 
• **Polarity:** Water is a **polar molecule**, making it effective in dissolving ionic and polar substances.
 
• **Importance:** Water is vital for life, acting as a medium for **biochemical reactions** and a solvent for nutrients.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Other Options:**
 
 
• **CO₂:** Carbon dioxide is a linear molecule with one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms. It is a greenhouse gas and not related to water composition.
 
• **O₂:** Oxygen gas consists of two oxygen atoms bonded by a double bond. It is essential for respiration but does not represent water.
 
• **NaCl:** Sodium chloride is an ionic compound made of sodium and chloride ions, commonly known as table salt. It does not resemble the molecular formula of water.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Universal Solvent:** Water’s ability to dissolve a wide range of substances is due to its **polar nature**.
 
• **States of Water:** Water exists in three states: **solid (ice)**, **liquid (water)**, and **gas (water vapor).**
 
• **Applications:** Water is used in **agriculture, industry, hydration, sanitation**, and numerous other fields.
 
• **Research:** Studies on water’s molecular structure have been crucial in understanding its role in **climate change**, **ecosystem balance**, and **cellular processes.**

• **Food adulteration** refers to the process of adding or mixing something inferior, harmful, or unnecessary to food items, reducing their quality, safety, and nutritional value.
 
• Authorities like the **Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI)** monitor and regulate food safety standards to prevent adulteration.
 
• Consumers are advised to purchase spices and food products from reputable sources and check for certifications indicating quality and safety standards.

question: The property of metals by the virtue of which they can be beaten into thin sheets is called:
solution:
The correct answer is **__Malleability.__**

**__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **Key Points__****

__
 
• The property by virtue of which metals can be beaten into thin sheets is known as **malleability.**
 
• Metals are** malleable**.
 
• Malleability is a substance's ability to deform **under pressure**.
 
• Malleability is a property of **material** by which in can be beaten to form its thin sheets. **Most** of the **metals** are **malleable**.
 
• The **crystal structure** of **harder metals** such as **antimony** and **bismuth,** makes it more **difficult** to press **atom**s into **new positions** without breaking. This is because the rows of atoms in the metal don't line-up.
 
• [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3d1f12151210d9bf29e17a7d878f4bc153c313c27fd835dd48a8435c77ee63ab.png] 
 
• Example of **Malleable Metals** are bellow.
 
• **Gold.**
 
• **Silver.**
 
• **Iron.**
 
• **Copper.**
 
• **Tin.**

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] Additional Information__**

 
 

 **Conductivity.**
 
 
Conductivity is the measure of the ease at which an** electric charge** or **heat** can pass through a **material**.

 
SI unit - **ohm metre**

 
In SI base units - **kg⋅m3⋅s−3⋅A−2**

 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/5557bda26bd799be661cbb5c1ad314606fad80d12c6c1a454d18d244a8c23de4.png] 

 
 
 

 **Rancidity.**
 
 
Rancidity condition produced by **aerial oxidation** of unsaturated **fat** present in foods and other products marked by unpleasant **odour** or **flavour.**

 
When a **fatty** substance is exposed to **air** its unsaturated components are converted into **hydroperoxides**, which break down into volatile **aldehydes**, **esters**, **alcohols**, **ketones**, and **hydrocarbons**, some of which have disagreeable** odours.**

 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ad0ec9cd3dab6ac53b416800733f2812e8eec0b9741661cc15e2bc413c296a11.png] 

 
 
 

 **Ductility.**
 
 
Ductility is when a **solid material** stretches under **tensile strain**.

 
Brittle materials, such as **glass**, cannot accommodate concentrations of **stress** because they **lack ductility**, and therefore **fracture easily.**

 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/80a8133e70fde93ba49643f0b9675f4487148e85a13b2f5f74bba01b3b2de049.png]

subject: GK
question: How is the molecular weight of a fatty acid determined?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Saponification value**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The saponification value** denotes the quantity of milligrams of **potassium hydroxide (KOH) or sodium hydroxide (NaOH)** needed to saponify one gram of fat, given specific conditions.
 
• This value serves as a gauge of the average molecular weight, or chain length, of the fatty acids contained within the sample in the form of triglycerides.
 
• In essence, a higher saponification value indicates a lower average length of fatty acids and a lighter mean molecular weight of triglycerides, while a lower value suggests the opposite.
 
• In practical terms, fats or oils possessing a high saponification value, such as coconut and palm oil, are more favorable for soap making.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **The peroxide value (PV)** of an edible oil quantifies the degree of primary oxidation of unsaturated fats within the oil, primarily through the conversion of molecular oxygen into hydroperoxides and peroxides.
 
• **The acid value (AV)** is a numerical representation of the acidity level of a chemical substance, typically expressed in terms of the quantity of potassium hydroxide (KOH) required to neutralize the free acids present in one gram of the substance.
 
• **The iodine value (IV)** measures the mass of iodine in grams consumed by 100 grams of a chemical substance. It serves as an indicator of the degree of unsaturation or the number of double bonds present in the fatty acids comprising the substance, with higher values indicating greater unsaturation.

question: Which of the following forms metallic bonds in elemental stage?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Bismuth**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• ** Bismuth (Bi)**:

 
 
• Bismuth is a chemical element with the symbol **Bi** and **atomic number 83**.
 
• It is a **post-transition metal, radioactive**, and one of the **pnictogens** with chemical properties resembling its** lighter group 15 **siblings arsenic and antimony. 
 
• Bismuth is the most naturally** diamagnetic** element and has one of the** lowest values of thermal conductivity** among metals.
 
• Bismuth is a** brittle metal **with a** dark, silver-pink hue**, often with an** iridescent oxide tarnish **showing many colours from** yellow to blue**.
 
• Elemental bismuth is** denser in the liquid phase than the solid,** a characteristic it shares with** germanium, silicon, gallium, and water**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/6e114b44718a613f01932654c6c60c7bd331281d8b9b8c6820fe27e942e4fc78.png] 

 
• Bismuth

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• ** Metallic Bond**:

 
 
• Metallic bonding is a type of chemical bonding that arises from the **electrostatic attractive force between conduction electrons **and **positively charged metal ions**.
 
• It may be described as the sharing of** free electrons** among a structure of** positively charged ions (cations)**.
 
• Metallic bonds have a **high melting point**.
 
• Metallic bonding accounts for many physical properties of metals, such as **strength, ductility, thermal and electrical resistivity and conductivity, opacity, and lustre**.
 
 
 
• **Phosphorus (P)**:
 
 
• Phosphorus is a chemical element with the **symbol P** and** atomic number 15**.
 
• Elemental phosphorus exists in two major forms,** white phosphorus and red phosphorus**, but because it is highly reactive, phosphorus is never found as a free element on Earth.
 
• Phosphorus is an element essential to sustaining life largely through** phosphates**.
 
• Phosphates are a component of** DNA, RNA, ATP, and phospholipids**, complex compounds** fundamental to cells**.
 
• Elemental phosphorus was first isolated from **human urine, and bone ash** was an important early phosphate source.
 
• Phosphate mines contain fossils because phosphate is present in the** fossilized deposits of animal remains and excreta**.
 
• **Low phosphate** levels are an important limit to growth in some **aquatic **systems.
 
• The vast majority of phosphorus compounds mined are consumed as** fertilisers**.
 
• Phosphate is needed to replace the phosphorus that plants remove from the soil, and its annual demand is rising nearly twice as fast as the growth of the **human population**. 
 
 
 
• **Arsenic (As)**:
 
 
• Arsenic is a chemical element with the **symbol As** and** atomic number 33**.
 
• Arsenic is a **metalloid**. It has various **allotropes**.
 
• The primary use of arsenic is in **alloys of lead** (for example, in** car batteries and ammunition**).
 
• Arsenic is a common** n-type dopant** in **semiconductor electronic devices**.
 
• It is also a component of the** III-V compound semiconductor gallium arsenide**.
 
• Arsenic and its compounds, especially **trioxide**, are used in the production of** pesticides, treated wood products, herbicides, and insecticides**. 
 
• **Arsenic contamination of groundwater is a problem that affects millions of people across the world**.
 
 
 
• **Antimony (Sb)**:
 
 
• Antimony is a chemical element with the** symbol Sb **and **atomic number 51**.
 
• It is a** lustrous grey metalloid**.
 
• The largest applications for metallic antimony are in alloys with** lead and tin**, which have improved properties for **solders, bullets, and plain bearings.**

subject: GK
question: Which of the following atmospheric layers contains the ozone layer, vital for absorbing harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Stratosphere**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Stratosphere** is the second major layer of Earth's atmosphere, located above the **Troposphere** and below the **Mesosphere**.

• It contains the **Ozone Layer**, which is a region of high **Ozone (O3)** concentration that absorbs most of the sun's harmful **Ultraviolet (UV) radiation**.

• Without the ozone layer in the stratosphere, the intense UV rays would reach the Earth's surface, leading to increased rates of **skin cancer**, **cataracts**, and damage to terrestrial and marine ecosystems.

• The **Troposphere** is the lowest layer where all **weather phenomena** occur, but it contains very little ozone compared to the stratosphere.

• The **Mesosphere** is the layer above the stratosphere where temperatures decrease with altitude and most **meteors** burn up upon entry.

• The **Thermosphere** is the layer above the mesosphere characterized by high temperatures and the presence of the **Ionosphere**, which aids in **radio communication**.

**Additional Information__**

• The **Stratosphere** extends from approximately 10 km to 50 km above the Earth's surface.

• The **Montreal Protocol**, signed in 1987, is a global agreement to phase out the production of **Ozone-Depleting Substances (ODS)** like **Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs)**.

• Temperature in the stratosphere actually **increases** with altitude because the ozone layer absorbs UV radiation and converts it into heat.

• The boundary between the troposphere and the stratosphere is known as the **Tropopause**.

• Commercial **jet aircraft** often fly in the lower stratosphere to avoid the turbulence found in the troposphere.
</ul

• The **exosphere** is the **outermost layer** of the atmosphere, which gradually fades into the vacuum of **outer space**.

This is often phrased as "For every **action**, there is an equal and opposite **reaction**." ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***
 
• **Force = mass × acceleration (F = ma)** is the mathematical representation of **Newton's Second Law of Motion**. It describes how the velocity of an object changes when it is subjected to an external **force**. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• The statement that **Energy cannot be created or destroyed**, only transformed from one form to another, is known as the **Law of Conservation of Energy**. This is a fundamental principle of **physics** and **thermodynamics**, not a law of motion. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• The observation that **acceleration is inversely proportional to mass** is a specific characteristic of **Newton's Second Law** ($a = F/m$). It implies that for a constant **force**, a larger **mass** will experience less **acceleration**. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***
 
• The **action and reaction forces** always act on **different bodies**. This is why they do not cancel each other out, even though they are equal in **magnitude** and opposite in **direction**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Historical Context:** **Sir Isaac Newton** first presented the three laws of motion in his work titled **"Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica,"** which was published in the year **1687**. These laws laid the foundation for **classical mechanics**.
 
• **Application in Rocketry:** One of the most famous applications of the **Third Law** is **rocket propulsion**. The rocket engine expels **exhaust gases** downward (action), and in response, the gases exert an equal and opposite upward **force** (thrust) on the rocket (reaction), allowing it to lift off.
 
• **Recoil of a Gun:** When a **bullet** is fired from a **gun**, the gun exerts a forward **force** on the bullet. According to **Newton’s Third Law**, the bullet exerts an equal and opposite backward **force** on the gun, which is felt by the shooter as **recoil**.
 
• **Walking and Swimming:** When a person **walks**, they push the **ground** backward with their feet (action), and the ground pushes the person forward (reaction). Similarly, in **swimming**, a swimmer pushes the **water** backward to move their **body** forward.
 
• **Nature of Forces:** The **action-reaction pair** consists of two **forces** that are of the **same nature**. For instance, if the action is a **gravitational force**, the reaction must also be a **gravitational force**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Simultaneity:** The **action** and **reaction** forces occur **simultaneously**. There is no **time lag** between the action and the reaction.
 
• **Conservation of Momentum:** **Newton's Third Law** is intrinsically linked to the **Law of Conservation of Momentum**. In an isolated system, the total **momentum** remains constant because internal **action-reaction** pairs cancel each other out within the system's total momentum calculation.
 
• **Vector Quantity:** Since **force** is a **vector quantity**, the **direction** is crucial. The mathematical form is often written as **$F_{AB} = -F_{BA}$**, where the **negative sign** indicates the opposite direction.
 
• **Universal Applicability:** These laws are applicable to all objects in the **macroscopic world** moving at speeds significantly lower than the **speed of light** (**300,000 km/s**). For subatomic particles or objects moving near the speed of light, **quantum mechanics** and **relativity** are used.

question: Why do seasons change throughout the year on Earth?

options.text: The tilt of the Earth's axis
The Earth's distance from the Sun

solution:
The correct answer is __**The tilt of the Earth's axis**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• The change in seasons is primarily caused by the **axial tilt** of the Earth, which is approximately **23.5 degrees** relative to its orbital plane (the ecliptic).

• As the Earth performs its **annual revolution** around the Sun, this fixed tilt causes different hemispheres to be angled toward or away from the Sun at different points in the orbit.

• When the **Northern Hemisphere** is tilted toward the Sun, it receives more direct **solar radiation** and experiences longer daylight hours, resulting in **summer**. At the same time, the **Southern Hemisphere** is tilted away, experiencing **winter**.

• The **Earth's distance from the Sun** is not the cause of seasons. Earth reaches its closest point to the Sun (**perihelion**) in January and its farthest point (**aphelion**) in July, which contradicts the seasonal temperatures in the Northern Hemisphere.

• The **rotation of the Earth** on its axis occurs once every 24 hours and is responsible for the cycle of **day and night**, not the yearly seasons.

• The **Moon's gravitational pull** is the primary force behind the **tides** in Earth's oceans and does not influence seasonal climate changes.

**Additional Information__**

• **Solstices** mark the times of the year when the tilt of the Earth's axis is most inclined toward or away from the Sun. The **Summer Solstice** (around June 21) is the longest day of the year in the Northern Hemisphere.

• **Equinoxes** occur when the Sun is positioned directly over the **Equator**, resulting in nearly equal lengths of day and night across the globe. These occur in March (**Vernal Equinox**) and September (**Autumnal Equinox**).

• The Earth's axis points consistently toward a fixed position in space, currently marked by the star **Polaris** (the North Star).

• Regions near the **Equator** experience very little seasonal variation because they receive relatively consistent direct sunlight throughout the year.
</ul

subject: GK
question: Which of the following scenarios best illustrates the principle of conservation of momentum?

options.text: A ball rolling down a frictionless incline increases its speed.
A car comes to a stop when the brakes are applied due to friction.
When a bullet is fired from a gun, the gun recoils in the opposite direction.
A satellite maintains a stable orbit around the Earth due to gravity.

solution:
The correct answer is __**When a bullet is fired from a gun, the gun recoils in the opposite direction**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• The **Law of Conservation of Momentum** states that the total **linear momentum** of a closed or **isolated system** remains constant if no **external force** acts on it. Momentum is defined as the product of an object's **mass** and its **velocity**.

• **Statement 1:** A ball rolling down a **frictionless incline** increases its speed because of the **external force** of **gravity** acting along the slope. Since an external force is accelerating the ball, the **momentum** of the ball is not conserved; it increases as the **velocity** increases. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***

• **Statement 2:** When a car comes to a stop due to **brakes**, the **external force** of **friction** between the tires and the **road** acts on the vehicle. This force changes the **momentum** of the car from its initial value to **zero**. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***

• **Statement 3:** When a **bullet** is fired from a **gun**, the system (gun + bullet) is initially at rest with a total **momentum** of **zero**. Upon firing, the **internal force** of the exploding gunpowder pushes the bullet forward and the gun backward. The forward **momentum** of the bullet is exactly balanced by the backward **recoil momentum** of the gun, keeping the total **system momentum** at **zero**. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***

• **Statement 4:** A **satellite** in a stable **orbit** is subject to the **external gravitational force** of the **Earth**. While the magnitude of its **velocity** (speed) might remain constant in a circular orbit, its direction is constantly changing due to **centripetal force**, meaning its **vector momentum** is continuously changing. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Mathematical Expression:** The principle is mathematically represented as **m1u1 + m2u2 = m1v1 + m2v2**, where **m** represents **mass**, **u** represents **initial velocity**, and **v** represents **final velocity** of the interacting bodies.

• **Newton’s Third Law Connection:** The conservation of **momentum** is a direct consequence of **Newton’s Third Law of Motion**, which states that for every action, there is an **equal and opposite reaction**. The forces between the bullet and the gun are internal **action-reaction pairs**.

• **Types of Collisions:** In **physics**, momentum is conserved in both **elastic** and **inelastic collisions**. However, **kinetic energy** is only conserved in **elastic collisions** (like ideal **gas molecules** or **billiard balls**), while it is partially converted to **heat** or **sound** in inelastic ones.

• **Applications:** This principle is fundamental in **rocket propulsion**. A **rocket** moves upward by ejecting **exhaust gases** downward at high **velocity**. The downward **momentum** of the gases provides an equal upward **momentum** to the rocket body.

• **Vector Nature:** Since **velocity** is a **vector**, **momentum** is also a **vector quantity**. This means that in **two-dimensional** or **three-dimensional** space, the **momentum** must be conserved independently along the **x, y, and z axes**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **System Definition:** For the conservation law to apply, one must clearly define the **isolated system**. In the gun-bullet example, if we only look at the bullet, its **momentum** is not conserved because the gun exerts a **force** on it. Conservation only applies when both objects are treated as a **single unit**.

• **Recoil Velocity:** The **recoil velocity** of a **gun** is much smaller than the **muzzle velocity** of the **bullet** because the **mass** of the gun is significantly larger than the **mass** of the bullet, as shown by the relation **V_gun = -(m_bullet * v_bullet) / M_gun**.

• **Impulse:** The change in **momentum** is known as **impulse**. When an **external force** is applied over a **time interval**, the **momentum** changes according to the **Impulse-Momentum Theorem** (**Force × Time = ΔMomentum**).

• **Historical Context:** While the concept of **momentum** was discussed by earlier scientists like **Descartes**, it was **Sir Isaac Newton** who formalized these laws in his work **Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica** published in **1687**.

7d:T2

options.text: A ball rolling down a frictionless incline increases its speed.

When a bullet is fired from a gun, the gun recoils in the opposite direction.
A satellite maintains a stable orbit around the Earth due to gravity.

solution:
The correct answer is __**When a bullet is fired from a gun, the gun recoils in the opposite direction**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• When a ball rolls down an incline, the **gravitational force** acts as an external force, causing the ball to accelerate and its momentum to increase. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***

• As a car brakes, **frictional force** between the tires and the road surface acts as an external net force that reduces the car's velocity to zero, transferring momentum to the Earth. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***

• In a gun-bullet system, the initial total momentum is zero; when fired, the **internal chemical energy** creates equal and opposite forces, resulting in the bullet moving forward and the gun moving backward with equal momentum, thus keeping the **total system momentum** conserved at zero. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***

• A satellite in orbit is subject to the **gravitational pull** of the Earth, which acts as an external **centripetal force** that continuously changes the satellite's direction and its momentum vector. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

 **Additional Information__**

• **Law of Conservation of Momentum**:

• Derived from **Newton's Second Law** and **Newton's Third Law**, it states that for a **closed system** with no external forces, the total vector sum of momenta remains constant.

• The mathematical representation for a two-body system is m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂.

• **Isolated System**:

• For the principle to hold, the system must be isolated from **external impulses**. In the gun recoil example, the explosion is an **internal force**, which does not change the total momentum of the gun-bullet system.

• **Recoil Velocity**:

• The velocity at which the gun moves backward is calculated as vg = −(mb × vb) ÷ mg. Because the mass of the gun is much larger than the bullet, the **recoil velocity** is significantly smaller.

</ul

question: Which principle explains how rockets are propelled forward when fuel is ejected in the opposite direction?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Newton's Third Law of Motion**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Newton's Third Law of Motion** states that for every **action**, there is an **equal and opposite reaction**. This is the fundamental principle that explains how a rocket moves.

• In a rocket engine, fuel is burned to produce high-pressure **exhaust gases**. These gases are expelled out of the back of the rocket at very high velocities. This downward or backward flow of gas is the **action**.

• The **reaction** to this action is an upward or forward force, called **thrust**, exerted by the gases on the rocket, which propels it forward.

• **Newton's First Law of Motion** (Law of Inertia) states that an object will remain at rest or in uniform motion unless acted upon by an external force. While it explains why a rocket needs a force to move, it doesn't explain the mechanism of propulsion itself.

• The **Law of Conservation of Mass** states that mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. While mass is conserved as fuel turns into gas, it does not explain the movement.

• The **Law of Gravitation** explains the force of attraction between two masses (like the Earth and the rocket). This force actually pulls the rocket back toward Earth and must be overcome by the rocket's thrust.

**Additional Information__**

• Rocket propulsion is also deeply rooted in the **Law of Conservation of Momentum**. The momentum gained by the expelled exhaust gases in one direction is exactly balanced by the momentum gained by the rocket in the opposite direction.

• Rockets are unique because they carry both **fuel** and an **oxidizer**. This allows them to function in the **vacuum of space**, where there is no oxygen to support combustion and no air to push against.

• The speed a rocket reaches depends on the velocity of the exhaust gases and the ratio of the rocket's initial mass to its final mass (after the fuel is spent), a relationship known as the **Tsiolkovsky rocket equation**.

• Common examples of **Newton's Third Law** in daily life include **recoil of a gun** when a bullet is fired and the movement of a **swimmer** pushing against water to move forward.
</ul

subject: GK
question: The phenomenon of total internal reflection can occur when light travels from:

options.text: A rarer medium to a denser medium at any angle of incidence.
A denser medium to a rarer medium at any angle of incidence.
A rarer medium to a denser medium at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle.
A denser medium to a rarer medium at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle.

solution:
The correct answer is __**A denser medium to a rarer medium at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle.**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Total Internal Reflection (TIR)** is an optical phenomenon that occurs when a light ray strikes a medium boundary at an angle larger than a particular **critical angle** with respect to the normal to the surface.

• For **Total Internal Reflection** to occur, two specific conditions must be met:

• The light must be traveling from an **optically denser medium** (e.g., glass, water) to an **optically rarer medium** (e.g., air).

• The **angle of incidence** must be **greater than the critical angle** for that pair of media.

• If light travels from a **rarer medium to a denser medium**, it will always undergo **refraction** and bend towards the normal, regardless of the angle of incidence. Thus, options 1 and 3 are incorrect.

• If the light travels from a denser to a rarer medium but the angle of incidence is **less than the critical angle**, it will refract into the rarer medium. If the angle is **exactly equal** to the critical angle, the light will graze the interface (refraction angle of 90 degrees). Therefore, TIR does not happen at 'any' angle, making option 2 incorrect.

**Additional Information__**

• **Critical Angle:** It is defined as the angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the **angle of refraction** in the rarer medium is **90 degrees**. It is given by the formula: theta_c = sin⁻¹ ((n₂)/(n₁)) , where n1 is the refractive index of the denser medium and n2 is the refractive index of the rarer medium.

• **Optical Fibers:** These utilize **Total Internal Reflection** to transmit light signals over long distances with extremely low power loss. They consist of a **core** and a **cladding** where the core has a higher refractive index than the cladding.

• **Sparkling of Diamonds:** The **refractive index** of diamond is very high (about 2.42), which makes its **critical angle** very small (about 24.4 degrees). This causes light entering the diamond to undergo multiple internal reflections before escaping, creating a brilliant sparkle.

• **Mirage:** This is an **optical illusion** caused by **Total Internal Reflection** in the atmosphere when layers of air at different temperatures have different refractive indices.
</ul

subject: GK
question: The phenomenon of interference in light waves is a direct consequence of:

options.text: The diffraction of light around obstacles.

solution:
The correct answer is __**The superposition principle of waves.**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• The phenomenon of **interference** occurs when two or more light waves overlap in space, leading to a redistribution of light energy. This phenomenon is a direct consequence of the **superposition principle**.

• The **superposition principle** states that when two or more waves of the same type cross at the same point, the resultant displacement at that point is equal to the **vector sum** of the displacements of the individual waves.

• **Constructive Interference:** This occurs when the waves are in phase (crest meets crest or trough meets trough), leading to a wave with a larger amplitude and **maximum intensity**.

• **Destructive Interference:** This occurs when the waves are out of phase (crest meets trough), leading to a wave with a smaller amplitude or zero amplitude, resulting in **minimum intensity**.

• **Why other options are incorrect:**

• **Light as particles (photons):** This particle nature explains the **photoelectric effect** and **blackbody radiation**, but interference is a wave-like property.

• **Diffraction:** While diffraction involves the bending of light around obstacles and also utilizes superposition, interference specifically refers to the interaction between waves from **coherent sources**.

• **Polarization:** This refers to the orientation of the oscillations of a **transverse wave** in a particular direction and is not the cause of interference.

**Additional Information__**

• The most famous demonstration of light interference is **Young's Double-Slit Experiment**, conducted by **Thomas Young** in 1801, which provided definitive proof of the **wave nature of light**.

• To observe a stable interference pattern, the sources must be **coherent**, meaning they emit light waves of the same frequency and maintain a **constant phase difference** over time.

• In interference, energy is not lost but is simply **redistributed** from the regions of destructive interference (dark fringes) to the regions of constructive interference (bright fringes), obeying the **law of conservation of energy**.

• The condition for **constructive interference** is that the path difference must be an integral multiple of the wavelength: Delta x = nlambda (where n = 0, 1, 2...).

• The condition for **destructive interference** is that the path difference must be an odd multiple of half the wavelength: Delta x = (n + (1)/(2))lambda .
</ul

question: What happens to the pupil in low light conditions?

options.text: It contracts to prevent excess light from entering
It expands to allow more light to enter

solution:
The correct answer is __**It expands to allow more light to enter**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
__

• The **pupil** is the dark circular opening in the center of the **iris** that regulates the amount of light entering the eye.

• In **low light conditions** or darkness, the pupil **dilates** (expands). This is a physiological response to allow the maximum possible amount of light to reach the **retina**, helping the person see better in the dark.

• This expansion is controlled by the **radial muscles** of the iris, which contract to pull the pupil open wider.

• In contrast, in **bright light**, the pupil **constricts** (shrinks) to prevent too much light from entering, which could damage the sensitive cells of the retina. This is controlled by the **circular muscles** of the iris.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• The **iris** is the colored part of the eye that acts like a shutter in a camera, adjusting the size of the pupil.

• The adjustment of the pupil size in response to light intensity is known as the **pupillary light reflex**.

• The **retina** contains two main types of photoreceptor cells: **rods**, which are sensitive to low light levels (scotopic vision), and **cones**, which are responsible for color vision and high spatial acuity (photopic vision).

• The **optic nerve** transmits the visual information from the retina to the **brain** for processing.

question:
Fill in the blank:
The phenomenon where the Sun, Earth, and Moon align to cause a total or partial shadow is called a _______
solution:
The correct answer is __**Eclipse**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• An **Eclipse** is an astronomical event that occurs when an astronomical object or spacecraft is temporarily obscured, either by passing into the shadow of another body or by having another body pass between it and the viewer.

• The specific alignment of three celestial bodies, such as the **Sun**, **Earth**, and **Moon**, in a straight line is scientifically referred to as **Syzygy**.

• A **Solar Eclipse** occurs when the **Moon** moves between the **Sun** and **Earth**, blocking the Sun's light and casting a shadow on a portion of the Earth.

• A **Lunar Eclipse** happens when the **Earth** comes between the **Sun** and the **Moon**, causing the Earth's shadow to fall on the Moon.

• **Transit** is a similar phenomenon but occurs when a much smaller celestial body passes in front of a larger one (e.g., the **Transit of Venus** across the Sun).

• **Conjunction** occurs when two celestial objects appear close to each other in the sky from the perspective of an observer, but they do not necessarily cause a shadow.

• **Revolution** is the term used for the orbital motion of one body around another, such as the **Earth's revolution** around the Sun, which takes approximately 365.25 days.

**Additional Information__**

• The shadow cast during an eclipse consists of two main parts: the **Umbra** (the darkest, central part) and the **Penumbra** (the lighter, outer part).

• An **Annular Solar Eclipse** occurs when the Moon is near **Apogee** (its farthest point from Earth), making it appear smaller than the Sun and creating a **Ring of Fire** effect.

• Eclipses do not occur every month because the **Moon's orbit** is tilted at an angle of about 5 degrees relative to the **Earth's orbit** around the Sun.

• A **Total Lunar Eclipse** often gives the Moon a reddish hue, a phenomenon frequently called a **Blood Moon**, caused by the scattering of sunlight through the Earth's atmosphere.
</ul

• A barometer is a scientific instrument used to measure** atmospheric pressure**, also called barometric pressure.

question:
Match the atmospheric phenomenon with its primary measurement instrument
1. Wind Speed
2. Humidity
3. Atmospheric Pressure
solution:
The correct answer is __**1-Anemometer, 2-Hygrometer, 3-Barometer**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Anemometer**: This is a **scientific instrument** used to measure **wind speed** and **wind pressure**. It is a fundamental tool for **meteorologists** who study weather patterns and for **physicists** who study the way air moves. The first description of an anemometer was given by **Leon Battista Alberti** around **1450**. *Hence, the match for wind speed is correct.*
 
• **Hygrometer**: A **hygrometer** is an instrument used to measure the **amount of water vapor** in the atmosphere, in soil, or in confined spaces. Humidity measurement is vital in **meteorology**, **agriculture**, and **industrial manufacturing**. The concept of the hygrometer dates back to the **15th century**, with significant improvements made by **Horace Bénédict de Saussure** in **1783** using a human hair to measure humidity. *Hence, the match for humidity is correct.*
 
• **Barometer**: A **barometer** is an instrument used to measure **atmospheric pressure**. Because atmospheric pressure changes with distance above or below sea level, a barometer can also be used to measure **altitude**. **Evangelista Torricelli**, an Italian physicist and mathematician, is generally credited with inventing the mercury barometer in **1643**. *Hence, the match for atmospheric pressure is correct.*
 
• The combination of these instruments allows for **weather forecasting** and the monitoring of **climatic conditions** across different **geographical locations**. *Hence, the statement representing option C is the correct match.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Wind Speed Measurement (Anemometer)**:
 
 
• There are several types of anemometers, including the **Cup Anemometer**, which consists of four cups that rotate with the wind, and the **Sonic Anemometer**, which uses **ultrasonic sound waves** to measure wind velocity.
 
• In addition to speed, a **Wind Vane** is often paired with an anemometer to determine the **direction** of the wind.
 
• These instruments are critical at **airports** for aviation safety and at **wind farms** to optimize **energy production**.
 
 
 
• **Humidity Measurement (Hygrometer)**:
 
 
• **Relative Humidity (RH)** is the most common way to express the amount of moisture in the air relative to the maximum amount the air could hold at that **temperature**.
 
• A **Psychrometer** is a specific type of hygrometer that uses two **thermometers** (one dry bulb and one wet bulb) to determine humidity through the **cooling effect of evaporation**.
 
• Modern **digital hygrometers** use **capacitive** or **resistive** sensors to measure moisture levels in **HVAC systems** and **museums** to preserve artifacts.
 
 
 
• **Atmospheric Pressure Measurement (Barometer)**:
 
 
• There are two main types of barometers: **Mercury Barometers** and **Aneroid Barometers**. The aneroid version is more portable and uses a small, flexible **metal box** called an aneroid cell.
 
• Atmospheric pressure is commonly measured in units of **hectopascals (hPa)**, **millibars (mb)**, or **inches of mercury (inHg)**.
 
• A **rising barometer** generally indicates **fair weather**, while a **falling barometer** suggests approaching **storms** or low-pressure systems.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Standard Atmospheric Pressure**: At **sea level**, the standard atmospheric pressure is approximately **1013.25 hPa** (or 14.7 pounds per square inch).
 
• **Instrument Calibration**: All meteorological instruments require regular **calibration** against **international standards** to ensure accuracy in global **weather reports** and **climate models**.
 
• **Other Meteorological Instruments**: Apart from the ones mentioned, a **Thermometer** is used for measuring temperature, and a **Rain Gauge** (or **Ombrometer**) is used to measure **liquid precipitation** over a set period.
 
• **Historical Context**: The development of these instruments during the **Scientific Revolution** in the **17th and 18th centuries** laid the groundwork for modern **meteorology**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **pyranometer **is specifically designed to **measure **the **total solar irradiance on a horizontal plane**, encompassing the entire hemisphere above the instrument.
 
• It is widely **used **in **meteorology** and **climatology **to monitor solar radiation levels, which play a crucial role in weather patterns, climate change studies, and **renewable energy applications**.
 
• A typical pyranometer **does not require any power to operate**. However, recent technical development includes use of electronics in pyranometers, which do require (low) external power.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__ **

 
• Hygrometer:

 
 
• It is a specialized device that determines the relative humidity in a closed or open space.
 
• The first hygrometer was created in 1783 by Swiss physicist and geologist Horace Bénédict de Saussur.
 
 
• He used human hair to measure humidity.
 
 
 
• It functions through a process called evaporative cooling.
 
 
 
• **Barometer**:
 
 
• ​A scientific device known as a barometer is used to** measure atmospheric pressure**, also known as **barometric pressure**.
 
• The layers of air encircling Earth are called the atmosphere. Gravity draws that air to Earth, where its weight causes it to press against everything it comes into contact with. This pressure is measured using barometers.
 
• The weather is influenced by variations in the atmosphere, particularly variations in air pressure. Barometers are used by meteorologists to forecast transient changes in the weather.
 
• An approaching** low-pressure system** is indicated by a **sharp decrease in air pressure**. It is commonly predicted that low pressure will **bring clouds**, **rain**, and **wind**.
 
• Air flows out of **high pressure zones**. **Clear skies **and **chilly**, **dry air **are typically associated with high pressure zones.
 
 
 
• **Anemometer**:
 
 
• ​An instrument used to **measure wind pressure** and **speed **is called an anemometer.
 
• When it comes to **studying weather patterns**, meteorologists rely heavily on anemometers. They are also crucial to the **study of air movement** by physicists.
 
• Anemometers with **three or four cups fastened to horizontal arms** are the most **popular kind**.
 
• A vertical rod is where the arms are fastened. The rod spins as a result of the cups rotating in the wind. The rod spins more quickly the greater the wind. To determine wind speed, the anemometer counts the number of rotations, or turns.
 
• The reason wind speed is often averaged over a brief duration is because wind speeds are not constant—there are gusts and lulls.

subject: GK
question: A major limitation of Rutherford's model was its inability to explain:

options.text: The stability of the atom and the atomic spectrum

solution:
The correct answer is __**the stability of the atom and the atomic spectrum**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Rutherford's atomic model** was proposed in **1911** after the famous **gold foil experiment**. He suggested that atoms consist of a dense, positively charged nucleus surrounded by electrons.
 
• The model explained the structure of the atom and the deflection of alpha particles during the experiment, proving the existence of a nucleus. However, it failed to explain certain crucial phenomena.
 
• One of the major limitations of Rutherford's model was its inability to explain the **stability of the atom**. According to classical electromagnetic theory, electrons revolving around the nucleus should emit radiation continuously, lose energy, and eventually spiral into the nucleus, leading to the collapse of the atom. This does not happen in reality.
 
• Additionally, Rutherford's model could not explain the **atomic spectrum**. Atoms emit radiation at specific wavelengths, resulting in discrete spectral lines (as observed in the hydrogen spectrum). Rutherford's model could not justify why atoms emit such specific wavelengths instead of a continuous spectrum.
 
• **The existence of isotopes**, though important, is unrelated to Rutherford's model, as isotopes are identified by differences in neutron numbers. Hence, Option 1 is incorrect.
 
• **The deflection of alpha particles** was already explained successfully by Rutherford's experiment and his model. Hence, Option 2 is incorrect.
 
• **The indivisible nature of atoms** was disproven with the discovery of subatomic particles like protons, neutrons, and electrons. Hence, Option 4 is incorrect.
 
• *Therefore, the inability to explain the stability of the atom and the atomic spectrum is the major limitation of Rutherford's model, making Option 3 the correct answer.*

**Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Rutherford's Gold Foil Experiment:**

 
 
• Rutherford bombarded a thin gold foil with alpha particles. Most particles passed through undeflected, but some were deflected at large angles, and a few even rebounded.
 
• This led to the conclusion that the atom consists of a dense, positively charged nucleus where most of the mass is concentrated, surrounded by empty space and electrons.
 
 
 
• **Limitations of Rutherford's Model:**
 
 
• It could not explain why electrons do not lose energy and collapse into the nucleus despite moving in circular orbits.
 
• The model failed to explain the discrete spectral lines observed in the atomic spectrum of elements like hydrogen.
 
 
 
• **Bohr's Model of the Atom:**
 
 
• Niels Bohr improved upon Rutherford's model in **1913**. He introduced the concept of **quantized orbits**, where electrons revolve in specific, stable energy levels without radiating energy.
 
• Bohr's model successfully explained the stability of atoms and the discrete spectral lines in the hydrogen spectrum.
 
 

**Important Points__**

 
• **Classical Electromagnetic Theory:**

 
 
• According to this theory, any charged particle in accelerated motion (like an electron in circular orbit) should emit electromagnetic radiation and lose energy.
 
• This would cause the electron to spiral into the nucleus, making the atom unstable. However, this does not occur, proving the limitation of Rutherford's model.
 
 
 
• **Atomic Spectrum:**
 
 
• The atomic spectrum consists of discrete lines corresponding to specific energy transitions in an atom. For example, the hydrogen spectrum has distinct series like Lyman, Balmer, and Paschen.
 
• Rutherford's model could not explain why only certain wavelengths are emitted or absorbed, a phenomenon later explained by Bohr's quantized energy levels.

question: To modify the magnitude of an alternating voltage without altering its frequency, which principle is applied in the functioning of a transformer?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Mutual induction**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• A **transformer** is a static electrical device that transfers electrical energy between two or more circuits through **electromagnetic induction**.

• The fundamental principle behind the operation of a transformer is **Mutual Induction**. This occurs when a changing magnetic flux produced by the **primary winding** links with the **secondary winding**, inducing an electromotive force (EMF) in it.

• The transformer modifies the **magnitude of alternating voltage** (stepping it up or down) while keeping the **frequency** of the power constant.

• **Self-induction** is the phenomenon where a change in current in a single coil induces an EMF in that same coil. While it occurs in the primary winding, the transfer of energy to the secondary is due to mutual induction.

• **Electromagnetic radiation** involves the emission of energy as waves (like radio waves), which is not the mechanism for power transformation in a transformer.

• **Capacitive coupling** involves the transfer of energy through an electric field between two points of a circuit, which is different from the magnetic coupling used in transformers.

**Additional Information__**

• A transformer consists of two inductive coils (**Primary** and **Secondary**) which are electrically separated but magnetically linked through a **ferromagnetic core**.

• The relationship between the voltages and the number of turns in the coils is given by the formula: (V_p)/(V_s) = (N_p)/(N_s) , where **V** represents voltage and **N** represents the number of turns.

• **Step-up transformers** increase the output voltage (Ns > Np), whereas **Step-down transformers** decrease the output voltage (Ns < Np).

• Transformers operate only on **Alternating Current (AC)** because **Direct Current (DC)** does not produce the changing magnetic flux necessary for induction.

• The efficiency of modern transformers is very high, often exceeding **95 percent**, as there are no moving parts and thus no mechanical friction losses.
</ul

subject: GK
question: What happens to the resistance of a conductor as temperature increases?
solution:
The correct answer is __**It increases**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Resistance of a Conductor:** Resistance is the property of a conductor that opposes the flow of electric current. It depends on factors like material, temperature, length, and cross-sectional area.
 
• When the temperature of a conductor increases, the atoms within the material vibrate more vigorously due to the added thermal energy.
 
• This increased atomic vibration causes more frequent collisions between the electrons (which are responsible for the conduction of electricity) and the atoms in the conductor. *Hence, resistance increases with temperature.*
 
• The increase in resistance is more pronounced in metallic conductors, as metals typically have free electrons that interact strongly with the vibrating atoms when temperature rises.
 
• This relationship between temperature and resistance is mathematically expressed as: **R = R₀(1 + αΔT)**, where **R** is the resistance at temperature T, **R₀** is the resistance at reference temperature, **α** is the temperature coefficient of resistance, and **ΔT** is the change in temperature. *Hence, the resistance increases as temperature rises.*
 
• In contrast, materials like semiconductors and insulators may show a decrease in resistance with temperature, as their conduction mechanism differs. *Thus, this explanation specifically applies to conductors.*
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is It increases.***

**Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Factors Affecting Resistance:**

 
 
• **Material:** Different materials have different electrical resistivities. Metals generally have low resistivity, making them good conductors.
 
• **Temperature:** As explained, resistance increases with temperature for conductors due to increased atomic vibrations and electron scattering.
 
• **Length:** Longer conductors have higher resistance because the electrons face more obstacles during their journey.
 
• **Cross-sectional Area:** A larger cross-sectional area reduces resistance as it provides more space for electrons to flow.
 
 
 
• **Applications:**
 
 
• Resistance is utilized in designing devices like **electric heaters**, where higher resistance generates heat.
 
• Conductors with low resistance, such as **copper and aluminum**, are widely used in electrical wiring.
 
• Temperature-dependent resistances are used in **thermistors**, which are sensors for temperature measurement.
 
 

**Important Points__**

 
• **Temperature Coefficient of Resistance:**

 
 
• The **temperature coefficient of resistance** (**α**) quantifies how much the resistance of a material changes with temperature. For metals, **α** is positive, indicating an increase in resistance.
 
• 
 
• 
• For semiconductors, **α** is negative, meaning resistance decreases with temperature.
 
 
 
• **Practical Examples:**
 
 
• **Electric Bulbs:** Filament resistance increases with temperature, causing the bulb to glow brightly.
 
• **Transmission Lines:** Resistance increases in transmission lines during hot weather, leading to energy losses.

question: A transformer works on the principle of:
solution:
The correct answer is __**Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• A **transformer** is a static electrical device that transfers electrical energy from one alternating-current circuit to another through the process of **mutual induction**.

• The fundamental principle behind its operation is **Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction**, which states that a time-varying magnetic flux through a loop induces an **electromotive force (EMF)** in that loop.

• In a transformer, an **alternating current** flowing through the **primary coil** creates a varying magnetic field in the core. This changing magnetic flux links with the **secondary coil**, inducing a voltage across its terminals.

• **Ohm's Law** (V = IR) describes the relationship between voltage, current, and resistance in a conductor but does not explain the transfer of energy between isolated circuits.

• **Lenz's Law** determines the **direction** of the induced EMF and current such that it opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it; it is a consequence of the law of conservation of energy.

• **Conservation of Charge** states that the total electric charge in an isolated system remains constant, which is a general physical principle but not the specific operational mechanism of a transformer.

**Additional Information__**

• Transformers are used to **Step-up** (increase) or **Step-down** (decrease) voltage levels in power systems while maintaining the same **frequency**.

• A transformer cannot work on **Direct Current (DC)** because DC produces a constant magnetic field, which results in zero change in flux and thus no induced EMF in the secondary winding.

• The relationship between the primary and secondary voltages and the number of turns is given by the transformer ratio: **Vₚ / Vₛ = Nₚ / Nₛ**.

• An **Ideal Transformer** is assumed to have no losses (no copper loss, iron loss, or flux leakage), meaning the input power equals the output power.

• The core of a transformer is usually made of **laminated silicon steel** to reduce energy losses caused by **eddy currents** and **hysteresis**.
</ul

question: If the length of a wire is doubled and its thickness (cross-sectional area) is reduced to half, what will be the effect on its electrical resistance?
solution:
The correct answer is __**It becomes four times**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **electrical resistance** (R) of a conductor is directly proportional to its **length** (L) and inversely proportional to its **cross-sectional area** (A). This relationship is expressed by the formula: R = rho (L)/(A) , where rho (rho) is the **resistivity** of the material.

• According to the question, the new length (L') is twice the original length (L' = 2L) and the new cross-sectional area (A') is half of the original area (A' = A/2).

• Substituting these new values into the resistance formula: Rₙₑw = rho (2L)/(A/2) .

• By simplifying the expression, we get: Rₙₑw = rho (2L times 2)/(A) = 4 times (rho (L)/(A)) .

• Therefore, the new resistance is **four times** the original resistance (R_new = 4R).

• **Option 1, 2, and 4** are incorrect because they do not satisfy the mathematical relationship derived from the doubling of length and halving of the area simultaneously.

**Additional Information__**

• **Resistivity** ( rho ) is an intrinsic property of a material and does not change with the dimensions (length or area) of the wire; it only changes with **temperature** and the **nature of the material**.

• The **SI unit** of electrical resistance is the **Ohm** (Ω).

• **Ohm's Law** states that the current through a conductor between two points is directly proportional to the voltage across the two points, provided temperature remains constant (V = IR).

• Factors affecting the resistance of a wire include:
 
 
• **Length**: Longer wires have more resistance.
 
• **Thickness (Area)**: Thicker wires have less resistance.
 
• **Temperature**: For most metals, resistance increases as temperature increases.
 
• **Material**: Different materials (like copper vs. nichrome) have different resistivities.

question: What type of radiation is responsible for ionizing atmospheric gases in the Earth's ionosphere?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Ultraviolet Radiation**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
__

• The **ionosphere** is a region of the Earth's upper atmosphere, extending from approximately 60 km to 1,000 km above the surface, where the air is ionized by solar energy.

• **Ultraviolet (UV) radiation** from the Sun is the primary agent responsible for this ionization. UV photons possess sufficient energy to knock electrons out of the atoms and molecules of atmospheric gases (such as **oxygen** and **nitrogen**), creating a layer of **free electrons** and **positive ions**.

• While **Solar Radiation** is the broad term for all energy emitted by the Sun, **Ultraviolet Radiation** (along with X-rays) is the specific component of the electromagnetic spectrum that drives the ionization process in the upper atmosphere.

• **Cosmic Radiation**, which originates from outside the solar system, does contribute to ionization, but its effect is significantly smaller than that of solar UV radiation within the ionosphere.

• **Gamma Radiation** is highly energetic but is not the primary source for the sustained ionization layers found in the Earth's ionosphere.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• The ionosphere is critical for **radio communication** because it reflects **high-frequency (HF)** or shortwave radio waves back to Earth, allowing for long-distance transmission beyond the horizon.

• It is composed of several layers, known as the **D, E, and F layers**. The **F layer** (also known as the **Appleton-Barnett layer**) has the highest electron density and is most important for skywave propagation.

• Ionization levels fluctuate based on the **diurnal cycle** (day and night), seasons, and the 11-year **solar cycle**. During the night, the D and E layers largely disappear as ions and electrons recombine in the absence of solar UV.

• Phenomena such as the **Aurora Borealis** (Northern Lights) occur when charged particles from the solar wind interact with the gases in the ionosphere near the Earth's magnetic poles.
</ul

question:
The Doppler effect describes the change in observed frequency of a wave when there is relative motion between the source of the wave and the observer.

Which of the following scenarios illustrates the Doppler effect for sound?

options.text: Light from a distant star appears shifted towards the red end of the spectrum.
A stationary observer hears a change in the pitch of a siren as an ambulance passes by.
Water waves bend as they move from deep to shallow water.
Sunlight is dispersed into different colors when it passes through a prism.

solution:
The correct answer is __**A stationary observer hears a change in the pitch of a siren as an ambulance passes by.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The Doppler Effect:** It is the change in the observed frequency or wavelength of a wave due to the relative motion between the source of the wave and the observer. This phenomenon applies to sound, light, and other types of waves.
 
• **Sound Waves:** In the given scenario, the pitch (frequency) of the ambulance siren appears higher as it approaches the stationary observer and lower as it moves away. This is due to the compression and stretching of sound waves caused by relative motion. This is the correct example of the Doppler effect.
 
• **Relative Motion:** The Doppler effect specifically occurs when there is relative motion between the wave source (ambulance siren) and the observer (stationary person). The frequency changes based on whether the source is moving toward or away from the observer.
 
• **Applications:** The Doppler effect for sound waves is widely used in applications like radar speed detection, medical ultrasound imaging, and astronomy to measure the velocity of moving objects.
 
• **Incorrect Options:** Other scenarios mentioned, like light shifts and wave bending, do not describe the Doppler effect for sound waves. They pertain to different physical phenomena like refraction or dispersion.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Redshift and Blueshift:** The Doppler effect also applies to light waves. When a light source moves away from the observer, its wavelength stretches, causing a redshift. Conversely, when it moves closer, the wavelength compresses, causing a blueshift. This is used in astronomy to study the movement of stars and galaxies.
 
• **Refraction:** The bending of waves, such as water waves moving from deep to shallow water, is due to a change in wave speed and direction. This phenomenon is not related to the Doppler effect.
 
• **Dispersion:** Sunlight splitting into different colors when passing through a prism is due to dispersion. Different wavelengths of light refract at slightly different angles, creating a spectrum. This is unrelated to the Doppler effect.
 
• **Applications of Doppler Effect:** In sound waves, it is used in technologies like Doppler radar, which measures the speed of objects such as vehicles. In medical settings, Doppler ultrasound is used to monitor blood flow and heart conditions.
 
• **Important Formula:** The change in observed frequency due to the Doppler effect for sound waves can be calculated using: f′=fv+vov+vs" id="MathJax-Element-1-Frame" role="presentation" style="position: relative;" tabindex="0">f′=fv+vov+vsf′=fv+vov+vs f′=fv+vov+vs f' = f \frac{v + v_o}{v + v_s} , where: - f' : Observed frequency - f : Actual frequency - v : Speed of sound - v_o : Speed of observer - v_s : Speed of source

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Option 1:** Light from a star shifted toward the red spectrum is an example of the Doppler effect for light waves, not sound waves.
 
• **Option 3:** Water waves bending due to a change in medium is refraction. It doesn’t involve frequency change due to motion.
 
• **Option 4:** Dispersion of sunlight into colors is caused by differences in refractive index, unrelated to the Doppler effect.
 
• **Real-Life Example:** The siren of an emergency vehicle passing by is the most common and relatable example of the Doppler effect for sound waves.
 
• **Discovery:** The Doppler effect was first described by Austrian physicist **Christian Doppler** in **1842**.

subject: GK
question: Which of the following is a practical example of convection?

options.text: Warming your hands by a fire

solution:
The correct answer is __**Heating water on a stove**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Convection** is the mode of heat transfer that takes place in **fluids** (liquids and gases) through the actual movement of the particles of the medium.

• When **heating water on a stove**, the water at the bottom of the container gets heated, its density decreases, and it rises. The cooler, denser water from the top moves down to replace it, creating **convection currents** that distribute heat throughout the liquid.

• **Warming your hands by a fire** is primarily an example of **Radiation**, as the heat is felt even without direct contact or a moving fluid medium between the fire and the hands (though some convection occurs if hands are held directly above the fire).

• **Heat transmission through a vacuum** is only possible via **Radiation**. Convection and conduction both require a material medium to transfer energy.

• **Heat transfer in metal** occurs through **Conduction**. In solids, heat is transferred from one molecule to another through vibrations and the movement of free electrons without the bulk movement of the material itself.

**Additional Information__**

• There are three primary modes of heat transfer: **Conduction**, **Convection**, and **Radiation**.

• **Natural Convection** occurs due to **buoyancy forces** (differences in density caused by temperature variations), such as **Sea breezes** and **Land breezes**.

• **Forced Convection** occurs when a fluid is forced to flow over a surface by external means like a **fan**, **pump**, or **suction device**.

• The rate of heat transfer in convection is often described by **Newtons Law of Cooling**.

• **Radiation** is the only method that can transfer heat through the **vacuum of space**, which is how thermal energy from the **Sun** reaches the Earth.
</ul

question: Triple point can be defined as:

options.text: the condition of temperature under which the gaseous and liquid phases of a substance can exist in equilibrium
the temperature at which solid is converted into liquid
the condition of pressure under which the solid and liquid phases of a substance can exist in equilibrium
the condition of temperature and pressure under which the gaseous, liquid and solid phases of a substance can exist in equilibrium

solution:
The Correct answer is **__the condition of temperature and pressure under which the gaseous, liquid and solid phases of a substance can exist in equilibrium__**. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** 

 
• The triple point of a substance is the temperature and pressure at which the three phases **(gas, liquid, and solid)** of that substance coexist in thermodynamic equilibrium.
 
• The triple point of water is used to define the Kelvin(K), the base unit of thermodynamic temperature in the International System of Units (SI).
 
• The triple point of water is **273.16K, 0.01° C, or 32.018° F**.
 
 
• **The graph of pressure plotted against temperature the following diagram explains**
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f4fece212bc77e370074dc5d77b5e169c5b7672fa5a13ca134b1a94e87d8005e.png] 

If the graph is for water then the three lines shown represent:

(a) the boiling curve (AB) is the locus of points where water and its vapour can exist in equilibrium;

(b) the sublimation curve (AC) is the locus of points where ice and its vapour can exist together in equilibrium;

(c) the solidification curve (AD) is the locus of points where water and ice can exist together.

 
• The triple point is at A where these three lines intersect and where water, water vapour and ice can exist in equilibrium.
 
• The temperature at which this occurs is defined as **273.16 K** on the thermodynamic temperature scale.
 
• The triple point is not exactly at 0° C because under the pressure of its own vapour ice melts at about **0.0075° C**.

• A **nanometre** is one billionth of a metre.
 
• It is often abbreviated as **nm** and is commonly used in fields such as physics, chemistry, and nanotechnology to measure extremely small lengths.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] Additional Information__
