question: Which national initiative aims to prevent and control non-communicable diseases such as diabetes and hypertension?

options.text: National Programme for Prevention and Control of NCDs

solution:
The correct answer is __**National Programme for Prevention and Control of NCDs**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **National Programme for Prevention and Control of Cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Diseases and Stroke (NPCDCS)**, which has been recently renamed as the **National Programme for Prevention and Control of Non-Communicable Diseases (NP-NCD)**, was launched in **2010**. It is the primary initiative in **India** dedicated to managing chronic lifestyle diseases.

• The program focuses on **health promotion**, **early diagnosis**, and **management** of **NCDs**. It aims to strengthen **infrastructure**, develop **human resources**, and provide **palliative care**. This is the correct option as it directly targets **diabetes** and **hypertension**.

• **Mission Indradhanush** is a health mission launched in **December 2014**. Its goal is to ensure full **immunization** coverage for children up to **2 years** of age and **pregnant women** against **12 vaccine-preventable diseases**. It does not focus on **NCDs** like **diabetes**. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***

• The **National Digital Health Mission (NDHM)**, now known as the **Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM)**, was launched in **August 2020**. It focuses on creating a **digital health ecosystem** including **Health IDs** and **Electronic Health Records**. It is a technological framework, not a clinical control program for **NCDs**. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***

• **Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY)** is the **insurance** component of **Ayushman Bharat**, providing a cover of **Rs. 5 lakh** per family per year for **secondary** and **tertiary care** hospitalization. While it covers treatment for **NCDs**, it is not a dedicated preventive and control initiative like **NP-NCD**. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Non-Communicable Diseases (NCDs)**: These are medical conditions that are not infectious and cannot be passed from person to person. In **India**, **NCDs** are responsible for nearly **63%** of all deaths. The four major types are **cardiovascular diseases**, **cancers**, **chronic respiratory diseases**, and **diabetes**.

• **75/25 Initiative**: Launched by the **Union Health Ministry**, this initiative aims to ensure that **75 million** people suffering from **hypertension** and **diabetes** are put on standard care by the year **2025** through **Primary Health Centres**.

• **Ayushman Bharat - Health and Wellness Centres (AB-HWCs)**: These centers are the frontline for **NCD** screening. Population-based screening for **hypertension**, **diabetes**, and common cancers (**oral**, **breast**, and **cervical**) is conducted for all individuals above the age of **30 years**.

• **Risk Factors**: The **NP-NCD** program specifically targets four major behavioral risk factors: **tobacco use**, **unhealthy diet**, **physical inactivity**, and **harmful use of alcohol**.

• **Global Targets**: **India** was the first country to adopt the **Global Monitoring Framework** for **NCDs**, aiming for a **25%** relative reduction in premature mortality from **NCDs** by **2025**, as aligned with the **Sustainable Development Goals (SDG)** target **3.4**.

**Important Points__**

• **India Hypertension Control Initiative (IHCI)**: This is a **multi-partner** initiative involving the **Ministry of Health and Family Welfare**, **ICMR**, and **WHO**. It won the **2022 UN Interagency Task Force** award for its excellence in scaling up **hypertension** control within the primary health care system.

• **National Health Policy (NHP) 2017**: This policy emphasizes the need for **preventive** and **promotive** health care. It set a target to reduce the prevalence of **tobacco use** by **15%** by **2020** and **30%** by **2025** to combat **NCDs**.

• **Portal for NCDs**: The government has developed a **National NCD Portal** to facilitate the **real-time monitoring** of screening and treatment data across the country, ensuring better follow-up for patients with **chronic conditions**.

• **Financial Support**: Under the **National Health Mission (NHM)**, states receive financial and technical support for setting up **NCD Clinics** at the **District** and **Community Health Centre (CHC)** levels.
</ul

• The **Ministry of Commerce and Industry** is the primary ministry responsible for the implementation of the **PM Gati Shakti National Master Plan**. Specifically, the **Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT)** acts as the nodal agency for this ambitious project.
 
• Launched on **13th October 2021** by Prime Minister **Narendra Modi**, the **PM Gati Shakti** is a **Digital Platform** that brings together **16 Ministries**, including **Railways** and **Roadways**, for integrated planning and coordinated implementation of infrastructure connectivity projects.
 
• The plan aims to provide **multimodal connectivity** to various **economic zones** across the country, ensuring that people, goods, and services move seamlessly from one mode of transport to another.
 
• While the **Ministry of Finance** (Option 1) manages the **budgetary allocations** and the **Ministry of Road Transport and Highways** (Option 2) and **Ministry of Railways** (Option 4) are key executing bodies for physical infrastructure, the **Ministry of Commerce and Industry** provides the overarching technological and administrative framework through the **National Master Plan (NMP)**.
 
• The project is designed to break **departmental silos** and institutionalize holistic planning for stakeholders across major infrastructure projects like **Bharatmala**, **Sagarmala**, and **inland waterways**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• The **PM Gati Shakti** plan is built on **six pillars**: **Comprehensiveness**, **Prioritization**, **Optimization**, **Synchronization**, **Analytical**, and **Dynamic**. These pillars ensure that all data is available in one place with **GIS-based spatial planning** tools.
 
• One of the major goals of this initiative is to reduce **logistics costs** in **India**, which currently stand at approximately **13-14% of GDP**, aiming to bring them down to around **8%** to match global standards and improve export competitiveness.
 
• The plan involves an investment of approximately **Rs. 100 lakh crore** and is closely linked with the **National Infrastructure Pipeline (NIP)**, which was launched in **2019** to improve the quality of life for citizens.
 
• An **Empowered Group of Secretaries (EGoS)**, headed by the **Cabinet Secretary**, has been constituted to oversee the implementation, while a **Network Planning Group (NPG)** provides technical support for the unified planning process.
 
• The **Unified Logistics Interface Platform (ULIP)** is a significant component under this plan, designed to provide **real-time information** to all stakeholders and simplify the documentation process in the **logistics sector**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **National Master Plan** uses **ISRO** (Indian Space Research Organisation) imagery and **BiSAG-N** (Bhaskaracharya National Institute for Space Applications and Geo-informatics) technology to provide **spatial planning** and analytical tools for better decision-making.
 
• It covers various **Economic Zones** such as **textile clusters**, **pharmaceutical clusters**, **defence corridors**, **industrial corridors**, and **agricultural zones** to ensure that infrastructure is built where it is most needed for economic growth.
 
• The **PM Gati Shakti** also integrates existing schemes like **UDAN** (Ude Desh ka Aam Naagrik) for regional air connectivity and **Digital India** to ensure that the infrastructure is future-ready and technologically advanced.
 
• By **2024-25**, the plan targets significant increases in the **National Highway network**, the creation of **200+ new airports/heliports/water aerodromes**, and a massive expansion of the **gas pipeline network** across **India**.

question: Which government official announced the Ladli Behna Yojana?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Chief Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Ladli Behna Yojana** was officially announced by the then **Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh**, **Shivraj Singh Chouhan**, on **January 28, 2023**.
 
• The announcement was made during the celebration of **Narmada Jayanti** in the **Narmadapuram** (formerly known as **Hoshangabad**) district of **Madhya Pradesh**.
 
• The primary objective of the scheme is to enhance the **economic independence** of women in the state, improve their **health and nutritional status**, and grant them a greater say in **family-level decision-making**.
 
• Initially, the scheme promised a monthly financial assistance of **Rs. 1,000** to every eligible woman, which was later enhanced to **Rs. 1,250 per month**.
 
• The scheme targets women from **economically weaker sections**, **middle-class families**, and **deprived categories**, aiming to provide them with a safety net for their daily personal expenses.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Eligibility Criteria**: To benefit from the **Ladli Behna Yojana**, the applicant must be a **permanent resident** of **Madhya Pradesh**. The **age** limit for the beneficiaries was originally set between **23 and 60 years**, but was later revised to include women aged **21 to 60 years**.
 
• **Economic Limitations**: The scheme is restricted to families whose total **annual income** is less than **Rs. 2.5 lakh**. Additionally, the family members should not be **Income Tax payers**.
 
• **Land Ownership Rule**: A critical feature of the eligibility is that the family of the beneficiary should not own more than **5 acres** of **agricultural land**.
 
• **Exclusion Factors**: Women who are already receiving a monthly amount of **Rs. 1,250** or more from other **Government of India** or **State Government** social security or pension schemes are not eligible to apply.
 
• **Historical Context**: This scheme is often seen as an extension of the **Ladli Laxmi Yojana**, which was also a flagship program of the **Madhya Pradesh** government focused on the welfare of **girl children**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Implementation and Disbursement**: The funds are transferred directly into the **Aadhaar-linked bank accounts** of the beneficiaries through the **Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT)** system on the **10th day** of every **month**.
 
• **Budgetary Allocation**: The **Madhya Pradesh government** allocated a substantial budget of approximately **Rs. 8,000 crore** for the first financial year to ensure the smooth rollout of the scheme across the state.
 
• **Application Process**: The registration was made accessible by setting up special **camps** at the **Gram Panchayat**, **Ward**, and **Anganwadi** levels to assist women with the **e-KYC** and application filing.
 
• **Scale of Impact**: It is estimated that more than **1.25 crore** women in **Madhya Pradesh** have been enrolled under this scheme, making it one of the largest **cash-transfer programs** for women in **India**.
 
• **Documentation Required**: Key documents required for the application include the **Samagra ID**, **Aadhaar Card**, **Mobile Number**, and a **bank account** that is enabled for **DBT**.

question: Which program was launched in 1975 to address rural poverty in India?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Twenty Point Program**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The Twenty Point Program (TPP)** was launched by the Government of India in **1975** during the tenure of Prime Minister **Indira Gandhi**. It aimed to eradicate **rural poverty**, reduce economic inequality, and improve the living conditions of the underprivileged.
 
• The program focused on areas such as **agriculture, education, employment, health, and housing**, with special emphasis on rural and marginalized communities.
 
• It also aimed to curb **corruption and improve administrative efficiency** in the delivery of public services to ensure the benefits reached the targeted sections of society.
 
• The TPP underwent revisions in subsequent years, such as in **1982, 1986, and 2006**, to align it with changing socio-economic priorities and challenges. These revisions expanded its scope and made it more effective in addressing rural poverty.
 
• The program included measures for **land reforms, welfare of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, and an increase in literacy rates**. It also emphasized **family planning, environmental protection, and the development of rural infrastructure**.
 
• The program played a crucial role in bringing attention to **inclusive growth** and ensuring that economic development reached the grassroots level, particularly in rural areas.
 
• *Hence, the Twenty Point Program was a significant initiative to address rural poverty in India.*

**Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Integrated Rural Development Program (IRDP):**

 
 
• Launched in **1978**, this program aimed to provide employment and promote self-reliance among rural poor families by offering them assets and skills.
 
• It focused on improving the economic conditions of marginalized groups like **Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and landless laborers**.
 
• However, the IRDP did not specifically address the broader socio-economic goals covered under the Twenty Point Program.
 
 
 
• **Minimum Needs Program (MNP):**
 
 
• Introduced in the **Fifth Five-Year Plan (1974-79)**, this program aimed to ensure the provision of basic amenities like **water supply, health services, education, and housing**.
 
• Though it contributed to improving living conditions, it was not directly focused on eradicating rural poverty in the same comprehensive way as the Twenty Point Program.
 
 
 
• **Employment Guarantee Scheme (EGS):**
 
 
• This was a state-level initiative introduced in **Maharashtra in 1972** to provide **employment opportunities to rural laborers** during periods of drought or unemployment.
 
• It laid the foundation for national programs like the **Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA)**, but its scope was more localized compared to the Twenty Point Program.
 
 

**Important Points__**

 
• **Objectives of the Twenty Point Program:**

 
 
• Address **poverty alleviation** and reduce economic inequalities in rural areas.
 
• Promote **agricultural growth** and ensure land reforms for equitable distribution.
 
• Improve the **living conditions of marginalized communities** by providing access to health, education, and housing.
 
 
 
• **Impact of the Program:**
 
 
• **Contributed to rural development:** Improved access to resources and services for the rural poor.
 
• **Boosted administrative reforms:** Increased efficiency in delivering welfare schemes and addressing corruption.

question: How does the Central Bank do debt monetization?

options.text: The central bank directly finances the government by purchasing its debt
The central bank increases interest rates to control inflation
The government borrows money from foreign countries
The central bank reduces the money supply in the economy

solution:
The correct answer is __**The central bank directly finances the government by purchasing its debt.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Debt monetization** refers to the process by which the **central bank** creates money to directly purchase government bonds or securities. This is a method of financing government deficits without borrowing from external sources or raising taxes.
 
• Through this mechanism, the central bank provides liquidity to the government by purchasing its debt, effectively injecting funds into the economy. This financing helps the government meet its expenditure requirements. *Hence, the correct option is the central bank directly finances the government by purchasing its debt.*
 
• Statement 2, “The central bank increases interest rates to control inflation,” is incorrect because increasing interest rates is a monetary policy tool to control inflation, not directly related to debt monetization.
 
• Statement 3, “The government borrows money from foreign countries,” is incorrect because borrowing from foreign countries involves external debt, not debt monetization.
 
• Statement 4, “The central bank reduces the money supply in the economy,” is incorrect because reducing the money supply is related to controlling inflation rather than financing government debt.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Debt monetization process:**

 
 
• In debt monetization, the central bank purchases government bonds directly, increasing the money supply in the economy. This process does not involve borrowing from commercial banks or external lenders.
 
• The new money created by the central bank is used to finance government expenditure, such as infrastructure projects, welfare programs, or other initiatives.
 
 
 
• **Features of debt monetization:**
 
 
• **Purpose:** Helps governments tackle budget deficits, especially during economic crises or emergencies.
 
• **Impact on inflation:** Debt monetization can lead to inflation if the money supply grows excessively compared to economic output.
 
• **Example:** During the **COVID-19 pandemic**, many governments relied on central banks to finance their expenditures through debt monetization.
 
 
 
• **Alternative financing mechanisms:**
 
 
• Governments can also borrow externally or raise taxes to finance deficits, but these methods may have different socio-economic impacts compared to debt monetization.
 
• Debt monetization is considered a last resort when other methods of financing are not viable or desirable.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Inflation risks:**

 
 
• Debt monetization increases the money supply, which can lead to **higher inflation** if not managed properly. This is particularly significant in developing economies.
 
• To mitigate inflation risks, central banks often monitor the economy closely and use monetary policy tools like interest rate adjustments.
 
 
 
• **Historical examples:**
 
 
• During **World War II**, countries like the **United States** and **United Kingdom** used debt monetization to finance their war efforts.
 
• In recent times, debt monetization has been used during economic crises, such as the **2008 global financial crisis** and the **COVID-19 pandemic**.

question: Name the situation when the central bank reduces interest rates to stimulate economic growth?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Expansionary monetary policy**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Expansionary monetary policy** is a macroeconomic strategy used by a **central bank** (like the **Reserve Bank of India** or the **Federal Reserve**) to stimulate the economy by increasing the **money supply**. This is primarily achieved by **reducing interest rates**, which makes borrowing cheaper for consumers and businesses. ***Hence, the correct answer is Expansionary monetary policy.***

• When the **central bank** lowers the **policy rates** (such as the **Repo Rate**), commercial banks typically lower their lending rates. This encourages **investment** and **consumption**, leading to higher **aggregate demand** and **economic growth**.

• **Contractionary monetary policy** is the opposite of expansionary policy. It involves **increasing interest rates** to reduce the money supply and slow down economic activity, usually to combat high **inflation**. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***

• **Fiscal stimulus** refers to measures taken by the **government**, such as increasing **public spending** or reducing **taxes**, to boost the economy. While it aims for growth, it is a tool of **fiscal policy**, not monetary policy managed by a central bank. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***

• **Quantitative easing** is an unconventional monetary policy where a central bank purchases **government bonds** or other financial assets from the market to inject **liquidity** directly into the economy. While it is expansionary in nature, the specific action of reducing interest rates is the standard definition of expansionary monetary policy. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)**: In **India**, the **MPC** is responsible for fixing the benchmark interest rate (**Repo Rate**). It consists of **6 members**, including the **Governor of the RBI**, and meets at least **4 times a year**.

• **Repo Rate**: This is the rate at which the **Reserve Bank of India** lends money to commercial banks in the event of any shortfall of funds. It is a key tool used to control **inflation** and **liquidity**.

• **Reverse Repo Rate**: This is the rate at which the **RBI** borrows money from commercial banks within the country. It helps the central bank to absorb excess **liquidity** from the banking system.

• **Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)**: This is a specific share of **Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL)** that banks must keep with the **RBI** in the form of **cash**. Increasing the **CRR** is a contractionary measure, while decreasing it is expansionary.

• **Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)**: This is the minimum percentage of deposits that a commercial bank has to maintain in the form of **liquid cash**, **gold**, or other **securities** before providing credit to customers.

**Important Points__**

• The primary objective of **monetary policy** in **India** is to maintain **price stability** while keeping in mind the objective of **growth**. The **RBI Act, 1934** was amended in **2016** to provide a statutory basis for the implementation of the flexible **inflation targeting** framework.

• The current **inflation target** set by the **Government of India** is **4%** with a tolerance band of **+/- 2%** (i.e., a range of **2% to 6%**).

• **Open Market Operations (OMO)**: These involve the simultaneous **purchase and sale** of **government securities** by the **RBI** to regulate the **money supply** in the economy over the long term.

• **Bank Rate**: It is the rate at which the **RBI** is ready to buy or rediscount bills of exchange or other commercial papers. It is also known as the **Discount Rate**.
</ul

question: Which of the following is another name for the Keynesian theory of demand for money?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Liquidity preference theory**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The **Keynesian theory of demand for money** is famously known as the **Liquidity Preference Theory**. It was proposed by the British economist **John Maynard Keynes** in his landmark book, **'The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money'**, published in **1936**.

• Keynes defined **liquidity preference** as the desire of the public to hold assets in the form of **cash** (the most liquid form) rather than in interest-bearing bonds or other investments.

• The theory posits that the **rate of interest** is the 'reward' for parting with liquidity for a specified period. Therefore, the demand for money is inversely related to the **interest rate**.

• Keynes identified **three distinct motives** for holding money: the **Transactionary Motive**, the **Precautionary Motive**, and the **Speculative Motive**.

• The **Transactionary Motive** and **Precautionary Motive** are primarily influenced by the **level of income** (Y), while the **Speculative Motive** is a function of the **rate of interest** (r).

• The **Cambridge theory** and **Cash balance approach** are pre-Keynesian neoclassical theories that focus on money as a store of value but do not emphasize the speculative demand as Keynes did. ***Hence, these options are incorrect.***

• The **Classical approach**, associated with economists like **Irving Fisher**, views money strictly as a **medium of exchange** and ignores the role of interest rates in determining money demand. ***Hence, this option is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**

__

• **Cambridge Theory / Cash Balance Approach:** Developed by **Alfred Marshall**, **A.C. Pigou**, and **D.H. Robertson** at the **University of Cambridge**. It is expressed by the equation M = kPY , where **'k'** represents the fraction of real income that people wish to hold in cash.

• **Classical Approach (Quantity Theory of Money):** This approach is best represented by **Irving Fisher’s Equation of Exchange**: MV = PT . Here, **M** is the money supply, **V** is the velocity of circulation, **P** is the price level, and **T** is the volume of transactions. It assumes that **V** and **T** are constant in the short run.

• **Liquidity Trap:** A specific situation in Keynesian economics where the **interest rate** is so low (near zero) that people prefer to hold all their wealth in cash rather than bonds. In this state, **monetary policy** becomes ineffective because any increase in the money supply is simply absorbed by the public as liquid holdings.

• **Speculative Demand for Money:** This is the most revolutionary part of Keynes's theory. It suggests that people hold money to avoid capital losses from holding bonds when they expect **interest rates** to rise in the future.

**Important Points__**

• **Transactionary Motive:** This refers to the demand for money to meet day-to-day expenses. Since income is received periodically (e.g., **monthly**) but expenditures occur continuously, individuals need to keep cash on hand.

• **Precautionary Motive:** This involves holding cash to provide for **unforeseen contingencies** or emergencies, such as sickness, accidents, or unemployment. Like the transactionary motive, it depends on the **income level**.

• **Relationship with Interest Rates:** In the **Liquidity Preference Theory**, when interest rates are high, the **opportunity cost** of holding cash is high, so people hold less money. Conversely, when interest rates are low, the demand for money increases.

• **Modern Developments:** Later economists like **William Baumol** and **James Tobin** refined the Keynesian model. The **Baumol-Tobin model** suggests that even the transactionary demand for money is sensitive to **interest rates**, not just income.

question: Which of the following does NOT refer to reserve money?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Savings money**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Reserve Money**, also known as **M0**, is the most fundamental measure of the money supply in **India**, representing the total monetary liabilities of the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)**.

• It is widely referred to as **Central Bank Money** because it consists of currency and deposits that are directly issued or held by the **Central Bank**. *Hence, statement 1 refers to reserve money.*

• The term **Base Money** is used because it forms the foundation upon which the entire money supply of the **economy** is built through the **banking system**. *Hence, statement 2 refers to reserve money.*

• It is also known as **High-Powered Money** because it has a multiplier effect on the total money supply; a small increase in **Reserve Money** can lead to a much larger increase in the total money supply through **bank lending**. *Hence, statement 3 refers to reserve money.*

• **Savings money**, typically referring to deposits in **savings accounts**, is a component of **Narrow Money (M1)** or **Broad Money (M3)**. It represents a liability of **commercial banks** to the public, not a liability of the **RBI**. *Hence, statement 4 does NOT refer to reserve money and is the correct answer.*

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Components of Reserve Money (M0)**: It includes **Currency in Circulation**, **Bankers' Deposits with RBI**, and **'Other' Deposits with RBI**. It is the most liquid measure of money from the perspective of the **Central Bank**.

• **Narrow Money (M1)**: This includes **Currency with the Public**, **Demand Deposits** with the banking system (such as **savings** and **current accounts**), and **'Other' Deposits with RBI**. It is highly liquid and used for immediate transactions.

• **Intermediate Money (M2)**: This is calculated as **M1** plus **Savings Deposits with Post Office Savings Banks**. This measure was more prominent before the **1998** working group recommendations.

• **Broad Money (M3)**: This is the most commonly used measure of money supply in **India**. It is calculated as **M1** plus **Time Deposits** (such as **Fixed Deposits**) with the banking system. It reflects the total volume of money available in the **economy**.

• **M4 Classification**: This includes **M3** plus **Total Deposits with Post Office Savings Organizations** (excluding **National Savings Certificates**).

**Important Points__**

• **Money Multiplier**: This is the ratio of **Broad Money (M3)** to **Reserve Money (M0)**. It indicates the capacity of the **banking system** to create money. If the **RBI** increases the **Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)**, the **money multiplier** usually decreases.

• **Monetary Policy Tools**: The **RBI** manages **Reserve Money** through various instruments like **Open Market Operations (OMO)**, **Repo Rate**, and **Reverse Repo Rate** to control **inflation** and **liquidity**.

• **Historical Context**: The current classification of money aggregates (**M0, M1, M2, M3**) was introduced based on the recommendations of the **Second Working Group on Money Supply** in **1977**.

• **Sources of Reserve Money**: The primary sources include **Net RBI Credit to the Government**, **RBI Credit to the Commercial Sector**, **RBI's Net Foreign Exchange Assets**, and **Government's Currency Liabilities to the Public**.

• **Liquidity Aggregates**: In addition to **M0-M3**, the **RBI** also tracks **L1, L2, and L3**, which include broader financial instruments like **term deposits** with financial institutions and **public deposits** with **Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs)**.
</ul

subject: GK
question: According to guidelines by the RBI (as of January 2022), how many payment banks currently active in India?
solution:
The correct answer is __**6.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• ​A committee headed by Dr Nachiket Mor in 2013 recommended setting up of 'Payments Bank' to cater to the lower-income groups and small businesses.
 
• The Reserve Bank of India has formed Payment Banks to facilitate **more transaction and savings accounts** for the underserved population who lack banking access.
 
• Payment Banks will assist those who have **little or no banking access **and **allow increased access to financial services.**
 
• **Currently,** there are **6 active payments banks in India:**
 
 
• ** Airtel Payments Bank**
 
• **India Post Pay ments Bank**
 
• **Fino Payments Bank**
 
• **Jio Payments Bank**
 
• **Paytm Payments Bank**
 
• **NSDL Payments Bank**
 
 

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] Additional Information__**

 
• **Payment Banks** are registered under the** Companies Act 2013** but are governed by a host of legislations such as **Banking Regulation Act, 1949; RBI Act, 1934; Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999, Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 etc.**
 
• Main features of Payment Banks:-
 
 
• Acceptance of demand deposit is restricted to holding a maximum balance of Rs 200,000 per individual customer. 
 
• While the payment banks can't issue credit cards, they can issue ATM and debit cards.
 
• They are not allowed to give loans. 
 
• Distribution of non-risk sharing simple financial products like mutual fund units and insurance products, etc.
 
 
• They are only allowed to invest the money received from customers' deposits into government securities.
 
 
 
• They cannot accept NRI deposits.

question: UPI is a system that powers multiple bank accounts into a single mobile application. What is the full form of UPI?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Unified Payments Interface**__.

__
 
• **Unified Payments Interface**

 
 
• Unified Payments Interface (UPI) is a system that powers multiple bank accounts into a single mobile application (of any participating bank), merging several banking features, seamless fund routing & merchant payments into one hood.
 
• It also caters to the “Peer to Peer” collect request which can be scheduled and paid as per requirement and convenience.
 
• NPCI conducted a pilot launch on 11th April 2016 by Dr Raghuram G Rajan, Governor, RBI at Mumbai.
 
• Banks have started to upload their UPI-enabled Apps on the Google Play store from 25th August 2016 onwards.
 
 
 
• **Participants in UPI**
 
 
• Payer PSP (Payment service Provider)
 
• Payee PSP
 
• Remitter Bank
 
• Beneficiary Bank
 
• NPCI (National Payments Corporation of India)
 
• Bank Account holders
 
• Merchant
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Mobile Banking**

 
 
• It refers to the use of a mobile device to carry out financial transactions anywhere.
 
• ​This service is provided by majorly all financial institutions, especially banks.
 
• Mobile banking enables customers to carry out various transactions, which may vary depending on the institutions.
 
• Mobile banking services can be categorized into, account information, transaction, investment, support service, content, and news.
 
• It can be done either through the internet or by SMS.
 
• In 2002 mobile banking was started in India by a way through SMS

subject: GK
question: Name the principle that states that as production increases, the cost per unit decreases?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Economies of scale**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Economies of scale** refer to the cost advantage that a business experiences when it increases its level of **output**. The main reason for this is the inverse relationship between the **quantity of production** and **per-unit fixed costs**. As more units are produced, **fixed costs** like **rent**, **administrative salaries**, and **machinery depreciation** are spread over a larger volume, reducing the **average cost per unit**.

• **Law of diminishing returns**: This principle states that if one **factor of production** (like labor) is increased while others (like capital/land) are held **constant**, the **marginal output** will eventually decrease. This typically occurs in the **short-run** and leads to an **increase** in **marginal cost** rather than a decrease in unit cost. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***

• **Economies of scale**: This principle specifically describes the **long-run** phenomenon where increasing the **scale of production** leads to lower **average total costs**. This is achieved through **specialization**, **bulk purchasing** of **raw materials**, and **technological improvements**. ***Hence, statement 2 is correct.***

• **Opportunity cost**: This is the value of the **next best alternative** foregone when a choice is made. It is a fundamental concept in **resource allocation** but does not describe the relationship between **production volume** and **unit cost**. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***

• **Marginal utility**: This is an **economic concept** from the consumer side, representing the **additional satisfaction** or benefit a consumer derives from consuming one **additional unit** of a good or service. It generally **decreases** as consumption increases (**Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility**). ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Internal Economies of Scale**: These are internal to the **firm** and result from its own actions.

• **Technical Economies**: Large firms can afford **expensive** and **advanced machinery** that is more efficient.

• **Managerial Economies**: Large companies can hire **specialized managers** (e.g., **HR**, **Finance**, **Marketing**) to improve **operational efficiency**.

• **Financial Economies**: Large organizations often have better **credit ratings** and can borrow **capital** at **lower interest rates** compared to small businesses.

• **Marketing Economies**: The **advertising cost** per unit is lower for a firm producing **millions of units** compared to a small-scale producer.

• **External Economies of Scale**: These occur outside of an individual firm but within the **entire industry**.

• **Infrastructure**: If an industry grows in a specific **location**, the **government** may provide better **transportation** and **communication** links, benefiting all firms in that area.

• **Specialized Labor**: A large industry attracts a **skilled workforce**, reducing **recruitment** and **training costs** for individual companies.

• **Real-World Examples**: Companies like **Walmart** and **Amazon** utilize **economies of scale** by purchasing **inventory** in massive **bulk**, which allows them to negotiate **lower prices** from **suppliers** and pass those savings to **consumers**.

**Important Points__**

• **Diseconomies of Scale**: This happens when a **firm** grows so large that **average costs** begin to **increase**. This is often due to **communication failures**, **bureaucracy**, **lack of motivation** among workers, and **coordination problems** in very large **organizations**.

• **Adam Smith**: The concept of **economies of scale** was famously illustrated by **Adam Smith** in his **1776** book, **The Wealth of Nations**, using the example of a **pin factory** where **division of labor** significantly increased **productivity**.

• **Minimum Efficient Scale (MES)**: This is the **lowest point** on the **long-run average cost curve** where a firm can produce its **output** at the **minimum possible cost**. Reaching **MES** is crucial for **competitiveness** in **global markets**.

• **Fixed vs Variable Costs**: Understanding the difference is vital. **Fixed costs** (e.g., **insurance**, **rent**) do not change with **output**, while **variable costs** (e.g., **raw materials**, **direct labor**) change in direct **proportion** to the **volume** produced.
</ul

question: Which of the following best explains the Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility?

options.text: Utility increases at an increasing rate
Total utility decreases with more consumption
Marginal utility declines with each additional unit consumed
Marginal Utility increases with Total Utility

solution:
The correct answer is __**Marginal utility declines with each additional unit consumed**__.

**__Key Points__**

• The **Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility** is a fundamental principle in **Economics** which states that as a person consumes more units of a specific commodity, the **utility** or satisfaction derived from each successive unit goes on **diminishing**.

• Statement 1: Utility increases at an increasing rate. This describes a situation of increasing marginal returns, which is the opposite of this law. In the context of consumption, the psychological intensity of desire for a good typically falls as one acquires more of it. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***

• Statement 2: Total utility decreases with more consumption. **Total Utility (TU)** only begins to decrease when **Marginal Utility (MU)** becomes **negative** (disutility). The law specifically addresses the decline in the **additional** satisfaction, not necessarily the total amount until a certain threshold is crossed. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***

• Statement 3: Marginal utility declines with each additional unit consumed. This is the core definition of the law. It suggests that the **first unit** of a good consumed provides the **highest utility**, and every **subsequent unit** provides less satisfaction than the one before it. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***

• Statement 4: Marginal Utility increases with Total Utilit

question: Consider the following two statements about types of economies:**Statement I:** In a centrally planned economy, the government takes all major decisions regarding production, exchange, and consumption of goods and services.**Statement II:** In a market economy, economic activities are restricted to physical marketplaces where buyers and sellers must interact face-to-face.**Which of the above statements is/are correct**?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Only Statement I is correct**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Statement I** is correct because in a **centrally planned economy**, also known as a **command economy**, the **government** or a **central authority** takes all major decisions regarding the **production**, **exchange**, and **consumption** of goods and services. The **state** owns the **means of production** and decides what to produce, how to produce, and for whom to produce, often prioritizing **social welfare** over individual **profit**.

• **Statement II** is incorrect because a **market economy** is not restricted to **physical marketplaces** or **face-to-face interactions**. In economic terms, a **market** is any **mechanism** or **arrangement** that brings **buyers and sellers** together to facilitate **exchange**. In the **21st century**, this includes **e-commerce platforms**, **digital stock exchanges**, and **global financial networks** where transactions occur **electronically** without any **physical contact**.

• In a **centrally planned economy**, the **allocation of resources** is determined by a **central plan** rather than the **price mechanism**. This system was historically prevalent in countries like the **Soviet Union** and is still observed in **North Korea**. **Hence, Statement I is correct.**

• In a **market economy**, economic activities are guided by the **invisible hand**, a term coined by **Adam Smith** in **1776**. Prices are determined by the forces of **supply and demand**, and the **private sector** plays the most significant role in **resource allocation**. **Hence, Statement II is incorrect.**

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Mixed Economy**: This is an **economic system** that combines elements of both **market** and **centrally planned** economies. In a **mixed economy**, both the **public sector** and the **private sector** coexist. **India** adopted a **mixed economic model** after **Independence** in **1947** to balance **economic growth** with **social justice**.

• **Laissez-faire**: This is a **French** term meaning **leave alone**. It describes an **economic environment** where **transactions** between **private parties** are free from **government intervention**, such as **regulations**, **subsidies**, or **tariffs**. It is the purest form of a **capitalist market economy**.

• **Price Mechanism**: This refers to the **system** where **price** acts as a **signal** for **producers** and **consumers**. In a **market economy**, if the **demand** for a product increases, its **price** rises, signaling **producers** to increase **production**.

• **Socialist Economy**: Often associated with **central planning**, this system emphasizes **collective ownership** and the **reduction of income inequality**. The **government** ensures that **essential goods** and **services** like **healthcare** and **education** are accessible to all **citizens**.

• **Capitalist Economy**: Characterized by **private ownership** of **capital goods** and **investments** determined by **private decision**. The **United States**, **United Kingdom**, and **Japan** are prominent **examples** of **market-driven capitalist economies**.

**Important Points__**

• **Economic Problems**: Every **economy**, regardless of its type, must solve three fundamental **economic problems**: **What to produce** (selection of goods), **How to produce** (choice of technology/labor vs. capital), and **For whom to produce** (distribution of income).

• **Global Trends**: Since the **1991 LPG Reforms** (**Liberalization, Privatization, and Globalization**), many **centrally planned economies** have transitioned toward **market-oriented** systems to improve **efficiency** and **global competitiveness**.

• **Role of Government**: Even in **market economies**, the **government** often intervenes to provide **public goods** (like **national defense**), regulate **monopolies**, and address **market failures** such as **pollution** or **economic recessions**.

• **Consumer Sovereignty**: In a **market economy**, **consumers** are considered **sovereign** because their **preferences** and **spending patterns** determine what **producers** will manufacture. In contrast, in a **centrally planned economy**, **consumer choice** is often **restricted** by **government quotas**.
</ul

subject: GK
question:
**Consider the following statements about market equilibrium:****Statement I: In equilibrium, the quantity that all firms wish to sell equals the quantity all consumers want to buy.
Statement II: Excess supply exists when the market demand is greater than the market supply.
Which of the above statements is/are correct**?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Only Statement I is correct**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Market Equilibrium** is defined as a situation in the market where the **Quantity Demanded** of a commodity is exactly equal to its **Quantity Supplied**. At this point, there is no inherent tendency for the price to change, and the market is said to be cleared.

• **Statement I** states that in equilibrium, the quantity that all firms wish to sell equals the quantity all consumers want to buy. This is the fundamental condition for equilibrium in a competitive market. At the **Equilibrium Price**, the intentions of buyers and sellers are perfectly synchronized. ***Hence, Statement I is correct.***

• **Statement II** suggests that **Excess Supply** exists when market demand is greater than market supply. This is economically inaccurate. **Excess Supply**, also known as a **Surplus**, occurs when the **Quantity Supplied** exceeds the **Quantity Demanded** at the prevailing market price. This usually happens when the market price is set above the equilibrium level.

• When the **Market Demand** is greater than the **Market Supply**, the condition is known as **Excess Demand** or a **Shortage**. This typically occurs when the market price is below the equilibrium level, leading to competition among buyers that eventually pushes the price upward. ***Hence, Statement II is incorrect.***

• The point where the **Demand Curve** and the **Supply Curve** intersect on a graph represents the **Market Equilibrium**, determining both the **Equilibrium Price** and the **Equilibrium Quantity**.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Law of Demand**: This law states that, keeping other factors constant (**Ceteris Paribus**), there is an inverse relationship between the price of a good and its **Quantity Demanded**. As the price falls, consumers are willing to buy more.

• **Law of Supply**: This law indicates a direct relationship between price and **Quantity Supplied**. As the market price increases, producers are incentivized to offer more of the good for sale to increase their **Profit Margins**.

• **Price Mechanism**: This refers to the process by which the forces of **Supply and Demand** interact to determine the prices of goods and services. It acts as a signal for resource allocation in a **Market Economy**.

• **Market Clearing**: A market is said to clear when the price adjusts such that the quantity supplied equals the quantity demanded, leaving no **Unsold Inventory** and no **Unmet Demand**.

• **Equilibrium Shifts**: Changes in external factors such as **Consumer Income**, **Technology**, **Input Prices**, or **Government Policy** can cause the demand or supply curves to shift, leading to a new **Market Equilibrium**.

**Important Points__**

• **Adam Smith**: The father of modern economics described the self-regulating nature of the market as the **Invisible Hand**. He argued that individuals pursuing their own self-interest in a free market lead to an efficient **Market Equilibrium**.

• **Alfred Marshall**: The **19th-century** economist **Alfred Marshall** is credited with standardizing the use of **Supply and Demand** diagrams to illustrate **Market Equilibrium** in his seminal work, **'Principles of Economics' (1890)**.

• **Price Floors and Ceilings**: Government interventions like a **Price Floor** (minimum price) can lead to persistent **Excess Supply**, while a **Price Ceiling** (maximum price) can lead to chronic **Excess Demand** or black markets.

• **Stability of Equilibrium**: An equilibrium is considered stable if, following a small **Displacement**, market forces (the **Price Mechanism**) push the price and quantity back toward the original equilibrium point.
</ul

question: Which of the following statements is/are **correct**?**Statement I:** Intermediate goods are goods used as inputs in the production of other goods**Statement II:** Capital goods are durable goods used in production that do not get transformed into the final product.

options.text: Both statements I and II are correct
Both statements I and II are incorrect
Statement I is correct, Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect, Statement II is correct

solution:
The correct answer is __**Both statements I and II are correct**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Intermediate goods** refer to those goods that are used as **inputs** in the **production** of other goods or services. These goods are either entirely consumed or undergo transformation during the production process within the same **accounting year**. For example, **flour** used by a **baker** to bake **bread** or **steel** used in the **manufacturing** of a **car** are intermediate goods. ***Hence, Statement I is correct.***

• **Capital goods** are **durable** goods used in the **production** process that do not get transformed into the **final product**. These are **fixed assets** of the producers, such as **machinery**, **equipment**, **tools**, and **factory buildings**. They can be used repeatedly in the production process for several years and do not lose their identity in the final output. ***Hence, Statement II is correct.***

• The classification of a good as **intermediate** or **capital** depends on its **end-use**. If a **machine** is purchased for **resale** by a dealer, it is treated as an **intermediate good**, but if it is purchased by a **factory** for use in production, it is a **capital good**.

• In **National Income** accounting, the value of **intermediate goods** is not included separately to avoid the problem of **double counting**, as their value is already merged into the value of the **final goods**. **Capital goods**, however, are included as they constitute **investment**.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Final Goods**: These are goods meant for **final consumption** by households or for **final investment** by firms. They are not intended for further **resale** or **transformation** within the same **year**.

• **Consumption Goods**: These are **final goods** that satisfy **human wants** directly. They are categorized into **durable goods** (e.g., **televisions**, **refrigerators**), **semi-durable goods** (e.g., **clothes**, **crockery**), **non-durable goods** (e.g., **milk**, **bread**), and **services** (e.g., **education**, **healthcare**).

• **Gross Investment**: This refers to the total addition made to the **capital stock** of an **economy** during a given period. It includes **Net Investment** and **Depreciation**.

• **Depreciation**: Also known as the **consumption of fixed capital**, it represents the loss in the value of **fixed assets** due to normal **wear and tear**, **accidental damages**, or **expected obsolescence** over a period of **time**.

• **Inventory**: This includes the stock of **finished goods**, **semi-finished goods**, and **raw materials** held by a **business** at a specific point in **time**. Change in **inventory** is considered a part of **investment**.

**Important Points__**

• The **Value-Added Method** of calculating **GDP** involves subtracting the value of **intermediate consumption** from the **Value of Output**. This ensures that only the **contribution** of each **production unit** is counted.

• **Capital goods** are a sub-category of **producer goods**. While all **capital goods** are **producer goods**, not all **producer goods** are **capital goods** (as raw materials are also producer goods but are not capital goods).

• In the **Indian context**, the **National Statistical Office (NSO)**, which operates under the **Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI)**, is the nodal agency for the **classification** and **estimation** of these **economic aggregates**.

• The **Circular Flow of Income** demonstrates how **expenditure** on **final goods** (including **capital goods**) becomes **income** for the **factors of production**, while **intermediate goods** remain within the **production boundary**.
</ul

subject: GK
question: Iso-utility curve is another name for ________ curve.
solution:
The correct answer is __**indifference**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• An **indifference curve** is a graph that shows various combinations of **two goods** that give a consumer the same level of **satisfaction** and **utility**. Because the consumer receives the same amount of utility at every point along the curve, it is also frequently referred to as an **Iso-utility curve** (where **Iso** means equal). ***Hence, option 4 is correct.***

• The **demand curve** represents the relationship between the **price** of a commodity and the **quantity demanded** by consumers. It typically slopes downwards, indicating that as price decreases, quantity demanded increases, but it does not represent constant utility. ***Hence, option 1 is incorrect.***

• The **supply curve** illustrates the relationship between the **market price** and the **quantity of goods** a producer is willing to supply. This curve is focused on production costs and profit margins rather than consumer satisfaction levels. ***Hence, option 2 is incorrect.***

• The **Phillips curve** is a macroeconomic concept that describes the inverse relationship between the rate of **unemployment** and the rate of **inflation** in an economy. It has no direct relation to microeconomic consumer utility theories. ***Hence, option 3 is incorrect.***

• The concept of the **indifference curve** was popularized by economists **J.R. Hicks** and **R.G.D. Allen** in **1934**. It forms the basis of **Ordinal Utility Theory**, which assumes that utility cannot be measured in exact numbers but can be ranked in order of preference.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Properties of Indifference Curves**: These curves are generally **downward sloping** from left to right, **convex to the origin**, and **never intersect** each other. A higher indifference curve indicates a **higher level of satisfaction**.

• **Marginal Rate of Substitution (MRS)**: This is the rate at which a consumer is willing to trade one good for another while maintaining the same level of utility. The **MRS** is the **slope** of the indifference curve, and it typically diminishes as the consumer moves down the curve, which explains the **convexity** of the curve.

• **Indifference Map**: An **indifference map** is a collection of multiple indifference curves on a single graph. It provides a complete picture of a consumer's **preferences** for different combinations of goods.

• **Assumptions of the Theory**: The analysis assumes **rationality** (the consumer seeks to maximize utility), **transitivity** (if A is preferred to B and B to C, then A is preferred to C), and **non-satiety** (more of a good is always preferred to less).

• **Budget Line**: This represents the **income constraint** of the consumer. It shows all combinations of two goods that a consumer can afford given their **total income** and the **market prices** of the goods.

**Important Points__**

• **Consumer Equilibrium**: A consumer is said to be in **equilibrium** when they reach the highest possible indifference curve given their **budget line**. This occurs at the point of **tangency** where the slope of the indifference curve (**MRS**) equals the slope of the budget line (**Price Ratio**).

• **Cardinal vs. Ordinal Utility**: **Alfred Marshall** proposed **Cardinal Utility**, suggesting utility could be measured in **utils**. However, the **Iso-utility/Indifference curve** approach belongs to the **Ordinalist school**, which argues that consumers only rank their preferences.

• **Exceptions to Convexity**: While most indifference curves are convex, they can be **straight lines** in the case of **perfect substitutes** or **L-shaped** (right-angled) in the case of **perfect complements**, such as left and right shoes.
</ul

subject: GK
question: The concept of "human development ethics" challenges the Human Development Index (HDI) for its:

options.text: Implicit assumptions about universal values and development goals.

solution:
The correct answer is __**Implicit assumptions about universal values and development goals**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Human development ethics** is a field of study that evaluates the normative foundations, goals, and procedures of development. It challenges the **Human Development Index (HDI)** primarily because the index relies on **implicit assumptions about universal values**. It suggests that the three dimensions of the **HDI** (health, education, and income) are the only or most important goals for all people, regardless of their cultural or social context. *Hence, statement 1 is correct.*

• The **HDI** was actually created to counter the **over-reliance on economic data** like **Gross Domestic Product (GDP)**. While it still includes **Gross National Income (GNI)**, its purpose was to broaden the definition of development. Therefore, the ethical challenge is not about the reliance on economic data itself, but how that data is weighted against other values. *Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.*

• **Military strength indicators** are generally excluded from human development frameworks because the focus is on **human-centric well-being** rather than state power. Human development ethics does not typically argue for the inclusion of military data, as military spending is often seen as a **diversion of resources** from social sectors. *Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.*

• The **lack of international trade analysis** is a critique related to **macroeconomics** or **dependency theory**, but it is not the core concern of **human development ethics**, which focuses on the **capabilities** and **freedoms** of individuals. *Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.*

• Ethicists argue that by using a **standardized metric**, the **HDI** might ignore the **plurality of cultures** and the importance of **local agency** in defining what a meaningful life looks like.

**Additional Information__**
__

• The **Human Development Index (HDI)** was introduced in **1990** by the **United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)** as a revolutionary way to measure national progress.

• The index was the brainchild of **Mahbub ul Haq**, a Pakistani economist, and **Amartya Sen**, an Indian Nobel laureate, who wanted to shift the focus of development economics from **national income accounting** to **people-centered policies**.

• The **HDI** is calculated based on three key dimensions:

• **Health:** Measured by **Life Expectancy at Birth**.

• **Education:** Measured by **Mean Years of Schooling** for adults and **Expected Years of Schooling** for children.

• **Standard of Living:** Measured by **GNI per capita** adjusted for **Purchasing Power Parity (PPP)**.

• The theoretical foundation of the **HDI** is the **Capability Approach**. This approach argues that the objective of development is to expand the **real freedoms** that people enjoy—their **capabilities** to lead the lives they have reason to value.

• The **UNDP** releases the **Human Development Report (HDR)** annually, which ranks countries into four tiers: **Very High**, **High**, **Medium**, and **Low** human development.

**Important Points__**

• To address various critiques, the **UNDP** has introduced supplementary indices over the years, such as the **Inequality-adjusted HDI (IHDI)** in **2010**, which discounts the **HDI** value according to the level of inequality in a country.

• The **Gender Inequality Index (GII)** and the **Gender Development Index (GDI)** were established to highlight disparities between men and women in **reproductive health**, **empowerment**, and **labor market participation**.

• In **2020**, the **Planetary pressures-adjusted HDI (PHDI)** was launched. This index accounts for a countrys **carbon dioxide emissions** and **material footprint**, addressing the ethical need for **environmental sustainability** in development.

• A major point in **human development ethics** is **Human Agency**. It emphasizes that individuals should not just be beneficiaries of **health** and **education** but should be **active participants** in the **democratic processes** that determine development priorities.

• Critics often point out that the **HDI** fails to capture **political freedom**, **human rights**, and **subjective well-being** (happiness), which are essential components of the **human experience**.

subject: GK
question: Which of the following is NOT an exception to the 'Law of Demand'?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Substitute goods**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Law of Demand**, popularized by **Alfred Marshall** in **1890**, states that there is an **inverse relationship** between the **price** of a good and its **quantity demanded**, assuming all other factors remain constant.
 
• **Giffen goods** are a unique category of **inferior goods** (such as **staple foods** like **bread** or **potatoes**) where the **income effect** is stronger than the **substitution effect**. When the **price** of a Giffen good **rises**, consumers, being too poor to afford expensive substitutes, actually buy more of the staple good. ***Hence, statement A is an exception to the law.***
 
• **Conspicuous goods**, also known as **Veblen goods** named after **Thorstein Veblen**, are **luxury items** like **designer watches**, **luxury cars**, or **diamonds**. These goods are purchased for **status** or **snob appeal**; as their **price increases**, they become more **exclusive** and **desirable**, leading to higher **demand**. ***Hence, statement B is an exception to the law.***
 
• **Speculative goods** involve assets where buyers **anticipate** future **price movements**. In **stock markets** or **real estate**, if the **price** of an asset **rises**, investors often buy more of it expecting the **price** to rise further in the **future** to secure a **profit**. ***Hence, statement C is an exception to the law.***
 
• **Substitute goods** are products that can replace each other, such as **Tea and Coffee** or **Pepsi and Coca-Cola**. While the **price** of one substitute affects the **demand** for another (**positive cross-price elasticity**), each good individually follows the standard **Law of Demand**; if the **price** of **Tea** rises, the **quantity demanded** for **Tea** itself will **fall**. ***Hence, statement D is NOT an exception to the law.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Cross-Price Elasticity**: This measures the **responsiveness** of the **quantity demanded** for one good to a **change in the price** of another good. For **substitute goods**, this value is **positive**, meaning an **increase** in the **price** of **Coffee** leads to an **increase** in the **demand** for **Tea**.
 
• **Veblen Effect**: First identified in the **1899** book **"The Theory of the Leisure Class"**, it describes **conspicuous consumption** where **utility** is derived from the **exhibit of wealth** rather than the **functional use** of the product.
 
• **Giffen Paradox**: Observed by **Sir Robert Giffen** during the **19th century** in **Ireland**, he noticed that a rise in the **price** of **potatoes** caused the **poor** to consume more of them because they had to cut back on **expensive meat** to afford the **basic staple**.
 
• **Complementary Goods**: These are goods used together, such as **Cars and Petrol** or **Printers and Ink Cartridges**. Unlike substitutes, they have a **negative cross-price elasticity**; if the **price** of **petrol** rises, the **demand** for **cars** typically **decreases**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Demand Curve Shape**: While a **normal demand curve** slopes **downward from left to right**, the demand curve for **exceptions** like **Giffen** or **Veblen goods** slopes **upward**, indicating a **direct relationship** between **price** and **quantity**.
 
• **Consumer Ignorance**: Sometimes, **consumers** judge the **quality** of a product by its **price**. They may buy more of a **high-priced product** assuming it is of **superior quality**, which acts as another **psychological exception** to the law.
 
• **Emergency Situations**: During times of **war**, **famine**, or **pandemics**, people tend to **hoard goods** even when **prices** are **skyrocketing** due to **fear of shortage**, bypassing the traditional **Law of Demand**.
 
• **Necessary Goods**: For **life-saving medicines** or **salt**, the **quantity demanded** remains relatively **stable** regardless of **price changes**, showing **low price elasticity**.
</ul

• **Substitute goods** are products that serve a similar purpose and can be used in place of one another, such as **tea and coffee** or **Pepsi and Coca-Cola**.
 
• When the price of a product increases, its **quantity demanded** decreases according to the law of demand; however, the demand for its **substitute good** increases as consumers seek cheaper alternatives.
 
• This movement does not represent an exception to the law of demand because the **price-demand relationship** for the specific good itself remains negative; the change in substitute demand is considered a **shift in the demand curve** due to a change in the price of **related goods**.
 
• The elasticity of substitution measures how easily a consumer can switch between these goods, which is a core determinant of market demand rather than an anomaly.

• **Giffen Goods**:

 
 
• These are **non-luxury, inferior goods** that lack close substitutes, named after **Sir Robert Giffen**.
 
• For these goods, the **income effect** outweighs the **substitution effect**, leading to an increase in demand even when prices rise, violating the law of demand.
 
 
 
• **Conspicuous Goods**:
 
 
• Also known as **Veblen goods**, these are items consumed to demonstrate **wealth or social status**, such as **diamond jewelry** or **luxury sports cars**.
 
• Demand for these goods often increases as the price rises because the **prestige value** associated with the high price makes them more attractive to certain consumers.
 
 
 
• **Speculative Goods**:
 
 
• This exception occurs in markets like **stocks**, **gold**, or **real estate** where price increases lead to expectations of further hikes.
 
• Consumers buy more at higher prices to avoid paying even higher prices in the future or to make a profit, creating a **positive price-demand correlation**.

subject: GK
question: What does HDI stand for?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Human Development Index**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **HDI** stands for **Human Development Index**, which is a statistical composite index used to measure the average achievements of a country in three basic dimensions of human development. ***Hence, the correct answer is Human Development Index.***

• The concept of the **Human Development Index** was created by the Pakistani economist **Mahbub ul Haq** and the Indian economist **Amartya Sen** in **1990**.

• It is published annually by the **United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)** as part of the **Human Development Report (HDR)**.

• The index was designed to shift the focus of development economics from national income accounting to people-centered policies, emphasizing that people and their capabilities should be the ultimate criteria for assessing the development of a country.

• It ranks countries into four levels of human development: **Very High**, **High**, **Medium**, and **Low** based on their cumulative score across various indicators.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Health Dimension**: This is assessed by **Life Expectancy at birth**, which is the average number of years a person is expected to live based on current mortality rates. It serves as a proxy for the overall health and nutrition status of a population.

• **Education Dimension**: This is calculated using two indicators: **Mean years of schooling** (the average number of years of education received by people ages **25** and older) and **Expected years of schooling** (the total number of years of schooling that a child of school-entry age can expect to receive).

• **Standard of Living**: This is assessed by **Gross National Income (GNI) per capita** at **Purchasing Power Parity (PPP)** in international **US Dollars**. This measure accounts for the differences in the cost of living and inflation between countries.

• The **HDI** score is a value between **0 and 1**. A score closer to **1** indicates a higher level of development, while a score closer to **0** indicates a lower level.

• The **UNDP** uses the **geometric mean** of the three normalized dimension indices to calculate the final **HDI** value, ensuring that a low achievement in one dimension is not linearly compensated by a high achievement in another.

**Important Points__**

• In the latest **Human Development Report 2023-24**, **India** was ranked **134th** out of **193 countries** with an **HDI** value of **0.644**, placing it in the **Medium** human development category.

• **Switzerland**, **Norway**, and **Iceland** consistently rank at the top of the global **Human Development Index** due to their high life expectancy and robust social security systems.

• The **UNDP** also tracks other vital indices like the **Gender Inequality Index (GII)**, where **India** ranked **108th** in the **2022** report, showing improvement in gender parity.

• The **Inequality-adjusted Human Development Index (IHDI)** accounts for the distribution of achievements within a population; the difference between the **HDI** and **IHDI** represents the loss in human development due to inequality.

• The **Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI)** complements the **HDI** by identifying overlapping deprivations at the household and individual level in health, education, and living standards, providing a more comprehensive view of poverty than income alone.
</ul

subject: GK
question: What is the term for the situation where demand exceeds supply in a market?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Shortage**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• A **Shortage**, also referred to as **excess demand**, is an economic state where the **quantity demanded** by consumers for a specific product or service is significantly higher than the **quantity supplied** by producers at the current **market price**. ***Hence, the correct answer is Shortage.***

• In a **free market**, a shortage typically occurs when the price of an item is set **below the equilibrium level**. Because the price is low, more people want to buy the good, but businesses find it less profitable to produce or sell it, creating a **market imbalance**. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***

• A **Surplus** is the exact opposite of a shortage; it occurs when the **quantity supplied** exceeds the **quantity demanded**, usually because the price is **above the equilibrium point**. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***

• **Equilibrium** is the condition where **market forces** are balanced. At the **equilibrium price**, the amount of goods buyers want to buy is exactly equal to the amount of goods sellers want to sell, resulting in no **shortage** or **surplus**. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***

• **Deflation** refers to a general **decrease in the price level** of goods and services across an entire economy over a specific period. It is a **macroeconomic** phenomenon related to the **purchasing power** of money rather than a specific supply-demand mismatch in a single market. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Price Ceilings and Shortages**: Governments sometimes implement a **Price Ceiling**, which is a **legal maximum price**. If this ceiling is set below the **natural equilibrium price**, it leads to a persistent **shortage** because prices cannot rise to clear the market. A classic example is **Rent Control** in cities like **New York** or **Mumbai**.

• **Market Mechanisms**: According to the **Law of Supply and Demand**, if a shortage exists, **market competition** among buyers will naturally drive the price up. As the price increases, the **quantity demanded** decreases and the **quantity supplied** increases until they meet at **equilibrium**.

• **Causes of Shortages**: Shortages can be caused by various factors including **supply chain disruptions**, **natural disasters**, **government regulations**, or sudden **shifts in consumer preferences**. For instance, the **Global Chip Shortage** that began in **2020** severely impacted the **automobile** and **electronics industries**.

• **Economic Impacts**: When a **shortage** occurs, it often leads to **rationing**, **long waiting lines** (queues), and the potential development of **black markets** where goods are traded illegally at prices much higher than the **official rate**.

• **Inventory Management**: In the **retail sector**, a shortage is often called a **stockout**. Modern businesses use **Just-in-Time (JIT)** inventory systems to keep costs low, but this makes them more vulnerable to **shortages** if there is a sudden **logistical delay** or **demand spike**.

**Important Points__**

• **Invisible Hand**: The concept introduced by **Adam Smith** in **1776** suggests that the **price mechanism** acts as an invisible hand that resolves **shortages** and **surpluses** automatically in a **laissez-faire** economy.

• **Elasticity**: The duration and severity of a **shortage** often depend on the **Price Elasticity of Demand**. If a good is a **necessity** (like medicine or basic food), a shortage can lead to drastic **price hikes** because consumers cannot easily reduce their consumption.

• **Historical Example**: The **1973 Oil Crisis** is a famous example of a global **shortage**. Following an **embargo** by **OPEC**, the supply of **petroleum** dropped sharply, leading to massive **price increases** and **fuel rationing** in many **Western countries**.
</ul
