question: The National Rural Employment Programme (NREP) was initiated in the ________ Five-Year Plan.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Sixth Five-Year Plan**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **National Rural Employment Programme (NREP)** was launched in **October 1980** during the **Sixth Five-Year Plan**. It was designed to replace the earlier **Food for Work Programme** to streamline employment generation in rural sectors.
 
• The primary objective of the **NREP** was to generate additional gainful employment for the unemployed and underemployed persons in the rural areas of **India**.
 
• This programme aimed at the creation of **durable community assets** for strengthening the rural infrastructure, such as **rural roads**, **school buildings**, and **panchayat ghars**.
 
• The funding for the **National Rural Employment Programme** was shared between the **Central Government** and the **State Governments** on a **50:50** basis.
 
• Under this initiative, a specific target was set to generate **300 to 400 million mandays** of employment per annum for the rural poor to ensure food security and income stability.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Sixth Five-Year Plan (1980–1985):**
 
 
• The **Sixth Five-Year Plan** marked the beginning of economic liberalization in **India** and focused heavily on **poverty alleviation** and **economic self-reliance**.
 
• The plan was launched under the leadership of **Prime Minister Indira Gandhi** with a target growth rate of **5.2%**, but it successfully achieved a growth rate of **5.7%**.
 
• It emphasized **family planning** to control the growing **population** and invested significantly in the **energy sector** and **agriculture**.
 
 
 
• **Evolution of Employment Schemes:**
 
 
• In **1983**, during the same plan period, the **Rural Landless Employment Guarantee Programme (RLEGP)** was introduced to provide a guarantee of employment to at least one member of every landless household for up to **100 days** in a **year**.
 
• Later, on **April 1, 1989**, both **NREP** and **RLEGP** were merged to form the **Jawahar Rozgar Yojana (JRY)**, which became a major flagship employment scheme.
 
 
 
• **Fifth Five-Year Plan (1974–1978):**
 
 
• This plan focused on **'Garibi Hatao'** (Removal of Poverty) and **Justice**. It was terminated **one year** early in **1978** by the **Janata Party government**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **Integrated Rural Development Programme (IRDP)** was another crucial scheme launched in **1980** to provide self-employment opportunities to the rural poor through **subsidies** and **bank loans**.
 
• The **National Rural Employment Programme** prioritized the **Scheduled Castes (SC)** and **Scheduled Tribes (ST)** for employment, ensuring that a portion of the funds was reserved for their **socio-economic development**.
 
• The **Sixth Plan** is often cited as the **'Plan of Infrastructure'** as it significantly expanded **irrigation projects** and **national highways** across the **country**.
 
• Currently, the spirit of these early employment programmes is carried forward by the **Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA)**, which was enacted in **2005** to provide a legal **Right to Work**.

question: How is the data for the Happiness Index collected?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Through self-reported surveys**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The data for the **World Happiness Index** is primarily collected through **self-reported surveys** conducted by the **Gallup World Poll**. This poll samples approximately **1,000** individuals from nearly every country annually to assess their **subjective well-being**. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***
 
• The core of the survey is the **Cantril Ladder**, where respondents are asked to think of a ladder, with the best possible life for them being a **10** and the worst possible life being a **0**. They then rate their own current lives on that **0 to 10 scale**.
 
• The index does not rely on **satellite images** to determine happiness, as these are typically used for environmental or geographical data rather than human emotion or life satisfaction. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• While **GDP per capita** is one of the six variables used to explain the variation in happiness across countries, the index is not calculated **by measuring GDP only**. It integrates socio-economic factors with individual perceptions. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• The report does not determine rankings **by analyzing internet usage**. While digital data can provide insights into behavior, the formal **World Happiness Report** methodology relies on direct human responses regarding their quality of life. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **The World Happiness Report (WHR)**: This is an annual publication by the **United Nations Sustainable Development Solutions Network (SDSN)**. It was first released in **2012** following the **UN High-Level Meeting** on "Happiness and Well-Being: Defining a New Economic Paradigm."
 
• **Six Key Variables**: To explain the differences in reported happiness levels, researchers analyze six factors: **GDP per capita**, **Social support** (having someone to count on), **Healthy life expectancy**, **Freedom to make life choices**, **Generosity** (donations to charity), and **Perceptions of corruption**.
 
• **Gross National Happiness (GNH)**: The concept of measuring happiness instead of just economic growth originated in **Bhutan**. In **1972**, the 4th King of Bhutan, **Jigme Singye Wangchuck**, declared that "Gross National Happiness is more important than Gross Domestic Product."
 
• **Top Performing Countries**: Nordic countries consistently dominate the top of the rankings. **Finland** has been ranked as the happiest country in the world for **seven consecutive years** as of the **2024** report. Other high-ranking nations include **Denmark**, **Iceland**, and **Sweden**.
 
• **India's Ranking**: In recent years, **India** has generally ranked lower on the index compared to many of its neighbors. In the **2024** report, India was ranked **126th** out of 143 countries surveyed.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Release Date**: The report is typically released annually on **March 20th**, which is recognized by the **United Nations** as the **International Day of Happiness**.
 
• **Methodology Stability**: To ensure data reliability and reduce the impact of outliers or temporary events, the report uses a **three-year average** of the **Gallup World Poll** data for its final rankings.
 
• **Dystopia**: The report uses a hypothetical country called **Dystopia**, representing the lowest national averages for each of the six key variables. This serves as a **regression benchmark** to compare how much each factor contributes to a real country's happiness score.
 
• **Subjective vs. Objective**: The primary rank is strictly **subjective** (based on what people say), while the six variables used for explanation are **objective** (based on national statistics and survey data on specific behaviors).
</ul

subject: GK
question: Which of the following is NOT a reason for a fiscal deficit?

options.text: High government expenditure on welfare schemes
Surplus in the balance of payments

solution:
The correct answer is __**Surplus in the balance of payments**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Fiscal Deficit** is defined as the excess of the **government's total expenditure** over its **total revenue**, excluding **borrowings**, during a specific **financial year**. It indicates the total **borrowing requirements** of the government.
 
• **High government expenditure on welfare schemes:** When the **government** increases spending on **social welfare**, **subsidies**, and **infrastructure** without a corresponding increase in **revenue**, the gap between income and expenditure widens. ***Hence, this statement is a correct reason for a fiscal deficit.***
 
• **Reduction in tax revenue:** A decline in **tax collection**, whether due to **economic slowdown**, **tax evasion**, or **tax cuts** implemented by the **Ministry of Finance**, reduces the **government's income**. This shortfall directly contributes to the **budgetary gap**. ***Hence, this statement is a correct reason for a fiscal deficit.***
 
• **Increase in public borrowings:** While **borrowing** is a way to finance a **deficit**, high levels of **public debt** lead to massive **interest payments** in subsequent years. These interest payments are a form of **revenue expenditure** that further inflates the **fiscal deficit**. ***Hence, this statement is a correct reason for a fiscal deficit.***
 
• **Surplus in the balance of payments:** This occurs when a **country's** total **exports** and **capital inflows** exceed its **imports** and **capital outflows**. This is an **international trade** metric and does not represent a shortfall in the **domestic budget** of the **government**. ***Hence, this statement is NOT a reason for a fiscal deficit.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Revenue Deficit:** This refers to the excess of **revenue expenditure** over **revenue receipts**. It signifies that the **government** is unable to cover its **day-to-day operational expenses** (like salaries and pensions) from its regular income.
 
• **Primary Deficit:** This is the **Fiscal Deficit** minus the **interest payments** on previous **borrowings**. It shows how much the **government** needs to borrow to meet its **current year** expenses, excluding the burden of **past debt**.
 
• **Fiscal Policy:** In **India**, fiscal policy is the tool used by the **Union Government** to monitor and influence the **economy** by adjusting **spending levels** and **tax rates**. It is managed primarily through the **Union Budget** presented every **February**.
 
• **Sources of Revenue:** The **government** earns through **tax revenue** (Direct taxes like **Income Tax** and **Corporate Tax**, and Indirect taxes like **GST**) and **non-tax revenue** (interest receipts, **dividends** from **PSUs**, and **external grants**).
 
• **Capital Receipts:** These include **recoveries of loans**, **disinvestment** of **Public Sector Undertakings**, and **borrowings**. Unlike **revenue receipts**, these either create a **liability** or reduce the **assets** of the **government**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **FRBM Act, 2003:** The **Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act** was enacted to ensure **inter-generational equity** in **fiscal management** and long-term **macro-economic stability**. It aimed to limit the **fiscal deficit** to **3% of the GDP**.
 
• **Deficit Financing:** To bridge the **fiscal gap**, the **government** may borrow from the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** or the **public**. If the **RBI** prints new **currency** to fund the **deficit**, it can lead to high **inflation** in the **economy**.
 
• **Impact of High Deficit:** Persistent **fiscal deficits** can lead to a **debt trap**, **crowding out** of **private investment** (as the **government** consumes most of the **market credit**), and a decrease in the **sovereign credit rating** of the **country**.
 
• **Grants-in-aid:** Under **Article 275** of the **Constitution of India**, the **Union** provides **grants** to **states**, which is a major **expenditure** item that impacts the **fiscal deficit** of the **Central Government**.
</ul

question: What is the term for the economic measure that tracks changes in the price level of a basket of goods and services?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Consumer Price Index (CPI)**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• It reflects the **purchasing power of a country's currency** and is a crucial measure of **inflation**.
 
• It is calculated by taking the price of a selected set of goods and services (referred to as the **basket**) in a base year, then comparing it to the prices in the current year.
 
• CPI is also used as a tool to protect consumers from the adverse effects of inflation and to ensure their purchasing power is maintained.

**Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Consumer Price Index (CPI):**

 
 
• In **India**, CPI is released by the **National Statistical Office (NSO)** under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI). It is reported on a monthly basis.
 
• **Gross Domestic Product (GDP):** GDP measures the **total monetary value of all goods and services** produced within a country's borders in a specific period, not the price levels or inflation. It is an indicator of economic performance, not the cost of living.
 
• **Balance of Payments (BoP):** BoP is a record of all monetary transactions between residents of a country and the rest of the world. It measures international trade and financial flows, not changes in domestic price levels.
 
 
 
• **Applications of CPI:**
 
 
• It helps central banks, such as the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)**, to formulate **monetary policies** by setting targets for inflation control.
 
• 
 
• 
• CPI data is also used in determining the cost-of-living adjustments for **social security benefits** and other government programs.
 
 

**Important Points__**

 
• **Base Year:** The base year for CPI calculation in India is **2012**. It serves as the reference point to compare current price levels.
 
• **Core Inflation:** CPI is used to calculate **core inflation**, which excludes volatile components like food and energy prices to understand the underlying inflation trend.
 
• **Global Use:** CPI is used internationally by organizations like the **International Monetary Fund (IMF)** and the **World Bank** to compare price levels and inflation rates across countries.

question: Which is the First country to introduce the idea of prioritizing happiness over economic growth?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Bhutan**__.

**__Key Points__**

• **Bhutan** is the first and only country in the world to officially prioritize **Gross National Happiness (GNH)** over **Gross Domestic Product (GDP)** as a measure of national progress.

• The concept of **Gross National Happiness** was coined by the **Fourth King of Bhutan, Jigme Singye Wangchuck**, in **1972**. He famously declared that **'Gross National Happiness is more important than Gross Domestic Product'**.

• The philosophy of **GNH** is based on the premise that true development of a society takes place when material and spiritual development occur side by side to complement and reinforce each other.

• The **GNH** framework is anchored by **four pillars**: **Sustainable and Equitable Socio-Economic Development**, **Environmental Conservation**, **Preservation and Promotion of Culture**, and **Good Governance**.

question: Suppose a firm increases all inputs by 50% and its output increases by 75%. What type of return to scale is this?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Increasing Returns to Scale**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Returns to Scale** refers to the change in output resulting from proportional changes in all inputs. It is a concept widely used in economics and production theory.
 
• In the given scenario, the firm increases its inputs (labor, capital, etc.) by **50%**, but the output increases by **75%**. This indicates that the output increases by a larger percentage than the input. Hence, the firm exhibits **Increasing Returns to Scale**.
 
• **Increasing Returns to Scale** occur when the proportional increase in output is greater than the proportional increase in inputs. It usually happens due to factors like better utilization of resources, specialization, or economies of scale. *Hence, the statement is correct.*
 
• It is important to distinguish between the three main types of returns to scale: **Constant Returns to Scale**, **Increasing Returns to Scale**, and **Decreasing Returns to Scale**. These help analyze the efficiency of production systems.
 
• The firm does not exhibit **Constant Returns to Scale**, as the output increase is not proportional to the input increase. Similarly, it does not exhibit **Decreasing Returns to Scale**, where the output increase would be less than the input increase. *Hence, the correct answer is Increasing Returns to Scale.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Types of Returns to Scale:**

 
 
• **Constant Returns to Scale:** When the output increases in the same proportion as the input increase. For example, if inputs are increased by **50%**, and output also increases by **50%**.
 
• **Increasing Returns to Scale:** When the output increases by a greater proportion than the input increase. It typically occurs due to advantages like specialization, reduced average costs, or efficient resource allocation.
 
• **Decreasing Returns to Scale:** When the output increases by a smaller proportion than the input increase. This can happen due to inefficiencies or overutilization of resources.
 
 
 
• **Factors Influencing Returns to Scale:**
 
 
• **Economies of Scale:** Larger production leads to reduced average costs, contributing to Increasing Returns to Scale.
 
• **Specialization:** Efficient division of labor and resource allocation can enhance productivity, leading to Increasing Returns to Scale.
 
• **Technological Advancements:** Improved technologies can result in higher output from the same level of inputs.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Returns to Scale:**
 
 
• Used in analyzing production systems in industries like manufacturing, agriculture, and services.
 
• Helps businesses determine the optimal scale of operation to maximize efficiency.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Characteristics:**

 
 
• **Increasing Returns to Scale** often occur at the initial stages of production when economies of scale are significant.
 
• As production scales up, firms may transition to **Constant** or **Decreasing Returns to Scale** due to factors like resource limitations or inefficiencies.
 
 
 
• **Real-World Example:**
 
 
• Large-scale industries, such as automobile manufacturing, often experience **Increasing Returns to Scale** due to high initial fixed costs and efficient production systems.
 
• In agriculture, technological advancements like modern irrigation systems can lead to **Increasing Returns to Scale**.

Reason (R): Privatization reduced government control and improved productivity in public enterprises.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Assertion (A):** The **New Economic Policy of 1991** led to more efficient and competitive markets in India. This is **correct**. The 1991 reforms introduced measures such as **liberalization, privatization, and globalization**, which reduced trade barriers and restrictions, opening up the economy to competition and efficiency.
 
• **Reason (R):** Privatization reduced government control and improved productivity in public enterprises. This is also **correct**. Privatization allowed private sectors to take over previously government-controlled businesses, leading to better management practices, increased productivity, and higher efficiency.
 
• The **Reason (R)** explains the **Assertion (A)** accurately. Privatization was a significant part of the 1991 reforms that contributed to the creation of competitive markets and improved the overall economic structure. *Hence, Option 1 is correct.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **New Economic Policy of 1991:**

 
 
• Introduced by the **Government of India** under **Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao** and **Finance Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh**.
 
• Focused on three pillars: **liberalization** (removal of restrictions and licensing), **privatization** (transfer of ownership from public to private), and **globalization** (integration with the global economy).
 
• Aimed to address the **balance of payments crisis** and economic stagnation, and to improve market efficiency.
 
• Key reforms included the abolition of the **License Raj**, reduction of tariffs, removal of trade barriers, and encouragement of foreign investments.
 
 
 
• **Privatization:**
 
 
• Involved transferring ownership of public sector enterprises to private entities to enhance efficiency and productivity.
 
• Led to better management practices and reduced bureaucratic inefficiencies.
 
• Examples: Disinvestment of companies like **Air India**, **VSNL**, and **Maruti Suzuki**.
 
 
 
• **Impact of New Economic Policy:**
 
 
• **Economic growth:** India's GDP grew significantly after the reforms.
 
• **Foreign investment:** Increased Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) inflows.
 
• **Competitive markets:** Removal of monopolies led to a more competitive environment.
 
• **Global integration:** India became a significant player in the global market.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key features of 1991 reforms:**

 
 
• **Liberalization:** Removed licensing and regulatory hurdles for businesses.
 
• **Privatization:** Focused on disinvesting public enterprises to improve efficiency.
 
• **Globalization:** Opened up the economy to foreign investment and trade.
 
 
 
• **Challenges and criticisms:**
 
 
• **Income inequality:** Critics argue that the reforms widened the gap between rich and poor.
 
• **Dependency on foreign investment:** Concerns over excessive reliance on foreign capital.
 
• **Environmental impact:** Increased industrialization led to ecological concerns.

• Goods and services tax (GST) is a tax levied when a consumer buys a good or service.
 
• It is meant to be a single, comprehensive tax that will subsume all the other smaller indirect taxes on consumption like service tax, etc.
 
• It is a single tax on the supply of goods and services, right from the manufacturer to the end consumer.
 
• This is how it is done in most developed countries.
 
• More than 160 countries have implemented this system of taxation.
 
• GST does not tax or get into specific commodities.

question: Which of the following is NOT included in the domain of Psychological Well-Being?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Pollution**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Psychological Well-Being (PWB)** is a multi-dimensional concept that refers to the **internal state** of a person, including their cognitive and emotional evaluations of their life as a whole.
 
• **Sense of purpose** is a core domain of psychological well-being as it provides **meaning** and a feeling that one's life has a **direction** and **goals**. *Hence, this is a part of the domain.*
 
• **Optimism** reflects a **positive outlook** and the expectation of good outcomes in the future, which is fundamental to **resilience** and emotional stability. *Hence, this is a part of the domain.*
 
• **Pollution** is an **external environmental factor** that belongs to the study of **Environmental Science** or **Public Health**; while it can negatively affect mental health, it is not an intrinsic psychological domain. *Hence, statement 3 is the correct choice as it is NOT included in the domain.*
 
• **Feeling of accomplishment** (or Achievement) is the satisfaction derived from **reaching milestones** or succeeding in tasks, which is a key pillar in psychological frameworks like the **PERMA model**. *Hence, this is a part of the domain.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Carol Ryff’s Six-Factor Model**: Developed in **1989**, this model is one of the most scientifically validated frameworks for measuring **Psychological Well-Being**. It includes **Self-acceptance**, **Personal growth**, **Purpose in life**, **Environmental mastery**, **Autonomy**, and **Positive relations with others**.
 
• **The PERMA Model**: Introduced by **Martin Seligman** (the founder of **Positive Psychology**) in his **2011** book *Flourish*, it outlines five elements of well-being: **Positive Emotion**, **Engagement**, **Relationships**, **Meaning**, and **Accomplishment**.
 
• **Subjective Well-Being (SWB) vs. PWB**: **Subjective Well-Being** (often termed **Hedonic** well-being) focuses on **happiness** and the balance of pleasure over pain, whereas **Psychological Well-Being** (**Eudaimonic** well-being) focuses on **human potential** and living a meaningful life.
 
• **Environmental Determinants**: While **Pollution** (including **air**, **noise**, and **water** pollution) is a significant **determinant** of mental health outcomes such as **Anxiety** or **Depression**, it is classified as a **stressor** or a **contextual factor** rather than a psychological domain itself.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **World Health Organization (WHO) Definition**: The **WHO** defines health as a state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity. This highlights that **Well-Being** is a proactive state.
 
• **Biological Factors**: Psychological well-being is often linked to the regulation of **neurotransmitters** such as **Serotonin**, **Dopamine**, and **Oxytocin**, which facilitate feelings of **reward**, **social bonding**, and **happiness**.
 
• **Demographic Influences**: Factors like **age** (well-being often follows a **U-shaped curve** across the lifespan), **socio-economic status**, and **cultural context** can influence how different domains like **autonomy** or **achievement** are prioritized by an individual.
 
• **Impact of Climate Change**: Modern psychological studies now recognize **Eco-anxiety**, which is the chronic fear of environmental doom caused by **Pollution** and **Climate Change**, further distinguishing the external cause from the internal psychological state.

question: What is the main focus of the Happiness Index?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Measuring happiness and wellbeing**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **World Happiness Report** is an annual publication that ranks **156 countries** based on how happy their citizens perceive themselves to be, with the primary focus on **measuring happiness and wellbeing**. *Hence, the statement 'Measuring happiness and wellbeing' is correct.*

• The index uses **subjective wellbeing** data to complement traditional objective indicators like **GDP** or **employment rates**, providing a more comprehensive view of **social progress**.

• The ranking is determined by six key variables: **GDP per capita**, **social support** (having someone to count on in times of trouble), **healthy life expectancy** at birth, **freedom to make life choices**, **generosity** (measured by recent donations), and **perceptions of corruption** in government and business.

• **Tracking population growth** is the primary function of **demographic surveys** and **national censuses**, which focus on **birth rates**, **death rates**, and **migration** rather than emotional wellbeing. *Hence, the statement 'Tracking population growth' is incorrect.*

• **Calculating government incoming** refers to **fiscal policy** and **revenue collection** metrics, which are monitored by **central banks** and **ministries of finance** to manage the **national budget**. *Hence, the statement 'Calculating government incoming' is incorrect.*

• **Checking school performance** involves educational assessments such as the **Program for International Student Assessment (PISA)** or **literacy rate** surveys, which evaluate **academic outcomes** rather than general life satisfaction. *Hence, the statement 'Checking school performance' is incorrect.*

**Additional Information__**
__

• The **World Happiness Report** is published by the **United Nations Sustainable Development Solutions Network (SDSN)** and was first released in **April 2012**.

• The report was launched to support the **United Nations High-Level Meeting on Happiness and Well-being**, following a **2011** **UN General Assembly** resolution inviting member countries to measure the happiness of their people.

• The data for the rankings comes primarily from the **Gallup World Poll**, which utilizes the **Cantril ladder** question: respondents are asked to think of a ladder, with the best possible life for them being a **10** and the worst possible life being a **0**.

• The concept of prioritizing happiness over economic indicators was pioneered by **Bhutan** in the **1970s**, when the **4th King**, **Jigme Singye Wangchuck**, introduced the **Gross National Happiness (GNH)** index as a more important metric than **Gross Domestic Product (GDP)**.

• **Nordic countries**, such as **Finland**, **Denmark**, **Iceland**, and **Norway**, consistently dominate the top of the index due to high levels of **social trust**, **low corruption**, and **effective welfare states**.

**Important Points__**

• In the **World Happiness Report 2024**, **Finland** was ranked as the happiest country in the world for the **seventh consecutive year**.

• **India** was ranked **126th** out of **143 countries** in the **2024** report, indicating that despite **economic growth**, there are significant challenges in **social support** and **perceived freedom**.

• The **2024** report also highlighted a **happiness gap** based on **age**, noting that in some regions, **younger populations** are reporting lower levels of happiness compared to **older generations** due to **social media** pressures and **economic instability**.

• The index serves as a critical tool for **policymakers** to shift the focus of **public policy** toward **mental health**, **community building**, and **environmental sustainability**.

options.text: United Nations Sustainable Development Solutions Network (SDSN)

solution:
The correct answer is __**United Nations Sustainable Development Solutions Network (SDSN)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **World Happiness Report** is an annual publication that ranks countries based on how happy their citizens perceive themselves to be. It is published by the **United Nations Sustainable Development Solutions Network (SDSN)**. **Hence, option 3 is correct.**
 
• The report was first released in **2012** to coincide with the **United Nations High-Level Meeting** on **Happiness and Well-being**. It has since become a global standard for measuring the quality of life and social progress.
 
• The rankings are primarily based on data from the **Gallup World Poll**, where respondents evaluate their own lives using the **Cantril Ladder** scale.
 
• The **United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)** is not the publisher of this report; it is well-known for publishing the **Human Development Report (HDR)** and the **Human Development Index (HDI)**. **Hence, option 1 is incorrect.**
 
• The **World Health Organization (WHO)** focuses on international public health and publishes reports such as the **World Health Statistics**, but it does not produce the World Happiness Report. **Hence, option 2 is incorrect.**
 
• The **World Economic Forum (WEF)** is an international non-governmental organization that publishes the **Global Gender Gap Report** and the **Global Risk Report**, but it is not responsible for the happiness rankings. **Hence, option 4 is incorrect.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Methodology of the Report:** The report uses six key variables to explain the variation in happiness levels across different nations: **GDP per capita**, **social support**, **healthy life expectancy**, **freedom to make life choices**, **generosity**, and **perceptions of corruption**.
 
• **Top Performing Countries:** Nordic countries consistently dominate the top of the rankings. **Finland** has been named the **happiest country in the world** for **seven consecutive years** as of the **2024** report. Other top-ranked nations include **Denmark**, **Iceland**, and **Sweden**.
 
• **India’s Ranking:** In the **2024 World Happiness Report**, **India** was ranked **126th** out of **143 countries**. This position remained unchanged from the previous year, indicating a need for improvement in social and economic well-being factors.
 
• **International Day of Happiness:** The report is typically released on or around **March 20**, which was designated as the **International Day of Happiness** by the **UN General Assembly** in **2012**.
 
• **The SDSN:** The **Sustainable Development Solutions Network (SDSN)** was established in **2012** under the auspices of the **UN Secretary-General**. It works to mobilize global scientific and technological expertise to promote practical problem-solving for **sustainable development**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Gross National Happiness (GNH):** The concept of measuring happiness as a metric of national progress was pioneered by **Bhutan**. In **1972**, the **Fourth King of Bhutan**, **Jigme Singye Wangchuck**, declared that **Gross National Happiness** is more important than **Gross Domestic Product (GDP)**.
 
• **Global Trends:** The **2024 report** noted a significant trend where **younger generations** in **North America** and parts of **Western Europe** reported lower happiness levels compared to older generations, a shift from historical patterns.
 
• **Policy Impact:** The findings of the **World Happiness Report** are increasingly used by governments to inform **public policy**. Countries like **New Zealand** and the **United Arab Emirates** have even appointed **Ministers of Happiness** or Well-being to integrate these metrics into governance.
 
• **Data Source:** The **Gallup World Poll** remains the primary data source, conducting surveys in more than **160 countries** and in over **140 languages** to capture a representative sample of the global population.

question: Which region in India has the highest population density due to fertile soil and abundant water resources?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Indo-Gangetic Plain**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Indo-Gangetic Plain**, also known as the **North Indian River Plain**, is a vast and **fertile** expanse of land that covers most of northern and eastern **India**. It is the most **densely populated** region in the country due to its favorable **geographical** features.
 
• This region is formed by the **alluvial deposits** brought down by three major **river systems**: the **Indus**, the **Ganga**, and the **Brahmaputra**, along with their numerous **tributaries**. The continuous deposition of **alluvium** over millions of years has created some of the most **fertile soil** in the world.
 
• The **abundant water resources** provided by these **perennial rivers** ensure a steady supply for **irrigation**, **domestic use**, and **industrial activities**. This availability of water makes the region highly suitable for **intensive agriculture**, allowing for multiple **cropping seasons** in a single **year**.
 
• The **topography** of the plain is mostly **flat** and level, which significantly facilitates the construction of **transportation networks** such as **roads** and **railways**, as well as the development of large **urban settlements** and **industrial hubs**.
 
• According to the **2011 Census** of India, states located within this plain exhibit the highest **population densities**. For example, **Bihar** has a density of **1,106** persons per square km, and **West Bengal** has **1,028** persons per square km, both of which are significantly higher than the **national average**. ***Hence, the Indo-Gangetic Plain is the correct option.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Thar Desert**:
 
 
• Located primarily in the state of **Rajasthan**, the **Thar Desert** (also known as the **Great Indian Desert**) is characterized by **arid** and **semi-arid** climatic conditions.
 
• Due to extremely low **rainfall** (less than **150 mm** per year) and high **evaporation rates**, **water resources** are scarce, leading to a very **low population density**. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***
 
 
 
• **Himalayan Region**:
 
 
• The **Himalayan Region** consists of young **fold mountains** with **rugged terrain**, **steep slopes**, and **harsh climatic conditions**.
 
• The lack of **arable land** and difficulties in **transportation** and **communication** make it one of the least **densely populated** areas in India. For instance, **Arunachal Pradesh** has a density of only **17** persons per square km as per the **2011 Census**. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***
 
 
 
• **Western Ghats**:
 
 
• The **Western Ghats** or **Sahyadri** is a **mountain range** that runs parallel to the **western coast** of the **Indian peninsula**. It is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** and a **biodiversity hotspot**.
 
• While the region receives **heavy rainfall**, its **undulating topography** and thick **forest cover** limit large-scale **agricultural expansion** and **urbanization** compared to the **Northern Plains**, resulting in a **moderate population density**. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***
 
 
 
• **Population Density Factors**:
 
 
• **Population density** is a measurement of the number of **people per unit land area** (usually per **square kilometer**). 
 
• In India, the **distribution of population** is highly **uneven** and is influenced by **physical factors** (climate, terrain, soil, water), **socio-economic factors** (industrialization, urbanization), and **historical factors** (early settlements).
 
• The **national average population density** of India was **382** persons per square km according to the **2011 Census** report.
 
 
</ul

question: **Read the statements given below carefully :****Statement 1:** The Deccan Trap region of the Peninsular Plateau is covered with black soil derived from igneous rocks.**Statement 2:** The Aravalli Hills are newly formed folded mountains stretching from Gujarat to Delhi.**Which of the above statements is/are correct?**
solution:
The correct answer is __**Only 1**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 

__ 
 
• **Statement 1:** The Deccan Trap region of the Peninsular Plateau is covered with **black soil** derived from **igneous rocks.** 
 
 
• The Deccan Trap is a large volcanic province in west-central India formed by extensive volcanic eruptions during the **Cretaceous period.** 
 
• The rocks in this region, primarily basalt, weather over time to form **fertile black soil**, also known as **regur soil.** 
 
• The black soil is highly suitable for growing crops like **cotton**, hence it is also called **black cotton soil.** 
 
• *Hence, this statement is correct.* 
 
 

 
• **Statement 2:** The Aravalli Hills are newly formed folded mountains stretching from Gujarat to Delhi. 
 
 
• The Aravalli Hills are among the **oldest mountain ranges** in the world, dating back to the **Precambrian era** (approximately 3.2 billion years ago). 
 
• They are not newly formed; rather, they are highly eroded and weathered over time due to their geological age. 
 
• The range extends from **Rajasthan** and **Haryana** through parts of **Gujarat** to **Delhi.** 
 
• *Hence, this statement is incorrect.* 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 

__ 
 
• **Black Soil Characteristics:** 
 
 
• Black soil is rich in **calcium carbonate, magnesium, potash, and lime**, making it highly fertile. 
 
• It has a high water retention capacity, which is beneficial for crops like **cotton, sugarcane, wheat, and oilseeds.** 
 
• This soil develops cracks during the dry season, which helps in better aeration. 
 
 

 
• **Formation of Deccan Trap:** 
 
 
• The Deccan Traps were formed by **successive volcanic eruptions** that occurred about **65 million years ago**. 
 
• The eruptions resulted in the creation of a massive layer of **igneous rocks** that later weathered to form black soil. 
 
 

 
• **Aravalli Hills Features:** 
 
 
• The Aravallis are composed of **ancient crystalline rocks**, such as granite, quartzite, and gneiss. 
 
• They are considered **relic mountains**, significantly eroded over millions of years. 
 
• The range is a critical source of **minerals**, including lead, zinc, and marble, and plays an important role in environmental conservation. 
 
 

 
• **Importance of Aravalli Range:** 
 
 
• The Aravalli Hills act as a natural barrier against the spread of the **Thar Desert** into the eastern parts of India. 
 
• They are home to a variety of **flora and fauna** and serve as a crucial ecological zone in the region. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 

 
 
• The Deccan Plateau covers a large part of southern India and is known for its **volcanic origin**. 
 
• The Aravallis have a significant role in influencing the **climate** of the region by blocking hot desert winds. 
 
• Black soil is found predominantly in the **Deccan Plateau** states such as Maharashtra, Gujarat, and Madhya Pradesh. 
 
• The Aravalli range has faced severe ecological degradation due to **deforestation, mining, and urbanization.**

question: What does the fertility rate measure?

options.text: Number of live births per 1000 people in the population
Number of women in the population between ages 15 and 49
Number of live births per 1000 women aged 15 to 49 in a given year
Number of children born per family regardless of age

solution:
The correct answer is __**Number of live births per 1000 women aged 15 to 49 in a given year**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **fertility rate**, specifically the **General Fertility Rate (GFR)**, is a demographic measure that calculates the **number of live births per 1000 women** of reproductive age in a specific **year**. This measure is more precise than the crude birth rate because it focuses only on the segment of the population capable of childbearing. *Hence, statement 3 is correct.*
 
• The **Crude Birth Rate (CBR)** is defined as the **number of live births per 1000 people** in the total population. Unlike the fertility rate, it includes men, children, and elderly women who are not in the reproductive age bracket, making it a broader but less refined indicator of fertility. *Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.*
 
• The **number of women in the population between ages 15 and 49** refers to the size of the **reproductive age group** or the **childbearing population**. While this data is essential for calculating fertility rates, the count itself is a demographic stock value and not a rate of birth. *Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.*
 
• The **number of children born per family** is a concept related to **family size** or **completed fertility** at a micro-level. However, in formal **demography**, the fertility rate is standardized per 1000 women to allow for comparisons across different regions and time periods, rather than being measured simply per household or family. *Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Total Fertility Rate (TFR)**: This is the average number of children a woman would have by the end of her reproductive years if she were to experience the current **age-specific fertility rates**. It is one of the most widely used indicators to track population trends globally.
 
• **Replacement Level Fertility**: This is the specific **TFR** at which a population exactly replaces itself from one generation to the next without migration. In most **countries**, this value is considered to be **2.1**.
 
• **India's Fertility Trends**: According to the **National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5)** conducted between **2019 and 2021**, India's **TFR** has declined to **2.0**, which is below the **replacement level**. This indicates a significant shift in the **country's** demographic trajectory.
 
• **Age-Specific Fertility Rate (ASFR)**: This measures the **number of live births per 1000 women** within specific age cohorts, such as **20 to 24 years** or **25 to 29 years**. It helps **governments** and **organisations** understand at what **age** childbearing is most concentrated in a society.
 
• **Factors Affecting Fertility**: Several socio-economic **features** influence these rates, including **female literacy**, **age at marriage**, economic status, and the availability of **contraception** and **healthcare** services.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Fecundity vs. Fertility**: In **demography**, **fecundity** refers to the biological potential or physical capacity to conceive, whereas **fertility** refers to the actual production of **live births**. A woman may be fecund but have zero fertility if she chooses not to have children.
 
• **Demographic Transition Model**: High **fertility rates** are typically observed in the early stages of the **Demographic Transition Model**, often seen in **developing nations**. As a **country** industrialises and **education** improves, it moves toward lower **birth rates** and **death rates**.
 
• **Global Context**: Many **developed countries** in **Europe** and **East Asia**, such as **Japan** and **South Korea**, are currently experiencing 'ultra-low' **fertility rates** (below **1.5**), leading to concerns about **ageing populations** and a shrinking **workforce**.

question: Which one of the following defines spatial distribution of population?

options.text: The movement of people from rural to urban areas
The pattern of how people are spread across a given area
The ratio or males to females in a population
The fertility rate of a population

solution:
The correct answer is __**The pattern of how people are spread across a given area**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Spatial distribution of population** refers to the **pattern of how people are spread** across a specific geographical area. It highlights the way populations are arranged in different regions, whether densely or sparsely populated.
 
• This concept emphasizes the **geographical distribution** of human populations, taking into account factors like urbanization, migration, and resource availability.
 
• It does not focus on the **movement of people** from rural to urban areas or fertility rates but primarily on the **static arrangement** of populations. *Hence, the correct answer is option 2.*
 
• In contrast to demographic measures like **male-to-female ratio** or fertility rate, spatial distribution is concerned with how population density varies across different regions.
 
• This measure is crucial for understanding economic development, urban planning, infrastructure requirements, and environmental impacts. *Hence, option 2 accurately defines spatial distribution of population.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Factors influencing spatial distribution:**

 
 
• **Physical geography:** Natural features like mountains, plains, rivers, and climate significantly impact population spread. For instance, areas with fertile soil and favorable climate tend to have higher population density.
 
• **Economic factors:** Regions with industrial development, employment opportunities, and better infrastructure attract larger populations. Urban areas typically have a higher population density compared to rural regions.
 
• **Social and political factors:** Historical migration patterns, government policies, and cultural preferences shape how populations are distributed.
 
 
 
• **Uses of spatial distribution analysis:**
 
 
• **Urban planning:** Understanding spatial distribution helps in designing cities, allocating resources, and ensuring equitable access to services.
 
• **Infrastructure development:** Insights into population spread are essential for building roads, schools, hospitals, and utilities where they are most needed.
 
• **Environmental conservation:** Identifying densely populated areas can aid efforts to reduce ecological strain and promote sustainable development.
 
 
 
• **Examples of spatial distribution:**
 
 
• In **India**, states like **Uttar Pradesh** and **Bihar** have high population densities, while regions like **Arunachal Pradesh** are sparsely populated due to geographical constraints.
 
• Global examples include dense populations in urban areas like **New York City**, while regions like **Sahara Desert** exhibit sparse distribution due to harsh living conditions.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Option-specific details:**

 
 
• **Option 1:** While migration affects population distribution over time, it does not define the spatial arrangement at a given moment.
 
• **Option 3:** The male-to-female ratio is a demographic measure focusing on gender balance, not spatial distribution.
 
• **Option 4:** Fertility rate reflects the number of births in a population but does not describe how individuals are geographically spread.
 
 
 
• **Significance of spatial distribution:**
 
 
• Understanding spatial distribution is crucial for addressing urbanization challenges, planning resource allocation, and ensuring sustainable development.

question: Which one of the following defines elderly dependency ratio?

options.text: The ratio of children to the working-age population
The ratio of elderly (65+) to the working-age population
The ratio of elderly to children in a population
The ratio of urban to rural elderly population

solution:
The correct answer is __**The ratio of elderly (65+) to the working-age population**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Elderly Dependency Ratio (EDR)** is a demographic measure that represents the number of elderly persons, typically those aged **65 years and above**, per **100** persons of **working age** (defined as those aged **15 to 64 years**). ***Hence, the correct answer is the ratio of elderly (65+) to the working-age population.***

• This ratio is a critical indicator used by **economists** and **policymakers** to determine the potential **socio-economic** support needed for the older population, who are generally considered to be outside the active **labor force**.

• The ratio of children (aged **0 to 14 years**) to the working-age population is known as the **Child Dependency Ratio**, which measures the pressure of the younger dependent population. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***

• The ratio of the elderly population to the number of children in a given population is called the **Aging Index** or **Elderly-Child Ratio**, which tracks the relative aging of a society. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***

• Comparing the urban elderly population to the rural elderly population is a measure of **geographical distribution** or **urbanization** trends and does not constitute a dependency ratio. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• The **Total Dependency Ratio** is the sum of the **Child Dependency Ratio** and the **Elderly Dependency Ratio**. It provides an overall assessment of the total number of dependents that the **productive population** must support.

• A rising **Elderly Dependency Ratio** is a common feature of the **Demographic Transition** in developed countries, where **life expectancy** is high and **fertility rates** have declined significantly.

• Countries such as **Japan**, **Italy**, and **Germany** currently exhibit some of the highest elderly dependency ratios in the world, leading to increased fiscal pressure on **pension systems** and **public healthcare**.

• Conversely, many developing nations are currently benefiting from a **Demographic Dividend**, where the **working-age population** is large relative to the dependent population, creating an opportunity for rapid **economic growth**.

• The **United Nations (UN)** and the **World Bank** utilize these ratios to help nations plan for **sustainable development** and to design social safety nets for an aging citizenry.

**Important Points__**

• The **Old-Age Support Ratio** is the numerical inverse of the elderly dependency ratio; it indicates how many individuals of **working age** are available to support a single person aged **65 years or older**.

• In the context of **India**, the elderly population (aged **60 years and above**) is projected to reach nearly **20%** of the total population by the year **2050**, according to the **India Ageing Report 2023**.

• A high dependency ratio can lead to a decrease in **national savings rates**, as a larger portion of the **GDP** is diverted toward the consumption, **social security**, and **geriatric care** of the non-working population.

• To address the challenges of a high ratio, governments may implement reforms such as increasing the **retirement age**, encouraging **private pension schemes**, and investing in **healthcare infrastructure**.

• Demographic data used to calculate these ratios is primarily sourced from national **Census** reports and large-scale surveys like the **National Family Health Survey (NFHS)** in India.
</ul

question: Read the following two statements carefully and choose the correct option:**Statement 1:** Rural-to-urban migration is a major contributor to urban growth in India.**Statement 2:** Better job opportunities and education facilities in cities attract migrants.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Only 1**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• **Rural-to-urban migration** refers to the movement of people from villages to cities, which significantly fuels the process of **urbanization** in India. This migration contributes to the rapid expansion of **Metropolitan cities** and the emergence of **Census Towns**, where rural settlements transition into urban entities based on population density and non-agricultural employment. **Hence, statement 1 is correct.**

• While cities offer various amenities, **Statement 2** is considered incorrect in a strict statistical context because **Marriage** remains the single largest reason for migration in India, particularly for the female demographic according to the **Census of India 2011**. Furthermore, much of the labor migration is driven by **Push Factors** like rural poverty and lack of agricultural land rather than the simple pull of urban **education facilities**. **Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.**

 **Additional Information__**

• **Types of Migration:**

• **Internal Migration:** Movement within the country, classified into four streams: **Rural-to-Rural**, **Rural-to-Urban**, **Urban-to-Urban**, and **Urban-to-Rural**.

• **Push Factors:** These are negative conditions in the place of origin, such as **natural disasters**, **political instability**, **poor health services**, and **unemployment**.

• **Pull Factors:** These are positive attractions in the destination, such as **higher wages**, **regular work**, and **better living conditions**.

• **Urban Growth Components:**

• Urban growth in India is driven by three main factors: **Natural Increase** (birth rate minus death rate), **Net Migration** (predominantly rural-to-urban), and **Reclassification** of rural areas into urban centers.

• The **Census of India** defines an urban area based on a minimum population of **5,000**, a population density of at least **400 persons per sq. km**, and at least **75 percent** of the male main working population engaged in **non-agricultural pursuits**.

</ul

question:
Read the following two statements carefully and choose the correct option:**
Statement 1:** India experienced a negative population growth rate between 1911 and 1921.**
Statement 2:** The influenza epidemic of 1918-19 caused widespread deaths during that period.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Both 1 and 2 are correct**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Statement 1** asserts that **India** experienced a **negative population growth rate** between **1911 and 1921**. This is historically accurate as the **Census of 1921** recorded a decrease in the total population from **25.21 crore** in **1911** to **25.13 crore** in **1921**. This decline resulted in a **negative growth rate** of **-0.31%**, which is the only instance of absolute decline in the history of the **Indian Census**. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• **Statement 2** explains that the **influenza epidemic of 1918-19** caused widespread deaths during that period. This pandemic, also known as the **Spanish Flu**, was devastating for **India**, resulting in the deaths of approximately **12 to 17 million** people, which accounted for nearly **5%** of the total population at the time. ***Hence, statement 2 is correct.***
 
• The decade of **1911-1921** was marked by several calamities including **famines**, **plague**, and **cholera**, which significantly increased the **mortality rate**. The impact of the **First World War** (1914-1918) also contributed to economic distress and health crises across the country.
 
• The year **1921** is officially designated as the **'Year of the Great Divide'** because it marks the transition from a period of **stagnant or fluctuating population** to a period of **steady and continuous growth**. Before **1921**, population growth was erratic due to high **birth rates** being offset by high **death rates**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Stages of Demographic Transition**: **India** has passed through distinct demographic phases. The **first stage** (1901-1921) was characterized by **stagnant growth**. The **second stage** (1921-1951) saw **steady growth** as **death rates** began to decline due to improved **sanitation** and **health services**. The **third stage** (1951-1981) is known as the period of **population explosion**.
 
• **Census History**: The first **non-synchronous census** in **India** was conducted in **1872** under **Lord Mayo**. The first **synchronous census**, covering the entire country simultaneously, was conducted in **1881** under **Lord Ripon**. Since then, the **Census** has been conducted every **10 years**.
 
• **Malthusian Theory**: The demographic conditions prior to **1921** are often cited as an example of **Malthusian checks**, where **natural calamities** and **epidemics** act as a check on **population growth** when it exceeds the **food supply**.
 
• **Post-Independence Trends**: After **1947**, the **Government of India** focused on **public health**, leading to a sharp drop in the **death rate**. However, the **birth rate** remained high for several decades, leading to a massive increase in the **total population**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **Registrar General and Census Commissioner of India**, under the **Ministry of Home Affairs**, is the nodal authority for conducting the **decennial census**.
 
• The **1918 Influenza** was particularly severe in **India** compared to other nations, as it coincided with a **weak monsoon** and subsequent **crop failures**, leaving the population **malnourished** and more susceptible to the **virus**.
 
• According to the **2011 Census**, **India's** population was **121.09 crore**, showing a **decadal growth rate** of **17.7%**, a significant contrast to the **negative growth** seen a century earlier in **1921**.

Read the following two statements carefully and choose the correct option:**
Statement 1:** Adolescents constitute nearly one-fifth of India's total population.**
Statement 2:** Adolescents are grouped in the age bracket of 10 to 19 years.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Both 1 and 2 are correct**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Statement 1** suggests that **adolescents** make up nearly **one-fifth** of the **total population** of **India**. According to the **Census of India 2011**, the **adolescent population** (individuals aged **10-19 years**) was recorded at approximately **253 million**, which accounts for about **20.9%** of the **country's** total **population**. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• **Statement 2** defines the **age bracket** for **adolescents** as **10 to 19 years**. This specific **age group** is the standard definition provided by the **World Health Organization (WHO)** and is strictly followed by the **Government of India** for **demographic** analysis and **policy formulation**. ***Hence, statement 2 is correct.***
 
• **Adolescents** are considered the most significant **human resource** for the **future** of the **nation**. They are in a **transitional phase** from **childhood** to **adulthood**, which is marked by rapid **physical**, **mental**, and **emotional** changes.
 
• The **nutritional requirements** of **adolescents** are significantly higher than those of a **child** or an **adult**. Poor **nutrition** during this **period** can lead to **deficiency diseases** and stunted **growth**, which is why **government programs** focus heavily on this **demographic**.
 
• In **India**, the **adolescent population** is characterized by a large **number** of individuals who require **special attention** regarding **education**, **health**, and **vocational training** to harness the **demographic dividend**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **National Youth Policy (NYP-2014)**: While **adolescents** are aged **10-19 years**, the **National Youth Policy 2014** defines **youth** as persons in the **age group** of **15 to 29 years**. This helps in **categorizing** different **stages** of **development** for **targeted interventions**.
 
• **Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram (RKSK)**: This **health program** was launched in **January 2014** by the **Ministry of Health and Family Welfare**. It aims to reach out to **253 million** **adolescents** in **India**, focusing on **nutrition**, **reproductive health**, **substance abuse**, and **mental health**.
 
• **Anemia among Adolescents**: A critical **health issue** in **India** is the high **prevalence** of **Anemia**, particularly among **adolescent girls**. The **Weekly Iron and Folic Acid Supplementation (WIFS)** program is a **government initiative** designed to address this **nutritional deficiency**.
 
• **Demographic Dividend**: **India** currently possesses a **youthful demographic profile**. The **adolescent** and **youth population** provides a **window of opportunity** for **economic growth**, provided there is adequate **investment** in their **skill development** and **health**.
 
• **Education and Literacy**: The **literacy rate** among **adolescents** has seen a **steady increase** over the **decades**, but **challenges** like **school dropouts** at the **secondary level** remain a **concern** for **policymakers**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Gender Concerns**: **Adolescent girls** often face **social barriers** such as **early marriage** and **restricted mobility**, which can impact their **educational** and **health outcomes** compared to **adolescent boys**.
 
• **Urban vs Rural Distribution**: A significant **portion** of **India's adolescents** resides in **rural areas**, where **access** to **quality healthcare** and **modern education** facilities is often **limited** compared to **urban centers**.
 
• **Right to Education (RTE)**: The **Constitution (Eighty-sixth Amendment) Act, 2002** inserted **Article 21-A** to provide **free and compulsory education** to all **children** in the **age group** of **six to fourteen years**, which covers the **early adolescent** years.
 
• **Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)**: **Empowering adolescents** is crucial for achieving **SDG 3** (Good Health and Well-being), **SDG 4** (Quality Education), and **SDG 5** (Gender Equality) by the **year 2030**.

question: Read the following two statements carefully and choose the correct option:**Statement 1:** India has completed its demographic transition as both death and birth rates have declined equally.**Statement 2:** In India, although mortality rates have reduced, the birth rate remains comparatively high.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Only 2**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Demographic Transition Model (DTM)** is a framework that explains the transformation of countries from high birth and death rates to low birth and death rates as they move from a pre-industrial to an industrialized economic system. India has not yet completed its demographic transition. It is currently situated in the **late third stage** of this transition. For a transition to be considered complete (Stage 4), both birth and death rates must be low and approximately equal, leading to a stable or stationary population. **Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.**

• In India, the **Mortality Rate** (Death Rate) has seen a sharp decline over the last several decades due to significant improvements in **medical technology**, **public health services**, **vaccination programs**, and **food security**. However, the **Birth Rate**, while declining, has not fallen as rapidly as the death rate. This lag between the falling death rate and the slowly declining birth rate is a characteristic of a developing economy undergoing transition. **Hence, statement 2 is correct.**

• According to the **Sample Registration System (SRS)** data, India’s **Crude Birth Rate (CBR)** has declined significantly from about **40.8 per 1000** in **1951** to approximately **19.5 per 1000** in recent years. Simultaneously, the **Crude Death Rate (CDR)** has dropped from **25.1 per 1000** in **1951** to around **6.0 per 1000**. The gap between these two rates explains why India’s population continues to grow despite the decline in fertility.

• The **National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5)** conducted between **2019-21** revealed that India’s **Total Fertility Rate (TFR)** has reached **2.0**, which is slightly below the **Replacement Level Fertility** of **2.1**. Despite reaching this milestone, the population continues to increase due to **Population Momentum**, which is the result of a large young population entering their reproductive years.

• The completion of the demographic transition would imply that the **Natural Growth Rate** (Birth Rate minus Death Rate) is near zero or negative. India’s growth rate, though slowing down, remains positive, indicating that the transition is still in progress.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Stages of Demographic Transition:**

• **Stage 1:** High Birth Rate and High Death Rate. Population remains stable but low. India was in this stage before the **1920s**. The year **1921** is known as the **Year of the Great Divide** because, after this year, the death rate started to decline consistently.

• **Stage 2:** High Birth Rate and rapidly falling Death Rate. This leads to a **Population Explosion**. India experienced this phase between **1951 and 1981**.

• **Stage 3:** Falling Birth Rate and low Death Rate. The population still grows but at a declining rate. India is currently in this phase.

• **Stage 4:** Low Birth Rate and Low Death Rate. The population becomes stable. Countries like **Japan** and many **European nations** are in this stage or moving into Stage 5 (declining population).

• **Factors for Declining Mortality:** The eradication of epidemics like **Smallpox**, control over diseases like **Malaria** and **Cholera**, and the success of the **Green Revolution** in ensuring food availability have been primary drivers in reducing the death rate in India.

• **Factors for High Birth Rate:** Socio-economic factors such as **universal marriage**, **early marriage** age, **poverty**, **illiteracy** (especially among females), and a traditional **preference for male children** have historically kept the birth rate higher than the death rate.

• **Demographic Dividend:** India is currently enjoying a **Demographic Dividend**, where the proportion of the **working-age population** (15-64 years) is larger than the dependent population. This provides a window of economic opportunity if supported by **education**, **skill development**, and **employment**.

**Important Points__**

• **Population Momentum:** This is a crucial concept in Indian demography. Even if every couple has only two children today, the population will continue to grow for a few decades because the number of people in the **reproductive age group** is very high due to high fertility in previous generations.

• **Regional Variations:** There is a significant disparity in demographic transition within India. States like **Kerala**, **Tamil Nadu**, and **Andhra Pradesh** have reached low birth and death rates (Stage 4), while states like **Bihar**, **Uttar Pradesh**, and **Madhya Pradesh** are still in the earlier phases of Stage 3 with higher fertility rates.

• **Government Initiatives:** The **National Population Policy (NPP) 2000** was formulated with the long-term objective of achieving a stable population by **2045**, which was later revised to **2070**, consistent with the requirements of sustainable economic growth.

• **Life Expectancy:** At the time of **Independence in 1947**, the average life expectancy in India was around **32 years**. Due to the demographic transition, it has increased to approximately **70 years** as of **2023**, reflecting the success in reducing mortality.

question:
Fill in the blank:
The Census in India is conducted every ______ years.
solution:
The correct answer is __**10**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Census** in **India** is a decennial exercise, which means it is conducted every **10 years**. This regularity ensures that the government has updated **demographic**, **social**, and **economic** data to formulate effective policies.

• The responsibility of conducting the decennial **Census** rests with the **Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner**, **India**, which operates under the **Ministry of Home Affairs**, **Government of India**.

• The legal framework for the census is provided by the **Census Act of 1948**. This act empowers the **Central Government** to take a census and makes it mandatory for citizens to answer the census questions truthfully while ensuring the **confidentiality** of the information provided.

• Historically, the first non-synchronous census in **India** was conducted in **1872** during the tenure of **Lord Mayo**. However, the first synchronous (complete and simultaneous) census was held in **1881** under **Lord Ripon**. Since **1881**, the census has been conducted uninterruptedly every **10 years**.

• The **2011 Census** marked the **15th** census of **India** since **1872** and the **7th** census since **Independence**. The other options like **5**, **15**, or **20** years are incorrect as they do not align with the statutory and historical practice of the **Indian** government.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Census 2011 Findings**: According to the **2011 Census**, the total population of **India** was **1,210,854,977** (approximately **1.21 billion**). The **literacy rate** was recorded at **74.04%**, and the **sex ratio** was **943** females per **1000** males.

• **Postponement of 2021 Census**: The **16th** Indian Census, which was scheduled to take place in **2021**, was postponed indefinitely due to the outbreak of the **COVID-19 pandemic**. This upcoming census is planned to be the first-ever **digital census**, where data will be collected through a mobile app.

• **Constitutional Status**: The **Census** is a **Union Subject** listed under **Entry 69** of the **Seventh Schedule** of the **Constitution of India**. This means only the **Parliament** has the power to legislate on matters related to the census.

• **Delimitation Process**: The data collected during the census is used for the **delimitation** of constituencies for the **Lok Sabha** and **State Legislative Assemblies** under **Article 82** and **Article 170** of the **Constitution**.

• **Socio-Economic and Caste Census (SECC)**: In **2011**, the government also conducted the **SECC** to identify households living below the **poverty line** (**BPL**) and to collect **caste-based** data for better targeting of social welfare schemes.

**Important Points__**

• **Motto of Census 2011**: The official motto of the **2011 Census** was **'Our Census, Our Future'**. This highlights the importance of the exercise in shaping the nation's developmental trajectory.

• **Stages of Census**: The census is typically conducted in two distinct phases: the **House Listing and Housing Census** and the **Population Enumeration**. The first phase identifies the residential status and amenities, while the second phase records individual details.

• **Registrar General of India**: The post of the **Registrar General and Census Commissioner** was created in **1949**. This official is responsible for overseeing the entire process and ensuring the **accuracy** and **integrity** of the data.

• **Global Context**: **India** is one of the few countries in the world that has maintained a consistent **decennial** census record for over **140 years**, providing a massive **longitudinal dataset** for researchers and historians.
</ul

question: Which State in India has the lowest population density?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Arunachal Pradesh**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• According to the **Census 2011**, **Arunachal Pradesh** has the lowest population density among all states in **India**, with only **17 persons per square kilometer**.

• The low population density is primarily due to the state's vast **geographical area** of **83,743 square kilometers** coupled with a relatively small **population** of approximately **1.38 million**.

• The **topography** of **Arunachal Pradesh**, characterized by the rugged **Eastern Himalayas**, deep valleys, and dense **forest cover** (over **80%** of its land), makes large parts of the state difficult to inhabit, leading to sparse settlements.

• Comparing the other options: **Sikkim** has a population density of **86**, **Nagaland** has **119**, and **Manipur** has **115** persons per square kilometer. While these are low compared to the national average, they are significantly higher than that of **Arunachal Pradesh**.

• The **Census 2011** was the **15th** official census of **India** and remains the primary source of **demographic data** used for administrative and planning purposes.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Highest Density State**: **Bihar** is the most densely populated state in **India** as per the **2011 Census**, with a density of **1,106 persons per square kilometer**.

• **National Average**: The overall **population density** of **India** was recorded at **382 persons per square kilometer** in **2011**, an increase from **325** in the **2001 Census**.

• **Union Territories**: Among **Union Territories**, **Delhi** has the highest population density at **11,320 persons per square kilometer**, while the **Andaman and Nicobar Islands** have the lowest at **46**.

• **Least Populous State**: Although **Arunachal Pradesh** has the lowest density, **Sikkim** is the **least populous state** in **India** with a total population of about **6.11 lakh**.

• **Growth Trends**: **Nagaland** was the only state in **India** to show a **negative decadal growth rate** of **-0.58%** between **2001** and **2011**.

**Important Points__**

• **Definition**: **Population Density** is defined as the number of persons living per unit of area (usually per **square kilometer**). It is a key indicator of **population distribution** and **urbanization**.

• **District Level Data**: Within **Arunachal Pradesh**, the **Dibang Valley** district has the lowest density in the entire country, with only about **1 person per square kilometer**.

• **Geographical Significance**: **Arunachal Pradesh** is the largest state in **Northeast India** by area and is known as the **Land of the Rising Sun** because it receives the first **sunlight** in **India** at **Dong Valley**.
