question: Which of the following species is endemic to the Great Nicobar Island and not naturally found anywhere else in the world?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Nicobar Megapod**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Nicobar Megapod** (**Megapodius nicobariensis**) is a ground-dwelling bird that is **endemic** to the **Nicobar Islands** in the **Bay of Bengal**. It is not found naturally anywhere else in the world. ***Hence, the correct answer is Nicobar Megapod.***
 
• The **Lion-tailed Macaque** (**Macaca silenus**) is an **Old World monkey** endemic to the **Western Ghats** of **South India**. It is primarily found in the states of **Kerala**, **Karnataka**, and **Tamil Nadu**. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***
 
• The **Indian Pangolin** (**Manis crassicaudata**) is a **scaly anteater** found in various habitats across **India**, **Sri Lanka**, **Nepal**, and **Pakistan**. It is not restricted to a single island group. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***
 
• The **Great Hornbill** (**Buceros bicornis**) is a large bird found in the **Indian subcontinent** and **Southeast Asia**. Its range includes the **Western Ghats**, the **Himalayan foothills**, and countries like **Thailand** and **Indonesia**. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• The **Nicobar Megapod** belongs to the **Megapodiidae** family, whose members are known as **mound-builders**. These birds are unique because they do not sit on their eggs to provide warmth; instead, they build large **incubation mounds** of soil and **decaying vegetation**. The heat generated by the decomposition of organic matter incubates the eggs.
 
• The species is primarily found in **coastal forests** and **mangrove** areas. Its population is concentrated on islands like **Great Nicobar**, **Little Nicobar**, **Teressa**, and **Nancowry**. It is about the size of a **domestic hen** and has **brown plumage** with **large, strong feet**.
 
• It is currently listed as **Vulnerable** on the **IUCN Red List**. The **2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami** caused a severe decline in its population, as many of its nesting mounds were located on the **beaches** and were destroyed by the waves.
 
• In **India**, the species is protected under **Schedule I** of the **Wildlife Protection Act, 1972**, which provides it the highest level of legal protection against hunting and trade.
 
• The **Great Nicobar Biosphere Reserve** was established to protect the unique biodiversity of the island. It covers approximately **85%** of the island's area and was designated a **UNESCO Biosphere Reserve** in **2013**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Great Nicobar Island** is the largest and **southernmost** island of the **Nicobar** group. It is located about **190 kilometers** north of the **Indonesian** island of **Sumatra**.
 
• The island features a **tropical wet evergreen forest** ecosystem, which supports various endemic fauna, including the **Nicobar Tree Shrew**, **Nicobar Serpent Eagle**, and the **Nicobar Long-tailed Macaque**.
 
• **Indira Point**, located at **6 degrees 4 minutes North** latitude, is the **southernmost point** of the **Indian Union** and is situated on this island.
 
• The island is home to the **Shompen** tribe, who are hunter-gatherers and classified as a **Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group (PVTG)**. They have lived in isolation in the interior forests for centuries.
 
• The **Galathea Bay** on **Great Nicobar** is one of the most significant **nesting sites** in the world for the **Giant Leatherback Turtle**, the largest of all living sea turtles.

question:
Which of the given statements is /are CORRECT?

1. Soil erosion and deforestation over a long period may convert arable land into a wasteland.
2. India has the largest land under plain areas as compared to Mountains and plateaus.
3. The net sown area in India is similar in all the states, excluding the North-Eastern states.
solution:
The correct answer is __**1 and 2 only**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Statement 1**: **Soil erosion** and **deforestation** are primary drivers of **land degradation**. When protective vegetation is removed and topsoil is washed away by **wind** or **water** over a long period, the land loses its fertility and moisture-retaining capacity. This process eventually converts **arable land** into **wasteland**, making it unfit for **agriculture**. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• **Statement 2**: India possesses diverse **relief features**. Approximately **43%** of the land area is **plain**, which provides facilities for **agriculture** and **industry**. **Mountains** account for **30%** of the total surface area, ensuring the perennial flow of some rivers and providing facilities for **tourism** and **ecology**. About **27%** of the area is the **plateau** region, which possesses rich reserves of **minerals**, **fossil fuels**, and **forests**. Since **43%** is the largest proportion, plains are the dominant relief feature. ***Hence, statement 2 is correct.***
 
• **Statement 3**: The pattern of **net sown area** varies greatly from one state to another. It is over **80%** of the total area in **Punjab** and **Haryana**, but it is less than **10%** in **Arunachal Pradesh**, **Mizoram**, **Manipur**, and the **Andaman Nicobar Islands**. This variation is not limited only to **North-Eastern states** but is seen across various regions due to **topography**, **climate**, and **soil types**. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is 1 and 2 only.***

**Additional Information__**

 
• **Land Use Pattern in India:**
 
 
• The use of land is determined both by **physical factors** such as **topography**, **climate**, **soil types** as well as **human factors** such as **population density**, **technological capability**, and **culture** and **traditions**.
 
• The total **geographical area** of **India** is **3.28 million square km**. However, **land use data** is available only for **93%** of the total area because reporting for most of the **North-East states** (except **Assam**) and some parts of **Jammu and Kashmir** has not been fully conducted.
 
• The **forest area** in the country is far lower than the desired **33%** of geographical area, as outlined in the **National Forest Policy (1952)**.
 
 
 
• **Land Degradation and Conservation:**
 
 
• At present, there are about **130 million hectares** of **degraded land** in **India**. Approximately **28%** of it belongs to the category of **forest degraded area**, **56%** is **water eroded area**, and the rest is affected by **saline** and **alkaline deposits**.
 
• Human activities such as **deforestation**, **overgrazing**, **mining**, and **quarrying** have contributed significantly to **land degradation**.
 
• In states like **Jharkhand**, **Chhattisgarh**, **Madhya Pradesh**, and **Odisha**, **deforestation** due to **mining** has caused severe land degradation.
 
• In states like **Gujarat**, **Rajasthan**, **Madhya Pradesh**, and **Maharashtra**, **overgrazing** is one of the main reasons for land degradation.
 
• In the states of **Punjab**, **Haryana**, and western **Uttar Pradesh**, **over-irrigation** is responsible for land degradation due to **waterlogging** leading to increase in **salinity** and **alkalinity** in the soil.
 
 
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• **Fallow Lands:** These are lands left without cultivation for one or less than one agricultural year to allow the soil to regain its fertility.
 
• **Culturable Wasteland:** Land left uncultivated for more than **5 agricultural years**.
 
• **Net Sown Area:** The physical extent of land on which crops are sown and harvested is known as **net sown area**.
 
 
</ul

question:
Which of the following is **correct** for the Indian Desert region?
1. It is a sandy plain with dunes.
2. It is heavily forested.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Only 1**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Indian Desert**, also known as the **Thar Desert**, is located towards the western margins of the **Aravalli Hills**. It is characterized as an undulating **sandy plain** covered with various types of **sand dunes**. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• This region receives very low rainfall, generally below **150 mm** per year. Due to this **arid climate** and extreme water scarcity, the region has very **low vegetation cover** and is certainly not **heavily forested**. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• The topography is dominated by **shifting sand dunes** and **sandy soils** that have very low organic matter. The lack of moisture prevents the growth of dense forests, limiting the flora to **thorny bushes** and **xerophytic** plants.
 
• Streams appear only during the **rainy season** and soon disappear into the sand as they do not have enough water to reach the sea. **Luni** is the only large river in this entire region.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Only 1.***

**Additional Information__**

 
• **Location and Extent:**
 
 
• The **Thar Desert** spans across the **Northwestern** part of the Indian subcontinent. About **85%** of the desert is located in **India**, primarily in the state of **Rajasthan**, while the remaining **15%** is in **Pakistan**.
 
• In India, it also extends into parts of **Gujarat**, **Haryana**, and **Punjab**.
 
 
 
• **Geological Features:**
 
 
• **Barchans**: These are **crescent-shaped sand dunes** that cover larger areas of the desert. However, **longitudinal dunes** become more prominent near the **Indo-Pakistan border**.
 
• The desert is a **northern extension** of the **Peninsular Plateau**. Evidence of marine deposits can be found at **Akal Wood Fossil Park** near **Jaisalmer**, indicating that this area was under the sea during the **Mesozoic Era**.
 
 
 
• **Climate and Vegetation:**
 
 
• The region experiences **extreme temperatures**, with very hot summers and cold winters. The **evaporation** rate is much higher than the **precipitation** rate.
 
• The natural vegetation is classified as **Tropical Thorn Forests**. Common species include **Khejri** (Prosopis cineraria), **Acacia**, and various types of **Cacti**.
 
 
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• **Indira Gandhi Canal**: This is the **longest canal** in India, which has significantly changed the **ecology** and **economy** of the northern part of the **Indian Desert** by providing water for **irrigation** and drinking.
 
• **Luni River**: Originating in the **Pushkar Valley** of the **Aravalli Range**, it flows through the **Thar Desert** and ends in the marshy lands of the **Rann of Kutch** in **Gujarat**.
 
• **Saline Lakes**: The region has several salt lakes like **Sambhar**, **Didwana**, and **Pachpadra**, which are important sources of **salt production** in India.
 
 
</ul

subject: GK
question: Which of these mountain ranges is not among the ones separating India from the rest of Asia?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Arakanyoma**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Indian Subcontinent** is geographically isolated from the rest of the **Asian** continent by a massive barrier of high mountain ranges in the north and northwest.

• The **Himalayas**, **Karakoram**, and **Hindukush** ranges collectively form this physical barrier that separates the **Indian** landmass from **Central Asia** and the **Tibetan Plateau**.

• **Hindukush mountains**: This range extends through **Afghanistan** and **Pakistan**, acting as the northwestern boundary of the subcontinent and separating it from **Central Asia**. ***Hence, this range is among those separating India from the rest of Asia.***

• **Karakoram mountains**: Situated in the regions of **Ladakh**, **Gilgit-Baltistan**, and **Xinjiang**, this range separates **India** from the **Tarim Basin** and **Central Asian** regions. ***Hence, this range is among those separating India from the rest of Asia.***

• **Himalayas**: This is the most prominent range that forms the northern boundary of **India**, separating the subcontinent from the **Tibetan Plateau** and the rest of the **Asian** continent. ***Hence, this range is among those separating India from the rest of Asia.***

• **Arakanyoma**: Also known as the **Rakhine Mountains**, this range is located in **Myanmar** and separates the **Irrawaddy** basin from the **Bay of Bengal**. While it forms a boundary between **India** and **Myanmar** in the east, it is not considered part of the primary northern mountain wall that separates the subcontinent from the rest of the **Asian** landmass. ***Hence, this range is not among the ones separating India from the rest of Asia.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Himalayas**: These are the youngest fold mountains in the world, formed approximately **50 million years** ago. They stretch for about **2,400 kilometers** from the **Indus River** in the west to the **Brahmaputra River** in the east, containing the world's highest peak, **Mount Everest**, at **8,848.86 meters**.

• **Karakoram Range**: This range contains the highest concentration of glaciers outside the polar regions, including the **Siachen Glacier**. It is home to **K2** (Mount Godwin-Austen), which is the second-highest peak in the world at **8,611 meters**.

• **Hindukush**: Stretching for about **800 kilometers**, this range is historically significant for the **Khyber Pass**, which served as a major trade and invasion route into the **Indian Subcontinent**. Its highest peak is **Tirich Mir**, located in **Pakistan**.

• **Arakanyoma**: This range is a southward extension of the **Himalayas** that arcs through **Myanmar**. It includes the **Patkai**, **Naga**, and **Lushai** hills on the **Indian** side. The highest point of this range is **Mount Victoria** (also known as **Nat Ma Taung**).

**Important Points__**

• **Climatic Barrier**: These northern mountain ranges protect the **Indian Subcontinent** from the freezing cold **Siberian** winds during winter and trap the moisture-laden **Southwest Monsoon** winds, ensuring heavy rainfall in the **Indo-Gangetic Plain**.

• **Biodiversity Hotspots**: The **Himalayas** and the **Indo-Burma** region (which includes the **Arakanyoma**) are recognized as global **Biodiversity Hotspots** due to their unique flora and fauna.

• **River Systems**: Major perennial rivers such as the **Indus**, **Ganges**, and **Brahmaputra** originate from these high mountain ranges, providing a vital source of water for agriculture and life in **India**.
</ul

question: Which type of vegetation is primarily found in the Himalayan region of India, characterized by coniferous trees and shrubs?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Temperate forests**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Temperate forests**, often referred to as **Montane Temperate forests** in the Indian context, are the primary vegetation type in the **Himalayan region** at altitudes ranging from **1500 to 3000 meters**. These forests are prominently characterized by the presence of **coniferous trees** and various **shrubs**. *Hence, this option is correct.*
 
• The **coniferous trees** found here, such as **Pine, Deodar, Silver Fir, Spruce, and Cedar**, have evolved needle-like leaves and a conical shape to survive the cold temperatures and heavy snowfall of the **Himalayas**. *Hence, the description matches this vegetation type.*
 
• **Tropical evergreen forests** are generally found in the **Terai region** and the **foothills** of the **Himalayas** up to an elevation of **1000 meters**, where the climate is warm and humid. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.*
 
• **Tundra vegetation** occurs at much higher altitudes, typically above **3600 to 4000 meters**, where the growth of tall trees is inhibited by extreme cold; this zone is dominated by **mosses, lichens**, and very short grasses. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.*
 
• **Desert vegetation** in the **Himalayan** context is restricted to the **rain-shadow areas** of the **Trans-Himalayas**, such as **Ladakh** and **Lahaul-Spiti**, which are classified as **cold deserts** with very sparse, stunted shrubs. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Geographic Distribution**: These **coniferous forests** cover a vast stretch of the **Himalayan range**, passing through the states and Union Territories of **Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim, and Arunachal Pradesh**.
 
• **Species Diversity**: In the **Western Himalayas**, the **Deodar (Cedrus deodara)** is a dominant species, prized for its durable timber. In the **Eastern Himalayas**, which receive higher **rainfall**, there is a greater variety of broad-leafed trees like **Oaks** mixed with **conifers**.
 
• **Economic Uses**: The **Chir Pine (Pinus roxburghii)** is highly valued for **timber** and for the extraction of **resin** and **turpentine**. **Silver Fir** and **Spruce** are extensively used for making **paper pulp** and **packing cases**.
 
• **Shrub Layer**: The undergrowth in these forests often consists of **Rhododendrons**, **Bamboo**, and various types of **ferns**, which thrive in the moist, cool environment of the mountain slopes.
 
• **Wildlife Habitats**: This vegetation zone is the **habitat** for unique fauna including the **Kashmir Stag (Hangul)**, **Snow Leopard** (at higher fringes), **Musk Deer**, and **Himalayan Black Bear**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Altitudinal Zonation**: The **Himalayan vegetation** shows a distinct **succession** of types based on **altitude**. It starts with **Tropical** at the base, followed by **Sub-tropical**, then **Temperate (Coniferous)**, and finally **Alpine** and **Tundra** at the highest reaches.
 
• **Climatic Influence**: The shift from **broad-leaved evergreen trees** to **needle-leaved conifers** is a direct result of the **lapse rate**, where the temperature drops by approximately **6.5 degrees Celsius** for every **1000 meters** of ascent.
 
• **Conservation**: Many areas within this **temperate belt** are protected under **National Parks** like the **Great Himalayan National Park** in **Himachal Pradesh**, which is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** known for its biodiversity.
 
• **Soil Type**: The soils in these **coniferous forests** are generally **podzolic** and **acidic** in nature, often covered with a thick layer of **humus** formed by the slow decomposition of needles.

question: The Deccan Traps were formed as a result of which geological event?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Volcanic eruptions**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Deccan Traps** are a massive **Large Igneous Province** located in west-central India. They were formed by the accumulation of multiple layers of solidified **flood basalt** resulting from intense volcanic activity.

• The primary geological event responsible for their formation was a series of **fissure-type volcanic eruptions**. These occurred as the **Indian Plate** moved over the **Reunion hotspot** in the **Indian Ocean** during its northward drift.

• **Earthquakes** are seismic vibrations caused by the sudden release of energy in the Earth's lithosphere. While they occur in volcanic regions, they do not deposit the massive layers of igneous rock that define the Deccan plateau. **Hence, this option is incorrect.**

• **Volcanic eruptions** involved the outpouring of low-viscosity **basaltic lava** that spread over vast areas, cooling to form the characteristic step-like topography of the region. **Hence, this option is correct.**

• **Glacial movement** refers to the flow of ice masses which shapes the landscape through erosion and the deposition of sediments like **moraines**. The Deccan region shows no evidence of massive glaciation during the **Mesozoic Era**. **Hence, this option is incorrect.**

• **Tectonic plate collision** is responsible for orogenic events, such as the formation of the **Himalayas** when the **Indian Plate** collided with the **Eurasian Plate**. However, the Deccan Traps are volcanic in origin and were formed before the main collision event. **Hence, this option is incorrect.**

**Additional Information__**
__

• The term **'Trap'** is derived from the **Swedish** word **'Trappa'**, which translates to **'stairs'**. This refers to the step-like or terraced appearance of the hills in the **Western Ghats**.

• Geographically, the traps cover a significant portion of India, primarily in the states of **Maharashtra**, **Gujarat**, and **Madhya Pradesh**, with smaller extensions into **Karnataka** and **Telangana**.

• The weathering of these volcanic basaltic rocks over millions of years has led to the formation of fertile **Black Soil**, also known as **Regur soil**.

• This **Black Soil** is highly valued for its moisture-retention capacity and is the primary soil type used for **Cotton** cultivation in the **Deccan** region.

• The total thickness of the lava flows varies across the region but reaches its maximum of over **2,000 meters** in the western part, particularly near the **Mumbai** coast.

**Important Points__**

• The eruptions took place approximately **66 million years ago**, coinciding with the end of the **Cretaceous period** and the beginning of the **Paleogene period**.

• Scientific research suggests that the massive release of volcanic gases, such as **carbon dioxide** and **sulfur dioxide**, during these eruptions contributed to global climate change and the **K-Pg mass extinction** event, which saw the end of the dinosaurs.

• The lava is primarily classified as **Tholeiitic basalt**, which is rich in iron and magnesium and has a low silica content, allowing it to flow easily over hundreds of kilometers.

• The **Deccan Traps** are one of the few examples of a continental flood basalt province on Earth, comparable in scale to the **Siberian Traps** in **Russia**.

• The volcanic activity is estimated to have lasted for a duration ranging from **30,000 to 1,000,000 years**, occurring in several distinct pulses of high-volume eruptions.
</ul

question: Which is the largest container port in India?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Jawaharlal Nehru Port (JNPT), Maharashtra**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Jawaharlal Nehru Port**, also widely known as **Nhava Sheva**, is the largest **container port** in India. It is located in **Navi Mumbai, Maharashtra**, along the **Arabian Sea** coast.
 
• It was commissioned on **May 26, 1989**, with the primary objective of de-congesting the **Mumbai Port** and serving as a hub for containerized traffic in the country.
 
• The port handles approximately **50%** of the total containerized cargo across all **major ports** in India. It is currently ranked among the top **30** container ports globally in terms of efficiency and volume.
 
• It serves as the gateway for India's international trade, particularly with **Europe, the Middle East, and the Americas**. The port handles diverse commodities including **textiles, chemicals, pharmaceuticals, carpets, and heavy machinery**.
 
• JNPT is the first major port in India to adopt the **Landlord Port Model**, where the port authority acts as a regulatory body and landlord, while port operations are carried out by **private terminal operators**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Mundra Port, Gujarat**:
 
 
• Located in the **Kutch district** of **Gujarat**, it is the largest **private port** and the largest **commercial port** in India by overall cargo volume.
 
• It is operated by **Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone Limited (APSEZ)** and has surpassed many major government ports in total tonnage handled annually.
 
 
 
• **Chennai Port, Tamil Nadu**:
 
 
• It is the **second largest** container port in India and the largest port in the **Bay of Bengal** region.
 
• Established in **1881**, it is an **artificial and all-weather port** that plays a crucial role in the handling of **automobiles, iron ore, and agricultural products**.
 
 
 
• **Kolkata Port, West Bengal**:
 
 
• Officially renamed the **Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port** in **2020**, it is the only **major riverine port** in India.
 
• Located about **203 kilometers** from the sea on the banks of the **Hooghly River**, it serves as a critical trade link for **North-East India** and landlocked neighbors like **Nepal and Bhutan**.
 
 
 
• **Mumbai Port, Maharashtra**:
 
 
• It is one of the **oldest modern ports** in India, used primarily for **bulk cargo** and **liquid chemicals**. Unlike JNPT, it is a **natural deep-water harbor**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Infrastructure and Connectivity**: **JNPT** is directly connected to the **Western Dedicated Freight Corridor (WDFC)**, which significantly reduces the transit time for goods moving between the port and the **National Capital Region (NCR)**.
 
• **TEU Capacity**: The port's performance is measured in **TEUs (Twenty-foot Equivalent Units)**. In the financial year **2022-2023**, JNPT handled a record-breaking **6.05 million TEUs**.
 
• **Special Economic Zone (SEZ)**: A dedicated **Multi-Product SEZ** has been developed at JNPT to promote **manufacturing-led exports** and enhance the "Make in India" initiative.
 
• **Digital Initiatives**: The port has implemented the **Centralized Parking Plaza (CPP)** and **Direct Port Delivery (DPD)** systems to ensure **transparency** and reduce the **Logistics Performance Index (LPI)** costs for traders.
</ul

question: What is the name of the geographical area from which all precipitation flows into a single river system?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Drainage basin**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **Drainage basin**, also known as a watershed or catchment area, is a geographical area where all precipitation, including rain, snow, and other forms of water, collects and flows into a single river system.
 
• The boundaries of a drainage basin are defined by **elevated landforms**, such as ridges or mountains, which direct the flow of water toward a particular river or its tributaries.
 
• Drainage basins are an essential aspect of hydrological studies as they help in understanding the flow of water, sediment transport, and nutrient cycles.
 
• Examples of major drainage basins in the world include the **Amazon Basin** (largest drainage basin in the world), the **Ganga-Brahmaputra Basin** in India, and the **Nile River Basin** in Africa.
 
• *Hence, "Drainage basin" is the correct answer.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Characteristics of a Drainage Basin:**

 
 
• The size of a drainage basin can vary from a few square kilometers to millions of square kilometers.
 
• Drainage basins often consist of a network of **tributaries**, smaller streams that feed into the main river.
 
• The water flow in a drainage basin is influenced by factors like **topography, climate, vegetation, and human activities**.
 
• Drainage basins serve as a critical source of water for agriculture, drinking, and industrial purposes.
 
 
 
• **Comparison of Other Options:**
 
 
• **Plateau:** A plateau is a flat, elevated landform that rises sharply above the surrounding area. It is not related to the collection of precipitation into a river system.
 
• **Waterfall zone:** This refers to an area where waterfalls are commonly found, usually due to steep gradients in rivers. It is not a geographical area where precipitation collects into a single river system.
 
• **Inland depression:** This is a low-lying area or a basin, often without an outlet to the sea. While it can collect water, it is not the same as a drainage basin, which specifically channels water to a river system.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Drainage Basins:**
 
 
• **Amazon Basin:** Located in South America, it is the largest drainage basin in the world, covering about 7 million square kilometers.
 
• **Mississippi River Basin:** Located in the United States, it is one of the largest drainage basins in North America.
 
• **Ganga-Brahmaputra Basin:** One of the most important drainage basins in India, supporting millions of people through its water resources.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Significance of Drainage Basins:**

 
 
• Drainage basins play a critical role in **water resource management**, as they determine how water flows and is distributed across regions.
 
• They are essential for maintaining biodiversity, as they provide habitats for various aquatic and terrestrial species.
 
• Drainage basins are also used in the planning and construction of **dams and irrigation systems**, which are vital for agriculture and energy production.
 
 
 
• **Global Drainage Systems:**
 
 
• Approximately **64% of the world's freshwater** flows through drainage basins.
 
• Many drainage basins are transboundary, meaning they span across multiple countries, leading to international agreements for water-sharing.

question: Which Indian port handles the highest volume of crude oil imports?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Kandla Port**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Kandla Port**, officially renamed as **Deendayal Port Trust** in **2017**, is located in the **Kutch District** of **Gujarat**. It is situated on the **Gulf of Kutch** and is one of the major ports on the west coast of India.

• It is recognized as the largest port in India by the volume of cargo handled. Specifically, it handles the highest volume of **Crude Oil** imports because it acts as the primary gateway for the massive oil refineries located in **Jamnagar** and **Vadinar**, as well as the landlocked refineries in **North India** via pipelines.

• The port is a **Tidal Port** and a **Natural Harbour**, making it geographically advantageous for large tankers. It manages a significant portion of India's **POL (Petroleum, Oil, and Lubricants)** traffic. ***Hence, option 1 is correct.***

• **Mumbai Port** is located in **Maharashtra** and is India's largest port by size and area. While it handles a substantial amount of liquid cargo and mineral oil, its total crude import volume is surpassed by **Kandla Port** due to the latter's proximity to high-capacity private and public refineries. ***Hence, option 2 is incorrect.***

• **Paradip Port** is an artificial deep-water port situated in **Odisha**. It is a major hub for **Iron Ore** and **Coal**. Although it handles crude oil for the **Indian Oil Corporation Limited (IOCL)** refinery in **Paradip**, its total volume is lower than that of the western ports. ***Hence, option 3 is incorrect.***

• **Visakhapatnam Port** is located in **Andhra Pradesh** and is the only **Natural Harbour** on the eastern coast of India. It is a **Landlocked Port** known for exporting **Iron Ore** to **Japan**. While it has oil handling facilities, it does not lead the country in crude import volume. ***Hence, option 4 is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Classification of Ports:** India has a coastline of approximately **7,516.6 kilometers**. The maritime administration is divided into **13 Major Ports** and over **200 Non-Major (Minor) Ports**. The **Major Ports** are under the jurisdiction of the **Central Government** (**Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways**), while **Minor Ports** fall under **State Governments**.

• **Mormugao Port:** Located in **Goa**, it is a premier **Iron Ore** exporting port in India. It was awarded the status of a major port in **1963**.

• **Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust (JNPT):** Also known as **Nhava Sheva**, located in **Maharashtra**, it is the largest **Container Port** in India. It was developed to decongest the **Mumbai Port**.

• **Chennai Port:** It is one of the oldest **Artificial Ports** on the eastern coast. It ranks second in terms of container traffic after **JNPT**.

• **Kolkata Port (Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port):** It is the only **Riverine Major Port** in India, located on the **Hooghly River**. It serves the entire **North-East India** and neighboring countries like **Nepal** and **Bhutan**.

**Important Points__**

• **Sagarmala Project:** Launched by the **Government of India** in **2015**, this flagship programme aims to promote **Port-led Development** in the country by modernizing ports and improving connectivity.

• **Major Port Authorities Act, 2021:** This **Act** was passed to provide greater autonomy and flexibility to the **Major Ports** in India and to professionalize their governance through the creation of **Boards of Port Authorities**.

• **Strategic Importance:** Over **95%** of India's trade by volume and **70%** by value is moved through maritime transport, making ports like **Kandla** vital for **Energy Security**.

• **Ennore Port (Kamarajar Port):** Located in **Tamil Nadu**, it is the first port in India which is a **Public Company** (**Corporate Port**).
</ul

subject: GK
question: Which among the following pairs is NOT correct about the indigenous dog breeds of India?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Chippiparai - Kerala**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Chippiparai** is an indigenous sighthound breed that originates from the **Tamil Nadu** state of India, specifically around the **Madurai**, **Theni**, and **Virudhunagar** districts. It was traditionally bred by royal families in **Chippiparai** near **Rajapalayam** for hunting small game like boar and deer. **Hence, the pair Chippiparai - Kerala is not correct.**
 
• **Gaddi Dog**, also known as the **Himalayan Sheepdog** or **Indian Panther Hound**, is found in the **Himalayan** region, including **Himachal Pradesh**, **Uttarakhand**, and parts of **Jammu and Kashmir**. It is a sturdy livestock guardian dog used by the **Gaddi** tribe. **Hence, the pair Gaddi Dog - Jammu and Kashmir is correct.**
 
• **Combai** (or **Kombai**) is a powerful and loyal terrier-type dog native to the **Theni** district of **Tamil Nadu**. Historically, they were used for hunting and guarding, and they are known for their distinctive ridge of hair on their back. **Hence, the pair Combai - Tamil Nadu is correct.**
 
• **Mudhol Hound** is a renowned sighthound from the **Mudhol** region of **Bagalkot** district in **Karnataka**. It is famous for its incredible speed, stamina, and sharp vision, making it an excellent hunter. **Hence, the pair Mudhol Hound - Karnataka is correct.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Rajapalayam**: This is another iconic breed from **Tamil Nadu**, characterized by its milky white coat, pink nose, and golden eyes. It was used by the **Nayakar** dynasty and later in the **Polygar Wars** against the British.
 
• **Rampur Hound**: Originating from the **Rampur** region of **Uttar Pradesh**, this sighthound was a favorite of the **Nawabs of Rampur**. It is built for speed and was used to hunt jackals, leopards, and even lions.
 
• **Kanni**: Closely related to the **Chippiparai**, the **Kanni** is a sighthound from **Tamil Nadu**. The name **Kanni** means **maiden**, as these dogs were traditionally given as part of a dowry to brides.
 
• **Jonangi**: This breed is native to the **Andhra Pradesh** region. It is unique for its short coat and its habit of making a **yodeling** sound instead of a typical bark. It was traditionally used for herding ducks.
 
• **Bakharwal Dog**: Found in the **Pir Panjal** range of the **Himalayas**, this breed is kept by the **Bakharwal** and **Gujjar** nomadic tribes of **Jammu and Kashmir** to protect their livestock from predators like wolves and bears.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **National Bureau of Animal Genetic Resources (NBAGR)**: Located in **Karnal**, **Haryana**, this institute under the **Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR)** is the nodal agency for the registration and documentation of indigenous animal breeds, including dogs.
 
• **Atmanirbhar Bharat and Indian Breeds**: In **August 2020**, Prime Minister **Narendra Modi** highlighted the importance of Indian dog breeds in his **Mann Ki Baat** address. He urged citizens to adopt local breeds to promote self-reliance and preserve India's biological heritage.
 
• **Military Induction**: The **Indian Army** made history in **2016** by inducting the **Mudhol Hound** into the **Remount Veterinary Corps (RVC)**. These dogs are trained for border surveillance, tracking, and explosive detection due to their high intelligence and physical agility.
 
• **Conservation Status**: Many indigenous breeds like the **Himalayan Mastiff** and **Alangu Mastiff** are facing the risk of extinction due to cross-breeding and the popularity of foreign breeds. Efforts are being made by various state governments to set up breeding centers to preserve their **genetic purity**.

__
 
• **Hooghly Region:** This is a major industrial area in India, primarily located in West Bengal. It includes industries like jute, textiles, engineering, and chemicals along the Hooghly River. *Hence, this is a major industrial region.*
 
• **Kolhapur-South Kannada Region:** This region is not considered a major industrial area compared to other regions in India. While it has industries, its scale and contribution to India's industrial output are relatively limited. *Hence, this is NOT a major industrial region.*
 
• **Gujarat Region:** Gujarat is one of India's most prominent industrial hubs, with major industries like petrochemicals, textiles, pharmaceuticals, and diamond cutting. *Hence, this is a major industrial region.*
 
• **Vishakhapatnam-Guntur Region:** Located in Andhra Pradesh, this region is a significant industrial center with industries like steel, shipbuilding, fertilizers, and chemicals. *Hence, this is a major industrial region.*
 
• **Durg-Raipur Region:** Situated in Chhattisgarh, this region is known for its steel and iron industries and is a key industrial area in central India. *Hence, this is a major industrial region.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Hooghly Industrial Region:**
 
 
• Located in **West Bengal**, this region is known for jute manufacturing, textiles, and engineering industries.
 
• It benefits from proximity to Kolkata, easy access to ports, and abundant labor.
 
• Major industries include **jute mills, paper mills, chemicals, and engineering products.**
 
 
 
• **Gujarat Industrial Region:**
 
 
• Gujarat is one of the fastest-growing industrial regions in India, with cities like Ahmedabad, Surat, and Vadodara leading the way.
 
• Key industries include **petrochemicals, pharmaceuticals, textiles, and diamond processing.**
 
• The state is well-known for its SEZs (Special Economic Zones) and ports.
 
 
 
• **Vishakhapatnam-Guntur Region:**
 
 
• This region is an important industrial hub in Andhra Pradesh, with major industries including steel plants, shipbuilding, and chemical production.
 
• Vishakhapatnam is home to India's **largest shipyard** and significant defense industries.
 
• It also has significant contributions to agriculture-based industries like fertilizers.
 
 
 
• **Durg-Raipur Industrial Region:**
 
 
• This region in Chhattisgarh is primarily known for its steel and iron industries.
 
• It houses the Bhilai Steel Plant, one of India's largest steel manufacturers.
 
• Other industries include **cement, aluminum, and power generation.**
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Industrial Regions in India:**
 
 
• Industrial regions are formed due to factors like resource availability, transportation facilities, skilled labor, and proximity to markets.
 
• India's industrial regions are concentrated in states like **Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal, and Karnataka.**
 
• Examples of major regions include Mumbai-Pune, Ahmedabad-Vadodara, Chennai-Coimbatore, and Delhi-Faridabad.
 
 
 
• **Role of Industrial Regions:**
 
 
• Industrial regions contribute significantly to India's GDP and employment.
 
• They act as hubs for innovation, technology, and manufacturing.
 
• These regions often facilitate international trade due to their proximity to ports and airports.
 
 
 
• **Kolhapur-South Kannada Region:**
 
 
• While this region has industries, it is not as prominent or developed as other major industrial hubs in India.
 
• Industries in this region are smaller in scale and focus on local and regional markets.
 
 
</ul

• **Polymers** are a dominant segment of the **petrochemical industry**, consisting of long-chain molecules produced through **polymerization**. These include **Polyethylene (PE)**, **Polypropylene (PP)**, and **Polyvinyl Chloride (PVC)**, which are utilized in **packaging**, **infrastructure**, and **automotive parts**. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• **Synthetic fibres** are man-made fibres created from **petrochemical sources** like **Ethylene** and **Para-xylene**. Major types in India include **Polyester**, **Nylon**, and **Acrylic**, which are critical for the **textile sector** and **industrial fabrics**. ***Hence, statement 2 is correct.***
 
• **Elastomers** refer to synthetic polymers with elastic properties, commonly known as **synthetic rubber**. Products like **Styrene-Butadiene Rubber (SBR)** and **Polybutadiene Rubber (PBR)** are essential for the **automobile industry** in the manufacturing of **tyres** and **tubes**. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***
 
• **Surfactant intermediates** are chemical compounds used as precursors for **detergents** and **cleaning agents**. The most prominent example is **Linear Alkyl Benzene (LAB)**, which is derived from **n-paraffins** and **benzene**. ***Hence, statement 4 is correct.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Overview of Petrochemical Industry**: The industry involves the transformation of **crude oil** and **natural gas** into useful products. **India** is the **6th largest** producer of chemicals globally and accounts for approximately **7%** of the global market share in the **chemical industry**.
 
• **Feedstocks**: The primary feedstocks used in the Indian petrochemical sector are **Naphtha**, **Natural Gas**, and **Ethane**. These are cracked to produce **olefins** (like **Ethylene** and **Propylene**) and **aromatics** (like **Benzene** and **Toluene**).
 
• **Government Policy**: The **Petroleum, Chemicals and Petrochemical Investment Regions (PCPIR)** policy aims to establish clusters for manufacturing. Notable regions include **Dahej** in **Gujarat**, **Paradip** in **Odisha**, and **Visakhapatnam** in **Andhra Pradesh**.
 
• **Market Trends**: The Indian market is seeing a shift towards **Specialty Chemicals**, which find applications in **pharmaceuticals**, **agrochemicals**, and **electronics**. The sector is projected to grow at a **CAGR** of around **10-12%** by **2030**.
 
• **Major Players**: The industry is led by giants like **Reliance Industries Limited (RIL)**, **Indian Oil Corporation (IOCL)**, and **GAIL (India) Limited**, which operate large-scale **cracker plants** across the **country**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Department of Chemicals and Petrochemicals**: This department, under the **Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers**, is the nodal agency for policy and planning. It oversees the **National Policy on Petrochemicals**, which aims to improve global competitiveness.
 
• **Environmental Regulations**: The industry is subject to strict guidelines by the **Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB)** regarding **effluent treatment** and **carbon emissions**, promoting **sustainable manufacturing** practices.
 
• **Import Dependence**: Despite high production, India still imports certain **specialty polymers** and **intermediates**. The **Make in India** initiative encourages domestic production to reduce the trade deficit in the **petrochemical sector**.
 
• **Applications**: Beyond household items, petrochemicals are vital for **healthcare** (medical devices), **telecommunications** (optical fibres), and **renewable energy** (components for **solar panels**).

question: Which of the following statements about the textile industry in India is correct?

options.text: It is dependent on foreign raw materials.
It is not involved in foreign exchange earnings.
It plays a key role in industrial output and jobs.

solution:
The correct answer is __**It plays a key role in industrial output and jobs**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **textile industry** is one of the oldest and most significant sectors in the **Indian economy**, contributing approximately **2% to 3% of the total Gross Domestic Product (GDP)** and about **7% of the total industrial output** in value terms. Hence, statement 3 is correct.

• It is the **second-largest employer** in **India** after agriculture, providing direct employment to over **45 million people** and indirect employment to another **60 million people**, including a large number of women and the rural population.

• The industry is **self-reliant** and not dependent on foreign raw materials; **India** is the **largest producer of cotton** and **jute** in the world and the **second-largest producer of silk**. Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.

• It is a major contributor to **foreign exchange earnings**, accounting for approximately **11% to 12% of India's total export earnings**, making it a vital sector for international trade. Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.

• The industry does not only manufacture low-value goods; it has a diverse range of products including **high-value garments**, **branded apparel**, and **technical textiles** used in specialized fields like **healthcare**, **defense**, and **automotive**. Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Raw Material Strength**: **India** produces all four types of silk: **Mulberry**, **Eri**, **Tasar**, and **Muga**. It is also the **world's second-largest producer of man-made fibers** like polyester and viscose.

• **Government Initiatives**: The **Government of India** has launched the **PM MITRA (Mega Integrated Textile Region and Apparel)** scheme to set up **7 mega textile parks** to boost investment and create **20 lakh jobs**.

• **FDI Policy**: To encourage growth, the government allows **100% Foreign Direct Investment (FDI)** in the textile sector under the **automatic route**.

• **Technical Textiles**: This is a sunrise sector in **India**, involving materials used for functional purposes such as **Meditech** (medical), **Agrotech** (agriculture), and **Geotech** (civil engineering), which are high-value-added products.

• **History**: The first modern textile mill in **India** was established at **Fort Gloster** near **Kolkata** in **1818**, though the industry saw real growth after the first cotton mill was set up in **Bombay (Mumbai)** in **1854** by **C.N. Davar**.

**Important Points__**

• **Linguistic and Cultural Impact**: The **handloom sector** is a significant part of the industry, preserving **India's heritage** and providing livelihoods to over **3.5 million weavers** across the country.

• **Global Position**: **India** is the **6th largest exporter** of textiles and apparel in the world, competing with nations like **China**, **Vietnam**, and **Bangladesh**.

• **Sustainability**: There is an increasing focus on **sustainable textiles** and **organic cotton**, with **India** being one of the leading producers of organic cotton globally to meet the demands of **environment-conscious** international markets.
</ul

question: What was the immediate outcome of Pakistan's objection to the SAARC Motor Vehicle Agreement in 2014?

options.text: India proposed a trilateral pact with China and Bhutan.
India shifted focus to BIMSTEC Maritime Agreement.
India advanced the BBIN Motor Vehicle Agreement.

solution:
The correct answer is __**India advanced the BBIN Motor Vehicle Agreement**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• During the **18th SAARC Summit** held in **Kathmandu, Nepal**, in **November 2014**, the member nations proposed the **SAARC Motor Vehicle Agreement (MVA)** to facilitate the seamless movement of people and goods across the region.

• **Pakistan** raised objections to the agreement, citing a lack of internal departmental clearances and security concerns, which effectively stalled the regional pact. **Hence, statement 4 is incorrect** as the organization did not halt all projects, but this specific regional agreement was blocked.

• As an immediate strategic response to bypass **Pakistan’s** veto, **India** shifted its focus toward a sub-regional framework involving willing neighbors. This led to the advancement of the **BBIN Motor Vehicle Agreement**. **Hence, statement 3 is correct.**

• The **BBIN MVA** was signed on **June 15, 2015**, in **Thimphu, Bhutan**, by the transport ministers of **Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, and Nepal**.

• The proposal for a trilateral pact with **China** and **Bhutan** was never the outcome, as **China** is not a member of **SAARC** and **India** maintains a distinct strategic policy regarding connectivity with **China**. **Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.**

• While **India** has increased its engagement with **BIMSTEC**, the immediate outcome of the **2014** deadlock was specifically the **BBIN** road connectivity pact, not a maritime agreement. **Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.**

**Additional Information__**

__

• The **BBIN** initiative (**Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Nepal**) is a sub-regional architecture aimed at improving economic integration through connectivity in power, water, and transport sectors.

• The **Asian Development Bank (ADB)** has been the lead technical and financial advisor for the **BBIN** project under its **South Asia Subregional Economic Cooperation (SASEC)** program.

• The **BBIN MVA** allows for **passenger, personal, and cargo vehicles** to travel across the borders of the four participating nations, reducing the cost and time of doing business.

• **Bhutan** faced domestic challenges in ratifying the agreement due to concerns regarding **environmental pollution** and the impact of heavy traffic on its infrastructure. Consequently, **Bhutan** opted for a temporary observer status while **India, Bangladesh, and Nepal** proceeded with implementation.

• In **March 2022**, **India, Bangladesh, and Nepal** finalized the enabling protocols to operationalize the **MVA**, marking a significant step toward regional integration without **Pakistan**.

**Important Points__**

• **SAARC** (South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation) was established on **December 8, 1985**, in **Dhaka**, with the goal of promoting the welfare of the people of **South Asia**.

• The **8 member states** of **SAARC** are **Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka**.

• The failure of the **SAARC MVA** in **2014** highlighted the **consensus-based decision-making** flaw of the organization, where a single member can veto regional progress.

• This event accelerated **India’s** **'Neighborhood First'** policy and its **'Act East'** policy, prioritizing groups like **BIMSTEC** (Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation) over **SAARC**.

• The **BBIN** model is often cited as a successful example of **'minilateralism'** in **South Asia**, where smaller groups of countries collaborate on specific functional areas to achieve faster results.

question:
Consider the following statements regarding the India–Bhutan Friendship Treaty signed in 2007:

1) The treaty affirms mutual respect for sovereignty and bans harmful use of each other’s territory.

2) Article 4 permits Bhutan to export arms to third countries with India’s consent.

3) The treaty promotes free trade and cultural cooperation in areas like education and health.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution:
The correct answer is __**1 and 3 only**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **India-Bhutan Friendship Treaty** was signed in **February 2007**, replacing the earlier treaty of **1949**. This updated treaty reflects the contemporary nature of the bilateral relationship, emphasizing mutual respect for each other's **sovereignty** and **territorial integrity**.
 
• **Statement 1**: The treaty affirms that both nations shall respect each other's independence and sovereignty. It explicitly mentions that neither government shall allow the use of its territory for activities harmful to the national security and interest of the other. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• **Statement 2**: **Article 4** of the **2007 Treaty** pertains to the **import** of arms and ammunition. It states that the **Government of Bhutan** is free to import arms, ammunition, and machinery required for its security from or through **India**, provided the intentions are friendly and do not pose a danger to **India**. It does not grant **Bhutan** the permission to **export** arms to third countries. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• **Statement 3**: The treaty significantly broadens the scope of cooperation. **Article 7** establishes **free trade** and commerce between the two territories, while **Article 8** encourages cooperation in various fields including **culture**, **education**, **health**, **sports**, and **science and technology**. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***
 
• The revision of the treaty was a landmark event that removed the clause from the **1949** version which stated that **Bhutan** would be 'guided by the advice' of **India** in its external relations, thereby granting **Bhutan** more **strategic autonomy**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Historical Context:** Diplomatic relations between **India** and **Bhutan** were formally established in **1968** with the appointment of a resident representative in **Thimphu**. The basic framework of their bilateral relations was the **Treaty of Friendship and Cooperation** signed in **1949**.
 
• **Strategic Importance:** **Bhutan** shares a border of approximately **699 km** with **India**, touching the states of **Sikkim**, **West Bengal**, **Assam**, and **Arunachal Pradesh**. It serves as a **buffer state** between **India** and **China**.
 
• **Economic Cooperation:** **India** is **Bhutan's** largest **trading partner**. The **hydropower** sector is the hallmark of this relationship. Several projects like the **Chukha** (336 MW), **Kurichhu** (60 MW), **Tala** (1020 MW), and **Mangdechhu** (720 MW) have been developed with **Indian** assistance.
 
• **Developmental Assistance:** **India** has been a major contributor to **Bhutan's Five-Year Plans** since their inception in **1961**. A significant portion of **India's** external aid budget is consistently allocated to **Bhutan** for infrastructure, **ICT**, and **social sectors**.
 
• **Security Cooperation:** Both countries cooperate closely on **border management**. In **2003**, the **Royal Bhutan Army** conducted **Operation All Clear** to flush out **Indian** insurgent groups (like **ULFA** and **NDFB**) operating from **Bhutanese** soil, demonstrating the strength of the security partnership.
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• The **2007 Treaty** was signed by the then **External Affairs Minister** of **India**, **Pranab Mukherjee**, and the then **Crown Prince** (now King) of **Bhutan**, **Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck**.
 
• The treaty provides for **extradition** of criminals and **mutual legal assistance** in criminal matters.
 
• It also ensures that **Bhutanese** citizens in **India** and **Indian** citizens in **Bhutan** shall enjoy the same facilities regarding trade and commerce as the locals.

question: Which of the following hill stations is also known as 'Satpura Ki Rani'?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Pachmari**__

**Pachmarhi** is widely known as **Satpura ki Rani (“Queen of Satpura”)**, situated at a** height of 1100 m** in a valley of the **Satpura Range in Hoshangabad district**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Pachmarhi is a hill station in the Hoshangabad district of Madhya Pradesh state.
 
• The name Pachmarhi is believed to be derived from the Hindi words Panch ("five") and Marhi ("caves").
 
• These caves were built by five Pandava brothers of the Mahabharatha era during their thirteen years of exile.
 
• The caves are situated on a hilltop and provide an excellent vantage point.
 
• Before the British, the Pachmarhi region came under the kingdom of the Gond king Bhawut Singh, although it was not a populated village or town at that time.
 
• Captain James Forsyth of the British Army along with Subhedar Major Nathoo Ramji Powar who was later made the Kotwal of Pachmarhi, spotted the plateau in the Pachmarhi region in 1857, while leading his troops on the way to Jhansi.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The Satpura Range is a range of hills in central India.
 
• The range rises in the eastern Gujarat state running east through the border of Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh to the east till Chhattisgarh.
 
• The range parallels the Vindhya Range to the north, and these two east-west ranges divide Indian Subcontinent into the Indo-Gangetic plain of northern India and the Deccan Plateau of the south. 
 
• The Narmada River originates from the north-eastern end of Satpura in Amarkantak.
 
• The Satpura Range is a horst mountain and is flanked by Narmada Graben in the north and much smaller but parallel Tapi Graben in the south.

question: Which linguistic group has the highest number of speakers in India?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Indo-Aryan**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Indo-Aryan** is the largest linguistic group in India, with the majority of the population speaking languages from this family.
 
• It is a subgroup of the larger Indo-European language family, which includes languages spoken in India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Nepal.
 
• Languages such as **Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Gujarati, Punjabi, Sindhi, and Odia** belong to the Indo-Aryan group. These are some of the most widely spoken languages in India.
 
• The Indo-Aryan group accounts for approximately **78% of India's population**, making it the most dominant linguistic family in the country.
 
• The languages in this group are primarily spoken in the northern, western, and eastern regions of India, covering a large geographical area and population.
 
• The Constitution of India recognizes several Indo-Aryan languages as **scheduled languages**, such as Hindi (which is also the official language of the Union government).
 
• The dominance of Indo-Aryan languages is a result of historical migration, cultural assimilation, and political developments over centuries.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Characteristics of Indo-Aryan Languages:**

 
 
• They are derived from **Sanskrit**, an ancient language that serves as the root for most Indo-Aryan languages.
 
• They are phonologically rich and characterized by a subject-object-verb (SOV) sentence structure.
 
 
 
• **Other Linguistic Groups in India:**
 
 
• **Sino-Tibetan:** Found in the northeastern regions, these languages include Manipuri, Bodo, and others. They are spoken by a smaller proportion of the population compared to Indo-Aryan.
 
• **Austric:** Includes languages such as Santhali, Mundari, and Khasi, primarily spoken by tribal communities in central and eastern India.
 
• **Dravidian:** Found predominantly in southern India, it includes Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, and Malayalam. Dravidian languages are spoken by a significant proportion of the population but still less compared to Indo-Aryan.
 
 
 
• **Facts and Data:**
 
 
• According to the **2011 Census of India**, Hindi alone is spoken by more than 43% of the Indian population, making it the most widely spoken Indo-Aryan language.
 
• Bengali is the second most spoken Indo-Aryan language, and it is also the official language of the state of West Bengal.
 
• Other widely spoken Indo-Aryan languages include Marathi, Gujarati, and Punjabi, each with millions of speakers.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Historical Significance:**

 
 
• The Indo-Aryan languages have deep historical roots and connections with **ancient Vedic culture** and literature.
 
• These languages played a crucial role in the spread of religion, art, and literature across the Indian subcontinent.
 
 
 
• **Modern Applications:**
 
 
• Indo-Aryan languages are used in government, media, education, and literature, contributing significantly to India's socio-economic and cultural development.
 
• They are also widely used in **Indian cinema**, including Bollywood, which has a global audience.

subject: GK
question: Which two tectonic plates are responsible for the formation of the Himalayas due to their collision?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Indian & Eurasian**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Himalayas** were formed due to the **collision** between the **Indian Plate** and the **Eurasian Plate**. This is a classic example of a **continent-continent convergent boundary**. ***Hence, the correct answer is Indian & Eurasian.***

• The **Indian Plate** was originally part of the ancient supercontinent **Gondwanaland**. About **200 million years** ago, it broke off and began moving **northward** toward the much larger **Eurasian Plate**.

• Before the collision, a vast sea called the **Tethys Sea** existed between the two plates. As the **Indian Plate** moved north, the sediments at the bottom of the **Tethys Sea** were compressed and uplifted to form the **Himalayan mountain range**.

• The **Indian & African** plates do not collide to form mountains; their interaction is primarily in the **Indian Ocean** along the **Central Indian Ridge**. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***

• The **Eurasian & Australian** plates meet in the **Southeast Asian** region, contributing to the formation of the **Indonesian archipelago** rather than the **Himalayas**. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***

• The **Pacific & Eurasian** plates interact along the **western Pacific**, forming **island arcs** and **oceanic trenches** like the **Japan Trench** through **subduction**. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• The **Himalayas** are classified as **Young Fold Mountains** because they were formed relatively recently in the **Earth's** geological history, approximately **40 to 50 million years** ago.

• The mountain range stretches over **2,400 kilometers** and passes through five countries: **India**, **Pakistan**, **China (Tibet)**, **Nepal**, and **Bhutan**.

• The **Himalayas** contain the world's highest peaks, including **Mount Everest**, which stands at **8,848.86 meters** above sea level.

• The **Tibetan Plateau** was also uplifted during this collision and is often referred to as the **'Roof of the World'** due to its high average elevation of over **4,500 meters**.

• The **Indian Plate** continues to move **northward** at a rate of about **5 centimeters per year**, causing the **Himalayas** to rise by approximately **5 to 10 millimeters** annually and making the region seismically active.

**Important Points__**

• **Plate Tectonics Theory:** This scientific theory describes the large-scale motion of seven large plates and several smaller plates of the **Earth's lithosphere**. It was developed in the **1960s** based on the earlier concept of **Continental Drift** proposed by **Alfred Wegener** in **1912**.

• **Types of Boundaries:** There are three main types of tectonic boundaries: **Convergent** (plates collide), **Divergent** (plates move apart), and **Transform** (plates slide past each other). The **Himalayas** are the result of a **Convergent Boundary**.

• **Impact on Climate:** The **Himalayan** range acts as a massive **climatic barrier**, preventing cold **Siberian** winds from entering the **Indian subcontinent** and forcing the **Monsoon** winds to shed their moisture over **India**.

• **River Systems:** Major perennial rivers like the **Indus**, **Ganges**, and **Brahmaputra** originate from the **Himalayan glaciers**, providing water to millions of people in **South Asia**.
</ul

• The roads are classified into **six** types: **National Highways**, **State Highways**, **District roads**, **Rural roads**, **Border Roads**, and **Expressways**.
 
• **National Highways** are the roads that connect one state with another and also connect important ports. These roads are constructed and laid by the **Central Public Works Department**(CPWD). They are designated with **NH**.
 
• **State Highways** are highways connecting major cities all over the state, it also connects other state highways of neighbouring states. It is designated by **SH**. • **District roads** are the roads where the districts are connected to each other. Other than a district, **Zila Parishads** also have the authority and responsibility to build roads.
 
• **Rural roads** are single-lane roads used to connect India's rural and remote areas. The roads are constructed and laid by **Panchayats** or by the project of **Pradhan Mantri Gramin Sadak Yojna**(PMGSY)
 
• **Border roads** are the roads constructed on the **North** and **North Eastern** borders of the country, constructed and maintained by the **Border Roads Organization **(BRO).
 
• **Expressways** are high-speed roads that are four or more lanes that have been designed for high-speed vehicular traffic, with all traffic flow regulated with toll roads. **National Expressways Authority of India** operates under the **Ministry of Road Transport and Highways**.

subject: GK
question: Who hand-calligraphed the original manuscript of the Indian Constitution?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Prem Behari Narain Raizada**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Prem Behari Narain Raizada** (Saxena) was the master calligrapher who hand-wrote the original manuscript of the **Constitution of India**. He belonged to a family of traditional calligraphers and learned the art from his grandfather.

• The original **Constitution** was not printed or typed; it was entirely **handwritten** in a flowing **italic style**. Raizada performed this monumental task in a room in **Constitution House** (now known as **Samvidhan Sadan**).

• When **Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru** approached him to write the document and asked about his fee, Raizada famously replied that he did not want a single penny. His only condition was that he be allowed to write his name on every page and his grandfather's name on the last page.

• He used approximately **432 pen nibs** (specifically **No. 303 nibs**) to complete the calligraphy of the **English** and **Hindi** versions. The entire process took about **six months** to finish.

• **B.N. Rau** (Sir Benegal Narsing Rau) served as the **Constitutional Advisor** to the **Constituent Assembly** and prepared the initial draft. *Hence, statement 1 is incorrect regarding calligraphy.*

• **S.N. Mukherjee** was the **Chief Draftsman** of the Constitution and was praised for his ability to put complex proposals into legal shape. *Hence, statement 3 is incorrect regarding calligraphy.*

• **Gopalaswami Ayyangar** was a key member of the **Drafting Committee** and played a significant role in drafting **Article 370**. *Hence, statement 4 is incorrect regarding calligraphy.*

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Artistic Decoration**: While Raizada did the calligraphy, the task of decorating and illuminating the pages was entrusted to artists from **Shantiniketan**. This team was led by **Nandalal Bose**.

• **Beohar Rammanohar Sinha**: He was a student of **Nandalal Bose** and is credited with the beautiful artwork on the **Preamble** page. His signature 'Ram' can be seen on the Preamble page.

• **Preservation**: The original handwritten copies of the Constitution (one in **English** and one in **Hindi**) are kept in special **helium-filled cases** in the **Library of the Parliament of India** in **New Delhi** to prevent deterioration.

• **Language**: The Constitution was originally written in both **Hindi** and **English**. Every member of the **Constituent Assembly** signed both copies on **January 24, 1950**.

• **Length**: The **Indian Constitution** is the **longest written constitution** of any sovereign nation in the world. At its inception, it contained **395 Articles**, **22 Parts**, and **8 Schedules**.

**Important Points__**

• **Drafting Committee**: Chaired by **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar**, who is known as the **Father of the Indian Constitution**. The committee was responsible for scrutinizing the draft prepared by the **Constitutional Advisor**.

• **Timeline**: The **Constituent Assembly** took exactly **2 years, 11 months, and 18 days** to complete the final draft of the Constitution.

• **Adoption and Enforcement**: The Constitution was adopted on **November 26, 1949** (celebrated as **Constitution Day** or **Samvidhan Divas**), and it came into full legal force on **January 26, 1950**.

• **Sovereignty**: With the commencement of the Constitution, the **Indian Independence Act of 1947** and the **Government of India Act of 1935** were repealed, and India became a **Republic**.
</ul

question: Who is regarded as the chief architect of the Indian Constitution?
solution:
The correct answer is __**B. R. Ambedkar**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Dr. B. R. Ambedkar** is widely regarded as the **Chief Architect of the Indian Constitution** and is also known as the **"Father of the Indian Constitution."**
 
• He was appointed as the **Chairman** of the **Drafting Committee** by the **Constituent Assembly** on **29 August 1947** to prepare a draft of the new Constitution for independent India.
 
• As the head of the **Drafting Committee**, he was responsible for synthesizing various administrative and political ideas into a single legal document that governs the nation.
 
• He played a crucial role in ensuring that the **Constitution** provided extensive safeguards and guarantees for **civil liberties**, including the **abolition of untouchability** and the prohibition of all forms of **discrimination**.
 
• His profound knowledge of **constitutional law** and his advocacy for the **depressed classes** ensured that the document reflected a commitment to **social justice** and **equality**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Mahatma Gandhi:** 
 
 
• Although he was the most prominent leader of the **Indian Independence Movement**, **Mahatma Gandhi** was **not a member** of the **Constituent Assembly**.
 
• His influence was nevertheless felt through the inclusion of **Gandhian principles**, such as the promotion of **cottage industries** and the establishment of **Village Panchayats**, primarily within the **Directive Principles of State Policy**.
 
 
 
• **Jawaharlal Nehru:** 
 
 
• The first **Prime Minister** of India, **Jawaharlal Nehru**, moved the historic **"Objectives Resolution"** on **13 December 1946**.
 
• This resolution outlined the **ideals** and **philosophy** that guided the framing of the Constitution, eventually becoming the basis for the **Preamble**.
 
 
 
• **Dr. Rajendra Prasad:** 
 
 
• He was elected as the permanent **President** of the **Constituent Assembly** on **11 December 1946**, following the temporary presidency of **Sachchidananda Sinha**.
 
• He presided over the deliberations of the Assembly and later became the **first President of India** in **1950**.
 
 
 
• **B.N. Rau:** 
 
 
• He was appointed as the **Constitutional Advisor** to the **Constituent Assembly**. He prepared the **initial draft** of the Constitution, which was then scrutinized and refined by the **Drafting Committee** led by **Ambedkar**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **Drafting Committee** consisted of **seven members**, including **K.M. Munshi**, **Alladi Krishnaswamy Iyer**, and **N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar**, with **Dr. B. R. Ambedkar** at the helm.
 
• The **Constitution of India** was formally **adopted** on **26 November 1949**, a date now celebrated annually as **Constitution Day (Samvidhan Divas)**.
 
• It officially **came into force** on **26 January 1950**, marking India's transition into a **Sovereign Democratic Republic**.
 
• **Dr. B. R. Ambedkar** served as India's first **Law Minister** in the **Union Cabinet** from **1947 to 1951**.
 
• He famously described **Article 32** (Right to Constitutional Remedies) as the **"heart and soul"** of the Constitution because it allows citizens to approach the **Supreme Court** for the enforcement of **Fundamental Rights**.
</ul

• The emergency provisions of the Indian Constitution are borrowed from the Government of India Act, **1935**.
 
• The Government of India Act 1935 was a comprehensive statute that laid the foundation for the federal structure and significant administrative reforms in British India.
 
• Provisions under this act included the establishment of a Federal Court, the division of powers between the centre and provinces, and emergency powers.
 
• The Indian Constitution adopted many features from this act, including the emergency provisions allowing the President to declare an emergency in case of war, external aggression, or armed rebellion.

• **The Government of India Act 1935** was the last pre-independence constitution of India, and it served as the basis for the Constitution of India adopted in 1950.
 
• It introduced provincial autonomy, which allowed Indian provinces to govern themselves to a certain extent, reducing the powers of the British Governor-General.
 
• The Act also provided for the establishment of a Federal Court and outlined a federal structure for India, which influenced the federal nature of the Indian Constitution.
 
• Many principles and administrative structures established by the 1935 Act were retained and refined in the Indian Constitution, contributing to the stability and continuity of governance post-independence.
 
• Emergency provisions were necessary to tackle unforeseen situations that could threaten the nation, thereby providing a constitutional mechanism to handle crises effectively.
