question: Which of the following powers did Jammu and Kashmir have under Article 370?

options.text: Decision-making in all matters except defence, foreign affairs, and communications

solution:
The correct answer is __**All of the above**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Article 370** of the **Indian Constitution** provided a special autonomous status to the state of **Jammu and Kashmir**. This article allowed the state to have **its own Constitution**, which was separate from the Constitution of India. This document governed the internal administration and legal framework of the state. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***

• Under the provisions of **Article 370**, the state was permitted to fly its own **separate flag** alongside the **National Flag of India**. The state flag was **red** in color with **three white vertical stripes** representing the three regions of the state (Jammu, Kashmir, and Ladakh) and a **white plough**. ***Hence, statement 2 is correct.***

• The **Parliament of India** had limited legislative powers over the state. Its authority was restricted primarily to matters of **defence, foreign affairs, finance, and communications**. For the application of any other central laws, the **concurrence of the State Government** was mandatory, giving the state significant **decision-making power** in most internal matters. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***

• Because all the mentioned powers—having a separate constitution, a distinct flag, and restricted central legislative jurisdiction—were integral features of the special status granted by **Article 370**, the correct choice is **All of the above**.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Historical Context:** **Article 370** was incorporated into the **Constitution of India** on **October 17, 1949**, as a **temporary provision**. It was drafted by **N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar** to manage the unique transition of the state into the **Union of India** following the **Instrument of Accession** signed by **Maharaja Hari Singh** in **1947**.

• **Article 35A:** This was a significant provision derived from **Article 370**, introduced through a **Presidential Order in 1954**. It empowered the **Jammu and Kashmir State Legislature** to define **permanent residents** of the state and provide them with exclusive rights regarding **government jobs**, **scholarships**, and the **purchase of immovable property**.

• **Abrogation of Article 370:** On **August 5, 2019**, the **President of India** issued the **Constitution (Application to Jammu and Kashmir) Order, 2019**, which effectively revoked the special status. This action made the **Constitution of India** fully applicable to the region and ended the state's separate constitution and flag.

• **Reorganization:** Following the abrogation, the **Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019** was enacted. This led to the **bifurcation** of the state into two **Union Territories**: **Jammu and Kashmir** (with a legislative assembly) and **Ladakh** (without a legislative assembly), effective from **October 31, 2019**.

**Important Points__**

• **Legislative Impact:** Before **2019**, **Article 360** (Financial Emergency) of the Indian Constitution did not apply to **Jammu and Kashmir**. Furthermore, the **Directive Principles of State Policy** and various **Fundamental Rights** were applicable only in a modified form or through state-specific legislation.

• **Judicial Oversight:** While the **Supreme Court of India** had jurisdiction over the state, the **High Court of Jammu and Kashmir** held a unique position, and certain central laws like the **Right to Information (RTI) Act** or the **Right to Education (RTE) Act** were not automatically applicable until the state legislature passed corresponding laws.

• **Current Status:** Since **October 2019**, the **Indian Penal Code (IPC)** has replaced the **Ranbir Penal Code (RPC)**, and all **central laws** and **welfare schemes** are now directly implemented in the **Union Territories** of **Jammu and Kashmir** and **Ladakh**.

question: Which act made the 'Governor-General of Bengal' as the 'Governor-General of India?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Charter Act of 1833**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Charter Act of 1833**, also known as the **Saint Helena Act 1833**, was a significant constitutional instrument that centralized the administration of **British India**.

• This act redesignated the **Governor-General of Bengal** as the **Governor-General of India**, vesting in him all **civil and military powers**. This was a major step toward the unification of the country under a single authority.

• **Lord William Bentinck** became the **first Governor-General of India** under the provisions of this act.

• The act deprived the **Governor of Bombay** and the **Governor of Madras** of their **legislative powers**, making the Governor-General of India the sole legislative authority for the entire British territory in India.

• It ended the activities of the **East India Company** as a **commercial body**, transforming it into a purely **administrative body**. The company’s territories in India were now held by it in trust for **His Majesty**, his heirs, and successors.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Charter Act of 1813**: This act renewed the **East India Company** charter for another **20 years**. It ended the company’s **trade monopoly** in India, except for trade in **tea** and trade with **China**. It also allotted **one lakh rupees** annually for the promotion of **education** in India and allowed **Christian missionaries** to enter the country.

• **Charter Act of 1853**: This was the last of the series of **Charter Acts** passed by the **British Parliament** between **1793** and **1853**. It separated the **legislative** and **executive functions** of the Governor-General’s council for the first time and introduced an **open competition system** for the selection and recruitment of **civil servants**.

• **Indian Council Act of 1861**: This act is an important landmark in the constitutional history of India as it initiated the process of **decentralization**. It restored the **legislative powers** to the **Bombay** and **Madras** Presidencies. It also introduced the **Portfolio system**, which was pioneered by **Lord Canning** in **1859**.

• **Regulating Act of 1773**: This was the first step taken by the **British Government** to control and regulate the affairs of the **East India Company** in India. It designated the **Governor of Bengal** as the **Governor-General of Bengal** and **Lord Warren Hastings** was the first person to hold this designation.

**Important Points__**

• The **Charter Act of 1833** introduced a **fourth member** to the Governor-General’s Council, known as the **Law Member**. **Lord Macaulay** was appointed as the first Law Member to assist in the codification of laws.

• The act mandated the establishment of the **First Law Commission** in **1834** under the chairmanship of **Lord Macaulay** to codify **Indian laws**, which eventually led to the creation of the **Indian Penal Code (IPC)**.

• An attempt was made by the **1833 Act** to introduce a system of **open competition** for the selection of **civil servants**, stating that Indians should not be debarred from holding any place, office, or employment under the Company. However, this provision was negated after opposition from the **Court of Directors**.

• The act also directed the **Governor-General-in-Council** to take steps for the **abolition of slavery** in India, which was eventually abolished in **1843**.

question: Which of the following is NOT a directive principle of international peace and security?

options.text: Promotion of international peace and security
Create opportunities of employment for foreigners
Respect for international laws and treaty obligations

solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The directive principles of international peace and security are guidelines for the government to follow in order to promote global harmony and stability.
 
• **Encourage settlements of international disputes**, **Promotion of international peace and security**, and **Respect for international laws and treaty obligations** are recognized as directive principles aimed at fostering peaceful international relations.
 
• **Create opportunities of employment for foreigners** is not a directive principle of international peace and security. It is more related to economic policies and employment strategies rather than international peace and security.

• The directive principles of state policy in India are enshrined in Part IV of the Constitution of India. They serve as guidelines to the central and state governments of India to be kept in mind while framing laws and policies.
 
• These principles are not enforceable by any court, but they are considered fundamental in the governance of the country, aiming to create social and economic conditions under which citizens can lead a good life.
 
• The directive principles related to international peace and security emphasize the importance of maintaining friendly relations with other nations and adhering to international laws and treaties.

• **The 42nd Amendment to the Indian Constitution**, enacted in **1976, **introduced significant changes, including the addition of four new directive principles.
 
• These directive principles are guidelines for the state to follow while formulating policies and laws, aiming to establish a just and equitable society.
 
• **Four Directive Principles** were added by the 42nd Amendment as follows:
 
• **Article 39:** This directive principle emphasizes that the state should direct its policies towards securing social justice and equality. It highlights several aspects, including equitable distribution of resources, prevention of concentration of wealth and means of production, and ensuring that the operation of the economic system does not result in the concentration of wealth and resources.
 
• **Article 39A: **This principle focuses on providing free legal aid and ensuring that justice is not denied to any citizen by reason of economic or other disabilities. It aims to ensure that opportunities for securing justice are not inaccessible to economically disadvantaged sections of society.
 
• **Article 43A: **This directive principle relates to participation of workers in management of industries. It emphasizes that the state shall take steps to secure the participation of workers in the management of undertakings, establishments, or other organizations engaged in any industry.
 
• **Article 48A: **This principle pertains to protection and improvement of environment and safeguarding forests and wildlife. It mandates that the state shall endeavor to protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife.

question: The 11th Fundamental Duty was added by which Amendment?
solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The 42nd Amendment Act of 1976 added 10 Fundamental Duties to the Indian Constitution.
 
• The 86th Amendment Act of 2002 later added the 11th fundamental duty to the list.
 
• The Swaran Singh Committee suggested the adoption of Fundamental Duties in 1976 after they were deemed necessary amid the internal problems of 1975–1977.
 
• The Fundamental Duties are covered by Article 51A of Part-IV A of the Indian Constitution.
 
• The basic requirements imposed by the 42nd Amendment Act of the Constitution in 1976 offer the legislature more ability to uphold these commitments in regard to the fundamental rights, in addition to promoting and producing culture.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The importance of fundamental duties:

 
 
• They serve as a reminder to Indian citizens of their obligations to society, their fellow citizens, and the country.
 
• They caution people to avoid engaging in anti-social and anti-national behavior.
 
• They motivate others and instill a sense of devotion and discipline in them.
 
• They assist the courts in reviewing and determining whether the statute is constitutional.
 
 
 
• There are 11 Fundamental Duties:
 
 
• ​To abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag, and the National Anthem.
 
• To cherish and follow the noble ideals that inspired the national struggle for freedom.
 
• To uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity, and integrity of India.
 
• To defend the country and render national service when called upon to do so.
 
• To promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood amongst all the people of India transcending religious, linguistic, and regional or sectional diversities and to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women.
 
• To value and preserve the rich heritage of the country’s composite culture.
 
• To protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers, and wildlife, and to have compassion for living creatures.
 
• To develop scientific temper, humanism, and the spirit of inquiry and reform.
 
• To safeguard public property and to abjure violence.
 
• To strive towards excellence in all spheres of individual and collective activity so that the nation constantly rises to higher levels of endeavor and achievement.
 
• To provide opportunities for education to his child or ward between the ages of six and fourteen years (added by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002)

question: Which article of the Constitution abolishes 'Untouchability'?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 17**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 17** of the **Constitution of India** specifically deals with the **abolition of untouchability**. It states that "Untouchability" is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden. ***Hence, Article 17 is the correct answer.***
 
• This article ensures that the enforcement of any disability arising out of **"Untouchability"** shall be an offense punishable in accordance with the **law**.
 
• It is a significant provision under **Part III** of the Constitution, which covers **Fundamental Rights**, aimed at establishing social equality and dignity for all citizens, especially those from marginalized communities.
 
• Unlike many other fundamental rights, **Article 17** is **absolute** in nature, meaning no exceptions are provided for its violation under any circumstances.
 
• The **Parliament** of India, exercising its power under **Article 35**, enacted the **Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955**, which was later renamed the **Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955**, to prescribe punishments for practicing untouchability.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Article 14**:

 
 
• This article guarantees **Equality before the law** and **Equal protection of the laws** within the territory of **India**.
 
• It prohibits **discrimination** and ensures that the state shall not deny any person equality. However, it does not specifically mention the abolition of untouchability. ***Hence, Article 14 is an incorrect option.***
 
 
 
• **Article 19**:
 
 
• This article protects **six fundamental freedoms** for the citizens of India, including freedom of **speech and expression**, assembly, association, movement, residence, and profession.
 
• These freedoms are subject to **reasonable restrictions** in the interest of the sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, etc. ***Hence, Article 19 is an incorrect option.***
 
 
 
• **Article 21**:
 
 
• This article provides for the **Protection of Life and Personal Liberty**. It states that no person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to **procedure established by law**.
 
• The **Supreme Court** has expanded its scope to include the right to **privacy**, right to clean environment, and right to education. ***Hence, Article 21 is an incorrect option.***
 
 
 
• **Article 15**:
 
 
• While not in the primary options, it is related as it prohibits discrimination on grounds only of **religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth**.
 
• It specifically provides access to **shops, public restaurants, hotels, and places of public entertainment** to all citizens.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Historical Context**: The inclusion of **Article 17** was a direct response to the centuries-old social evil of untouchability in India. **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar**, the father of the Indian Constitution, was a leading proponent of this provision.
 
• **Terminology**: Interestingly, the word **"Untouchability"** is placed within quotation marks in the Constitution because it is not defined in the Constitution or the Act. Courts have interpreted it to mean the social practice as it developed historically in India.
 
• **Enforcement Acts**:
 
 
• **Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955**: Provides penalties for preventing a person from entering a place of public worship or taking water from a public well/tank.
 
• **Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989**: This act was passed to prevent atrocities against members of **SC and ST** communities and to provide for special courts for the trial of such offenses.
 
 
 
• **Nature of Right**: Article 17 is enforceable not just against the **State** but also against **private individuals**. It is the duty of the State to take necessary steps to ensure this right is not violated.

question: Which Article of the Indian Constitution guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the laws?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 14**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 14** of the **Constitution of India** provides that the **State** shall not deny to any person **equality before the law** or the **equal protection of the laws** within the territory of **India**. *Hence, this option is correct.*
 
• The term **"Equality before the law"** is of **British origin** and implies the absence of any special privileges in favor of any individual. It signifies the equal subjection of all persons to the ordinary law of the land.
 
• The term **"Equal protection of the laws"** is derived from **Section 1** of the **14th Amendment** of the **U.S. Constitution**. It implies that among equals, the law should be equal and equally administered, and that like should be treated alike.
 
• This right is available to all **persons**, whether **citizens** or **foreigners**. It also extends to **legal persons**, such as **statutory corporations**, **companies**, **registered societies**, or any other type of legal entity.
 
• The **Supreme Court** has held that **Article 14** is a **"Basic Structure"** of the **Constitution**. Therefore, it cannot be destroyed even by an amendment to the Constitution under **Article 368**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Article 19:**
 
 
• It guarantees to all citizens the **six rights** regarding freedom of: (a) **speech and expression**, (b) **assembly**, (c) **association**, (d) **movement**, (e) **residence**, and (f) **profession**.
 
• These rights are available only to **citizens** and not to foreigners or legal entities like companies. *Hence, Article 19 is not the correct answer.*
 
 
 
• **Article 21:**
 
 
• It declares that no person shall be deprived of his **life or personal liberty** except according to **procedure established by law**.
 
• This right is available to both **citizens and non-citizens**. Over the years, the judiciary has expanded its scope to include the **right to privacy**, **right to health**, and **right to free legal aid**. *Hence, Article 21 is not the correct answer.*
 
 
 
• **Article 32:**
 
 
• It provides the **Right to Constitutional Remedies**, allowing citizens to move the **Supreme Court** for the enforcement of **Fundamental Rights**.
 
• **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar** described this article as the **"Heart and Soul of the Constitution"**. Under this, the court can issue **writs** like **Habeas Corpus**, **Mandamus**, and **Certiorari**. *Hence, Article 32 is not the correct answer.*
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The concept of **Rule of Law** is the basis of **Article 14**. It was famously propounded by the British jurist **A.V. Dicey**. His theory has three elements: absence of arbitrary power, equality before the law, and the primacy of the rights of the individual.
 
• There are certain **exceptions** to the rule of equality. For instance, the **President of India** and the **Governors of States** enjoy immunities under **Article 361**. They are not answerable to any court for the exercise and performance of the powers and duties of their office.
 
• **Article 31-C** is also an exception; the **Supreme Court** held that "where **Article 31-C** comes in, **Article 14** goes out." This relates to laws giving effect to certain **Directive Principles** (Article 39(b) and 39(c)).
 
• Foreign sovereigns (ambassadors and diplomats) enjoy immunity from **civil and criminal proceedings** in **India**, as per international conventions.
</ul

question: In which section of the Indian Constitution are Fundamental Rights outlined?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Part III**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Fundamental Rights** are outlined in **Part III** of the **Indian Constitution**, from **Articles 12 to 35**. These rights are guaranteed to all citizens and are enforceable by courts.
 
• They aim to ensure the protection of individual liberties and equality, regardless of caste, religion, gender, or background.
 
• **Part III** is often referred to as the **‘Magna Carta’** of India because it encapsulates the basic human rights essential for the development of individuals and the nation.
 
• Some of the key rights included in this part are the **Right to Equality** (Articles 14–18), the **Right to Freedom** (Articles 19–22), the **Right against Exploitation** (Articles 23–24), the **Right to Freedom of Religion** (Articles 25–28), **Cultural and Educational Rights** (Articles 29–30), and the **Right to Constitutional Remedies** (Article 32).
 
• These rights form the foundation of India’s democratic framework, ensuring the rule of law and the protection of individual dignity and freedom.
 
• The **Supreme Court of India** and the **High Courts** have the power to enforce these rights through writs such as **habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto,** and **certiorari**.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Part III.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Part I of the Constitution:**

 
 
• This part deals with the **Union and its Territory**. It includes Articles 1 to 4, which define India as a Union of States and outline the process for the reorganization of states.
 
• It specifies how new states can be formed, old states can be altered, and union territories can be administered.
 
 
 
• **Part II of the Constitution:**
 
 
• This part addresses **Citizenship**, including Articles 5 to 11. It lays down the conditions for acquiring, terminating, and determining Indian citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution.
 
• It explains the rights and responsibilities associated with Indian citizenship but does not include Fundamental Rights.
 
 
 
• **Part III of the Constitution:**
 
 
• As mentioned earlier, it includes **Fundamental Rights**, which are central to the democratic framework of the country. These rights are justiciable and enforceable by courts of law.
 
• The **Right to Constitutional Remedies** (Article 32) is considered the heart and soul of the Constitution as it empowers individuals to move the Supreme Court to enforce their Fundamental Rights.
 
 
 
• **Part IV of the Constitution:**
 
 
• This part deals with the **Directive Principles of State Policy** (Articles 36 to 51). These are non-justiciable principles that guide the government in framing laws and policies for the welfare of its people.
 
• While Fundamental Rights focus on individual rights, the Directive Principles emphasize collective welfare and socio-economic justice.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Enforcement of Fundamental Rights:**

 
 
• Fundamental Rights are enforceable in courts. If they are violated, individuals can approach the **Supreme Court** or **High Courts** for redressal under **Article 32** and **Article 226**, respectively.
 
• The writ jurisdiction of the courts ensures that the government or any authority complies with the provisions of Fundamental Rights.
 
 
 
• **Unique Features of Fundamental Rights:**
 
 
• They are not absolute and are subject to reasonable restrictions for the sake of public order, morality, and security of the state.
 
• Some rights, such as those under Articles 20 and 21, are available even to non-citizens.
 
• Fundamental Rights can be suspended during a **national emergency**, except for Articles 20 and 21.

subject: GK
question:
Match the below writs' with their correct constitutional purpose':

 
 

 
 
**Column A: Writs**

 
 
 
**Column B: Purpose**

 
 
 

 
 
1.

 
 Habeas Corpus
 
 
a.

 
 Direct a person to perform public duty
 
 

 
 
2.

 
 Mandamus
 
 
b.

 
 To prevent unlawful detention
 
 

 
 
3.

 
 Certiorari
 
 
c.

 
 Transfer of pending case
 
 

 
 
4.

 
 Quo Warranto
 
 
d.

 
 To inquire into illegal occupation of office
solution:
The correct answer is __**1 - b, 2 - a, 3 - c, 4 - d**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Habeas Corpus:**

 
 
• The term "Habeas Corpus" translates to "You may have the body."
 
• This writ is issued to ensure that no person is detained unlawfully, without sufficient legal justification.
 
• The purpose is to safeguard an individual's fundamental right to freedom under **Article 21** of the Indian Constitution.
 
• *Hence, it is correctly matched with "To prevent unlawful detention."*
 
 
 
• **Mandamus:**
 
 
• This writ is issued by a higher court to a lower court, tribunal, or public authority to perform a public or statutory duty.
 
• The term "Mandamus" means "We command."
 
• It is typically issued when a public official or body fails to perform their legal duty.
 
• *Hence, it is correctly matched with "Direct a person to perform public duty."*
 
 
 
• **Certiorari:**
 
 
• The writ of Certiorari is issued by a higher court to a lower court to transfer a case to itself or to quash an order given by the lower court.
 
• This writ is primarily used to ensure that the subordinate courts function within their jurisdiction.
 
• It is corrective in nature and is used to prevent judicial overreach or errors.
 
• *Hence, it is correctly matched with "Transfer of pending case."*
 
 
 
• **Quo Warranto:**
 
 
• The term "Quo Warranto" means "By what authority."
 
• This writ is issued to inquire into the legality of a person’s claim to a public office.
 
• It prevents the illegal occupation of a public office by an unauthorized person.
 
• *Hence, it is correctly matched with "To inquire into illegal occupation of office."*
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Writs in India:**

 
 
• Under the Indian Constitution, writs are issued by the Supreme Court and High Courts to enforce fundamental rights.
 
• These writs are provided under **Articles 32** (Supreme Court) and **226** (High Courts).
 
• There are five types of writs: **Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Certiorari, Quo Warranto, and Prohibition.**
 
 
 
• **Features and Functions of Writs:**
 
 
• **Habeas Corpus:** Protects individual liberty and ensures that no person is detained without lawful justification.
 
• **Mandamus:** Enforces public duties and ensures accountability in governance.
 
• **Certiorari:** Prevents the misuse of judicial authority by lower courts.
 
• **Quo Warranto:** Ensures that public offices are not occupied illegally.
 
• **Prohibition:** Stops lower courts from exceeding their jurisdiction.
 
 
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• The writ jurisdiction of the Supreme Court is limited to cases involving fundamental rights.
 
• High Courts can issue writs not only for fundamental rights but also for other legal rights.
 
• Writs are an essential tool to ensure judicial review and uphold the rule of law in India.

question: Directive Principles of State Policy strive to make India ________.
solution:
The correct answer is __**a welfare state**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The Directive Principles of State Policy aim to establish India as a **welfare state**.
 
• These principles are enshrined in Part IV of the Constitution of India and are intended to guide the state in formulating policies and laws.
 
• They emphasize social and economic democracy, aiming to reduce inequalities and ensure a decent standard of living for all citizens.
 
• Key areas include providing adequate means of livelihood, equal pay for equal work, protection of children and youth, and securing a social order based on justice and equality.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The Directive Principles are non-justiciable, meaning they are not enforceable by any court, but they are fundamental in the governance of the country.
 
• The Constitution of India was adopted on **26th November 1949** and came into effect on **26th January 1950**.
 
• The principles are inspired by the Irish Constitution and the objective is to create a social framework that supports the well-being of all citizens.
 
• Though non-justiciable, the principles act as a moral compass for the state in creating laws and policies aimed at social welfare and public good.
 
• The implementation of these principles is seen as crucial for achieving the goals of justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity as enshrined in the Preamble of the Constitution.

question:
Read the given statements and select the correct option.

A. Directive Principles of State Policy consists of all the ideals which the state should follow and keep in mind while formulating policies and enacting laws for the country.

B. It can be enforced by the Judiciary.

C. They can be suspended during a national emergency.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Only A**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

Directive Principles of State Policy

 
• Articles 36-51 under Part-IV of the Indian Constitution deal with Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP).
 
• They are borrowed from the Constitution of Ireland, which had copied it from the Spanish Constitution.
 
• It refers to the ideals that the State should keep in mind while formulating policies and enacting laws. e.g. the Government should try to ensure equal pay for equal work for men and women etc. 
 
• Non-justiciable nature on recommendations of Tej Bahadur committee Report
 
• Positive Connotation – Establishes social and economic democracy.
 
• Promote the concept of a Welfare State and Inclusive Growth.
 
• Precursors of Panchayat Raj Institution (Art. 40- Village Panchayat)
 
• Fundamental in governance and apply in policy makings – Art. 37
 
• Novel features and Soul of the constitution – B.R Ambedkar
 
• DPSP is the Conscience of the constitution – Granville Austin
 
• Constitutional instructions to – Legislature, executive, and administration of the state.
 
• Enabling in nature – Enables government for a comprehensive program of social and economic justice, unlike FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS.
 
• Non-justiciable, Non-self-executory, non-enforceable by a court of law.
 
• Government can implement provisions of DPSP by legislative actions.

Significance of DPSP

 
• Helps courts as Guiding Light in determining and examining the constitutional validity of acts/rules/regulations.
 
• Symbolizes the idea of a welfare state and amplifies social and economic justice as entailed in the Preamble.
 
• They impose a moral obligation on the state authorities for their application, however, public opinion is the real force behind them.
 
• Serves as moral precepts for – Legislature, executive, and administration of state
 
• They serve as a Common Minimum Programme for every government irrespective of their manifestos and political ideologies.
 
• The Directives are the life-giving provisions of the Constitution. They constitute the stuff of the Constitution and its philosophy of social justice. – L. M Singhvi. Hence, Option 1 is correct.
 
• Directives lay down that the goal of Indian polity is ‘economic democracy’ as distinguished from ‘political democracy’ (Fundamental rights) – R. Ambedkar
 
• Supplements and complements Fundamental Rights (Part III).
 
• Serves as benchmarks and yardstick for people to gauge the performance of govt.
 
• DPSPs are intended to be a guide, friends, and philosophers of the ruling party in legislative and executive acts.
 
• Serves as an important tool for opposition parties to ensure accountability of the executive and exercise influence and control over the government.

• This principle is rooted in the notion of fairness and justice, ensuring that individuals are not subjected to repeated legal proceedings for the same act.

subject: GK
question:
Which of the following are included under the scope of Article 21 as interpreted by the Supreme Court?
1. Right to sleep
2. Right to shelter
3. Right to reputation
4. Right to die
solution:
The correct answer is __**1, 2 and 3 only**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Right to sleep**: The **Supreme Court**, in the **Ramlila Maidan Incident v. Home Secretary, Union of India (2012)**, held that the **right to sleep** is a fundamental right. The court stated that sleep is essential for a human being to maintain the biological balance and health of the body, and disturbing it constitutes a violation of **Article 21**. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.*** 
• **Right to shelter**: In the case of **Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985)** and **Shantistar Builders v. Narayan Khimalal Totame (1990)**, the **Supreme Court** ruled that the **right to life** includes the **right to shelter**. It emphasized that for a human being, a house is not just a place to live but a place for physical, mental, and intellectual growth. ***Hence, statement 2 is correct.*** 
• **Right to reputation**: The **Supreme Court**, in the case of **Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India (2016)**, held that the **right to reputation** is an integral part of **Article 21**. The court observed that a person's reputation is an inseparable facet of their dignity and life. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.*** 
• **Right to die**: In the landmark judgment of **Gian Kaur v. State of Punjab (1996)**, a five-judge bench of the **Supreme Court** held that the **right to life** under **Article 21** does not include the **right to die** or the right to be killed. While the court later allowed **passive euthanasia** under strict guidelines in the **Common Cause (2018)** case, the general "right to die" (as in suicide) is not recognized as a fundamental right. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.*** 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
• **Article 21 of the Indian Constitution**: 
• It declares that "No person shall be deprived of his **life or personal liberty** except according to **procedure established by law**." This right is available to both **citizens and non-citizens**. 
• This article has been described as the "**heart of fundamental rights**" due to its wide and evolving interpretation by the judiciary. 
• **Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)**: 
• This case was a turning point for **Article 21**. The **Supreme Court** established that the "**procedure established by law**" must be **just, fair, and reasonable** (introducing the American concept of **Substantive Due Process**). 
• It ruled that "**Personal Liberty**" has the widest amplitude and covers a variety of rights that go to constitute the personal liberty of a man. 
• **Other Rights under Article 21**: 
• Over the years, the **Supreme Court** has included several rights under its scope, such as the **Right to Privacy (Justice K.S. Puttaswamy case, 2017)**, **Right to a Clean Environment**, **Right to Free Legal Aid**, **Right to Education**, and **Right to Speedy Trial**. 
• It also includes the **Right against Handcuffing** and the **Right to Travel Abroad**. 
• **Protection during Emergency**: 
• By the **44th Amendment Act (1978)**, it was mandated that the enforcement of the rights guaranteed by **Articles 20 and 21** cannot be suspended even during the operation of a **National Emergency** under **Article 352**. </ul

• **Directive Principles of State Policy** motive to generate** social and economic** conditions under which the citizens can lead a good life. 
 
• They as well motive to start **social and economic democracy** through a welfare state.
 
• The main aim of the Directive Principle of State Policy **listed in Part 4 of the Indian Constitution** is to give economic justice and to avoid the** concentration of wealth in the hands of a few people**.
 
• So, no government **can afford to ignore them.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The **Directive Principles** together with the Fundamental Rights hold the** philosophy of the Constitution and are the soul of the Constitution.**
 
• **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar** reported these principles as** 'novel features' **of the Indian Constitution.​ 
 
• **Part IV of the Constitution of India (Article 36–51)** holds the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP).

question: Which of the following statements is NOT correct about the Directive Principles of State Policy?

options.text: They are fundamental in the governance of the country.
The idea of Directive Principles of State Policy has been taken from the Irish Republic.
They were incorporated in our Constitution in order to provide economic justice.

solution:
The correct answer is __**these principles are justiciable**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Option 1** is the correct answer because the **Directive Principles of State Policy are not justiciable**, meaning they are** not enforceable by any court**.
 
• The Directive Principles are **fundamental in the governance of the country** and aim to create social and economic conditions under which the citizens can lead a good life.
 
• The idea of Directive Principles of State Policy has indeed been **taken from the Irish Republic** and incorporated into the Indian Constitution.
 
• They were included in our Constitution to **provide economic justice** and to help achieve a welfare state.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The Directive Principles of State Policy are listed in **Part IV **of the Indian Constitution from **Article 36 to Article 51**.
 
• They are guidelines for the framing of laws by the government and aim at ensuring **socio-economic justice**.
 
• Though they are non-justiciable, they are considered fundamental in the governance of the country and act as a yardstick in the making of laws.
 
• These principles reflect the ideals that the state should strive to achieve to promote the welfare of the people.
 
• Unlike the **Fundamental Rights, which are enforceable by the courts,** the Directive Principles are not enforceable by any court but are considered fundamental in the governance of the country.

question: Which of the following articles guarantees the Right to Equality before the Law and the Right to Equal Protection of the Laws?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 14**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 14** of the Indian Constitution guarantees the Right to Equality before the Law and the Right to Equal Protection of the Laws.
 
• This article is a fundamental right that ensures all individuals are treated equally by the law.
 
• It prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth.
 
• Article 14 applies to both citizens and non-citizens.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The Constitution of India was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 26th November 1949 and came into effect on 26th January 1950.
 
• It lays down the framework defining fundamental political principles, establishes the structure, procedures, powers, and duties of government institutions, and sets out fundamental rights, directive principles, and the duties of citizens.
 
• The Constitution of India is the longest written constitution of any country in the world.
 
• It declares India a sovereign, socialist, secular, and democratic republic, assuring its citizens justice, equality, and liberty, and endeavors to promote fraternity.
 
• Article 14 is part of the Fundamental Rights enshrined in Part III of the Constitution.
 
• The right to equality is a cornerstone of the Indian legal system and is crucial for maintaining the rule of law in the country.

question: Which of the following articles lays down for protection from self-incrimination i.e. protection from standing trial against oneself?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 20**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 20** of the Indian Constitution provides protection against self-incrimination.
 
• It ensures that no person accused of any offense shall be compelled to be a witness against themselves.
 
• This article includes provisions that safeguard individuals from being tried and punished more than once for the same offense (double jeopardy) and from retrospective criminal legislation.
 
• The protection under Article 20 is available to both citizens and non-citizens.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 20(1)** states that no person shall be convicted of any offense except for violation of a law in force at the time of the commission of the act charged as an offense.
 
• **Article 20(2)** ensures that no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offense more than once.
 
• **Article 20(3)** guarantees that no person accused of any offense shall be compelled to be a witness against themselves.
 
• These protections are fundamental rights and form part of the basic structure of the Constitution, ensuring fair treatment in the judicial process.

question: Under which article of the Indian Constitution is the Right to Equality guaranteed?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 14 to Article 18**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Right to Equality** is guaranteed under **Articles 14 to 18** of the Indian Constitution. It is one of the fundamental rights provided to citizens of India.
 
• **Article 14:** Guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the laws within the territory of India. This ensures no discrimination against individuals on any grounds.
 
• **Article 15:** Prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth. It also enables the state to make special provisions for women, children, and socially disadvantaged groups.
 
• **Article 16:** Ensures equality of opportunity in matters of public employment. It prohibits discrimination in employment based on religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, or residence.
 
• **Article 17:** Abolishes "untouchability" and forbids its practice in any form. This article is a step towards eradicating caste-based discrimination in society.
 
• **Article 18:** Abolishes titles except for military and academic distinctions. It aims to prevent the creation of artificial hierarchies in Indian society.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Fundamental Rights in the Indian Constitution:**

 
 
• Fundamental Rights are enshrined in Part III of the Indian Constitution, providing citizens with basic human rights essential for their development.
 
• These rights are enforceable by the courts, ensuring protection against arbitrary actions by the state.
 
• They include the Right to Equality, Right to Freedom, Right against Exploitation, Right to Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights, and Right to Constitutional Remedies.
 
 
 
• **Article 14:**
 
 
• It emphasizes equality before the law, ensuring that every individual is subject to the same laws without favoritism.
 
• The concept of "equal protection of the laws" guarantees that individuals in similar circumstances will be treated equally.
 
 
 
• **Article 15:**
 
 
• It prohibits discrimination on specific grounds, fostering inclusivity and social justice.
 
• The state is empowered to make affirmative actions like reservations for disadvantaged groups.
 
 
 
• **Article 17:**
 
 
• This article is instrumental in abolishing untouchability, a social evil prevalent in India.
 
• It ensures that individuals belonging to the lower castes are treated equally and with dignity.
 
 
 
• **Article 18:**
 
 
• It prevents individuals from using titles that create social hierarchies, ensuring a classless society.
 
• Military and academic distinctions are exceptions under this article.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Fundamental Rights vs Directive Principles:**

 
 
• Fundamental Rights are enforceable by courts, while Directive Principles of State Policy are non-enforceable guidelines for governance.
 
• Both aim to establish a welfare state but differ in their legal binding nature.
 
 
 
• **Equality vs Equity:**
 
 
• Equality ensures equal treatment for all, while equity focuses on fairness and addressing disparities.
 
• Articles 15 and 16 incorporate elements of equity through affirmative actions like reservations.
 
 
 
• **Judicial Interpretation:**
 
 
• The judiciary plays a crucial role in interpreting and safeguarding fundamental rights.
 
• Landmark cases like Kesavananda Bharati vs State of Kerala reaffirm the importance of fundamental rights in India's constitutional framework.

question: Which constitutional article ensures the protection of the cultural and educational rights of minorities?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 29**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 29** of the **Constitution of India** specifically deals with the **protection of interests of minorities**. It ensures that any section of the **citizens** residing in the territory of **India** having a distinct **language**, **script**, or **culture** of its own shall have the right to conserve the same. ***Hence, the option Article 29 is correct.***
 
• It serves two primary purposes: Clause (1) protects the right of a group to maintain its **cultural** and **linguistic** identity, while Clause (2) guarantees the individual right of a **citizen** not to be denied admission into **educational institutions** maintained by the **State** or receiving aid out of **State funds** on grounds only of **religion**, **race**, **caste**, **language**, or any of them.
 
• Though the heading of **Article 29** mentions "minorities," the use of the phrase "**section of citizens**" in the text indicates that the protection is available to both **minorities** as well as the **majority** community in certain contexts, as interpreted by the **Supreme Court of India**.
 
• This article is part of the **Cultural and Educational Rights** (Articles **29** and **30**) enshrined in **Part III** of the **Indian Constitution**, which are fundamental to the **secular** fabric of the **country**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Article 15**:
 
 
• This article prohibits **discrimination** by the **State** against any **citizen** on grounds only of **religion**, **race**, **caste**, **sex**, or **place of birth**.
 
• It is a facet of the **Right to Equality** (Articles **14** to **18**). It ensures equal access to **public places** like shops, restaurants, and wells. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect in the context of specific minority cultural rights.***
 
 
 
• **Article 25**:
 
 
• It provides for the **freedom of conscience** and the right to freely **profess**, **practice**, and **propagate** **religion** to all persons.
 
• This right is not absolute and is subject to **public order**, **morality**, and **health**. It also allows the **State** to regulate **economic**, **financial**, or **political** activities associated with **religious practice**. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect as it deals with religious freedom rather than specific cultural/educational rights.***
 
 
 
• **Article 32**:
 
 
• Commonly referred to as the "**Right to Constitutional Remedies**," it allows **citizens** to move the **Supreme Court** for the enforcement of **Fundamental Rights**.
 
• **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar** famously described this article as the "**Heart and Soul of the Constitution**." It empowers the **court** to issue **writs** like **Habeas Corpus**, **Mandamus**, **Prohibition**, **Quo Warranto**, and **Certiorari**. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect as it is a remedial right.***
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Article 30**: Complementary to **Article 29**, it grants all **minorities** (whether based on **religion** or **language**) the right to **establish** and **administer** **educational institutions** of their choice.
 
• The **Constitution of India** does not define the word "**minority**." However, **Article 30** recognizes minorities based on **religion** and **language**.
 
• In the **T.M.A. Pai Foundation case (2002)**, the **Supreme Court** ruled that for the purpose of **Article 30**, the unit for determining **minority status** is the **State**, not the whole of **India**.
 
• **Fundamental Rights** were borrowed from the **Constitution of the USA** (**Bill of Rights**) and are **justiciable** in nature, meaning they are enforceable by **courts**.
 
• The **National Commission for Minorities Act, 1992**, identifies six **religious minorities** in **India**: **Muslims**, **Christians**, **Sikhs**, **Buddhists**, **Zoroastrians (Parsis)**, and **Jains** (added in **2014**).
</ul

• Part IV A of the Indian Constitution contains Article 51A, which deals with the Fundamental Duties.
 
• The Soviet Constitution (USSR) is where the idea of fundamental duties originated.
 
• Fundamental Duties were recommended in 1976 by the Swaran Singh Committee.
 
• Ten Fundamental Duties were added to the Indian Constitution by the 42nd Amendment Act of 1976.
 
• Fundamental duties are not subject to legal action unless specifically stated in a provision, in contrast to fundamental rights, which are justiciable.

• The 86th Amendment to the Constitution was passed in 2002, adding the eleventh fundamental duty.

9.

10.

solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Article 32 of the Indian Constitution has been described as the ‘heart and soul’ of the Indian Constitution by Dr B. R. Ambedkar.
 
• It gives a citizen the right to approach the Supreme Court to get resorted to any of the fundamental rights in case of their violation.
 
• It is also known as the Right to Constitutional Remedies__.

 
 

 __Article__
 __Consists of__
 
 

 **Article 32**
 
 
Right to move the Supreme court for the enforcement of fundamental rights including the **writs**.

 __
 
• habeas corpus
 
• mandamus
 
• prohibition
 
• certiorari
 
• quo warranto
 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

Extra facts:

__
 
• Habeas Corpus: 

 
 
• This writ is issued to produce a person who has been detained whether in prison or in private custody, before a court and to release him if such detention is found illegal.
 
 
 
• Mandamus:
 
 
• The writ of command is issued by the supreme or high court when any government, court, corporation, or any public authority has to do a public duty but fails to do so.
 
 
 
• Prohibition:
 
 
• It is a writ issued with a view to restraining a person from holding a public office to which he is not entitled.
 
 
 
• Certiorari: 
 
 
• The writ of certiorari can be issued by the supreme or high court for quashing the order already passed by an inferior court, tribunal or quasi-judicial authority.
 
 
 
• Quo-Warranto: 
 
 
• The writ of quo-warranto can be issued by the supreme or high court for asking by what authority or warrant.
 
• It is issued by the court to enquire into the legality of a claim of a person to a public office.

• Speech and expression
 
• Assembly
 
• Association
 
• Movement
 
• Residence
 
• Profession
 
 
 
• Article 25 of the Indian constitution guarantees the Right to Freedom of Religion to its citizens.
 
 
• It provides freedom of conscience and free profession, practice, and propagation of religion.
 
• It is a basic human right guarantee that cannot be subverted or misinterpreted in any manner.
 
• Article 25 to Article 28 of the Indian constitution deals with the Right to Freedom of Religion.

subject: GK
question: The 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act (1992) aimed at legal reform in which of the following areas?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Local self-governance at rural level**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992** was a landmark legislation in India aimed at decentralizing power and establishing **local self-governance at the rural level**. It provided a constitutional foundation for the **Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs)**. *Hence, statement 3 is correct.*
 
• The act added a new **Part IX** to the **Constitution of India**, titled **The Panchayats**, which consists of provisions from **Article 243 to 243-O**. It also introduced the **Eleventh Schedule**, which lists **29 functional items** that are placed under the care of the Panchayats.
 
• **Industrial disputes management** is primarily governed by the **Industrial Disputes Act, 1947**, which focuses on the investigation and settlement of industrial conflicts between employers and workmen. It is not the subject of the 73rd Amendment. *Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.*
 
• **Environmental protection at the grassroot level** is addressed through various laws like the **Environment Protection Act, 1986** and the **Forest Rights Act, 2006**. While Panchayats have some roles in social forestry, the 73rd Amendment's primary legal reform was the institutionalization of the governance structure itself. *Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.*
 
• **Consumer protection rights** are regulated by the **Consumer Protection Act, 1986** (later replaced by the **2019 Act**), which establishes consumer councils and authorities for the settlement of disputes. This is unrelated to the structural reform of rural local bodies. *Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Historical Background:** The **73rd Amendment Act** was passed during the tenure of **Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao**. It came into force on **April 24, 1993**. This date is now commemorated annually as **National Panchayati Raj Day** in India.
 
• **Three-Tier System:** The Act mandates a uniform **three-tier structure** of Panchayati Raj across the country: the **Gram Panchayat** at the village level, the **Panchayat Samiti** at the intermediate (block) level, and the **Zila Parishad** at the district level. States with a population below **20 lakh** have the option not to constitute the intermediate level.
 
• **Gram Sabha:** The Act establishes the **Gram Sabha** as the foundation of the Panchayati Raj system. It is a body consisting of all persons registered in the electoral rolls of a village within the area of the Panchayat.
 
• **Reservation of Seats:** To ensure social justice, the Act provides for the **reservation of seats** for **Scheduled Castes (SCs)** and **Scheduled Tribes (STs)** in proportion to their population. Most importantly, it mandates that **not less than one-third (33%)** of the total number of seats and offices of chairpersons must be reserved for **women**.
 
• **Duration and Elections:** Every Panchayat is given a fixed tenure of **5 years**. In case of dissolution, elections must be held within a period of **6 months**. The minimum age for contesting elections to Panchayats is **21 years**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **State Election Commission:** The Act provides for the constitution of a **State Election Commission** in every state. This independent body is responsible for the superintendence, direction, and control of the preparation of electoral rolls and the conduct of all **elections to the Panchayats**.
 
• **State Finance Commission:** To ensure the financial viability of these local bodies, the **Governor** of a state is required to constitute a **State Finance Commission** every **5 years**. This commission reviews the financial position of the Panchayats and recommends the principles for the distribution of **net proceeds of taxes** between the State and the Panchayats.
 
• **Eleventh Schedule Subjects:** The **29 subjects** transferred to the Panchayats include **Agriculture**, **Land Improvement**, **Minor Irrigation**, **Animal Husbandry**, **Fisheries**, **Social Forestry**, **Small Scale Industries**, **Rural Housing**, **Drinking Water**, and **Education**.
 
• **Article 40:** The 73rd Amendment gave practical shape to **Article 40** of the **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)**, which directs the State to organize village panchayats and endow them with such powers and authority as may be necessary to enable them to function as units of **self-government**.

question: Name the location of the National Institute of Rehabilitation Training and Research (NIRTAR)?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Cuttack, Odisha**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **National Institute of Rehabilitation Training and Research (NIRTAR)**, now officially known as the **Swami Vivekanand National Institute of Rehabilitation Training and Research (SVNIRTAR)**, is located in **Olatpur**, which is approximately **30 kilometers** from **Cuttack** in the state of **Odisha**.

• It is a premier **autonomous body** functioning under the **Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities (Divyangjan)**, which is part of the **Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment**, **Government of India**.

• The institute was originally established in **1975** as a service center under the **Artificial Limbs Manufacturing Corporation of India (ALIMCO)** and later achieved its current **autonomous status** in **1984**.

• The core objective of the institute is to provide high-quality **rehabilitation services** for persons with **locomotor disabilities**, conduct **research** in the field of **rehabilitation engineering** and **medical sciences**, and develop trained **human resources**.

• The location in **Cuttack** serves as a vital medical hub for patients from across **Eastern India**, offering specialized **rehabilitative surgery** and **vocational training** to help individuals lead independent lives.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Academic Excellence**: **SVNIRTAR** offers several undergraduate and postgraduate courses, including **Bachelor of Physiotherapy (BPT)**, **Bachelor of Occupational Therapy (BOT)**, and **Bachelor of Prosthetics and Orthotics (BPO)**, all of which are affiliated with **Utkal University**.

• **Hospital Infrastructure**: The institute operates a **100-bed hospital** that specializes in **orthopedic surgery** for conditions such as **polio**, **cerebral palsy**, **congenital deformities**, and **spinal cord injuries**.

• **National Network**: The **Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment** manages several other national institutes, such as the **National Institute for the Empowerment of Persons with Visual Disabilities (NIEPVD)** in **Dehradun** and the **Ali Yavar Jung National Institute of Speech and Hearing Disabilities (AYJNISHD)** in **Mumbai**.

• **Outreach Services**: The institute actively organizes **assessment camps** and **outreach programs** under the **ADIP Scheme (Assistance to Disabled Persons for Purchase/Fitting of Aids and Appliances)** to distribute free **assistive devices** in rural and underserved areas.

• **Regional Presence**: To expand its reach, **SVNIRTAR** manages **Composite Regional Centres (CRCs)** located in **Ranchi**, **Guwahati**, and **Sikkim**, providing localized support for the **Divyangjan** population.

**Important Points__**

• The institute is named after the great philosopher **Swami Vivekanand**, reflecting its mission of selfless service to humanity and the empowerment of the marginalized.

• It plays a critical role in implementing the **Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act, 2016**, which mandates accessible healthcare and equal opportunities for persons with **21 recognized types of disabilities**.

• The **Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities** was officially given a separate identity within the Ministry in **May 2012** to focus specifically on policy issues and welfare schemes for the disabled.

• **SVNIRTAR** is also a recognized center for **DNB (Diplomate of National Board)** training in **Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation (PMR)**, contributing to the development of specialized medical professionals in **India**.
</ul

__
 
• **Finance Commission:** - The Finance Commission is primarily responsible for **tax distribution**. It recommends the division of tax revenues between the Union and the States and among the States themselves. - It plays a crucial role in ensuring fiscal federalism. - Hence, **Finance Commission matches with R.**
 
• **Article 282:** - Article 282 of the Indian Constitution allows the Union or the State governments to provide **discretionary grants** for public purposes. - These grants are not bound by specific constitutional provisions but can be given at the discretion of the government. - Hence, **Article 282 matches with P.**
 
• **Consolidated Fund:** - The Consolidated Fund is the repository of **all Union revenues**, including direct and indirect taxes, non-tax revenues, and borrowings. - It is used for various expenditures, and no money can be withdrawn from it without parliamentary approval. - Hence, **Consolidated Fund matches with S.**
 
• **Contingency Fund:** - The Contingency Fund is used to meet **unexpected expenses** that may arise during emergencies. - It is kept at the disposal of the President and is replenished from the Consolidated Fund. - Hence, **Contingency Fund matches with Q.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Finance Commission (Article 280):**

 
 
• The Finance Commission is a constitutional body established under **Article 280** of the Indian Constitution.
 
• It is appointed every **five years** by the President to recommend financial distributions between the Union and States.
 
• The recommendations include principles for tax distribution and grants-in-aid for States.
 
 
 
• **Article 282:**
 
 
• Article 282 of the Constitution provides discretionary powers to the Union and State governments to allocate grants for **public purposes**.
 
• These grants are not tied to specific constitutional provisions but are offered based on necessity.
 
 
 
• **Consolidated Fund of India:**
 
 
• It is the most significant fund managed by the Indian government and includes **all revenues received by the Union government.**
 
• Expenditures from the Consolidated Fund require prior approval from the **Parliament**.
 
• The fund ensures accountability in financial transactions of the government.
 
 
 
• **Contingency Fund:**
 
 
• It serves as an emergency fund for **unexpected and urgent expenses.**
 
• The fund is maintained under the authority of the **President** and can only be used for unforeseen circumstances.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Finance Commission:** - The Finance Commission ensures equitable financial distribution and strengthens fiscal federalism. - Example: The **15th Finance Commission (2020-25)** recommended tax devolution rates.
 
• **Article 282:** - Discretionary grants under Article 282 are used for specific purposes like disaster relief or special schemes.
 
• **Consolidated Fund:** - It covers regular government expenditures like salaries, infrastructure, and welfare schemes.
 
• **Contingency Fund:** - It is utilized during emergencies like natural disasters or wartime situations. - Example: The **Contingency Fund of India** is maintained at Rs. 500 crores.

question: Which of the following Articles of the Constitution of India provides that there shall be a Legislative Assembly for the National Capital Territory of Delhi?
solution:
The Correct Answer is** Article 239AA.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The status of** Delhi **being a **Union Territory under Schedule 1** of the Constitution but christened the **‘National Capital Territory’ **under **Article 239AA.**
 
• The** 69th amendment** to the Constitution of India inserted **Article 239AA**, which declared the Union Territory of Delhi to be administered by a LG who works on aid and advice of the elected legislative assembly.
 
• However, the **‘aid and advice’ **clause pertains only to matters on which the elected Assembly has powers under the **State and Concurrent Lists** with the exception of **public order, police, and land.**
 
• Further, the** Article 239AA **also notes that LG has to either act on the aid and advice of the **Council of Ministers**, or he is bound to implement the decision taken by the President on a reference being made by him.
 
• Also, **Article 239AA**, empowers the LG to refer a difference of opinion on ‘any matter’ with the Council of Ministers to the President.
 
• Thus, this dual control between LG and the elected government leads to a power tussle.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The **National Capital Region (NCR) **is a planning region centred upon the National Capital Territory (NCT) of Delhi in India.
 
• It encompasses Delhi and several districts surrounding it from the states of Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, and Rajasthan.
 
• Delhi is of great historical significance as an important commercial, transport, and cultural hub, as well as the political centre of India.
 
• According to legend, the city was named for Raja Dhilu, a king who reigned in the region in the 1st century BC.

question: Constitutional provisions related to Panchayats are in which part of the Constitution of India?
solution:
The correct answer is __**IX.​**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Part IX **of the Constitution has the** provisions for Panchayati Raj System.**
 
• **Panchayati Raj** is the system of local self-government of villages in rural India as opposed to urban and suburban municipalities.
 
• Part IX of the Indian Constitution is the section of the Constitution relating to the Panchayats.
 
• The **Panchayats must include members of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the same proportion as in the general population.**
 
• **One-third of all seats and chairperson posts must be reserved for women,** in some states half of all seats and chairperson posts.
 
• **The modern Panchayati Raj system **was introduced in India by the** 73rd constitutional amendment in 1992 **and added as an** Eleventh Schedule** of the Constitution.
 
• The Panchayati Raj now functions as a system of governance in which gram panchayats are the basic units of local administration.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The original text of the Indian Constitution consisted of **22 parts **and after **amendments**, currently, it contains** 25 parts.**
 
• The 25 parts of the Indian Constitution are tabled below:

 
 

 **Parts **
 **Articles**
 
 

 Part I – The Union and its Territories
 **1 – 4**
 
 

 Part II – Citizenship
 **5 -11**
 
 

 Part III – Fundamental Rights
 **12 – 35**
 
 

 Part IV – Directive Principles of State Policy
 **36 – 51**
 
 

 Part IV A – Fundamental Duties 
 **51A**
 
 

 Part V – The Union
 **52 – 151**
 
 

 Part VI – The States
 **152 – 237**
 
 

 Part VII – The States in Part B of the First Schedule
 **238 [Repealed]**
 
 

 Part VIII – The Union Territories
 **239 – 242**
 
 

 Part IX – The Panchayats
 **243 – 243O**
 
 

 Part IXA – The Municipalities
 **243P –243ZG**
 
 

 Part IXB – The Co-operative Societies
 **243ZH – 243ZT**
 
 

 Part X – The Scheduled and Tribal Areas
 **244 – 244A**
 
 

 Part XI – Relation between the Union and the States
 **245 – 263**
 
 

 Part XII – Finance, Property, Contracts, and Suits
 **264 – 300A**
 
 

 Part XIII – Trade, Commerce, and Intercourse within the territory of India
 **301 – 307**
 
 

 Part XIV – Services Under the Union and the States
 **308 – 323**
 
 

 Part XIVA – Tribunals
 **323A – 323B**
 
 

 Part XV – Elections
 **324 – 329A**
 
 

 Part XVI – Special provisions relating to certain classes
 **330 – 342**
 
 

 Part XVII – Official language
 **343 – 351**
 
 

 Part XVIII – Emergency Provisions
 **352 – 360**
 
 

 Part XIX – Miscellaneous
 **361 – 367**
 
 

 Part XX – Amendment of the Constitution
 **368**
 
 

 Part XXI – Temporary, Transitional, and Special Provisions
 **369 – 392**

• **95th Amendment**
 
 
• The** 95th Amendment Act of 2009 **extended the special representation for** Anglo-Indians** and the reserve of seats for SCs and STs in the **Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies for an additional ten years.**

question: Who was appointed as the chairman of the National Commission for Backward classes in December 2022?
solution:
The correct answer is__** Hansraj Gangaram Ahir**__. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Hansraj Gangaram Ahir was appointed as the chairman of the National Commission for Backward Classes (NCBC) in December 2022.
 
• He is a **former Union Minister of State for Home Affairs.**
 
• Ahir has been a prominent leader from Maharashtra and has served as a Member of Parliament.

**National Commission for Backward Classes (NCBC)**

 
• **102nd Constitution Amendment Act, 2018** granted constitutional status to the NCBC.
 
• **Article 338B** provides the NCBC with the authority to investigate and monitor all matters relating to the safeguards provided for the socially and educationally backward classes under the Constitution or under any other law.
 
• **Constitution (127th Amendment) bill, 2021:** This amendment allows states and union territories to prepare and maintain their own lists of SEBCs.
 
• **Article 342A:** Initially, this article empowered only the President to specify SEBCs in consultation with the Governor of the concerned state. The 2021 amendment restored the states’ authority in this matter.
 
• **Mandal Commission** established in 1979, it recommended reservations for OBCs in government jobs and educational institutions, leading to the implementation of** 27% reservation** for OBCs in 1990.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__** **Development Process of NCBC**

 
• The** first backward classes commission** was established under the chairmanship of **Kaka Kalelkar** to identify the socially and educationally backward classes.
 
• The commission submitted its report in 1955, but its recommendations were not implemented.
 
• Second Backward Classes Commission (1979) (Mandal Commission):Headed by **B.P. Mandal,** this commission was tasked with identifying the **criteria for defining** socially and educationally backward classes.
 
• The Mandal Commission’s report, submitted in 1980,** recommended a 27% reservation** for OBCs in government jobs and educational institutions. These recommendations were implemented in 1990.
 
• The Supreme Court, in the landmark **Indra Sawhney & Others v. Union of India case**, directed the establishment of a permanent body to examine and recommend the inclusion and exclusion of various Backward Classes. This led to the creation of the NCBC.
 
• The NCBC was constituted as a **statutory body under National Commission for Backward Classes Act, 1993 **to address the issues of backward classes.

**Structure of NCBC**

 
• **Chairperson:** Appointed by the President
 
• Vice-Chairperson
 
• **Three Other Members: **These members are appointed by the President and include individuals with special knowledge or experience in matters related to backward classes.
