question: Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which of the following has been emphasized for the first time in criminal law regarding sexual offences?

options.text: Marital rape as a punishable offense
Consent must be explicitly defined and recorded
Death penalty for all rape cases
Gender neutrality in sexual assault definitions

solution:
The correct answer is __**Gender neutrality in sexual assault definitions**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
__

• The **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023**, which replaces the **Indian Penal Code (IPC), 1860**, has introduced several significant changes to modernize criminal jurisprudence in India.

• One of the most notable shifts is the emphasis on **gender neutrality** regarding certain sexual offences, particularly those involving **children**. While the definition of rape under **Section 63** remains gender-specific (perpetrated by a man against a woman), the law has moved toward gender-neutral terminology in several other sections to ensure that all victims, regardless of gender, are protected under the law.

• The **BNS** aims to address the limitations of the **IPC** by recognizing that sexual assault can be committed against individuals of any gender, especially in cases of **minors**, where the term **'child'** is used neutrally.

• Regarding the other options: **Marital rape** (Exception 2 to Section 63) still remains an exception and is not a punishable offence unless the wife is under 18 years of age. The **death penalty** is not mandatory for all rape cases but is reserved for the most heinous instances, such as the rape of a girl below 12 years (**Section 65**) or repeat offenders.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• The **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS)** was enacted by the **Parliament of India** in **December 2023** and officially came into effect on **July 1, 2024**.

• It consists of **358 sections**, significantly streamlining the **511 sections** found in the original **IPC**.

• The **BNS** introduces **Community Service** as a new form of punishment for petty offences, reflecting a shift toward **restorative justice**.

• New categories of crime such as **Mob Lynching** and **Organized Crime** have been specifically defined and penalized for the first time under the general penal law.

• The act also introduces **Section 69**, which criminalizes sexual intercourse by **deceitful means** or making false promises of marriage, a specific addition not explicitly present in the same form in the **IPC**.
</ul

question: Which constitutional authority decides on the disqualification of a Member of State Legislature under the Anti-Defection Law?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Speaker of the Legislative Assembly**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The **Anti-Defection Law** was incorporated into the **Indian Constitution** via the **52nd Amendment Act, 1985**, which introduced the **Tenth Schedule**.

• According to **Paragraph 6** of the **Tenth Schedule**, any question regarding the disqualification of a member of a House arising from defection is to be decided by the **Presiding Officer** of that House.

• For the **State Legislative Assembly**, the designated authority is the **Speaker**, while for the **State Legislative Council**, it is the **Chairman**.

• The law was designed to prevent political instability caused by legislators changing parties for personal gain, a practice colloquially known as **Aaya Ram Gaya Ram**.

• The decision of the **Speaker** was initially intended to be final; however, the **Supreme Court** ruled that it is subject to **Judicial Review** to prevent arbitrariness.

 **Additional Information__**

• **Governor**:

• Under **Article 192**, the **Governor** is the deciding authority for disqualifications of members of the **State Legislature** on grounds other than defection, such as holding an **Office of Profit** or being of unsound mind.

• In these cases, the **Governor** is constitutionally mandated to obtain the opinion of the **Election Commission of India** and must act according to that opinion.

• **Election Commission**:

• The commission provides a binding opinion to the **President** (for MPs) or the **Governor** (for MLAs) regarding disqualification under **Articles 103** and **192**, but it has no direct decision-making power under the **Tenth Schedule**.

• **Kihoto Hollohan Case (1992)**:

• In this landmark judgment, the **Supreme Court** held that the **Speaker** acts as a **Tribunal** while deciding defection cases, making their decisions reviewable by the **High Courts** and the **Supreme Court** under their writ jurisdiction.

• **91st Amendment Act, 2003**:

• This amendment strengthened the law by requiring at least **two-thirds** of the members of a legislative party to agree to a merger with another party to avoid disqualification, removing the earlier provision that protected a **one-third** split.

</ul

question: Which authority can alter the boundaries of Indian states?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Parliament of India**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• **Article 3** of the **Constitution of India** explicitly grants the **Parliament** the exclusive power to form new states and alter the areas, boundaries, or names of existing states. This ensures that the **Union** has the authority to reorganize the internal map of the country for administrative or political reasons.

• The **Parliament** can, by law, increase the area of any state, diminish the area of any state, or alter the boundaries of any state. This process requires only a **simple majority** in both the **Lok Sabha** and the **Rajya Sabha**.

• The **Supreme Court** (Option 1) acts as the guardian of the **Constitution** and the arbiter of disputes between the **Union** and **States**, but it does not possess the legislative power to redraw state boundaries. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***

• The **State Legislative Assemblies** (Option 2) do not have the power to alter their own boundaries. While the **President** refers the reorganization bill to the concerned **State Legislature** for its views, those views are not binding on the **Parliament**. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***

• The **President of India** (Option 3) plays a procedural role by recommending the introduction of the bill in **Parliament** and referring it to the **State Legislature**, but the actual authority to enact the change lies solely with the **Parliament**. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***

• The **Parliament of India** (Option 4) is the supreme legislative body that exercises this power under **Part I** of the **Constitution**. ***Hence, statement 4 is correct.***

**Additional Information__**

__

• **Article 2 vs. Article 3**: While **Article 2** deals with the admission or establishment of new states that were not part of the **Union of India** (like **Sikkim** in **1975**), **Article 3** deals with the internal reorganization of existing states already within the **Union**.

• **Indestructible Union of Destructible States**: This phrase highlights that while the **Union of India** is permanent and cannot be dissolved, the individual states can be reorganized, merged, or renamed by the **Parliament** without the consent of the states.

• **States Reorganisation Act, 1956**: This was a major piece of legislation that reorganized the boundaries of Indian states and territories, primarily along **linguistic lines**, following the recommendations of the **Fazal Ali Commission**.

• **Recent Examples**: The **Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014** led to the creation of **Telangana**. The **Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019** reconstituted the state into two **Union Territories**: **Jammu and Kashmir** and **Ladakh**.

• **Historical Changes**: In **1950**, the **United Provinces** was renamed **Uttar Pradesh**. In **1969**, **Madras** was renamed **Tamil Nadu**, and in **1973**, **Mysore** became **Karnataka**.

**Important Points__**

• **Presidential Recommendation**: A bill for the purpose of altering state boundaries can be introduced in either **House of Parliament** only on the prior recommendation of the **President**.

• **State Legislature Consultation**: Before recommending the bill, the **President** must refer it to the **State Legislature** concerned for expressing its views within a specified period. However, the **Parliament** is free to accept or reject those views.

• **Simple Majority**: Laws made under **Article 3** are not considered amendments to the **Constitution** under **Article 368**. This means they can be passed like ordinary legislation with a **simple majority**.

• **Berubari Union Case (1960)**: The **Supreme Court** held that the power of **Parliament** to diminish the area of a state (under **Article 3**) does not include the power to cede Indian territory to a foreign state. Cession of territory requires a **Constitutional Amendment** under **Article 368**.

• **100th Constitutional Amendment Act (2015)**: This amendment was passed to give effect to the **Land Boundary Agreement** between **India** and **Bangladesh**, involving the exchange of certain enclaves.
</ul

subject: GK
question: Which organization preceded the WTO?
solution:
The correct answer is __**GATT**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT)** was the legal agreement that preceded the **World Trade Organization (WTO)**. It was signed by **23 nations** in **Geneva** on **October 30, 1947**, and came into effect on **January 1, 1948**. ***Hence, this option is correct.***

• The **GATT** was established to eliminate harmful trade protectionism and restore economic health to the world after the **Second World War**. It functioned as a multilateral treaty rather than a formal international organization.

• The **Uruguay Round** of negotiations, which lasted from **1986 to 1994**, led to the **Marrakesh Agreement**. This agreement transformed the **GATT** framework into the **World Trade Organization (WTO)** on **January 1, 1995**.

• The **United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)** was formed in **1965** to help countries eliminate poverty and achieve sustainable human development. It has no direct role in the institutional history of global trade regulation. ***Hence, this option is incorrect.***

• The **International Monetary Fund (IMF)** and the **World Bank** were both established at the **Bretton Woods Conference** in **1944**. While they are part of the **Bretton Woods** system alongside the trade regime, they focus on financial stability and development loans rather than trade rules. ***Hence, these options are incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• The **World Trade Organization (WTO)** is the only global international organization dealing with the rules of trade between nations. It is headquartered in **Geneva, Switzerland**.

• While **GATT** primarily focused on **trade in goods**, the **WTO** expanded its mandate to include **trade in services** (under the **General Agreement on Trade in Services - GATS**) and **intellectual property** (under the **TRIPS** agreement).

• The **WTO** currently has **164 member states**, which account for more than **98%** of total world trade. Decisions are typically made by **consensus** among all members.

• The **GATT** was originally intended to be a temporary arrangement until the **International Trade Organization (ITO)** was established via the **Havana Charter**. However, the **ITO** failed to be ratified by the **United States**, leaving **GATT** as the de facto trade regulator for nearly **50 years**.

• The **WTO** features a much more sophisticated **dispute settlement mechanism** compared to the old **GATT** system, allowing for more effective enforcement of trade agreements.

**Important Points__**

• The **Most-Favored-Nation (MFN)** principle is a core tenet of the **WTO**, requiring that any trade concession granted to one member must be granted to all other members.

• The **National Treatment** principle ensures that imported goods and services are treated no less favorably than locally-produced ones once they have entered the market.

• The current **Director-General** of the **WTO** is **Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala**, who made history in **March 2021** as the first woman and the first African to lead the organization.

• The **Ministerial Conference** is the highest decision-making body of the **WTO** and usually meets every **two years** to discuss major trade issues and policy directions.
</ul

question: How many members of the State Legislative Council are nominated by the Governor?
solution:
The correct answer is__** One-sixth**__.

__
 
• The **State Legislative Council** referred to as **Vidhan Parishad**, is the **upper house** in those states of India that have a **bicameral state legislature*** *whereas* *the **lower house** is the State** Legislative Assembly**.

 
 
• There are **6 states** that have a State Legislative Council. These are **Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Telangana, Maharashtra, Bihar, and Uttar Pradesh**.

 __

• **One sixth member are nominated by the Governor **from the persons having knowledge or practical experience in fields such as literature, science, arts, the cooperative movement and social services.
 
• **One twelfth member** are elected by persons **who are graduates** of three years' standing as residents of that state.
 
• **One twelfth member** are elected by **teachers** who had at least three years of experience in teaching in educational institutions within the state not below secondary schools, including colleges and universities.

In the 28 states and 3 union territories with having a** unicameral state legislature**, it's the only legislative body and in **6 states it is the lower house legislature** with the upper house being the State Legislative Council.

question: Which organization publishes the Ease of Doing Business (EODB) report?
solution:
The correct answer is __**World Bank**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Ease of Doing Business (EODB)** report was a flagship annual publication of the **World Bank Group**. It was first launched in **2003** and provided a detailed assessment of the business environment in **190 economies** by measuring the impact of government regulations on local firms.

• The **World Bank** used a set of **10 to 12 indicators** to rank countries. These indicators included **Starting a Business**, **Dealing with Construction Permits**, **Getting Electricity**, **Registering Property**, **Getting Credit**, **Protecting Minority Investors**, **Paying Taxes**, **Trading across Borders**, **Enforcing Contracts**, and **Resolving Insolvency**.

• In **September 2021**, the **World Bank** officially discontinued the **Doing Business** report. This decision was made following an internal audit and an independent investigation by the law firm **WilmerHale**, which uncovered data irregularities and ethical concerns regarding the **2018** and **2020** reports, specifically involving pressure on staff to alter data for certain countries like **China** and **Saudi Arabia**.

• The **World Bank** has since introduced a new project called **Business Ready (B-READY)** to replace the EODB. This new framework aims to provide a more comprehensive and transparent assessment of the business and investment climate, focusing on both the regulatory framework and the actual provision of public services.

• The other options provided are incorrect because the **IMF** focuses on global financial stability, the **WTO** regulates international trade rules, and the **UNDP** focuses on human development and poverty reduction. None of these organizations published the **Ease of Doing Business** report.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **World Bank Group**: Established in **1944** at the **Bretton Woods Conference**, it is headquartered in **Washington, D.C., USA**. It consists of five institutions, including the **International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD)** and the **International Development Association (IDA)**. Its primary mission is to provide financial and technical assistance to developing countries.

• **International Monetary Fund (IMF)**: Also founded in **1944**, the **IMF** is an organization of **190 countries** working to foster global monetary cooperation, secure financial stability, and facilitate international trade. It is well-known for publishing the **World Economic Outlook** and the **Global Financial Stability Report**.

• **World Trade Organization (WTO)**: Established on **January 1, 1995**, under the **Marrakesh Agreement**, the **WTO** replaced the **General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT)**. Headquartered in **Geneva, Switzerland**, it is the only global international organization dealing with the rules of trade between nations.

• **United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)**: Formed in **1965**, the **UNDP** is the **United Nations'** global development network. It helps countries eliminate poverty and achieve sustainable human development. It publishes the **Human Development Report (HDR)**, which includes the **Human Development Index (HDI)**.

**Important Points__**

• **India's Performance**: India showed a significant improvement in the **Ease of Doing Business** rankings over the last decade. India was ranked **142nd** in **2014** and jumped to the **63rd** position in the **2020** report. This progress was attributed to major reforms such as the **Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC)** of **2016** and the **Goods and Services Tax (GST)** implemented in **2017**.

• **Business Reform Action Plan (BRAP)**: In India, the **Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT)**, under the **Ministry of Commerce and Industry**, releases the **BRAP** rankings. This initiative ranks Indian states and Union Territories based on their implementation of business reforms, fostering competitive federalism within the country.

• **Data Integrity Issues**: The discontinuation of the EODB report highlighted the critical need for **data integrity** and **transparency** in global indices. The investigation revealed that data for **China**, **Azerbaijan**, **United Arab Emirates**, and **Saudi Arabia** had been manipulated, leading to a loss of credibility for the index.
</ul

question: Which two BRICS nations are permanent members of the UN Security Council?
solution:
The correct answer is __**China and Russia**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **United Nations Security Council (UNSC)** is composed of **15 members**, including **five permanent members (P5)** and **ten non-permanent members**. The **P5** nations are **China**, **France**, **Russia**, the **United Kingdom**, and the **United States**.

• **BRICS** is an influential bloc of emerging economies that originally consisted of **Brazil**, **Russia**, **India**, **China**, and **South Africa**. When comparing the membership of both organizations, only **China** and **Russia** hold permanent seats on the **UNSC**. ***Hence, the statement identifying China and Russia as the two BRICS nations in the UNSC P5 is correct.***

• In **Option 1**, while **Russia** is a permanent member, **Brazil** is not. **Brazil** has frequently served as a **non-permanent member** but does not possess **veto power**. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***

• In **Option 2**, **China** is a permanent member, but **India** is not. **India** is a member of the **G4 nations** and has been actively seeking a permanent seat on the **Security Council** for several years. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***

• In **Option 4**, neither **India** nor **South Africa** are permanent members of the **UNSC**. Both countries are significant regional powers that advocate for **UNSC reforms** to include more representation from the **Global South**. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• The **Permanent Members (P5)** of the **UNSC** possess the **Veto Power**, which allows any one of them to prevent the adoption of any 'substantive' resolution. This power was established at the **founding of the United Nations** in **1945** following **World War II**.

• **Russia's** seat was originally held by the **Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR)**. After the **dissolution of the Soviet Union** in **December 1991**, the **Russian Federation** was recognized as its legal successor state in the **United Nations**.

• The **BRICS** group held its first formal summit in **Yekaterinburg**, **Russia**, in **2009**. The acronym was coined by **Jim O'Neill** of **Goldman Sachs** in **2001** to describe the fast-growing economies that would dominate the global market by **2050**.

• **South Africa** was officially invited to join the group in **December 2010**, changing the acronym from **BRIC** to **BRICS**. Its inclusion was intended to provide a voice for the **African continent** within the bloc.

**Important Points__**

• The **16th BRICS Summit** was held in **Kazan**, **Russia**, in **October 2024**. The summit focused on strengthening **multilateralism** and the **Kazan Declaration** emphasized the need for a more **equitable international order**.

question: What is the supreme law of India?
solution:
pThe correct answer is __**Indian Constitution**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Indian Constitution** is the **supreme law of India** because it establishes the framework that defines fundamental political principles, establishes the structure, procedures, powers, and duties of government institutions, and sets out fundamental rights, directive principles, and the duties of citizens.

• All laws enacted by the **Parliament** or state legislatures, and all executive actions taken by the **President** or Governors, must be in conformity with the **Constitution**. If any law violates the provisions of the Constitution, the **Judiciary** has the power to declare it null and void.

• The **Supreme Court Judgment** is considered the law of the land under **Article 141**, but it is an interpretation of the law and the Constitution, not the supreme law itself. Judgments must align with constitutional mandates. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***

• The **Parliament** of India is the supreme legislative body, but its powers are derived from and limited by the **Constitution**. It cannot pass laws that override the **Basic Structure** of the Constitution as defined in the **Kesavananda Bharati case (1973)**. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***

• The **Indian Constitution** was adopted by the **Constituent Assembly** on **26 November 1949** and became effective on **26 January 1950**. It imparts **constitutional supremacy** rather than parliamentary supremacy. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***

• A **President's Order** (such as an **Ordinance** under **Article 123**) has the same force as an Act of Parliament but is temporary and subject to the **Constitution** and judicial review. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• The **Constitution of India** is the **longest written constitution** of any sovereign country in the world, originally containing **395 Articles** in **22 Parts** and **8 Schedules**.

• Currently, after various amendments, it has approximately **448 Articles** grouped into **25 Parts** and **12 Schedules**.

• **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar**, the Chairman of the **Drafting Committee**, is widely regarded as the **Chief Architect** or the **Father of the Indian Constitution**.

• The **Preamble** of the Constitution declares India to be a **Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, and Democratic Republic**, ensuring justice, liberty, and equality to all its citizens.

• The **Constitution** was not printed but **calligraphed** in both **Hindi** and **English** by **Prem Behari Narain Raizada**.

• The **Constituent Assembly** took exactly **2 years, 11 months, and 18 days** to complete the final draft of the **Constitution**.

**Important Points__**

• **Article 13**: This article explicitly provides for the doctrine of **Judicial Review**. It states that all laws in force in the territory of India immediately before the commencement of the Constitution, in so far as they are inconsistent with the provisions of **Fundamental Rights (Part III)**, shall be void.

• **Basic Structure Doctrine**: Established by the **Supreme Court** in **1973**, this doctrine prevents the **Parliament** from using its amendment powers under **Article 368** to alter the essential features of the **Constitution**, such as **Secularism**, **Federalism**, and **Democracy**.

• **Constitutional Supremacy vs. Parliamentary Supremacy**: Unlike the **United Kingdom**, where **Parliament** is supreme, India follows **Constitutional Supremacy**, where the **Constitution** is the highest legal authority.

• **Emergency Provisions**: Under **Articles 352, 356, and 360**, the **Constitution** provides for the suspension of certain rights and the shifting of the federal structure to a unitary one, yet even these actions must follow the **Constitutional** procedure.
</ul

question: Who was the chairman of the drafting committee of the constituent assembly?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Dr. B. R. Ambedkar**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Dr. B. R. Ambedkar** was appointed as the **Chairman of the Drafting Committee** of the **Constituent Assembly of India**, which was tasked with drafting the Constitution of India.
 
• The Drafting Committee, chaired by **Dr. B. R. Ambedkar**, consisted of seven members, including notable leaders like **Alladi Krishnaswamy Iyer**, **K. M. Munshi**, and **Gopalaswami Ayyangar**.
 
• **Dr. Ambedkar** played a pivotal role in shaping the Indian Constitution and is often referred to as the "**Father of the Indian Constitution**" due to his significant contributions.
 
• The Drafting Committee was formed on **29th August 1947**, and Dr. B. R. Ambedkar was unanimously chosen as its Chairman owing to his expertise in law, economics, and social reforms.
 
• The Indian Constitution, drafted under the guidance of **Dr. Ambedkar**, was adopted on **26th November 1949** and came into effect on **26th January 1950**.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Dr. B. R. Ambedkar.***

**Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Role of the Drafting Committee:**

 
 
• The Drafting Committee was responsible for preparing the **draft Constitution of India**. It worked on incorporating various principles and provisions to ensure justice, equality, liberty, and fraternity for all citizens.
 
• The committee deliberated on issues such as **fundamental rights, directive principles of state policy, federal structure**, and the separation of powers.
 
 
 
• **Dr. B. R. Ambedkar's Contributions:**
 
 
• **Dr. Ambedkar** was a renowned social reformer, jurist, and economist. His vision shaped the Constitution to address issues of **social inequality and discrimination**.
 
• He advocated for provisions to eliminate caste-based discrimination and ensure equal opportunities for all, including the **reservation system** for Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs).
 
• He emphasized the importance of **individual rights, secularism, and social justice**, which became the cornerstone of the Indian Constitution.
 
 
 
• **Other Members of the Drafting Committee:**
 
 
• **Alladi Krishnaswamy Iyer:** A legal luminary who contributed to framing the federal structure.
 
• **K. M. Munshi:** Played a significant role in drafting the preamble and ensuring linguistic and cultural preservation.
 
• **Gopalaswami Ayyangar:** Contributed to discussions on state reorganization and the federal system.
 
 

**Important Points__**

 
• **Formation of Constituent Assembly:**

 
 
• The **Constituent Assembly of India** was formed in **1946** under the Cabinet Mission Plan. It consisted of members elected by provincial assemblies and nominated by princely states.
 
• The Assembly had **299 members**, representing diverse regions, communities, and interests.
 
 
 
• **Adoption of the Constitution:**
 
 
• The Constitution was adopted on **26th November 1949** and enforced on **26th January 1950**, marking the beginning of India as a sovereign, socialist, secular, and democratic republic.
 
• The date **26th January** was chosen to commemorate the **Purna Swaraj Declaration of 1930**.

question: In which year was the Indian ‘Wildlife (Protection) Act’ implemented?
solution:
The correct answer is **__1972____.__**

**__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• The Wild Life **Protection Act,** **1972** is an Act of the** Parliament of India** enacted for the protection of plants and **animal species**.
 
• Before **1972**, India had only **five** designated **national parks**.
 
• According to this Act, **hunting**, **harvesting,** and** harming** of **animals **is **strictly prohibited**. It also imposed **restrictions** on **harvesting** forest resources.
 
• This Act provides for the **protection** of the country’s **wild animals**, **birds**, and **plant species**, in order to ensure **environmental **and **ecological** security.
 
• Among other things, the Act lays down restrictions on** hunting** many **animal species**. The Act was last **amended** in the year **2006**.

​**Constitutional Provisions for the Wildlife Act :**

 
• **​Article 48A** of the Constitution of India directs the State to **protect **and** improve** the **environment** and **safeguard wildlife** and **forests**. This article was added to the Constitution by the **42nd Amendment in 1976**.
 
• **Article 51A** imposes certain **fundamental duties** for the **people** of** India**. One of them is to protect and **improve** the** natural environment** including **forests**,** lakes**, **rivers**, and **wildlife,** and to have compassion for living creatures.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__** 

**History of wildlife protection legislation in India:**

 
• **​**The** first** such **law** was passed by the **British Indian Government **in **1887** called the **Wild Birds Protection** Act, **1887**. The law sought to prohibit the possession and **sale** of specified **wild birds** that were either** killed** or** captured** during a breeding session.
 
• A **second** **law** was enacted in **1912** called the **Wild Birds and Animals Protection Act**. This was amended in **1935** when the Wild **Birds** and **Animals Protection** (Amendment) Act **1935 **was passed.
 
• During the **British Raj**, **wildlife **protection was **not accorded** a **priority**. It was only in **1960** that the issue of **protection** of** wildlife** and the prevention of certain **species** from becoming extinct came to the fore.

question: When a non-minister proposes a bill, it is called:
solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **Private Member's Bill** is a bill introduced by a member of parliament or a legislative assembly who is not a minister.
 
• This is in contrast to a **Government Bill**, which is introduced by a minister on behalf of the government.
 
• Private Member's Bills can cover a wide range of issues and allow legislators not in the executive branch to propose new laws or amendments to existing ones.
 
• Such bills are an important tool for raising issues of public interest and can sometimes lead to significant legislative changes.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Private Member's Bills** are typically discussed only on Fridays when the parliament is in session.
 
• While the success rate of Private Member's Bills is relatively low compared to Government Bills, they play a crucial role in parliamentary democracy.
 
• One of the notable Private Member's Bills that became law was the **Transplantation of Human Organs Act, 1994** in India.
 
• Private Member's Bills must go through the same stages of scrutiny and debate as Government Bills, including multiple readings and committee reviews.
 
• The introduction of Private Member's Bills encourages a more participatory legislative process and ensures diverse viewpoints are considered in lawmaking.

__
 
• **Artificial Habitats**:

 
 
• **This topic is not explicitly mentioned in the Concurrent List.**
 
• **It generally pertains to environmental management and conservation measures, w**hich are primarily under the jurisdiction of the states.
 
• The** Indian Constitution divides legislative powers between the Centre and the States** through three lists: the Union List, the State List, and the Concurrent List.
 
• The **Concurrent List** contains subjects on which both the **Centre and the States** can legislate.
 
• However, in case of any conflict, the law made by the **Central Government** prevails over the State law.
 
• This list contains areas of common interest where a unified legal framework might be beneficial, such as education, marriage laws, and social security.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Medical Education**:

 
 
• This falls under the Concurrent List, allowing both the Centre and the states to legislate on this subject.
 
 
 
• **Protection of Wildlife**:

subject: GK
question: Identify the correct option base on given statements:**Assertion (A):** The Union Government alone can legislate on matters related to the deployment and jurisdiction of armed forces within Indian states.**Reason (R):** The Constitution includes the deployment of Union forces in aid of civil power, regulation of cantonments, and control over arms and atomic energy in the Union List

options.text: A and R are correct, and R is the correct reason for A
A and R both true, but R is not the appropriate explanation for A
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true

solution:
The correct answer is __**A and R are correct, and R is the correct reason for A**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• **Assertion (A)** states that the **Union Government** alone has the authority to legislate on matters concerning the deployment and jurisdiction of **armed forces** within **Indian states**. Under **Article 246** of the **Constitution of India**, the **Parliament** has exclusive power to make laws with respect to any of the matters enumerated in **List I** of the **Seventh Schedule**. Hence, statement **A** is correct.

• **Reason (R)** explains that the **Constitution** includes the deployment of **Union forces** in aid of civil power, regulation of **cantonments**, and control over **arms** and **atomic energy** in the **Union List**. These subjects are specifically mentioned under **Entry 2A**, **Entry 3**, **Entry 5**, and **Entry 6** of the **Union List** respectively. Hence, statement **R** is correct.

• The **Union List** (List I) is a list of **100 items** (originally 97) over which the **Union Government** or the **Parliament of India** has exclusive jurisdiction. Because the subjects mentioned in the reason are part of this list, the **Union** alone can legislate on them, which directly justifies the assertion.

• The deployment of **armed forces** in aid of civil power (**Entry 2A**) was notably inserted by the **42nd Amendment Act, 1976**, ensuring that the **Union** can assist states in maintaining public order while retaining legislative control over those forces.

• Since the legislative competence for the subjects in **Reason (R)** belongs solely to the **Union**, it provides the legal basis for the claim made in **Assertion (A)**. Hence, the correct answer is **A and R are correct, and R is the correct reason for A**.

**Additional Information__**

• **Seventh Schedule**: This schedule of the **Indian Constitution** provides for the distribution of powers and responsibilities between the **Union** and the **States**. It contains three lists: the **Union List**, the **State List**, and the **Concurrent List**.

• **Union List (List I)**: It includes subjects of national importance that require a uniform law across the **country**. Examples include **Defense** (Entry 1), **Foreign Affairs** (Entry 10), **Railways** (Entry 22), **Banking** (Entry 45), and **Census** (Entry 69).

• **Cantonments (Entry 3)**: The **Union** is responsible for the delimitation of **cantonment areas** and the constitution and powers of **cantonment authorities**. This ensures that military stations are governed by federal regulations rather than varying state laws.

• **Arms and Atomic Energy**: **Entry 5** covers **arms, firearms, ammunition, and explosives**, while **Entry 6** covers **atomic energy** and mineral resources necessary for its production. These are kept under **Union** control for **national security** and **strategic interests**.

• **Article 248 (Residuary Powers)**: The **Parliament** has exclusive power to make any law with respect to any matter not enumerated in the **Concurrent List** or **State List**. This reinforces the **Union's** legislative supremacy in **India**.

• **Role of the President**: While the **Parliament** legislates, the **President of India** is the **Supreme Commander** of the **Armed Forces** under **Article 53(2)**, though the exercise of this power is regulated by law.
</ul

__
 
• **Droupadi Murmu** assumed office as the **15th President of India** on **July 25, 2022**. She succeeded **Ram Nath Kovind** after winning the **2022 Presidential Election** as the nominee of the **National Democratic Alliance (NDA)**.
 
• She is the first person belonging to a **Scheduled Tribe** (specifically the **Santhal** community) to hold the highest constitutional office in the country. Her journey from the **Mayurbhanj** district of **Odisha** to **Rashtrapati Bhavan** is a significant milestone in Indian democracy.
 
• Born on **June 20, 1958**, she is the **youngest person** to ever hold the office of the President and the first to be born in **post-Independence India**.
 
• Before her presidency, she served as the **9th Governor of Jharkhand** from **2015 to 2021**, becoming the first woman governor of that state to complete a full five-year term.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Pratibha Patil**:
 
 
• She served as the **12th President of India** from **2007 to 2012**.
 
• She holds the distinction of being the **first woman** to occupy the office of the President. Prior to this, she served as the **Governor of Rajasthan**.
 
 
 
• **Pranab Mukherjee**:
 
 
• He was the **13th President of India**, serving from **2012 to 2017**.
 
• A veteran statesman, he held various key portfolios in the Union Cabinet, including **Finance, Defence, and External Affairs**. He was posthumously awarded the **Bharat Ratna** in **2019**.
 
 
 
• **Ram Nath Kovind**:

• Before his tenure as President, he was the **Governor of Bihar**. He was the second **Dalit** president of India after **K. R. Narayanan**.
 
 
 
• **Constitutional Role of the President**:
 
 
• The President is the **nominal head** of the executive, the **first citizen** of India, and the **Supreme Commander of the Indian Armed Forces**.
 
• Under **Article 53** of the **Constitution of India**, the executive power of the Union is vested in the President and exercised either directly or through officers subordinate to them.

• **Article 52**: Explicitly states that "There shall be a **President of India**."
 
• **Article 54**: Defines the **Electoral College** for the election of the President, which includes elected members of both Houses of **Parliament** and the **Legislative Assemblies** of the States and Union Territories of **Delhi and Puducherry**.
 
• **Article 56**: Specifies the **term of office**, which is **five years** from the date the President enters upon their office.
 
• **Article 60**: Pertains to the **oath or affirmation** by the President, usually administered by the **Chief Justice of India**.
 
• **Article 61**: Outlines the procedure for **impeachment** if the President violates the Constitution.

• **Seniority Principle**: The appointment of the **Chief Justice of India** usually follows the **seniority convention**, where the senior-most judge of the Supreme Court is recommended by the outgoing CJI and appointed by the **President**.
 
• **Collegium System**: Judicial appointments to the Supreme Court and High Courts are made via the **Collegium System**, which consists of the **CJI** and the **four senior-most judges** of the Supreme Court.
 
• **Gender Representation**: Since the inception of the Supreme Court on **January 26, 1950**, there has been a significant gender gap. Out of over **250 judges** appointed to the apex court till date, only a small fraction (around **11**) have been women.
 
• **Retirement Rules**: Under the Indian Constitution, Supreme Court judges retire at **65 years**, while High Court judges retire at **62 years**. This age limit is a critical factor in determining the succession line for the **Chief Justice** position.
 
• **Oath of Office**: Every judge of the Supreme Court is required to take an **oath or affirmation** before the **President** or a person appointed by them, as per the **Third Schedule** of the Constitution.

subject: GK
question: When there is a disagreement between Union and State laws on a matter listed in the Concurrent List, which law takes precedence?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Union Law**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 254** of the **Indian Constitution** deals with situations where there is an inconsistency between laws made by the Parliament and the State Legislature in the **Concurrent List**.
 
• The **Concurrent List** is one of the three lists in the Seventh Schedule of the Indian Constitution, where both the Union and State Governments have the authority to legislate.
 
• If there is a conflict between a Union Law and a State Law on a subject in the Concurrent List, **Union Law will prevail**, provided it has been enacted by the Parliament. *Hence, Union Law takes precedence.*
 
• **Article 254(2)** gives an exception where a State Law, if inconsistent with Union Law, can prevail in that state. However, this requires the **President's assent**.
 
• The principle of Union Law prevailing ensures a uniform legal framework across the country and avoids discrepancies caused by conflicting State Laws.
 
• This provision reflects the federal structure of India, where the Union holds supremacy in certain matters to maintain national integrity and cohesiveness.

**Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Concurrent List:**

 
 
• The **Concurrent List** in the Seventh Schedule of the Indian Constitution contains subjects on which both the Parliament and State Legislatures can make laws. Examples include **education, marriage and divorce, bankruptcy, forests, and protection of wildlife**.
 
• If both governments pass laws on the same subject and there is a conflict, the Union Law prevails unless the State Law has received **Presidential assent** under Article 254(2).
 
 
 
• **Supremacy of Union Law:**
 
 
• The provision for Union Law to prevail ensures uniformity across the country in areas of national importance.
 
• For example, if both Parliament and a State Legislature legislate on a subject like **education**, the law made by Parliament will be considered valid in case of inconsistency.
 
 
 
• **Role of the President:**
 
 
• Under **Article 254(2)**, a State Law inconsistent with Union Law can prevail within the state only if it has received the **President's assent**.
 
• However, even after the President's assent, Parliament retains the authority to repeal or amend such State Law.
 
 

**Important Points__**

 
• **Key Features of Article 254:**

 
 
• Union Law will always override State Law on matters in the **Concurrent List** in case of conflict unless the State Law has received Presidential assent.
 
• If the President assents to a State Law inconsistent with Union Law, the State Law will prevail within that particular state unless Parliament amends or repeals it.
 
 
 
• **Examples:**
 
 
• The **Essential Commodities Act, 1955**, a Union Law, prevails over any conflicting State Law as it is related to maintaining the supply of essential goods.
 
• In the case of education reforms, Union Laws like the **Right to Education Act, 2009** have precedence over State Laws.

subject: GK
question: When is a 'Vote on Account' necessary?

options.text: To ensure continuity of government operations until the budget is passed

solution:
The correct answer is __**To ensure continuity of government operations until the budget is passed**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Article 116** of the **Constitution of India** provides for a **Vote on Account**, which is a grant in advance made by the **Parliament** to the **Executive**.

• The primary purpose of a **Vote on Account** is to ensure the **continuity of government operations**. Since the **financial year** begins on **April 1st** and the **Budget** (the **Annual Financial Statement**) usually takes a few months to be debated and passed, the government needs funds to cover its essential **expenditure** during this transition period. ***Hence, the statement is correct.***

• It serves as a temporary authorization to withdraw money from the **Consolidated Fund of India**. Without this, the government would legally be unable to spend money after **March 31st**, leading to a shutdown of public services.

• A **Vote on Account** does not deal with **new taxation policies**. Changes in taxes are proposed through the **Finance Bill** as part of the regular budget process. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***

• It is not a tool used to **reduce fiscal deficit**. Fiscal deficit management involves long-term policy decisions, **expenditure** control, and **revenue** generation strategies, often guided by the **FRBM Act, 2003**. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***

• **Supplementary grants** are governed by **Article 115** and are sought when the amount authorized for a specific service in the **Appropriation Act** for the current **financial year** is found to be insufficient. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Duration and Amount**: By convention, a **Vote on Account** is usually passed for a period of **two months**. The amount granted is typically **one-sixth (1/6th)** of the total estimated **expenditure** presented in the **Budget** for the entire **financial year**.

• **Interim Budget vs. Vote on Account**: While a **Vote on Account** only deals with the **expenditure** side of the government's ledger, an **Interim Budget** (presented during an **election year**) includes both **expenditure** and **receipts** (revenue) estimates.

• **Consolidated Fund of India**: Defined under **Article 266**, this fund contains all **revenues** received by the government, **loans** raised, and **money** received in repayment of loans. No amount can be withdrawn from it without an **Appropriation Act** passed by the **Parliament**.

• **Appropriation Bill**: Under **Article 114**, the **Appropriation Bill** is introduced in the **Lok Sabha** after the **demands for grants** are voted upon. It gives legal authority to the government to withdraw funds from the **Consolidated Fund**.

• **Shift in Budget Date**: Since **2017**, the **Union Budget** has been presented on **February 1st** instead of the last day of February. This change was implemented to complete the legislative process before the start of the new **financial year** on **April 1st**, thereby minimizing the need for a **Vote on Account** in normal years.

**Important Points__**

• **Exclusive Power of Lok Sabha**: The **Vote on Account** is a special provision where the **Lok Sabha** can pass the grant without a full-scale discussion, ensuring that the **administrative machinery** does not come to a halt.

• **No Policy Changes**: It is a formal convention that the government does not announce major **policy changes** or **new schemes** during a **Vote on Account** or an **Interim Budget**, leaving such decisions to the **new government** formed after **elections**.

• **Constitutional Requirement**: **Article 265** states that no **tax** shall be levied or collected except by **authority of law**, and **Article 266** ensures **Parliamentary control** over **expenditure**, making the **Vote on Account** a vital constitutional mechanism for **fiscal accountability**.
</ul

question: What is the primary function of the Inter-State Council?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Resolve disputes between states**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Inter-State Council** is a **constitutional body** established under **Article 263** of the **Constitution of India**. Its primary mandate is to facilitate coordination between the states and the center.

• One of its core functions, as defined in **Article 263(a)**, is **inquiring into and advising upon disputes** which may have arisen between states. This mechanism helps in the peaceful resolution of conflicts through dialogue and recommendation. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***

• The council also investigates and discusses subjects in which the states or the Union have a **common interest**, aiming for better coordination of policy and action.

• The **Inter-State Council** was formally established by a **Presidential Order** on **28 May 1990**, based on the recommendations of the **Sarkaria Commission (1988)**.

• The function of **controlling inter-state trade** is primarily governed by **Articles 301 to 307** of the Constitution and is regulated by **Parliament**, not the Inter-State Council. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***

• The **allocation of central funds** to the states is the primary responsibility of the **Finance Commission**, a constitutional body constituted under **Article 280** every **five years**. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***

• The **election of the President** of India is conducted by an **Electoral College** as per **Article 54**, consisting of elected members of both Houses of Parliament and Legislative Assemblies of the States. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Composition of the Council:** The **Inter-State Council** is chaired by the **Prime Minister**. Its members include the **Chief Ministers** of all states, **Chief Ministers** of Union Territories having a Legislative Assembly, and **Administrators** of UTs not having a Legislative Assembly.

• **Union Cabinet Presence:** The council also includes **six Ministers of Cabinet rank** in the Union Council of Ministers, nominated by the **Prime Minister**.

• **Standing Committee:** A **Standing Committee** of the Inter-State Council was set up in **1996** for continuous consultation and processing of matters for the Council's consideration. It is chaired by the **Union Home Minister**.

• **Nature of Recommendations:** The **Inter-State Council** is a **recommendatory body**. Its advice is not legally binding on the governments, but it carries significant political and administrative weight in a federal setup.

• **Secretariat:** The Council is assisted by a **Secretariat**, which was set up in **1991** and is headed by a **Secretary** to the **Government of India**. Since **2011**, it also functions as the Secretariat for the **Zonal Councils**.

**Important Points__**

• **Article 262 vs Article 263:** While **Article 263** deals with general coordination and dispute inquiry, **Article 262** specifically provides for the **adjudication of disputes** relating to the **waters of inter-state rivers** or river valleys.

• **Sarkaria Commission:** This commission was appointed in **1983** to examine the relationship and balance of power between state and central governments. Its recommendation to make the **Inter-State Council** a permanent body was a landmark in **Indian federalism**.

• **Zonal Councils:** Unlike the Inter-State Council, **Zonal Councils** are **statutory bodies** established under the **States Reorganisation Act, 1956**. There are currently **five** Zonal Councils (Northern, Central, Eastern, Western, and Southern), and the **North-Eastern Council** was created by a separate Act in **1971**.

• **Frequency of Meetings:** According to the **1990 Presidential Order**, the Council should meet at least **three times a year**, though in practice, meetings have been held less frequently.
</ul

question: Which of the following statement about federalism in India is true?

options.text: States have the right to secede from the Union
There is rigid division of powers

solution:
The correct answer is __**The Union has overriding authority**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 1** of the **Constitution of India** describes India as a **"Union of States"** rather than a "Federation of States." This terminology signifies that the Indian federation is not the result of an agreement among the states, and consequently, no state has the **right to secede** from the Union. *Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.*
 
• The Indian **federal system** follows a **flexible division of powers** rather than a rigid one. While the **Seventh Schedule** provides three lists (Union, State, and Concurrent), the Union government holds **residuary powers** and can influence state legislation under specific conditions. *Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.*
 
• The **Union has overriding authority** over the states, which is a defining feature of India's **quasi-federal** structure. Under **Article 249**, Parliament can legislate on subjects in the State List in the **national interest** if the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution. Similarly, during a **National Emergency (Article 352)**, the federal structure transforms into a unitary one. *Hence, statement 3 is correct.*
 
• In India, states are not **sovereign entities**. The **Parliament of India** has the power under **Article 3** to increase or diminish the area of any state, alter its boundaries, or change its name, even without the state legislature's ultimate consent. *Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.*
 
• The **supremacy of the Union** is also evident in the **Concurrent List**, where in case of a conflict between a central law and a state law, the **central law prevails** as per **Article 254**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Nature of Indian Federalism:** 
 
 
• Experts like **K.C. Wheare** have described the Indian Constitution as **"quasi-federal"** because it contains both federal and unitary features with a strong tilt towards the **Center**.
 
• Other scholars, such as **Morris Jones**, termed it **"bargaining federalism,"** while **Granville Austin** called it **"cooperative federalism"** because of the interdependence between the Union and the States.
 
 
 
• **The Seventh Schedule:** 
 
 
• The **Union List** contains **100 subjects** (originally 97) such as **defense, foreign affairs, and banking**, over which only the Parliament can legislate.
 
• The **State List** consists of **61 subjects** (originally 66) like **police, public health, and agriculture**.
 
• The **Concurrent List** includes **52 subjects** (originally 47) such as **education, forests, and marriage**, where both tiers can legislate.
 
 
 
• **Unitary Features:** Features like a **Single Constitution**, **Single Citizenship**, **Integrated Judiciary**, and the appointment of the **Governor** by the **President** strengthen the Union's position.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **S.R. Bommai vs Union of India (1994):** In this landmark judgment, the **Supreme Court** ruled that **federalism** is a part of the **"Basic Structure"** of the Constitution. However, it also acknowledged the **superior powers** of the Union in matters of national integrity and security.
 
• **Residuary Powers:** Under **Article 248**, the power to legislate on any matter not mentioned in any of the three lists (Residuary Powers) is vested solely in the **Union Parliament**. This is a departure from the **U.S. federal model** where residuary powers rest with the states.
 
• **Article 356 (President's Rule):** This provision allows the Union to take over the **executive and legislative powers** of a state if the constitutional machinery fails, further illustrating the **overriding authority** of the Union.
</ul

subject: GK
question: Under what circumstances can the Parliament legislate on a subject in the State List?

options.text: When Rajya Sabha passes a resolution

solution:
The correct answer is __**When Rajya Sabha passes a resolution**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Under **Article 249** of the **Constitution of India**, the **Parliament** can legislate on a subject in the **State List** if the **Rajya Sabha** passes a resolution.
 
• This resolution must be supported by **not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting**, declaring that it is necessary or expedient in the **national interest** for the Parliament to make laws with respect to any matter enumerated in the **State List**. ***Hence, the correct answer is When Rajya Sabha passes a resolution.***
 
• A law made under **Article 249** remains in force for a period of **one year** at a time. However, the **Rajya Sabha** can renew the resolution for subsequent periods of **one year** indefinitely.
 
• This provision highlights the **quasi-federal** nature of the **Indian Constitution**, where the **Union** is given overriding powers over state subjects under specific circumstances.
 
• Such a law ceases to have effect after **six months** from the date on which the resolution expires.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Article 250 (During National Emergency)**: 
 
 
• The **Parliament** acquires the power to legislate with respect to any matter in the **State List** while a **Proclamation of Emergency** (under **Article 352**) is in operation.
 
• Such laws become inoperative **six months** after the emergency has ceased to operate.
 
 
 
• **Article 252 (Request by States)**: 
 
 
• If the **legislatures of two or more states** pass a resolution requesting the **Parliament** to enact laws on a **State List** subject, the Parliament can make such a law for those specific states.
 
• Any other state can adopt such a law later by passing a resolution in its legislature.
 
 
 
• **Article 253 (International Agreements)**: 
 
 
• The **Parliament** can make laws on any subject (including the **State List**) for implementing **international treaties**, **agreements**, or **conventions** with other countries or international bodies.
 
 
 
• **Article 356 (President’s Rule)**: 
 
 
• When **President’s Rule** is imposed in a state, the **Parliament** is authorized to exercise the legislative powers of that **State Legislature**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **Seventh Schedule** of the **Indian Constitution** divides legislative powers into three lists: the **Union List (List I)**, the **State List (List II)**, and the **Concurrent List (List III)**.
 
• The **Rajya Sabha**, acting as the **Council of States**, serves as the protector of the states' interests. Therefore, its consent is mandatory under **Article 249** to allow central interference in state subjects.
 
• During a **Financial Emergency** (under **Article 360**), the **Union** can give directions to states regarding **financial propriety** and the reservation of **Money Bills** for the **President's** consideration, but it does not automatically transfer the entire **State List** legislative power to **Parliament**.
 
• The **issuance of an ordinance** by the **President** (under **Article 123**) generally applies to matters on which the **Parliament** can legislate; hence, it cannot be used to legislate on **State List** subjects unless the aforementioned special circumstances (like Emergency or Rajya Sabha resolution) already exist.

question: Which law prevails in case of a conflict between Union and State laws on a subject in the Concurrent List?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Union law**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In the case of a conflict between **Union and State laws** on a subject in the **Concurrent List**, the **Union law prevails** as per **Article 254(1) of the Indian Constitution**.
 
• The **Concurrent List** includes subjects where both the Union and State governments can legislate. However, in case of inconsistency, the **Union law** will supersede the State law.
 
• If a State law receives the **President's assent** under **Article 254(2)**, it can prevail over Union law in that particular state. However, Parliament retains the power to override such state laws by making a law on the same subject. *Hence, Union law takes precedence in most cases.*
 
• The primary purpose of giving precedence to Union law is to maintain **uniformity** across the country on matters of national importance.
 
• This principle ensures that there is no conflict in laws affecting citizens across different states and facilitates a cohesive legal framework. *Hence, the correct answer is Union law.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Article 254 of the Indian Constitution:**

 
 
• **Article 254(1)**: When there is a conflict between a law made by the Parliament and a law made by the State Legislature on a subject in the **Concurrent List**, the law made by Parliament shall prevail.
 
• **Article 254(2)**: If a State law on a Concurrent List subject conflicts with an existing Union law, and the State law receives the **President's assent**, the State law can prevail in that particular state. However, the Parliament can override the State law by making another law on the same subject.
 
 
 
• **Concurrent List of the Indian Constitution:**
 
 
• The **Concurrent List** is one of the three lists in the **Seventh Schedule** of the Constitution. It includes subjects where both the Union and State legislatures can legislate.
 
• Examples of subjects in the Concurrent List include **education, criminal law, marriage and divorce, bankruptcy, forests, and protection of wildlife**.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Union Law Supremacy:**
 
 
• The supremacy of Union law ensures that there is a **uniform legal system** on subjects of national importance, avoiding discrepancies between states.
 
• This principle also ensures that the Union government can address issues of national interest effectively without being constrained by conflicting State laws.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Considerations in Article 254:**

 
 
• The **Concurrent List** subjects require careful legislation to avoid conflicts. Parliament has the final authority to ensure uniformity in laws.
 
• The **President's assent** is critical when State laws conflict with Union laws. This provides a constitutional mechanism to resolve conflicts.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Union Law Supremacy:**
 
 
• The Union government enacted the **Environment Protection Act, 1986**, which superseded State laws on environmental protection for uniform implementation across India.
 
• In the case of **education policies**, the Union government has consistently framed laws to ensure a standard education system across states, even when State laws differed.

question: If someone becomes a minister or the Prime Minister without being a Member of Parliament, they must get elected to the Parliament within _______ months or they will have to vacate the office.
solution:
The correct answer is __**six months**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 75(5)** of the **Indian Constitution** states that a person who is not a Member of Parliament (MP) can still be appointed as a minister, including the **Prime Minister**. However, such a person must become an MP within a period of **six months** from the date of their appointment.
 
• If the appointed person fails to get elected to either the **Lok Sabha** or the **Rajya Sabha** within this six-month period, they must resign from their ministerial position. Hence, option 2 is correct.
 
• This provision ensures that the **executive branch** remains accountable to the legislative branch, which is a crucial aspect of the **parliamentary system of governance**.
 
• The rule applies to both the **Union government** (Prime Minister and Union Ministers) and the **state governments** (Chief Ministers and State Ministers).
 
• The six-month provision allows flexibility in governance, ensuring that capable individuals can assume key positions temporarily even if they are not immediately elected members of the legislature.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Article 75 of the Indian Constitution:**

 
 
• **Article 75(1):** It states that the Prime Minister is appointed by the President, and the other ministers are appointed on the advice of the Prime Minister.
 
• **Article 75(5):** It mandates that a minister who is not a member of either House of Parliament must become a member within six months of their appointment.
 
• This article ensures that the **executive branch** is accountable to the **legislature**, which is a cornerstone of India's parliamentary democracy.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Application:**
 
 
• **PV Narasimha Rao:** He was appointed as the **Prime Minister** in 1991 and contested elections to become a member of the Parliament within six months.
 
• **Jayalalithaa:** In 2001, she was sworn in as the Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu but had to resign after being disqualified from contesting elections.
 
 
 
• **Parliamentary System of Government:**
 
 
• India follows a **parliamentary system of governance**, where the executive is responsible to the legislature.
 
• The system ensures that ministers, including the Prime Minister, remain answerable to the Parliament, reinforcing the principles of **democracy** and **accountability**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Legal Considerations:**

 
 
• The six-month provision is crucial in allowing the government to function smoothly while ensuring that all executive members hold a legitimate mandate from the legislature.
 
• The **President of India** plays a key role in appointing ministers, including individuals who are not MPs, based on the advice of the Prime Minister.
 
 
 
• **Significance of the Six-Month Rule:**
 
 
• It provides a mechanism for appointing non-legislators as ministers or Prime Minister temporarily, ensuring that governance is not hindered.
 
• This provision has been used multiple times in India, highlighting its practical importance in the country's political framework.

question: The executive power of the Union in India rests with _______.
solution:
The correct answer is __**President**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **As per the Indian Constitution**, the **executive authority of the Union** is vested in the **President,** who may exercise it directly or through subordinate officers.
 
• However, the practical exercise of executive power is primarily conducted by the **Council of Ministers,** under the leadership of the Prime Minister.
 
• The Prime Minister, a member of **either the Lok Sabha or the Rajya Sabha**, must meet certain eligibility criteria.
 
• They must be **at least 25 years old if they are a Lok Sabha member, or at least 30 years **old if they are a Rajya Sabha member.
 
• Additionally, they must be a citizen of India and cannot hold any profit-making office under the Indian government.
 
• While there is no term limit for the Prime Minister, they must maintain the confidence of both the President and the Lok Sabha to remain in office.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **The President of India **is elected by an electoral college composed of elected members from both Houses of Parliament and the Legislative Assemblies of the states.
 
• This election is conducted through the system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote method.
 
• To ensure fairness and equity, each vote is given suitable weightage to maintain uniformity among states and parity between the states and the Union.
 
• The President must fulfill certain eligibility criteria, including being a citizen of India, at least 35 years of age, and qualified for election as a member of the Lok Sabha.
 
• Their term of office spans five years, and they are eligible for re-election. Removal from office follows the procedure outlined in Article 61 of the Constitution.

• There shall be a **Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister** at the head to aid and advise the** President of India**.

• The President is mandated to act in accordance with the advice tendered by the Council of Ministers.
 
• However, the President retains the prerogative to request the Council of Ministers to review their advice, yet must ultimately adhere to their counsel following reconsideration.
 
• **The 42nd Amendment of the Constitution of India,** enacted in 1976, explicitly delineated that the President is bound to act in accordance with the advice tendered by the Council of Ministers.
 
• This amendment was ratified on** January 3, 1977,** thus solidifying the principle of executive accountability and the supremacy of the Council of Ministers in guiding the President's actions.

• **The Attorney General for India** serves as the principal legal advisor to the Government of India. Appointed by the President of India upon the recommendation of the Union Cabinet in accordance with Article 76(1) of the Constitution, the attorney general holds office at the pleasure of the President.

question: Who among the following presides over any joint sitting of both the houses of the Parliament of India, convened to resolve deadlock over any bill?

options.text: Any person appointed by the President

solution:
The correct answer is** ​__Speaker of the Lok Sabha.__**

__
 
• The **Constitution** of **India** provides **joint sittings** of both the **Houses** to break in the case of a **deadlock** between the **two houses** of **parliament**.
 
• The joint sitting of the Parliament is called by the **President** and is presided over by the **Speaker **or, in his **absence**, by the **Deputy Speaker** of the **Lok Sabha** or in his absence the Deputy-Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
 
• If any of the above officers are not present then any **other member** of the **Parliament** can preside by consensus of both the House.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **Key Points__**

 
• **Article 108** of the Indian Constitution of India provides for Joint sitting of both Houses.

 
 
• Joint sitting of both Houses in certain cases

 (1) If after a Bill has been passed by one House and transmitted to the other House
 
 
• the Bill is rejected by the other House; or
 
• the Houses have finally disagreed as to the amendments to be made in the Bill; or
 
• more than six months elapse from the date of the reception of the Bill by the other House without the Bill being passed by it the President may, unless the Bill has lapsed by reason of a dissolution of the House of the People, notify to the Houses by message if they are sitting or by public notification if they are not sitting, his** intention to summon **them to meet in a joint sitting for the purpose of deliberating and voting on the Bill: Provided that nothing in this clause shall apply to a Money Bill
 
 
 
 
 
• The time of sitting, the **duration, **and** adjournment** of the joint sitting is determined by the **Speaker.**
 
• The **quorum** to constitute a joint sitting shall be **one tenth** of the **total number** of members of the Houses.
 
• **Om Birla** is the new Lok Sabha Speaker of the **17th Lok Sabha** as on February 2021.

• If there is no quorum in the House, it shall be the duty of the Chairman, either to adjourn the House or to suspend the meeting until there is a quorum.
 
• The total membership of the Rajya Sabha is 245, therefore, the presence of 25 members is the quorum sufficient to constitute its meeting.

question: Which Article allows the President to impose President's Rule in a state?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 356**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 356** of the **Constitution of India** provides the **President** with the authority to impose **President's Rule** in a state if there is a **failure of constitutional machinery**. This occurs when the **State Government** cannot function according to the provisions of the **Constitution**. **Hence, statement 2 is correct.**
 
• The proclamation of **President's Rule** can be issued by the **President** based on a report from the **Governor** of the respective state or even if the **President** is satisfied 'otherwise' that such a situation exists.
 
• Upon the imposition of **Article 356**, the **State Council of Ministers**, including the **Chief Minister**, is dismissed. The **Governor**, acting on behalf of the **President**, takes over the administration of the state, often assisted by **advisors** or the **Chief Secretary**.
 
• Every proclamation issued under **Article 356** must be laid before both **Houses of Parliament** (**Lok Sabha** and **Rajya Sabha**) and must be approved within **two months** from the date of its issue by a **simple majority**.
 
• If approved, the **President's Rule** remains in force for **six months**. It can be extended for a maximum period of **three years**, subject to **Parliamentary** approval every **six months**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Article 352 (National Emergency):** This article empowers the **President** to declare a **National Emergency** when the security of **India** is threatened by **war**, **external aggression**, or **armed rebellion**. It has been proclaimed in **India** during the years **1962**, **1971**, and **1975**. **Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.**
 
• **Article 360 (Financial Emergency):** This article allows the **President** to declare a **Financial Emergency** if the financial stability or credit of **India** or any part of its territory is threatened. Notably, a **Financial Emergency** has **never been declared** in **India** since the **Constitution** came into effect. **Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.**
 
• **Article 365:** This article states that if a state fails to comply with or give effect to any direction from the **Union**, it shall be lawful for the **President** to hold that a situation has arisen in which the government of the state cannot be carried on in accordance with the **Constitution**. This often serves as a ground for invoking **Article 356**. **Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.**
 
• **S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994):** This landmark **Supreme Court** judgment restricted the arbitrary use of **Article 356**. The court ruled that the **President's** satisfaction is subject to **judicial review** and that the **State Legislative Assembly** should only be dissolved after **Parliament** approves the proclamation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The first instance of **President's Rule** in independent **India** was in the state of **Punjab** in **1951**. Since then, it has been used over **100 times** across various states.
 
• The **44th Amendment Act of 1978** introduced a significant check: **President's Rule** cannot be extended beyond **one year** unless a **National Emergency** is in operation or the **Election Commission of India** certifies that elections to the **State Legislative Assembly** cannot be held.
 
• During the period of **President's Rule**, the **Parliament** assumes the power to make laws for the state, and the **State Budget** is also passed by the **Parliament**.
 
• The **President** has the power to either **suspend** or **dissolve** the **State Legislative Assembly**. If suspended, the assembly can be restored once the proclamation is revoked; if dissolved, fresh **elections** must be conducted.
