question: The origin of the Ganga River is from which of the following?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Gangotri Glacier**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Ganga River** originates from the **Gangotri Glacier**, which is located in the **Uttarkashi district of Uttarakhand**, India.
 
• The river emerges in the form of the **Bhagirathi River** from **Gaumukh**, a cave-like structure at the snout of the glacier.
 
• The **Bhagirathi** later converges with the **Alaknanda River** at **Devprayag**, marking the official beginning of the Ganga River.
 
• The **Gangotri Glacier** is around **30.2 kilometers long** and **2 to 4 kilometers wide**, making it one of the largest glaciers in the Himalayas.
 
• The glacier is situated at an altitude of approximately **7,100 meters above sea level**, surrounded by peaks like **Chaukhamba, Shivling, and Bhagirathi**.
 
• *Hence, the correct answer is Gangotri Glacier.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Gangotri Glacier:**

 
 
• The glacier is a primary source of water for the Ganga River, which is considered sacred in Hinduism.
 
• It is a retreating glacier, with its snout (Gaumukh) receding approximately 10 to 30 meters annually due to **climate change** and global warming.
 
 
 
• **Other Options:**
 
 
• **Siachen Glacier:** Located in the eastern Karakoram range in Ladakh, it is the largest glacier in the Indian subcontinent but does not contribute to the Ganga River.
 
• **Zemu Glacier:** Found in Sikkim, this glacier feeds the Teesta River, which flows through Sikkim and West Bengal.
 
• **Pindari Glacier:** Located in the Kumaon region of Uttarakhand, it forms the Pindar River, a tributary of the Alaknanda River.
 
 
 
• **Importance of the Ganga River:**
 
 
• The Ganga is considered the **lifeline** of millions of people in India, providing water for drinking, agriculture, and industrial use.
 
• It is revered as a **goddess** in Hindu culture and worshipped during festivals such as **Ganga Dussehra** and **Chhath Puja**.
 
• The river basin supports approximately **600 million people** and spans an area of around **861,404 square kilometers**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Conservation Efforts:**

 
 
• The **National Mission for Clean Ganga (NMCG)** was launched in 2014 under the **Namami Gange Programme** to rejuvenate the river.
 
• Efforts focus on reducing pollution levels, afforestation, and biodiversity conservation.
 
 
 
• **Religious Significance:**
 
 
• The Ganga is believed to cleanse sins and is a major site for **ritual bathing** and cremation along its ghats.
 
• Prominent pilgrimage sites along the river include **Haridwar, Varanasi, and Prayagraj**.

question: Who among the following was the author of the book ‘Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi’?

The correct answer is __**Ziauddin Barani**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Ziauddin Barani **was the author of the book **‘Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi’.**
 
• **The Tarikh-i Firoz Shahi **stands as a remarkable example of **Indo-Persian historiography** from the Sultanate era in India.
 
• Completed in **1357 CE**, it was dedicated to the reigning monarch of the time.
 
• Ziauddin Barani, an Indian Muslim political thinker** during the reigns of Muhammad bin Tughlaq and Firuz Shah**, was renowned for his authorship of the Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi (also known as Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi).
 
• This historical work provides insights into medieval India, spanning from the rule of Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq to the initial years of Firuz Shah Tughluq's reign.
 
• Barani's Fatwa-i-Jahandari, while promoting a hierarchy among Muslim communities in the Indian subcontinent, was not strictly based on race or caste.
 
• It drew inspiration from the Sassanid Iran model, which emphasized aristocracy through birth.
 
• This concept, according to some scholars, aligned with the evolving Islamic thought of the time, as evident in the works of contemporaries like Ibn Khaldun.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Minhaj-us-Siraj** was a Persian historian born in the Ghurid region during the 13th century. In 1227, he migrated to Ucch and later settled in Delhi.
 
• **Abu Fazl **was an Indian writer, historian, and statesman who held the position of grand vizier in the Mughal Empire from his appointment in 1579 until his passing in 1602.
 
• **Syedna Mohammed Badruddin **served as the 46th Da'i al-Mutlaq of the Dawoodi Bohra community. He succeeded Syedna Tayyeb Zainuddin as the religious leader.

• The **earliest source on Sanskrit grammar **still in existence is the** Ashtadhyayi. **
 
• **It is **a **prehistoric Indian text** that was written sometime between the** fifth and fourth centuries BCE.**
 
• The** Indian grammarian Panini** was the author.
 
• It condenses the **phonetic and grammatical knowledge** that has developed inside the **Vedic religion** into **4,000 sutras.**
 
• **Ashtadhyayi's grammar** has been compared to the **Turing machine,** a** mathematically idealized model** that distils any computing device's logical architecture to its most basic components.
 
• In ancient India, Panini was a** renowned scholar, grammarian, and Sanskrit philologist.**
 
• Panini has been referred to as the** "first descriptive linguist"** and **"the father of linguistics."**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Tulsidas:**
 
 
• Tulsidas, also referred to as **Goswami Tulsidas, **was a** poet** and **Ramanandi Vaishnava Hindu saint.**
 
• The **Hanuman Chalisa **and the** epic Ramcharitmanas**, which is a translation of the Sanskrit Ramayana based on the biography of Rama in the** Awadhi dialect**, are works that bear his name.
 
 
 
• **Kabir:**
 
 
• Hinduism's Bhakti movement was influenced by the writings of **Kabir Das,** an** Indian mystic poet **and** saint** who lived in the 15th century.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The **Delhi Sultanate** was a Muslim kingdom based mostly in Delhi that stretched over large parts of the Indian subcontinent for 320 years (1206–1526).

• The Lodi dynasty was the last dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate before it was conquered by the Mughal Empire.
 
• The Lodi dynasty is known for its architectural contributions and the establishment of new cities, including Agra.

subject: GK
question: Which fort is an example of Rajput military architecture?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Chittorgarh Fort**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Chittorgarh Fort** is widely considered one of the most outstanding examples of **Rajput military architecture**. It is located in the **Chittorgarh** district of **Rajasthan**, India, and stands as a symbol of Rajput bravery and resistance.
 
• Spanning over an area of approximately **700 acres** and situated on a **180-meter high hill**, it is one of the largest forts in India. It served as the capital of the **Mewar Kingdom** for centuries.
 
• In **2013**, it was designated as a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** under the "Hill Forts of Rajasthan" group, highlighting its **historical significance** and structural brilliance.
 
• The fort features seven massive gates (called **Pols**), such as the **Padan Pol** and **Bhairon Pol**, designed to hinder enemy advancement. It also contains iconic structures like the **Vijay Stambh** (Tower of Victory), built by **Rana Kumbha** in **1448** to commemorate his victory over the armies of Malwa and Gujarat.
 
• The architecture showcases the use of **natural topography** for defense, a hallmark of **Rajput** engineering, which prioritized high elevation and massive stone **ramparts** to withstand long sieges.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Red Fort (Delhi)**: This fort is a prime example of **Mughal architecture**. It was commissioned by Emperor **Shah Jahan** in **1639** and completed in **1648**. Its **features** include massive walls of **red sandstone** and a layout that represents the zenith of Mughal creativity, blending Persian, Timurid, and Indian styles.
 
• **Agra Fort**: Located in **Agra**, **Uttar Pradesh**, this fort is another **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. While it has ancient origins as a brick fort called **Badalgarh**, it was rebuilt in its current form by Mughal Emperor **Akbar** starting in **1565**. It served as the main residence of the Mughal dynasty until **1638**.
 
• **Golkonda Fort**: Situated in **Hyderabad**, **Telangana**, it was the capital of the **Qutb Shahi dynasty** (**1512–1687**). It is famous for its **acoustic features**; a handclap at the entrance can be heard at the **Bala Hissar** pavilion, which is the highest point of the fort. It was also once the center of the global **diamond trade**.
 
• **Rajput vs. Mughal Styles**: While **Mughal architecture** often focused on symmetry, **charbagh gardens**, and marble inlay (pietra dura), **Rajput military architecture** was characterized by ruggedness, **jharokhas** (overhanging balconies), **chhatris** (cenotaphs), and defensive **bastions** tailored to the desert or hilly terrain of **Rajasthan**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **Chittorgarh Fort** is immortalized in history due to the three **Jauhars** (mass self-immolation) performed by the women of the fort during defeats, most notably the one led by **Rani Padmini** in **1303** when **Alauddin Khalji** attacked.
 
• The fort's **water management system** was highly advanced for its time, consisting of **84 water bodies** (reservoirs, wells, and step-wells) that could store enough water to sustain an army of **50,000 soldiers** for four years without external supply.
 
• **Kirti Stambh**, another major landmark within the fort, is a **22-meter high** tower dedicated to the first Jain Tirthankara, **Rishabhanatha**, highlighting the **religious diversity** present in Rajput kingdoms during the **12th century**.
 
• The battle of **Haldighati** (**1576**) and the subsequent struggles of **Maharana Pratap** are closely linked to the legacy of the **Mewar** resistance centered around this architectural marvel.

question: Alauddin Khilji's reign is marked by his successful defense against which foreign invader?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Mongols**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Alauddin Khilji**, who ruled the **Delhi Sultanate** from **1296 to 1316**, is celebrated in history for his successful defense of India against the **Mongol** invasions. The **Mongols** of the **Chagatai Khanate** launched several large-scale attacks during his reign, aiming to conquer the heart of North India.
 
• The major **Mongol** invasions occurred in **1297-98**, **1299**, **1303**, and **1305**. Unlike his predecessors, **Alauddin Khilji** adopted a proactive military stance, defeating the **Mongol** forces in battles such as the **Battle of Jalandhar (1298)** and the **Battle of Kili (1299)**. **Hence, the option Mongols is correct.**
 
• To protect the capital, **Delhi**, from **Mongol** raids, he constructed the **Siri Fort** around **1303**. This fort served as a massive defensive garrison and the second city of **Delhi**.
 
• **Alauddin Khilji** implemented rigorous military reforms to sustain a large army. He introduced the **Dagh** system (branding of horses) and the **Chehra** system (descriptive rolls of soldiers) to ensure the quality and loyalty of his troops.
 
• His **Market Control Policy** or **Price Control Measures** were specifically designed to keep the cost of living low, enabling him to maintain a massive standing army with relatively low salaries, which was essential for the continuous defense against **Mongol** threats.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Timur (Tamerlane)**: He was a **Turco-Mongol** conqueror who invaded India much later, in the year **1398**. His invasion took place during the reign of **Nasir-ud-Din Mahmud Shah Tughluq** of the **Tughlaq Dynasty**. **Timur** sacked **Delhi**, causing widespread destruction, but this was long after **Alauddin Khilji** had died. **Hence, the option Timur is incorrect.**
 
• **Babur**: He was the founder of the **Mughal Empire** in India. **Babur** invaded India in the **16th century** and defeated **Ibrahim Lodi** in the **First Battle of Panipat** in **1526**. His era is distinct from the **Khilji** period by over two centuries. **Hence, the option Babur is incorrect.**
 
• **Mahmud of Ghazni**: He was the ruler of the **Ghaznavid Empire** who conducted **17 raids** into India between **1000 and 1027 AD**. His primary motive was to plunder the wealth of Indian temples, such as the **Somnath Temple** in **1025 AD**. He predates the **Khilji Dynasty** by nearly 300 years. **Hence, the option Mahmud of Ghazni is incorrect.**
 
• **Khilji Dynasty**: It was the second dynasty to rule the **Delhi Sultanate**, founded by **Jalal-ud-din Firuz Khilji** in **1290**. **Alauddin Khilji** was the most powerful ruler of this dynasty, known for his administrative reforms and territorial expansions into **South India** under his general **Malik Kafur**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Zafar Khan**: He was one of **Alauddin Khilji**'s most valiant generals who played a crucial role in repelling the **Mongols**. He died heroically in the **Battle of Kili** in **1299** while fighting the forces of **Qutlugh Khwaja**.
 
• **Administrative Centralization**: To prevent internal rebellions while focusing on external **Mongol** threats, **Alauddin** prohibited the social gatherings of nobles and banned the use of wine and intoxicants.
 
• **Revenue Reforms**: He was the first Sultan to insist that in the **Doab** region, land revenue should be assessed on the basis of measuring the land (**Paimash**). This ensured a steady flow of income to the state to fund the military.
 
• **Economic Impact**: His strict enforcement of prices for grains, cloth, and other necessities ensured that even during **Mongol** sieges, the supply chain and economic stability of **Delhi** remained intact.

subject: GK
question: The Battle of Plassey (1757) marked the beginning of British rule in India. Which earlier battle marked the decline of the Delhi Sultanate?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Battle of Panipat (1526)**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **First Battle of Panipat**, fought on **21 April 1526**, is the landmark event that marked the end of the **Delhi Sultanate** and the beginning of the **Mughal Empire** in India. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***

• The battle was fought between the invading forces of **Zahir-ud-din Muhammad Babur** and the **Lodi Dynasty** led by **Ibrahim Lodi**. **Ibrahim Lodi** was the last Sultan of the **Delhi Sultanate**, and his death on the battlefield signified the total collapse of the Sultanate rule that had lasted since **1206**.

• The **Battle of Talikota (1565)** was a watershed battle fought between the **Vijayanagara Empire** and the **Deccan Sultanates** (Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, and Bidar). This battle led to the decline of the **Vijayanagara Empire** in South India, not the Delhi Sultanate. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***

• The **Battle of Khanwa (1527)** took place a year after the fall of the Delhi Sultanate. It was fought between **Babur** and the **Rajput** forces led by **Rana Sanga** of **Mewar**. This battle consolidated **Mughal** power but did not mark the decline of the Sultanate as it had already ceased to exist. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***

• The **Battle of Tarain (1192)**, specifically the **Second Battle of Tarain**, saw **Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad Ghori** defeat **Prithviraj Chauhan**. This event is historically recognized as the **establishment** and **foundation** of Muslim rule and the **Delhi Sultanate** in India, rather than its decline. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• **The Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526):** The Sultanate era spanned over **three centuries** and was characterized by five successive dynasties: the **Mamluk (Slave) Dynasty**, the **Khalji Dynasty**, the **Tughlaq Dynasty**, the **Sayyid Dynasty**, and the **Lodi Dynasty**. The **Lodi Dynasty** was the final phase, ending with **Ibrahim Lodi**.

• **Military Innovation at Panipat:** **Babur** was able to defeat a much larger army of **Ibrahim Lodi** (estimated at **100,000 soldiers** and **1,000 elephants**) primarily due to his use of **field artillery** and **gunpowder firearms**, which were relatively new to **Northern India** at the time. He employed the **Tulughma** (encirclement) tactic and the **Araba** (carts tied together to protect artillery) system.

• **The Role of Invitations:** **Babur**, the ruler of **Kabul**, was invited to invade India by **Daulat Khan Lodi** (the Governor of **Punjab**) and **Alam Khan** (uncle of Ibrahim Lodi), who were dissatisfied with **Ibrahim Lodi’s** tyrannical rule.

• **The Battle of Plassey (1757):** Fought on **23 June 1757**, this battle saw the **British East India Company**, led by **Robert Clive**, defeat the **Nawab of Bengal**, **Siraj-ud-Daulah**. It is considered the starting point of **British Colonial rule** in India, much like Panipat started the **Mughal** era.

• **Successive Panipat Battles:** The **Second Battle of Panipat (1556)** was fought between **Akbar** and **Hemu**, securing the Mughal throne. The **Third Battle of Panipat (1761)** was fought between the **Maratha Empire** and the **Afghan** invader **Ahmad Shah Abdali**, which weakened Maratha power and indirectly aided British expansion.

**Important Points__**

• **Ibrahim Lodi** holds the distinction of being the only **Sultan of Delhi** to have been killed on the **battlefield**.

• The **Lodi Dynasty** was of **Afghan** origin, founded by **Bahlul Lodi** in **1451**, following the decline of the **Sayyid Dynasty**.

• The transition from the **Delhi Sultanate** to the **Mughal Empire** shifted the political center of gravity and introduced a new era of **Indo-Islamic architecture** and **administrative reforms** that peaked under **Akbar**.

• While the **Battle of Panipat** ended the Sultanate, the **Battle of Buxar (1764)** is often cited alongside the **Battle of Plassey** as the final seal on **British political authority** over the **Mughal Emperor** and the **Nawab of Awadh**.

question: Name the Lodhi ruler shifted the capital from Delhi to Agra?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Sikandar Lodhi**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Sikandar Lodhi** was the second ruler of the **Lodhi dynasty**, who reigned from **1489 to 1517 CE**.
 
• He is credited with shifting the capital of his kingdom from **Delhi** to **Agra** in **1504 CE**.
 
• The reason for moving the capital to Agra was its **geographical location**, which was more strategic for administrative and military purposes.
 
• Sikandar Lodhi founded the city of **Agra** and developed it as a prominent administrative center.
 
• Under his rule, Agra became a hub for **trade, commerce, and cultural activities**, attracting merchants and artisans.
 
• This decision to shift the capital also symbolized Sikandar Lodhi’s attempt to expand and consolidate his empire in the **Doab region**, situated between the Ganga and Yamuna rivers.
 
• He was known for his administrative reforms, including the introduction of **market regulations** to stabilize prices and improve trade.
 
• Sikandar Lodhi was also a patron of art and literature, promoting the use of the **Persian language** in his court.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Lodhi Dynasty:**

 
 
• The Lodhi dynasty was the last dynasty of the **Delhi Sultanate**, ruling from **1451 to 1526 CE**.
 
• It was founded by **Bahlul Lodhi**, a Pashtun noble who established control over Delhi in 1451 CE.
 
• The dynasty is known for its efforts to consolidate power in North India and for its contributions to architecture and culture.
 
 
 
• **Other Rulers of the Lodhi Dynasty:**
 
 
• **Bahlul Lodhi:** He was the founder of the Lodhi dynasty and ruled from **1451 to 1489 CE**. His reign was marked by the consolidation of power and territorial expansion.
 
• **Ibrahim Lodhi:** The last ruler of the dynasty, he reigned from **1517 to 1526 CE**. His defeat at the **Battle of Panipat** in 1526 by Babur marked the end of the Delhi Sultanate and the beginning of the Mughal Empire.
 
 
 
• **Agra as a Capital:**
 
 
• Agra became a key administrative and cultural center under the Lodhi dynasty and later under the Mughals.
 
• Its strategic location in the fertile Doab region contributed to its prosperity as a center of agriculture and trade.
 
• The city was further developed by Mughal emperors like Akbar, Jahangir, and Shah Jahan, who built iconic monuments such as the **Taj Mahal** and **Agra Fort**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Strategic Importance of Agra:**

 
 
• Agra’s location between the Ganga and Yamuna rivers made it a vital region for trade and agriculture.
 
• It served as a base for military campaigns in North and Central India.
 
 
 
• **Sikandar Lodhi’s Contributions:**
 
 
• He introduced several administrative reforms, including **price regulation** and efficient tax collection.
 
• Sikandar Lodhi was a patron of **arts, literature, and architecture**, encouraging the construction of mosques and gardens.

question: Which one of the following pairs of ruler and length of their reign, is correctly matched?
solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Raziyya Sultan** (also known as **Razia Sultana**) reigned from **1236** to **1240**. She was the first and only female ruler of the **Delhi Sultanate**. Her reign lasted for approximately **4 years**. ***Hence, statement B is correct.***
 
• **Muhammad bin Tughluq** ascended the throne in **1325** and ruled until his death in **1351**. His total reign spanned **26 years**, during which he was known for ambitious yet controversial administrative experiments. ***Hence, statement A is incorrect.***
 
• **Alauddin Khalji**, the most powerful ruler of the **Khalji dynasty**, reigned from **1296** to **1316**. His rule lasted for **20 years** and was characterized by massive territorial expansion and economic reforms in **India**. ***Hence, statement C is incorrect.***
 
• **Ghiyasuddin Balban** served as the Sultan of **Delhi** from **1266** to **1287**. His reign lasted for **21 years**. He is credited with consolidating the power of the **Mamluk dynasty** through his policy of **"Iron and Blood."** ***Hence, statement D is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Raziyya Sultan:** She was the daughter of **Iltutmish**, who nominated her as his successor over his sons. Despite being an able administrator and a brave warrior, she faced heavy opposition from the **Turkish nobility** (the **Chahalgani**) because she was a woman. She was eventually defeated and killed near **Kaithal** in the year **1240**.
 
• **Muhammad bin Tughluq:** Often referred to as a **"wise fool"** by historians like **Ibn Battuta**, he introduced **token currency** in **1329** and ordered the transfer of the capital from **Delhi** to **Devagiri** (renamed **Daulatabad**). These projects resulted in significant economic loss and administrative chaos.
 
• **Alauddin Khalji:** He was the first Sultan to invade **South India**, led by his general **Malik Kafur**. He introduced strict **price control** mechanisms and market regulations to maintain a large standing army. He also built the **Alai Darwaza** and the city of **Siri** in **Delhi**.
 
• **Ghiyasuddin Balban:** He introduced the Persian customs of **Sijda** (prostration) and **Paibos** (kissing the Sultan's feet) to elevate the status of the monarch. He established a separate military department called **Diwan-i-Arz** to strengthen the internal security of the **Delhi Sultanate** against **Mongol** invasions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **Delhi Sultanate** comprised five successive dynasties: the **Mamluk/Slave Dynasty** (**1206–1290**), the **Khalji Dynasty** (**1290–1320**), the **Tughlaq Dynasty** (**1320–1414**), the **Sayyid Dynasty** (**1414–1451**), and the **Lodi Dynasty** (**1451–1526**).
 
• The **Slave Dynasty** was established by **Qutb-ud-din Aibak**, a former slave of **Muhammad Ghori**, in the year **1206**.
 
• The **Tughlaq Dynasty** enjoyed the longest period of rule among all the Sultanate dynasties, lasting for nearly **94 years**, while the **Khalji Dynasty** had the shortest span of approximately **30 years**.
 
• The **Sultanate period** ended in **1526** with the **First Battle of Panipat**, where **Babur** defeated **Ibrahim Lodi**, leading to the foundation of the **Mughal Empire** in **India**.

subject: GK
question:
**Consider the following statements:****
Statement 1.** Alauddin Khalji is remembered for administrative reforms and military expansion in the north.**
Statement 2.** Muhammad Bin Tughlaq's project to transfer the capital from Delhi to Daulatabad ultimately failed.**
Which of the statements is/are correct**?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Both 1 and 2 are correct**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Alauddin Khalji**, who reigned from **1296** to **1316**, was the most powerful ruler of the **Khalji Dynasty**. He is widely remembered for his extensive **administrative reforms**, particularly the **market control system** and **land revenue reforms**, which were designed to sustain a massive **standing army**. His **military expansion** in the **North** was significant, as he conquered territories like **Gujarat** in **1299**, **Ranthambore** in **1301**, **Chittor** in **1303**, and **Malwa** in **1305**. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• **Muhammad Bin Tughlaq**, who ruled from **1325** to **1351**, was known for his ambitious but controversial administrative experiments. One of his most famous projects was the **transfer of the capital** from **Delhi** to **Daulatabad** (formerly **Devagiri**) in **1327**. He believed that a central location would allow him to control both **North India** and the **Deccan** more effectively. However, the forced migration of the entire population of **Delhi** over a distance of **1500 kilometers** led to immense hardship and deaths. The project ultimately failed as he realized the difficulty of defending the northern borders from **Daulatabad**, leading him to order the population to move back to **Delhi**. ***Hence, statement 2 is correct.***
 
• Since both the provided statements accurately describe the historical actions and outcomes associated with these two rulers of the **Delhi Sultanate**, the overall conclusion is that both are valid. ***Hence, the correct answer is Both 1 and 2 are correct.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Administrative Reforms of Alauddin Khalji:**

 
 
• He introduced the **Dag** system (branding of horses) and the **Chehra** or **Huliya** system (descriptive roll of soldiers) to eliminate corruption and false muster in the **military**.
 
• He established the **Diwan-i-Mustakhraj**, a special department to look after and realize the arrears of **land revenue**.
 
• His **market reforms** involved fixing the prices of essential commodities and appointing officers like the **Shahna-i-Mandi** to supervise the markets in **Delhi**.
 
 
 
• **Projects of Muhammad Bin Tughlaq:**
 
 
• **Token Currency:** In **1329-30**, he introduced **copper** and **brass** coins as **token currency** to be used at par with **gold** and **silver** coins. This failed due to widespread illegal minting by the public.
 
• **Agriculture:** He created a separate department of **agriculture** known as **Diwan-i-Amir-Kohi** to bring more land under cultivation and provide loans (**Sondhar**) to farmers.
 
• **Taxation in Doab:** He increased the **land tax** in the fertile **Ganga-Yamuna Doab** region during a period of **famine**, which led to a massive peasant revolt.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Dynastic Context:** The **Khalji Dynasty** (**1290-1320**) was the second dynasty to rule the **Delhi Sultanate**, followed by the **Tughlaq Dynasty** (**1320-1414**).
 
• **Mongol Invasions:** **Alauddin Khalji** successfully defended **India** against several **Mongol** invasions, which necessitated his focus on **military** strength and **administrative** efficiency.
 
• **Historical Sources:** Much of the information regarding these rulers comes from the writings of contemporary chroniclers like **Ziauddin Barani**, who wrote the **Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi**, and the Moroccan traveler **Ibn Battuta**, who visited the court of **Muhammad Bin Tughlaq** in **1333**.
 
• **Architectural Contributions:** **Alauddin Khalji** built the **Alai Darwaza**, the **Siri Fort**, and the **Hauz Khas** in **Delhi**. **Muhammad Bin Tughlaq** built the city of **Jahanpanah**.

question: Who was the first Sultan of the Delhi Sultanate to start military expeditions into southern India?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Alauddin Khalji**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Alauddin Khalji** was the **first Sultan of the Delhi Sultanate** to start **military expeditions into southern India**.
 
• **Alauddin Khalji** ​:
 
 
• He was the **nephew **and son-in-law **of Jalaluddin Khilji**, who laid the **foundation of the Khilji dynasty** in **1290**.
 
• He was named Amir-i-Tuzuk because he had supported his uncle in his quest for dominance.
 
• Alauddin led two successful expeditions during Jalaluddin's rule.
 
• In addition to the Iqta of Kara, Bhilsa (Vidisa) was granted the Iqta of Awadh during his first expedition in AD 1292.
 
• In addition, he was** named Arizi-i-Mumalik**, or Minister of War. He** oversaw the first Turkish expedition to southern India in AD 1294**, during which they pillaged Devagiri.
 
• The expedition's triumph demonstrated Alauddin's skill as a military leader and effective organizer.
 
• He **slew Jalaluddin Khilji in July of the year 1296** and appointed **himself as the Sultan**.
 
• Alauddin made the decision to bring back Balban's brutal political practices.
 
• He made the decision to** limit the nobility's authority and the ulema's** (Islamic scholars') meddling in domestic affairs.
 
• In the early years of his reign, he also had to deal with a few secessions, one after another.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Ghiyas-ud-din Balban** was one of the most potent sultans of the Middle Ages, he was the **Sultan of Delhi** from **1266 until 1287 AD**.

 
 
• Like his mentor, **Iltutmish**, he ascended to prominence and assumed the title of Sultan of Delhi.
 
• Balban **belonged to** the renowned **Iltutmish's **group of **40 Turkish slaves**.
 
• He brought peace and order back to the realm, together with the authority and dignity of the sultan, after thirty years of near-anarchy since the days of Iltutmish.
 
• Balban also** forced officials to respect the Sultan**. They needed to touch his feet and bow. It was known as **Sijda**.
 
• He created a **spy system** to watch over officials who were called **Barids**.
 
• He also **introduced **the** Iqta system**, which **granted land to officials** in exchange for their services.
 
• He made **reforms **to the **police system**. He created a** separate police force** called the **Kotwali**, which had the authority to enforce the law and punish offenders.
 
 
 
• Muhammad bin Tughluq (MBT) was the son of Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq, also known as Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, who founded the Tughlaq dynasty by subduing the Delhi Sultanate. 
 
 
• Other names for him are Ulugh Khan and Prince Fakhr Malik Jauna Khan.
 
• The Deccan region of India, which is now Maharashtra, is home to Daulatabad, also called Devagiri, and it was Tughluq who ordered the relocation of his capital from Delhi.
 
• He introduced token money in the form of brass and copper coins with a par value with gold and silver coins.
 
 
 
• **Iltutmish **was the** first Muslim ruler to rule from Delhi **and that's why he was regarded as the **effective founder of the Delhi Sultanate**.
 
 
• He was also the **first Sultan of India** to be** recognised by the Khalifa**.
 
• He was successful in protecting Delhi's throne from the Mongol invasion as well as Yeldoz and Qubacha attacks.
 
• He shattered the Rajput powers in the north and established his dominance over them.
 
• He made his rule hereditary, issued coins in his honour, and **made Delhi** a beautiful **capital**.
 
• He **completed **the **construction **of the **Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque** and the **Qutb Minar**.
 
• He unveiled the **Sultanate's two coinage**, the **copper jital **and the **silver tanka**.
 
• He **introduced **the **Iqtadari system**, which divided the country into Iqtas and allocated them to nobles in return for pay.
 
• Since he did not think his sons were capable of carrying out the role, he **passed away in 1236** and was **succeeded by **his daughter, **Razia Sultana**.

question: _______ was land granted to a Brahmana, who was usually exempted from paying land revenue and other dues to the king, and was often given the right to collect these dues.
solution:
The correct answer is __**An agrahara.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• 
 Agrahara in Sanskrit refers to “land exempt from leasing rights”.

 
 
• Agrahara was land, village, or fields that were given to Brahmaṇas.
 
• The **Agraharas **were exempted from taxes and had other administrative immunities.
 
• Agrahara was also known as Agraharam, Chaturvedimangalams, Ghatoka, and Boya in ancient times.
 
• Agraharas were built and maintained by dynasties like Cholas and Pallavas.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• Other important keywords:__

 
 
• Ardhika: A cultivator who tills the land of others and gets half the crop as his share. 
 
• Brahmadeya: Generally tax-free land or village was given as a gift to Brahmanas.
 
• Dana: The idea of dana or gift to Brahmanas was developed by Brahmanical texts as the surest means of acquiring merit (Punya) and destroying sin (**Pataka**).
 
• Devadana: grants to the temple, either plots of Land or a Whole village, were known as Devadana in the south Indian context.

question: Gaumukh Kund is a reservoir located in which of the following forts?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Chittorgarh.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• **Gaumukh Kund** is a sacred water body situated on the western part of the famous **Chittorgarh Fort. **
 
• 'Gaumukh' literally means the** 'mouth of a cow'.** The water flows through the cracks in the rocks and in due course, falls into the reservoir.
 
• The Chittorgarh Fort **is also known as** **Chittorgarh or Chittor Fort.**
 
• Chittorgarh Fort is the largest fort in India and Asia.
 
• It is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site.**
 
• The fort used to be the **capital of Mewar rulers.**
 
• It is **located in** the present-day town of **Chittorgarh in Rajasthan.**
 
• Built-in the 7th century AD, Chittorgarh Fort has withstood three major Muslim invasions starting from Alauddin Khilji in 1303, in 1535 by Bahadur Shah of Gujarat, and in 1568 by Akbar.

 
• It is situated on the bank of Berach river (Banas River tributary).
 
• Chittorgarh Fort has a total of seven gates and the main gate is named the Ram Pol.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/98b862fde257d6b28c87df75978a0762ad5aa7a34906b381410c669e3edf201b.png] 

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] Additional Information__**

 
• Kumbhalgarh Fort:

 
 
• **Kumbhalgarh Fort** is located in the Rajsamand district of **Rajasthan.**
 
• Built by **Rana Kumbha **from the Sisodia Rajput dynasty.
 
• Longwall of the 36-kilometer length makes it the great wall of India.
 
• A special attraction in the fort is the Lakhola tank, Ganesh temple, and Parsvanatha temple.
 
• Kumbhalgarh is well known as the birthplace of Maharana Pratap.
 
 
 
• **Gwalior Fort**
 
 
• Gwalior Fort is known as Gibraltar of India.
 
• It was given the name ”The Perl in the necklace of the forts of Hind” by Mughal Emperor Babur.
 
• It was built in 525 AD century and it is one of the biggest forts in India.
 
• It was built by Suraj Sen.
 
• Temple Teli-ka-mandir is the most famous temple constructed in the Dravidian style of temple architecture.
 
 
 
• **Datia Mahal**
 
 
• Datia Mahal is a 7-storied architecture with two floors positioned in the basement.
 
• It is only made out of stone and bricks without any usage of wood or iron. So, the whole 7- storied building stands without any support of metal or even wood. 
 
• Datia Mahal is one of the great examples of Indo-Islamic architecture in India. A blend of Rajputana and Mughal styles gives it a luxurious look.

question: In which of the following years was Tipu Sultan killed?
solution:
The correct answer is __**1799**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• **Tipu Sultan**:

 
 
• In the **Fourth Anglo-Mysore War**, a combined force of **British East India Company** troops,** supported by the Marathas and the Nizam of Hyderabad defeated Tipu**. He was** killed on 4 May 1799** while defending his stronghold of **Seringapatam**.
 
• Tipu Sultan also known as the **Tiger of Mysore **was the ruler of the** Kingdom of Mysore, Karnataka**.
 
• He introduced a number of administrative innovations during his rule, including a **new coinage system **and **Mauludi Lunisolar calendar **and a **new land revenue system**.
 
• He initiated the growth of the** Mysore silk industry.**
 
• He was also a patron of **science and technology** and is credited as the **‘pioneer of rocket technology in India'**. He expanded the **iron-cased Mysorean rockets **and commissioned the military manual **Fathul Mujahidin**.
 
• He deployed the rockets against the advances of British forces and their allies during the** Anglo-Mysore Wars**, including the **Battle of Pollilur** and the** Siege of Srirangapatna**.
 
• He won important victories against the British in the **Second Anglo-Mysore War**. He negotiated the **1784 Treaty of Mangalore **with them after his father** Hyder Ali **died from** cancer** in **December 1782** during the **Second Anglo-Mysore War**.
 
• In the **Third Anglo-Mysore War**, he was forced into the** Treaty of Seringapatam**, losing a number of previously conquered territories, including **Malabar and Mangalore**.
 
• He sent emissaries to foreign states, including the** Ottoman Empire, Afghanistan, and France**, in an attempt to rally opposition to the British.
 
• Tipu was a great lover of democracy and a great diplomat who gave his support to the **French soldiers at Seringapatam** in setting up a** Jacobin Club in 1797.** Tipu himself became a** member of the Jacobin Club** and allowed himself to be called Citizen Tipu.
 
• He planted the** Tree of Liberty at Seringapatam**.
 
 
 
• **Important treaties with the British**:
 
 
• Four wars were fought with Mysore** (1767-69, 1780-84, 1790-92 and 1799)**.
 
 
• 1767-69: **Treaty of Madras**
 
• 1780-84: **Treaty of Mangalore**
 
• 1790-92:** Treaty of Seringapatam**
 
• 1799: **Subsidiary Alliance**
 
 
 
 

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/08444cc8babef048bdbb69f2f6cd5922613a4ef08ed6056b8a8b439356366f84.png] **

 
• Tipu Sultan

question: In which battle was Ibrahim Lodhi defeated by Babur ?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Battle of Panipat (1526)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Battle of Panipat**, fought in **1526**, was a decisive conflict between **Babur**, the founder of the **Mughal Empire**, and **Ibrahim Lodhi**, the Sultan of the Delhi Sultanate.
 
• This battle marked the end of the **Lodhi Dynasty** and the establishment of the **Mughal Empire in India**.
 
• The battle took place on the **plains of Panipat**, located in present-day **Haryana**, India.
 
• Babur’s army, though numerically smaller, employed superior tactics, including the use of **artillery and flanking maneuvers**, which were revolutionary for the Indian subcontinent at that time.
 
• The **death of Ibrahim Lodhi** during the battle signified the collapse of the Delhi Sultanate, paving the way for Mughal dominance in northern India.
 
• This victory also showcased Babur's military acumen and his ability to adapt to the conditions of the Indian terrain.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Battle of Panipat (1526).***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Battle of Panipat (1526):**

 
 
• This battle was the first of the **three famous battles of Panipat**. It marked the beginning of Mughal rule in India.
 
• Babur's forces used **gunpowder firearms and field artillery**, which gave them a significant advantage over Ibrahim Lodhi's army.
 
• The battle is considered one of the earliest examples of modern warfare in the Indian subcontinent.
 
 
 
• **Other Important Battles:**
 
 
• **Battle of Khanwa (1527):** Fought between Babur and Rana Sanga of Mewar, it solidified Babur's position in India after his victory at Panipat.
 
• **Battle of Chausa (1539):** Fought between Mughal Emperor Humayun and Sher Shah Suri, marking the rise of Sher Shah Suri.
 
• **Battle of Ghagra (1529):** Another significant battle where Babur defeated the Afghan chiefs and consolidated his empire.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Babur’s Victory:**
 
 
• Babur's victories introduced new military strategies, including the use of **field artillery**, which became a staple of Mughal warfare.
 
• The establishment of the Mughal Empire led to significant cultural, political, and architectural advancements in India.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Features of Babur’s Army:**

 
 
• Babur introduced the **Tulughma strategy**, which involved dividing the army into left, right, and center flanks for effective combat.
 
• The use of **gunpowder and artillery** was a game-changer in the Indian subcontinent, giving Babur an edge over his adversaries.
 
 
 
• **Historical Impact of the Battle:**
 
 
• The victory at Panipat marked the end of the **Delhi Sultanate** and the beginning of Mughal dominance in India.
 
• Babur’s rule laid the foundation for a centralized administration and a flourishing Indo-Islamic culture in the region.

question: The famous tripartite struggle was fought for control over ________ in early medieval period.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Kannauj**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The Tripartite Struggle,** commonly referred to as the **Kannauj Triangle Wars,** transpired in the ninth century, revolving around the **battle for dominance in northern India** among three prominent empires**: the Gurjara-Pratihara Empire, the Pala Empire, and the Rashtrakuta Empire.**
 
• This intense conflict primarily revolved around asserting control over the city of Kannauj, which served as a pivotal symbol of authority over the Ganges plain.
 
• During this period, the** Palas of Bengal, the Pratiharas of Central India, and the Rashtrakutas of the Deccan** engaged in fierce warfare to secure their influence over Kannauj.
 
• Ultimately, the Pratiharas emerged as the triumphant force, consolidating their power and dominance in the region.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Kannauj, **located in the Indian state of Uttar Pradesh, serves as both a city and an administrative center, functioning as a municipal board or Nagar Palika Parishad within Kannauj district. The name "Kannauj" is an evolved form of the classical name "Kanyakubja".
 
• Historically, it was also known as "Mahodaya" during the reign of Mihira Bhoja. Positioned 104 kilometers west of the state capital, Lucknow, Kannauj has been a significant center throughout Classical India, serving as a focal point for various imperial Indian dynasties.
 
• Among these dynasties, the earliest was the Maukhari dynasty, followed by Emperor Harsha of the Vardhana dynasty. Subsequently, Kannauj came under the rule of the Gahadavala dynasty, attaining unprecedented glory under the reign of Govindachandra.

question: The Battle of Haldighati (1576) was fought between which two leaders?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Akbar and Rana Pratap**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Battle of Haldighati** was a significant historical conflict fought on **June 18, 1576**. It took place between the forces of the **Mughal Emperor Akbar** and the **Rajput** king of **Mewar**, **Maharana Pratap**. *Hence, statement 1 is correct.*

• The **Mughal** army was led by **Raja Man Singh I** of **Amber**, who was one of **Akbar**'s most trusted generals. On the other side, **Maharana Pratap** led the **Mewar** forces, defending his kingdom's sovereignty against **Mughal** expansion.

• The battle occurred at **Haldighati**, a narrow mountain pass in the **Aravalli Range** near **Gogunda** in **Rajasthan**. The name **Haldighati** is derived from the turmeric-colored (yellow) soil of the region.

• While the **Mughal** forces technically won the battle by occupying the ground, they failed to capture **Maharana Pratap**. **Pratap** managed to escape to the hills, from where he continued a long-term **guerrilla warfare** against the **Mughal Empire**.

• Regarding the other options: The **Battle of Khanwa** in **1527** was fought between **Babur and Rana Sanga**. The **Battle of Chausa (1539)** and **Battle of Kannauj (1540)** were fought between **Sher Shah Suri and Humayun**. **Jahangir and Rana Amar Singh** (son of Pratap) eventually ended the long-standing conflict through a peace treaty in **1615**.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Maharana Pratap (1540–1597):** He was the **13th King of Mewar** and is celebrated as a national hero in **India** for his bravery and refusal to submit to the **Mughal** authority. He spent much of his life in the **Aravalli** mountains, organizing resistance.

• **Chetak:** This was the name of **Maharana Pratap**'s legendary horse. During the **Battle of Haldighati**, **Chetak** is said to have carried his master to safety despite being severely injured, eventually collapsing and dying. A memorial for **Chetak** stands at **Haldighati** today.

• **Hakim Khan Suri:** Interestingly, the vanguard of **Maharana Pratap**'s army was led by an **Afghan** general named **Hakim Khan Suri**, showing that the battle was a political struggle for independence rather than a purely religious one.

• **Raja Man Singh I:** He was the **Kachwaha Rajput** King of **Amber** and a primary commander in the **Mughal** army. His leadership at **Haldighati** represented **Akbar**'s policy of incorporating **Rajput** rulers into the **Mughal** administrative and military hierarchy.

• **Guerrilla Warfare:** After the battle, **Maharana Pratap** utilized the difficult terrain of the **Aravallis** to conduct **guerrilla tactics**. By the time of his death in **1597**, he had successfully recovered most of his ancestral territories, including **Udaipur** and **Kumbhalgarh**, though **Chittorgarh** remained under **Mughal** control.

**Important Points__**

• **Strength of Forces:** Historical accounts vary, but it is generally accepted that the **Mughal** army significantly outnumbered the **Mewar** forces. The **Mughals** had approximately **5,000 to 10,000** soldiers, while **Pratap** had around **3,000** horsemen and **400 Bhil** archers.

• **Bhil Community:** The local **Bhil** tribes played a crucial role in supporting **Maharana Pratap**. Their expertise in the hilly terrain and **archery** was vital for the **Rajput** resistance during and after the battle.

• **Historical Significance:** The **Battle of Haldighati** is often cited as a classic example of a smaller force using **geography** and **valor** to withstand a much larger imperial power, cementing **Maharana Pratap**'s legacy in **Indian** folklore.

question:
Consider the following statements:
Statement 1. Babur was of Mongol and Timurid descent and founded the Mughal Empire after defeating Ibrahim Lodi.
Statement 2. Babur was overthrown by Sher Shah and later succeeded by his grandson Akbar.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Only 1**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Zahir-ud-din Muhammad Babur** was the founder of the **Mughal Empire** in the Indian subcontinent. He possessed a distinguished lineage, being a descendant of **Timur** (the **Turco-Mongol** conqueror) from his father **Umar Sheikh Mirza**'s side and a descendant of **Genghis Khan** (the **Mongol** ruler) from his mother **Qutlugh Nigar Khanum**'s side.

• In **1526**, **Babur** invaded India and defeated **Ibrahim Lodi**, the last ruler of the **Lodi Dynasty**, in the **First Battle of Panipat**. This victory effectively ended the **Delhi Sultanate** and established the foundation of the **Mughal Empire**. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***

• **Babur** ruled from **1526** until his death in **1530**. He was not overthrown by **Sher Shah Suri**; rather, it was his son and successor, **Humayun**, who was defeated and ousted by **Sher Shah Suri**.

• **Sher Shah Suri** defeated **Humayun** in the **Battle of Chausa** (**1539**) and the **Battle of Kannauj** (**1540**), forcing **Humayun** into exile for nearly **15 years**. **Babur** was succeeded by his son **Humayun**, and **Akbar** (Babur's grandson) succeeded **Humayun** in **1556**. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Babur (Reign: 1526–1530):**

• He was born in **Andijan**, in the **Fergana Valley** (modern-day **Uzbekistan**), in **1483**.

• He is credited with introducing **gunpowder** and **field artillery** in Indian warfare, using the **Tulughma** and **Araba** methods.

• He wrote his autobiography, **Baburnama** (also known as **Tuzuk-i-Baburi**), in **Chagatai Turkic**, which was later translated into **Persian** during **Akbar**'s reign.

• Other significant battles fought by him include the **Battle of Khanwa** (**1527**) against **Rana Sanga** of **Mewar** and the **Battle of Ghagra** (**1529**) against the **Afghans**.

• **Sher Shah Suri (Reign: 1540–1545):**

• He was the founder of the **Suri Empire** with its capital at **Sasaram** (modern-day **Bihar**).

• He is renowned for his administrative brilliance, including the introduction of the **Rupiya** (currency) and the reconstruction of the **Grand Trunk Road** (**Sadak-e-Azam**), which connected **Chittagong** to **Kabul**.

• **Akbar (Reign: 1556–1605):**

• The third **Mughal Emperor**, who ascended the throne at the **age** of **13** after the accidental death of **Humayun**.

• He consolidated the empire through the **Second Battle of Panipat** (**1556**) against **Hemu** and is famous for his **Mansabdari system** and religious policy of **Din-i-Ilahi**.

**Important Points__**

• The **Mughal** succession followed a pattern of **Babur** (founder) -> **Humayun** (son) -> **Akbar** (grandson) -> **Jahangir** -> **Shah Jahan** -> **Aurangzeb**.

• The term **Mughal** is derived from **Mongol**, reflecting the dynasty's central Asian roots.

• The **Suri Dynasty** interrupted **Mughal** rule for a period of **15 years** (**1540–1555**) before **Humayun** recaptured **Delhi** shortly before his death.

question:
Consider the following statements about 'Bibi ka Maqbara':
1. It was built by Mughal emperor Aurangzeb in memory of his wife.
2. It is located in Chhatrapati Sambhaji Nagar and is called the "Taj Mahal of the Deccan."
3. It was constructed in the early 1500s during Babur's reign.
Which among these following is/are correct?
solution:
The correct answer is __**1 and 2 only**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Bibi ka Maqbara** was commissioned by the **Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb** in **1660** in memory of his first wife and chief consort, **Dilras Banu Begum**. She was posthumously known as **Rabia-ud-Daurani**. While some historical records suggest that his son, **Azam Shah**, oversaw the construction, it was built during the reign of **Aurangzeb** to honor his wife. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***

• The mausoleum is located in **Chhatrapati Sambhaji Nagar** (formerly known as **Aurangabad**) in the state of **Maharashtra**, **India**. It is famously called the **Taj of the Deccan** or **Dakkhani Taj** because its design was heavily inspired by the **Taj Mahal** in **Agra**. It stands as a major landmark and a symbol of **Mughal architecture** in the southern part of the empire. ***Hence, statement 2 is correct.***

• The construction of the **Bibi ka Maqbara** took place between **1651** and **1661 AD**, which is in the **17th century**. **Babur**, the founder of the **Mughal Empire**, reigned from **1526** to **1530 AD** in the **early 16th century**. Therefore, the monument was built more than a century after **Babur** reign ended. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***

• ***Hence, the correct answer is 1 and 2 only.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Architectural Details**: The monument was designed by the architect **Ata-ullah**, who was the son of **Ustad Ahmad Lahauri**, the principal designer of the **Taj Mahal**. This lineage explains the striking similarities between the two structures. The engineering work was carried out by **Hanspat Rai**.

• **Materials and Construction**: Unlike the **Taj Mahal**, which is constructed entirely of white **marble**, the **Bibi ka Maqbara** uses **marble** only for the main dome and the lattice screens. The rest of the structure is built with **basaltic trap** stone and finished with a fine **polished plaster** that gives it a marble-like appearance.

• **Garden Layout**: The tomb is set in the center of a **Charbagh** (four-fold garden) layout. It features axial ponds, fountains, and water channels, surrounded by high enclosure walls with **pavilions** and **minarets**.

• **Historical Context**: **Dilras Banu Begum** was a princess of the **Safavid dynasty** of **Persia**. She died in **1657** due to complications following the birth of her fifth child, **Akbar II**. Her death deeply affected **Aurangzeb**, leading to the commissioning of this grand tomb.

• **City Name Change**: The city where the monument is located, **Aurangabad**, was officially renamed **Chhatrapati Sambhaji Nagar** by the **Government of Maharashtra** in **2023**, in honor of the second **Chhatrapati** of the **Maratha Empire**.

**Important Points__**

• **Cost of Construction**: Historical inscriptions indicate that the mausoleum was built at a cost of approximately **6,68,203 Rupees** and **7 Annas**. This was significantly less than the cost of the **Taj Mahal**, which is why it is sometimes referred to as a more modest version of the **Agra** monument.

• **Comparison with Taj Mahal**: While the **Taj Mahal** represents the peak of **Mughal architecture** under **Shah Jahan**, the **Bibi ka Maqbara** reflects the transition and the beginning of the decline in the lavishness of **Mughal** buildings during **Aurangzeb** reign.

• **Tourism**: It is currently a protected monument under the **Archaeological Survey of India (ASI)** and remains one of the most visited historical sites in **Maharashtra**.
</ul

subject: GK
question: Which of the following statements about the Mughal mansabdari system is/are correct?**Statement I.** A mansab indicated both the rank (zat) and salary of a noble.**Statement II.** Every mansabdar was required to reside personally in the jagir whose revenue he drew.

options.text: Both I and II are correct

solution:
The correct answer is __**Only I**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Mansabdari system** was the administrative and military framework of the **Mughal Empire**, introduced by Emperor **Akbar** in **1571**. It was designed to organize the nobility and ensure a steady supply of military troops for the state.

• **Statement I**: The term **Mansab** refers to a rank or position held by an official. Each **Mansabdar** was assigned a dual rank: **Zat** and **Sawar**. The **Zat** rank was a numerical value that indicated the personal status of the noble in the imperial hierarchy and directly determined the **salary** they were entitled to receive. ***Hence, statement I is correct.***

• **Statement II**: While **Mansabdars** were often remunerated through **Jagirs** (assignments of land revenue), they were not required to reside personally in the **Jagir** from which they drew their income. In fact, **Mughal** policy encouraged the frequent transfer of **Mansabdars** from one post to another to prevent them from developing local power bases or becoming independent rulers. They usually collected revenue from their assigned **Jagirs** through their agents, known as **Amils**. ***Hence, statement II is incorrect.***

• The system ensured that the **Emperor** maintained absolute control over the military and administrative officials by making their positions dependent on imperial favor rather than hereditary right.

• ***Hence, the correct answer is Only I.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Zat and Sawar Ranks**: The **Zat** rank fixed the personal status and **salary** of the officer, while the **Sawar** rank indicated the number of **cavalrymen** (horses and riders) the **Mansabdar** was required to maintain for the **Mughal** army.

• **Classification of Ranks**: There were approximately **33** to **66** grades of **Mansabdars**. The lowest rank was **10**, and the highest for commoners was generally **5,000**. Ranks above **5,000**, such as **7,000** or **10,000**, were typically reserved for **Princes** of the royal blood.

• **Payment Methods**: **Mansabdars** were classified into two types based on their payment: **Naqdi** (those paid in cash from the royal treasury) and **Jagirdars** (those paid through the assignment of land revenue from a specific territory).

• **Evolution under Later Emperors**:

• Emperor **Jahangir** introduced the **Du-aspa Sih-aspa** (two-horse, three-horse) system, which allowed him to increase the military strength of a **Mansabdar** without increasing his **Zat** rank or personal **salary**.

• Emperor **Shah Jahan** introduced the **Month-scale** or **Month-ratio** system to manage the discrepancy between the estimated revenue (**Jama**) and the actual revenue collected (**Hasil**) from the **Jagirs**.

**Important Points__**

• **Non-Hereditary Nature**: A **Mansab** was not hereditary. It was granted by the **Emperor** and could be revoked or changed at any time. Upon the death of a **Mansabdar**, his **Mansab** lapsed, and his property was often seized by the state under the **Law of Escheat** to settle any outstanding debts to the treasury.

• **Military Obligations**: Every **Mansabdar** had to bring his contingent for periodic inspection. To prevent fraud, **Akbar** enforced the **Dagh** (branding of horses) and **Chehra** (descriptive rolls of soldiers) systems, which were originally introduced by **Alauddin Khalji**.

• **Administrative Roles**: **Mansabdars** were not just military commanders; they also served as **Governors**, **Ministers**, and other high-ranking civil officials within the **Mughal** administration.
</ul

question: Which feature of Mughal architecture was inspired by Persian styles?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Large domes and iwans (vaulted halls)**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Mughal architecture** is a remarkably symmetrical and decorative amalgam of **Persian**, **Turki**, and **Indian** architectural styles that flourished in the **Indian subcontinent** from the **16th** to the **18th century**.

• The feature of **Large domes** and **iwans** (vaulted halls) was directly inspired by **Persian (Safavid)** and **Central Asian (Timurid)** traditions. An **Iwan** is a rectangular hall or space, usually vaulted, walled on three sides, with one end entirely open; this became a signature element of **Mughal** gateways and mosque facades. ***Hence, statement 2 is correct.***

• **Flat roofs and simple courtyards** are more characteristic of **indigenous Indian** styles or the earlier **Delhi Sultanate** period, rather than being a specific **Persian** innovation introduced by the **Mughals**. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***

• **Stepwells** (known as **Baolis**) and elaborate **pavilions** are traditional **Indian** architectural features found extensively in **Rajasthan** and **Gujarat** long before the **Mughal** era. While **Mughals** built them, they were not **Persian** inspirations. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***

• **Minimal ornamentation** is the opposite of **Mughal** aesthetics, which are world-renowned for **lavish decoration**, including **carvings**, **frescoes**, and **inlay work**. **Persian** influence actually brought more complex decorative patterns to **India**. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Humayun’s Tomb**: Built in **1570** in **Delhi**, it was the first major **Mughal** structure to showcase strong **Persian** influence, designed by the **Persian architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas**. It introduced the **double dome** and the **Charbagh** layout to **India**.

• **Charbagh Layout**: This is a **Persian-style** garden layout where a quadrilateral garden is divided by **walkways** or **flowing water** into four smaller parts. This symbolizes the **Islamic** concept of **Paradise**.

• **Pietra Dura**: During the reign of **Shah Jahan** (**1628–1658**), the **Persian** technique of **Pietra Dura** (inlaying semi-precious stones like **lapis lazuli**, **jade**, and **crystal** into **marble**) reached its zenith, most famously seen in the **Taj Mahal**.

• **Double Dome**: This **Persian** architectural technique involves an inner shell to provide a ceiling in proportion with the interior and an outer shell to give the building a **monumental height** and **grandeur** from the outside.

**Important Points__**

• **Evolution of Materials**: Early **Mughal** structures under **Emperor Akbar** primarily used **Red Sandstone** (e.g., **Fatehpur Sikri**, built in **1571**), while later structures under **Shah Jahan** shifted toward **White Marble** to reflect **purity** and **elegance**.

• **Bulbous Domes**: The **onion-shaped** or **bulbous dome**, a distinct **Persian** feature, became more pronounced in later **Mughal** architecture, such as the **Taj Mahal** (completed in **1653**) and the **Bibi Ka Maqbara** in **Aurangabad**.

• **Calligraphy**: **Persian** influence also brought the use of **Arabic** and **Persian calligraphy** as a form of architectural decoration, often featuring **Quranic verses** inscribed on the **iwans** and **arches**.

• **Symmetry**: A core principle of **Persian** design adopted by the **Mughals** was **absolute bilateral symmetry**, where every element on one side of an axis is mirrored on the other, creating a sense of **harmony** and **balance**.

• **The Battle of Khanwa was fought in 1527 between the Mughal Emperor Babur and the Rajput forces led by Rana Sanga of Mewar.**

• **The battle was triggered by Babur's desire to expand his empire **and control the fertile plains of North India.
 
• Rana Sanga,** as the leading Rajput ruler, opposed Babur's ambitions and formed a confederacy of Rajput states to resist Mughal expansion.**
 
• The **battle took place on March 17, 1527,** near the town of Khanwa in Rajasthan.
 
• Babur employed innovative military tactics, including the use of artillery and the "chakar-i-barbar" (the "whirlwind" formation), to defeat the Rajput forces.

• Medini Rai:

• He joined Rana Sanga's confederacy against Babur but was defeated and killed in the Battle of Khanwa

solution:
The correct answer is __**Philosopher’s stone**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **In Western alchemy, the philosopher's stone** is a mysterious substance believed to possess the **extraordinary ability to transform** base metals like iron into precious gold.
 
• Also referred to as **"the tincture" or "the powder,"** this elusive stone was thought to hold immense power beyond mere transmutation.
 
• Alchemists held the belief that the philosopher's stone could remedy ailments, bestow eternal youth, and even grant immortality. Contrary to its name, the philosopher's stone was not a physical rock but was believed to exist in various forms such as a magical wax, liquid, or powder.
 
• The philosopher's stone occupied a central place in the esoteric language of alchemy, embodying ideals of perfection, divine enlightenment, and celestial joy.
 
• The pursuit of uncovering the philosopher's stone was encapsulated in the concept known as the Magnum Opus, or "Great Work," representing the alchemist's quest for ultimate knowledge and transformation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Emerald** is a gemstone that belongs to the beryl mineral family and is distinguished by its vibrant green hue, which is attributed to the presence of trace amounts of chromium or, in some cases, vanadium.
 
• **Jade** is a broad term encompassing two distinct types of ornamental rocks: nephrite and jadeite. These stones are highly valued for their beauty and durability, and they are commonly utilized in jewelry, decorative items, and various other applications.

subject: GK
question: Which of the following pairs of rulers and their immediate successors is correctly matched?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Ibrahim Lodi - Babur**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• **Ibrahim Lodi** was the last **Sultan** of the **Delhi Sultanate** and the final ruler of the **Lodi Dynasty**. He was defeated and killed in the **First Battle of Panipat** on **April 21, 1526**, by **Babur**. Consequently, **Babur** became the immediate successor to the throne of **Delhi** and founded the **Mughal Empire**. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***

• **Alauddin Khalji** (ruled **1296–1316**) belonged to the **Khalji Dynasty**. Upon his death, he was succeeded by **Shihabuddin Omar** and later **Qutbuddin Mubarak Shah**. **Muhammad Bin Tughlaq** was a ruler of the **Tughlaq Dynasty** who reigned from **1325 to 1351**, making him a much later ruler rather than an immediate successor. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***

• **Muhammad Bin Tughlaq** (**1325–1351**) was part of the **Tughlaq Dynasty**. **Iltutmish** (ruled **1211–1236**) was the third ruler of the **Slave Dynasty** (Mamluk Dynasty), which existed nearly a century before the **Tughlaqs**. Therefore, **Iltutmish** was a predecessor to the **Tughlaq** era, not a successor. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***

• **Babur** (ruled **1526–1530**) was the founder of the **Mughal Empire**. He was succeeded by his eldest son, **Humayun**, in **1530**. **Sher Shah Suri** was an **Afghan** ruler who established the **Suri Empire** after defeating **Humayun** in **1540**, but he was not the immediate successor of **Babur**. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**

__

• The **Lodi Dynasty** (**1451–1526**) was the first **Afghan** dynasty to rule the **Delhi Sultanate**. It was founded by **Bahlul Lodi**, followed by **Sikandar Lodi**, and ended with **Ibrahim Lodi**. The dynasty was known for its decentralized administrative structure where the **Sultan** was considered **first among equals** by the **Afghan** nobles.

• **Babur**, originally named **Zahir-ud-din Muhammad**, came from **Fergana** (modern-day **Uzbekistan**). He was a descendant of **Timur** on his father's side and **Genghis Khan** on his mother's side. His victory at **Panipat** was largely due to his innovative use of **artillery** and **gunpowder**, which were relatively new to **Indian** warfare.

• The **First Battle of Panipat** (**1526**) marked a significant turning point in **Indian** history. **Babur's** army was significantly smaller than **Ibrahim Lodi's**, but his use of **Tulughma** (flanking tactics) and **Araba** (carts for artillery) secured his victory and the end of the **Delhi Sultanate**.

• **Sher Shah Suri** (ruled **1540–1545**) is known for his brilliant administrative and fiscal reforms. He introduced the **Rupiya** currency and rebuilt the **Grand Trunk Road**. His administration served as a model for later **Mughal** rulers, especially **Akbar**, in areas of land revenue and military organization.

**Important Points__**

• The **Delhi Sultanate** sequence of dynasties is: **Slave Dynasty** (**1206–1290**), **Khalji Dynasty** (**1290–1320**), **Tughlaq Dynasty** (**1320–1414**), **Sayyid Dynasty** (**1414–1451**), and **Lodi Dynasty** (**1451–1526**).

• **Iltutmish** is often regarded as the real consolidator of the **Slave Dynasty** and was the first to receive a **Manshur** (letter of investiture) from the **Caliph** of **Baghdad**, legitimizing his rule as the **Sultan**.

• **Alauddin Khalji** is famous for his **market reforms** and **price control system**, as well as his successful defense against multiple **Mongol** invasions. He was the first **Sultan** to venture into **South India** through his general **Malik Kafur**.

• **Muhammad Bin Tughlaq** is known for his ambitious but failed projects, such as the **transfer of capital** from **Delhi** to **Daulatabad** and the introduction of **token currency**, which led to economic instability during his reign.

question:
Consider the following statements regarding South Indian dynasties in the 12th and 13th centuries:
Statement I: The Kakatiyas, ruling from Manyakheta, were the primary successors to the Later Chalukyas in the western Deccan.
Statement II: The Hoysalas, based in Devagiri, were the sole dynasty responsible for the complete overthrow of the Later Chalukyas across all their territories.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Neither 1 nor statement 2**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Statement I** is incorrect because the **Kakatiyas** did not rule from **Manyakheta**; their capital was **Warangal** (also known as **Orugallu**). **Manyakheta** (modern-day **Malkhed**) was actually the capital of the **Rashtrakuta Dynasty**. Furthermore, the **Kakatiyas** were the primary successors to the **Later Chalukyas** in the **Eastern Deccan** (modern-day **Telangana** and **Andhra Pradesh**), whereas the **Yadavas of Devagiri** were the successors in the **Western Deccan**.

• **Statement II** is incorrect because the **Hoysalas** were based in **Dwarasamudra** (modern-day **Halebidu** in **Karnataka**), not **Devagiri**. **Devagiri** (modern-day **Daulatabad**) was the capital of the **Yadava Dynasty** (also known as the **Seuna Dynasty**).

• The downfall of the **Later Chalukyas** (also known as the **Chalukyas of Kalyani**) was not caused by a single dynasty. Instead, their empire was partitioned among three major powers during the late **12th century**: the **Yadavas of Devagiri**, the **Hoysalas of Dwarasamudra**, and the **Kakatiyas of Warangal**. **Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.**

• The **Later Chalukya** power declined significantly after the death of **Vikramaditya VI** in **1126 AD**. By the year **1189 AD**, the last ruler **Someshvara IV** lost control as the empire fragmented into these three successor states. **Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.**

**Additional Information__**

• **Kakatiya Dynasty (1163–1323 AD):** This dynasty emerged as a sovereign power under **Prataparudra I** (also known as **Kakatiya Rudradeva**). They are famous for their unique **Vesara** style of architecture, exemplified by the **Thousand Pillar Temple** in **Hanamkonda** and the **Ramappa Temple** (a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**). Notable rulers include **Rani Rudramadevi**, one of the few female monarchs in Indian history, and **Prataparudra II**, the last king who faced the invasions of the **Delhi Sultanate**.

• **Hoysala Dynasty (1026–1343 AD):** Originally feudatories of the **Western Chalukyas**, they became independent under **Vishnuvardhana** (reigned **1108–1152 AD**). Their capital **Dwarasamudra** became a center for art and culture. They are renowned for their intricate soapstone carvings and star-shaped temple plans, such as the **Chennakesava Temple** at **Belur** and the **Hoysaleswara Temple** at **Halebidu**.

• **Yadava Dynasty of Devagiri (1187–1317 AD):** Founded by **Bhillama V**, they ruled over the **Western Deccan** region comprising modern **Maharashtra** and parts of **North Karnataka**. They reached their peak under **Simhana II**. The **Yadavas** were the first major kingdom to face the southern expeditions of **Alauddin Khalji** and his general **Malik Kafur** in the early **14th century**.

• **Later Chalukyas (973–1189 AD):** Also known as the **Western Chalukyas**, they established their capital at **Kalyani** (modern **Basavakalyan**). They were constant rivals of the **Cholas** of **Tanjore**. Their reign saw the birth of **Kannada** literature and the **Virashaiva** movement led by **Basavanna** in the **12th century**.

question: The Bibi Ka Maqbara, the burial place of Aurangzeb’s wife, Rabia-ud-Durrani near Aurangabad city is an imitation of which of the following monuments?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Taj Mahal at Agra**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Bibi Ka Maqbara **__

 __
 
• Bibi Ka Maqbara in **Aurangabad** is a magnificent mausoleum.
 
• It exhibits exceptional architectural beauty. 
 
• It was constructed in** 1668-69 by Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb.**
 
• It was constructed as a memorial to his first wife **Rabia-Ul-Daurani aka Dilras Banu Begum.**
 
• It is a fine example of Mughal architecture.
 
• **Bibi Ka Maqbara** is located on a raised square platform that is 19 feet high. 
 
• Four minarets, each with a height of 72 feet and featuring 144 stairs that lead to the top, stand at the four corners of the platform.
 
• There is also a mosque to the west of the structure. 
 
• The portion up to the dado level and the dome are constructed in marble while the rest of the tomb features basaltic trap construction.
 
• Bibi Ka Maqbara is one of the finest structures and a top tourist attraction in Aurangabad. 
 
• **It is often referred to as the Dakkhani Taj or the Taj of Deccan as it was modeled on the iconic Taj Mahal.** 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Jama Masjid at Delhi** - The Masjid-i Jehan-Numa, commonly known as the Jama Masjid of Delhi, is one of the largest mosques in India. It was built by the Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan between 1650 and 1656.
 
• **Safdarjung's Tomb at New Delhi** - Safdarjung's Tomb is a sandstone and marble mausoleum in Delhi, India. It was built in 1754 in the late Mughal Empire style for Nawab Safdarjung. 
 
• **Humayun's Tomb at New Delhi** - Humayun's tomb is the tomb of the Mughal Emperor Humayun in Delhi, India. The tomb was commissioned by Humayun's chief consort, Empress Bega Begum, in 1558, and designed by Mirak Mirza Ghiyas and his son, Sayyid Muhammad, Persian architects chosen by her.
