subject: GK
question: The Kailasa Temple at Ellora was built by which ruler?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Krishna I**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Krishna I** (reigned **756–774 CE**) was the successor to **Dantidurga** and a prominent ruler of the **Rashtrakuta Dynasty**. He is the monarch credited with the construction of the magnificent **Kailasa Temple**.
 
• The **Kailasa Temple** is located at **Ellora** (Cave 16) in the **Sambhaji Nagar** (formerly Aurangabad) district of **Maharashtra**. It is one of the most remarkable **monolithic** structures in the world.
 
• The temple is carved out of a single, massive **basalt** cliff. Uniquely, the artisans employed a **top-down** carving method, starting from the summit of the mountain and working downwards to the base.
 
• It is dedicated to **Lord Shiva** and was designed to symbolize **Mount Kailash**, the celestial abode of the deity in the Himalayas.
 
• The construction was an immense engineering feat of the **8th century**, involving the excavation of approximately **200,000 to 400,000 tonnes** of rock over several decades.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Rashtrakuta Dynasty**: 
 
 
• Founded by **Dantidurga** in the **8th century**, this dynasty ruled large parts of the **Deccan** and southern India.
 
• Their capital was located at **Manyakheta**. They were renowned patrons of **art**, **architecture**, and literature, fostering a culture where **Hinduism**, **Buddhism**, and **Jainism** flourished.
 
 
 
• **Ellora Caves**: 
 
 
• A **UNESCO World Heritage Site** since **1983**, it comprises **34 caves** carved into the **Charanandri hills**.
 
• The site includes **12 Buddhist** caves, **17 Hindu** caves, and **5 Jain** caves, reflecting the **religious tolerance** of ancient Indian society.
 
 
 
• **Other Rulers Mentioned**:
 
 
• **Ashoka**: The third **Mauryan Emperor** (**268–232 BCE**) known for spreading **Buddhism** and his **Rock Edicts**. His reign occurred nearly a millennium before the construction of the Kailasa Temple.
 
• **Rajaraja Chola I**: A powerful ruler of the **Chola Empire** (**985–1014 CE**) who built the structural **Brihadeeswarar Temple** at **Thanjavur**, which is distinct from the rock-cut style of Ellora.
 
• **Chandragupta II**: A famous ruler of the **Gupta Dynasty** (c. **375–415 CE**) associated with the **Golden Age** of India. While art flourished under the Guptas, the monolithic Ellora temples belong to the later **Rashtrakuta** period.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Architectural Style**: The temple mainly follows the **Dravidian** architectural style, characterized by a **Vimana** (tower) and a flat-roofed **Mandapa** (pillared hall).
 
• **Sculptural Mastery**: The temple walls feature intricate relief panels, most notably the **Ravana Phadi**, which depicts the demon king **Ravana** attempting to lift **Mount Kailash**.
 
• **Dimensions**: The temple is roughly **32 meters** high, making it one of the largest single monolithic excavations in human history, surpassing even the **Parthenon** in scale.

solution:
The correct answer is __**Jama Masjid**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The Buland Darwaza **serves as the primary entrance to the **Jama Masjid located in Fatehpur Sikri**.
 
• It known as** "Door of Victory," **it was constructed by the **Mughal emperor Akbar in 1575** to commemorate his triumph over Gujarat.
 
• Renowned for its Mughal architecture, the Buland Darwaza stands as the world's tallest gateway, soaring at a height of 53.63 meters and spanning 35 meters in width, accessible via 42 steps.
 
• The Jama Masjid, a magnificent mosque, was completed in 1571.
 
• It features a central nave, along with two colonnaded halls and two square chambers crowned by domes.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **The Jama Masjid **is a 16th-century congregational mosque situated within the UNESCO World Heritage Site of Fatehpur Sikri, located in Uttar Pradesh, India.
 
• Constructed by the Mughal emperor Akbar, it held the distinction of being the largest mosque within the empire during its construction period.
 
• Drawing inspiration from earlier mosques built by various pre-Mughal sultanates, the Jama Masjid served as a significant influence on subsequent Mughal architectural styles.
 
• Within the mosque complex, notable monuments include the Buland Darwaza, which functions as the southern gateway to the mosque, and the Tomb of Salim Chishti.
 
• This tomb is dedicated to the revered saint Salim Chishti, in whose honor the mosque was originally erected.

• **Bahmani kingdom** was a Muslim state of the Deccan in southern India and was one of the great medieval Indian kingdoms.

• Rivalry with the Vijayanagar kingdom over the fertile region of Raichur doab started during his period and continued till the last of Bahaman rule.

question: Khush Mahal within the walls of Warangal Fort, was built in which of the following dynasties?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Tughlaq.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• During the **reign of Tughlak**, the** Khush Mahal **is claimed to have been built on the location of the **Kakatiya palace.**
 
• It was constructed in the** 14th century **as an **audience hall.**
 
• The fort has **four ornamental gates** known as **Kakatiya Kala Thoranam,** which were once the entrances to a now-destroyed huge **Shiva temple.**
 
• Following the bifurcation of Andhra Pradesh, the **Kakatiyan arch** was accepted and officially included in **Telangana's insignia.**
 
• On **September 10, 2010**, the Permanent Delegation of India to UNESCO submitted the fort to the "tentative list" of** UNESCO World Heritage Sites.**
 
• **Tughlaqs:**
 
 
• The Tughlaqs were a **Turkic-speaking Muslim family.**
 
• Between **AD 1330 and 1335**, when **Muhammad Bin Tughlaq** launched a military campaign, the dynasty achieved its pinnacle.
 
• The **founder **of the Tughlaq dynasty is **Ghiyas-ud-Din-Tughlaq.**
 
• **Nasir-ud-Din Mahmud Shah Tughluq** also known as Nasiruddin Mohammad Shah, was the** last sultan** of the Tughlaq dynasty to rule the **Islamic Delhi Sultanate.**
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Lodi dynasty__:**

 __
 
• The Lodi dynasty was an** Afghan dynasty** that ruled the **Delhi Sultanate** from **1451 to 1526.**
 
• It was the** fifth and final dynasty** of the Delhi Sultanate and was** founded** by** Bahlul Khan Lodi **when he replaced the Sayyid dynasty.
 
• In the** First Battle of Panipat **in **1526 CE,** **Babur defeated** Ibrahim Lodi, the final prince of the Lodi dynasty.
 
• The Lodi dynasty, as well as the Delhi Sultanate, came to an end in this battle.
 
 
 
• **Chola Dynasty__:**
 __
 
• The Chola Dynasty was a **Tamil thalassocratic empire** in southern India, and it was one of the **world's longest-ruling empires.**
 
• **Vijayalaya**, the first feudatory of the **Pallavas of Kanchi**, founded the Chola Empire.
 
• In the year **850 A.D.**, he conquered **Tanjore**. He built a temple dedicated to the goddess **Nishumbhasudini (Durga)** there.
 
• **Aditya I **was** victorious** over Vijayalaya.
 
• The conquest of the Chola empire by the **Pandyas in 1257** resulted in the** end **of the Chola empire in **1279.**
 
 
 
• **Khilji Dynasty**__**:**
 
 
• The Khalji or Khilji dynasty was a **Turco-Afghan dynasty** that ruled over the Delhi Sultanate for about** three decades, from 1290 to 1320.**
 
• This is the **second dynasty** to reign the Delhi Sultanate of India,** founded** by **Jalal ud din Firuz Khalji.**
 
• **Malik Kafur** was **assassinated** by **Mubarak Khan**, Shihab-ud-older din's brother, who eventually deposed Shihab-ud-din and became the king of the Khilji Dynasty. **In 1320**, Mubarak Khan's officer** Khusrav Khan** assassinated him and other Khilji family members, putting an **end** to the Khilji Dynasty.

question: Which of the following kings of Tuluva dynasty assumed the title of ‘Yavanarajya Sthapanacharya’?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Krishnadevaraya** was a prominent king of the Tuluva dynasty who ruled the Vijayanagara Empire from 1509 to 1529.
 
• He assumed the title of **'Yavanarajya Sthapanacharya'**, which signifies his efforts in establishing control over territories previously held by the Yavanas (foreigners).
 
• Krishnadevaraya is considered one of the greatest rulers in Indian history due to his military prowess, administrative acumen, and patronage of arts and literature.
 
• His reign is often regarded as the golden age of the Vijayanagara Empire, marked by extensive territorial expansion and cultural achievements.
 
• He was a patron of Telugu, Kannada, and Sanskrit literature and initiated several architectural projects, including the famous Vithala Temple in Hampi.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• Krishnadevaraya's reign is well-documented by several contemporary sources, including the writings of Portuguese travelers such as Domingo Paes and Fernao Nuniz.
 
• He was succeeded by his half-brother Achyuta Deva Raya after his death in 1529.
 
• Krishnadevaraya's military campaigns included successful expeditions against the Bahmani Sultanate, the Gajapatis of Odisha, and the Portuguese, solidifying his dominance in the Deccan region.

question: The Vijayanagara empire included people from different cultural regions. Which of the following regions was NOT a part of it?

__
 
• The Maratha region was not part of the Vijayanagara Empire.
 
• The empire mainly encompassed regions of **southern India, while the Maratha region is in western India** (modern-day Maharashtra).
 
• The Vijayanagara Empire primarily controlled regions to the south of the Maratha lands during its height.
 
• The Maratha region gained prominence later under the Maratha Empire, which** rose after the decline of the Vijayanagara Empire in the 17th century.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Tamil:**

 
 
• The Tamil region was a** significant part **of the Vijayanagara Empire.
 
• The empire** included Tamil-speaking areas**, particularly in present-day Tamil Nadu.
 
• Vijayanagara rulers had close ties with Tamil dynasties and controlled important Tamil centers like Madurai.
 
 
 
• **Karnataka:**
 
 
• Karnataka was the** core region** of the Vijayanagara Empire.
 
• The empire was founded in this region,** with Hampi (in present-day Karnataka) as its capital.**
 
• Many of the Vijayanagara rulers were of Kannada-speaking origin.
 
 
 
• **Telugu:**
 
 
• The Telugu region (modern-day Andhra Pradesh) was a **crucial part **of the Vijayanagara Empire.
 
• Telugu warriors and nobles played significant roles in the administration and military.
 
• The empire's founders also had **Telugu roots, and Telugu culture flourished** under their rule.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The Vijayanagara Empire was **founded in 1336 by the brothers Harihara I and Bukka Raya I.** 
 
• The empire was named after its capital city, Vijayanagara, which is now the ruined city of** Hampi in Karnataka**, India. 
 
• The empire was predominantly** Hindu but also accepted other faiths such as Jainism and Islam.** 
 
• The empire was known for its art and culture, including architecture, literature, and religious tolerance. 
 
• The empire reached its peak in the early 16th century under the rule of** Krishnadevaraya, who wrote the epic poem Amuktamalyada.** 
 
• The empire's power declined after the** Battle of Talikota in 1565** when the combined armies of the Deccan sultanates defeated the Vijayanagara army and destroyed the capital city. The empire fell in 1646. 
 
• The ruins of the Vijayanagara Empire are a **UNESCO World Heritage Site. **
 
• The largest festival in the Vijayanagara Empire was** Mahanavami, also known as Navaratri or Dussehra.**

• Organized into four administrative provinces, known as "Taraf," the kingdom comprised *Daultabad, Bidar, Berar, and Gulbarga, *each overseen by a tarafdar or subedar.
 
• The governance of the Bahmani kingdom followed a feudal system.
 
• Encompassing the entirety of the Deccan up to the Krishna river, the Bahmani sultanate reached its zenith of influence during the tenure of Mahmud Gawan as vizier from 1466 to 1481.

• Positioned 568 km north of Bangalore, the state capital, Kalaburagi was integrated into the newly formed Mysore State (now Karnataka) under the States Reorganisation Act in 1956. 
 
• Noteworthy architectural wonders from the Bahamani Kingdom era adorn Kalaburagi, including the Jama Masjid within Kalaburagi Fort. Moreover, Kalaburagi hosts the circuit bench of the High Court of Karnataka. 
 
• In 2014, UNESCO placed several structures in the city on its "tentative list" for potential recognition as a World Heritage Site, along with others in the vicinity, under the collective name Monuments and Forts of the Deccan Sultanate.

• Under **Lord Hastings** a new policy of** “paramountcy” **was initiated. In this policy the Company claimed that its authority was paramount or supreme, hence its power was greater than that of Indian states.

• This policy asserted the supremacy of the** British East India **Company's authority over Indian states, justifying their annexation or the threat thereof.
 
• It granted the Governor-General the power to intervene in the internal affairs of princely states and even supersede their authority when deemed necessary.
 
• This policy remained in effect for 45 years, from 1813 to 1858. During this period, the British solidified their dominance and established themselves as the ultimate authority over Indian territories.
 
• However, they did not formally integrate Princely India into their claim over the Indian subcontinent. Following the uprising of 1857, known as the Indian Rebellion or the First War of Independence, the British initiated the sub-ordinate unity program.
 
• This program aimed to strengthen British control and governance, ultimately lasting until India gained independence in 1947.

__
 
• **Delhi, the capital of India** has a strong historical background.
 
• It was **ruled **by some of the** most powerful emperors** in Indian history.
 
• The town was known as** Indraprastha, where Pandavas** used to live.
 
• In due course, **eight more cities** came alive adjacent to Indraprastha:
 
 
• Lal Kot, Siri, Dinpanah, Quila Rai Pithora, Ferozabad, Jahanpanah, Tughlakabad and Shahjahanabad.
 
 
 
• Delhi has been a witness to political turmoil for over five centuries.
 
• It was **ruled by the Mughals in succession to Khiljis and Tughlaqs**.

• In **1911**, the **British shifted their capital from Calcutta to Delhi**.
 
• It again became the center of all the governing activities.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **In 1801, the Nawab of Awadh, Saadat Ali Khan II,** entered into the **Subsidiary Alliance** with the British.
 
• This alliance was devised as a political and military strategy by** Lord Wellesley, **the **Governor-General of British India, in 1798**.
 
• The terms of the Subsidiary Alliance included several stipulations:
 
 
• The Nawab was required to cede nearly half of his kingdom to the British, encompassing territories such as Rohilkhand and the region between the Ganga and the Jamuna rivers.
 
• The Nawab had to disband his own troops and rely instead on a British-managed army.
 
• The Nawab was obligated to pay substantial subsidies, often amounting to several lakhs of rupees.
 
• Article IV of the treaty affirmed that the forces provided by the British East India Company were deemed adequate to safeguard the ruler of Awadh.
 
• These terms effectively diminished the autonomy of the Nawab and established British dominance in Awadh.

• The** reason** behind the battle was due to** Mir Qasim's discontent over the British East India Company's continuous expansion in Bengal and other parts, as well as its misuse of Farmans and Dastaks, legal instruments of the Nawab**.
 
• The British forces were under the command of the** British East India Company** led by** Hector Munro**.
 
• The battle was between the British troops against the combined armies o**f Mir Qasim, Nawab of Bengal **till 1764; **the Nawab of Awadh**, **Shuja-ud-Daula**; and the **Mughal Emperor, Shah Alam II**.
 
• The battle was fought at Buxar, a **"strong fortified town"** located within the territory of** Bihar**.
 
• The war was brought to an end by the** Treaty of Allahabad in 1765**.
 
• After the defeat,** Mir Qasim also fled with his 3 million rupees worth of gemstones and later died in poverty in 1777**.
 
• **Shah Alam II surrendered **himself to the British.
 
• **Shah Shuja fled west hotly pursued by the victors**. He eventually **surrendered by 1765**.
 
• Then the** British** had become the **virtual rulers of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa**.

• The ruler of any princely state which governed directly or indirectly by the British does not have a legal male heir then his state will be annexed by the British.

• It is considered a significant step towards the centralization of the administration in India.

question: When was the Majority Act, which defines the age of the majority of Indian citizens, passed?
solution:
The correct answer is __**1875.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

 
• The **Majority Act of 1875 **is divided into two sections:
 
• **Section 3(1)**
 
 
• Every person domiciled in India shall attain the age of majority on completion of 18 years and not before. 
 
• Unless a particular personal law specifies otherwise, every person domiciled in India is deemed to have attained majority upon completion of 18 years of age. 
 
 
 
• **Section 3(2)**
 
 
• In computing the age of any person, the day on which he was born is to be included as a whole day and he shall be deemed to have attained majority at the beginning of the eighteenth anniversary of that day. 
 
• But if the child born is appointed a guardian or he/she is under the court of wards then he/she attains majority after his completion of 21 years of age.

question: Which act introduced separate electorates for Hindus and Muslims in British India?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Morley-Minto Reforms 1909**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Morley-Minto Reforms**, officially known as the **Indian Councils Act 1909**, introduced the system of **separate electorates** for **Muslims** in **British India**. This meant that **Muslim** representatives were to be elected exclusively by **Muslim voters**.

• The act was named after **Lord Morley**, the then **Secretary of State for India**, and **Lord Minto**, the then **Viceroy of India**. Due to the introduction of this communal representation, **Lord Minto** is often referred to as the **'Father of Communal Electorate'**.

• The **Indian Councils Act 1892** is incorrect because it primarily focused on increasing the number of members in the **Legislative Councils** and introduced a limited and indirect use of **elections**, but it did not establish **separate electorates** based on religion.

• The **Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms 1919** (or the **Government of India Act 1919**) is incorrect as the starting point because it **extended** the principle of **separate electorates** to other communities like **Sikhs**, **Indian Christians**, **Anglo-Indians**, and **Europeans**, rather than introducing it.

• The **Government of India Act 1935** is incorrect because it was a much later piece of legislation that introduced **Provincial Autonomy** and further extended **separate electorates** to **depressed classes (scheduled castes)**, **women**, and **labor**.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Simla Deputation (1906)**: A group of **Muslim** leaders led by the **Aga Khan** met **Lord Minto** in **October 1906** to demand **separate electorates** and **proportional representation** for **Muslims**, which heavily influenced the **1909 reforms**.

• **Expansion of Councils**: The **1909 Act** significantly increased the size of the **Legislative Councils**. The number of members in the **Central Legislative Council** was raised from **16 to 60**.

• **Indian Participation**: For the first time, the act provided for the association of **Indians** with the **Executive Councils** of the **Viceroy** and **Governors**. **Satyendra Prasad Sinha** became the first **Indian** to join the **Viceroy’s Executive Council** as a **Law Member**.

• **Powers of Legislators**: The act empowered members of the **Legislative Councils** to ask **supplementary questions** and move **resolutions** on the **budget**, although they were not allowed to vote on the budget as a whole.

**Important Points__**

• The **1919 Act** introduced **Dyarchy** in the provinces, which divided provincial subjects into two parts: **'Transferred'** and **'Reserved'**. This was a major step toward **responsible government** in **India**.

• The **1935 Act** proposed the establishment of an **All-India Federation** consisting of **Provinces** and **Princely States**. It also abolished **Dyarchy** in the provinces and introduced **Provincial Autonomy**.

• The **Indian Councils Act 1892** allowed the councils to discuss the **annual financial statement** (budget) and address questions to the **Executive**, which was a significant advancement over the **1861 Act**.

• The introduction of **separate electorates** in **1909** is widely viewed by historians as a part of the British **'Divide and Rule'** policy, which eventually contributed to the **partition of India** in **1947**.

question: The Ilbert Bill controversy of 1883 was related to which issue?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Rights of Indian judges**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Ilbert Bill** was a legislative measure introduced in **1883** during the viceroyalty of **Lord Ripon**. It was drafted by **Sir Courtenay Peregrine Ilbert**, who was the **Legal Member** of the **Viceroy's Executive Council**.

• The primary objective of the bill was to address the issue of **judicial disqualification** based on race. Before this bill, according to the **Criminal Procedure Code of 1873**, **Indian judges** and **magistrates** in the interior (mofussil) were not allowed to try **European British subjects** in criminal cases, even if the Indian judge was senior in rank.

• The bill proposed to grant **Indian District Magistrates** and **Sessions Judges** the same jurisdiction and **Rights of Indian judges** as their European counterparts to try Europeans. *Hence, statement 1 is correct.*

• The bill did not deal with the **Introduction of income tax**. Income tax in **India** was first introduced in **1860** by **James Wilson** to overcome the financial difficulties caused by the **Revolt of 1857**. *Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.*

• The **Expansion of railways** was a process that began much earlier, with the first train running between **Bombay** and **Thane** in **1853** under **Lord Dalhousie**. The **Ilbert Bill** had no relation to railway infrastructure. *Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.*

• The **Indianisation of the army** was a political demand that gained significant momentum during the **20th century**, particularly after **World War I**, and was not the subject of the **1883** controversy. *Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.*

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Lord Ripon**, who served as **Viceroy** from **1880** to **1884**, is regarded as one of the most liberal administrators in **British India**. He is known for the **Repeal of the Vernacular Press Act (1882)** and the **Resolution on Local Self-Government (1882)**.

• The **European community** in **India**, especially the **indigo and tea planters** in **Bengal**, reacted with extreme hostility to the bill. They viewed it as an insult to their racial superiority and formed the **European and Anglo-Indian Defence Association** to protest against it.

• This organized resistance by the British settlers is often referred to as the **White Mutiny**. They raised a fund of over **1.5 lakh rupees** and lobbied the government in **London** to withdraw the bill.

• Due to the intense pressure, a **compromise** was reached in **January 1884**. The amended bill allowed **Indian judges** to try Europeans, but the accused were given the right to demand a **jury**, of which at least **50%** of the members had to be **Europeans or Americans**.

• The **Ilbert Bill controversy** acted as a major catalyst for **Indian Nationalism**. It demonstrated to the **Indian intelligentsia** that they would never receive equal treatment under **British rule** without a unified political struggle.

**Important Points__**

• The controversy highlighted the **institutionalized racism** inherent in the **British colonial administration**. Even liberal reforms were thwarted by the collective pressure of the ruling race.

• **Surendranath Banerjee** and the **Indian National Association** (founded in **1876**) played a pivotal role in organizing counter-protests and support for the bill, which helped in the **political awakening** of the Indian middle class.

• The lessons learned from the **Ilbert Bill** agitation directly contributed to the formation of the **Indian National Congress** in **December 1885** at **Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College** in **Bombay**.

• The **compromise of 1884** was seen as a defeat for **Lord Ripon**, who eventually resigned from his post and returned to **England**, though he remained a hero to the **Indian people** for his efforts toward equality.
</ul

subject: GK
question: The Partition of Bengal in 1905 was carried out under which Viceroy?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Lord Curzon**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Partition of Bengal** was carried out in **1905** by **Lord Curzon**, who served as the **Viceroy of India** from **1899 to 1905**. This decision is considered one of the most controversial acts of his tenure. ***Hence, the statement regarding Lord Curzon is correct.***

• The partition was officially announced on **July 19, 1905**, and it was formally implemented on **October 16, 1905**. The British government claimed that the **Bengal Presidency**, which included **Bengal, Bihar, and Odisha**, was too large (with a population of nearly **80 million**) to be administered efficiently.

• The real political motive behind the partition was to weaken the **Indian National Movement**, which was centered in **Bengal**. By dividing the province, the British aimed to create a communal rift between the **Hindu-majority West Bengal** and the **Muslim-majority East Bengal and Assam**.

• **Lord Ripon (1880-1884)** was known for the **Ilbert Bill** and the **repeal of the Vernacular Press Act**. He is often called the **Father of Local Self-Government** in India. He was not associated with the 1905 partition. ***Hence, the option Lord Ripon is incorrect.***

• **Lord Lytton (1876-1880)** is remembered for the **Vernacular Press Act (1878)**, the **Arms Act (1878)**, and the **Second Anglo-Afghan War**. His term ended long before the partition occurred. ***Hence, the option Lord Lytton is incorrect.***

• **Lord Dalhousie (1848-1856)** is famous for the **Doctrine of Lapse**, the introduction of the **Railways (1853)**, and the **Post and Telegraph** system. He left India nearly half a century before the partition. ***Hence, the option Lord Dalhousie is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Swadeshi Movement:** The partition triggered the **Swadeshi Movement**, which focused on the **boycott of British goods** and the promotion of **Indian-made products**. Leaders like **Surendranath Banerjee**, **Bipin Chandra Pal**, and **Lala Lajpat Rai** played a pivotal role in this mass agitation.

• **Annulment of Partition:** Due to relentless protests and the rise of revolutionary activities, the **Partition of Bengal** was finally **annulled in 1911** by **Lord Hardinge II** during the **Delhi Durbar**.

• **Capital Shift:** In the same year (**1911**), the British government decided to shift the **capital of India** from **Calcutta** to **Delhi** to ensure better administrative control and to appease the sentiments of the people.

• **Cultural Impact:** **Rabindranath Tagore** composed the song **'Amar Sonar Bangla'** (now the national anthem of Bangladesh) as a mark of protest. He also encouraged people to tie **Rakhi** on each other's wrists as a symbol of **Hindu-Muslim unity** on the day the partition came into effect.

• **Formation of Muslim League:** One of the long-term consequences of the communal divide fostered by the partition was the formation of the **All India Muslim League** in **1906** at **Dacca** (now Dhaka) under the leadership of **Nawab Salimullah**.

**Important Points__**

• **Administrative Reforms of Curzon:** Apart from the partition, **Lord Curzon** is known for the **Ancient Monuments Preservation Act (1904)**, the establishment of the **Archaeological Survey of India (ASI)**, and the **Indian Universities Act (1904)**.

• **Surat Split (1907):** The difference in opinion regarding the methods of the **Anti-Partition Movement** (Moderates vs. Extremists) eventually led to the **Surat Split** of the **Indian National Congress** in **1907**.

• **Geographical Division:** The **Eastern Province** included **Assam** and the districts of **Dacca, Rajshahi, and Chittagong**, with its capital at **Dacca**. The **Western Province** included **Bihar and Orissa**, with its capital at **Calcutta**.
</ul

question: The Government of India Act 1935 proposed which major reform?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Establishment of federal government**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Government of India Act 1935** was a significant milestone in the constitutional history of India, proposing the establishment of an **All-India Federation**. This federation was intended to consist of **British Indian provinces** and **Princely States** as constituent units. Hence, the statement regarding the establishment of a federal government is correct.
 
• The Act introduced a clear division of powers between the **Centre** and the **Provinces** by categorizing subjects into three lists: the **Federal List** (59 items), the **Provincial List** (54 items), and the **Concurrent List** (36 items). **Residuary powers** were vested in the **Viceroy**.
 
• It abolished the system of **Dyarchy** in the provinces and introduced **Provincial Autonomy**, allowing provinces to act as autonomous units of administration. However, it simultaneously introduced **Dyarchy at the Centre** for federal subjects.
 
• The **Abolition of the Zamindari system** was not a part of this Act; it was a post-independence reform initiated through various state laws and the **1st Amendment** to the Constitution in **1951**. Hence, this statement is incorrect.
 
• The **Introduction of separate electorates** originally dates back to the **Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909**. While the 1935 Act extended this principle to **Scheduled Castes**, **women**, and **labor**, it was not the primary structural reform proposed. Hence, this statement is incorrect.
 
• The Act did not grant **Full independence** to India. It provided for limited self-governance while keeping the ultimate authority with the **British Parliament** and the **Viceroy**. Hence, this statement is incorrect.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• The **Government of India Act 1935** was the longest Act passed by the **British Parliament** at that time, containing **321 sections** and **10 schedules**.
 
• It led to the establishment of the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** in **1935** to regulate the currency and credit system of the country, following the recommendations of the **Hilton Young Commission**.
 
• The Act provided for the creation of a **Federal Court**, which was inaugurated in **1937** in **Delhi**. This court served as the precursor to the modern **Supreme Court of India**.
 
• Under this Act, **Burma** (now **Myanmar**) was officially separated from **British India** in **1937**, and two new provinces, **Sindh** and **Orissa**, were created.
 
• The **franchise** (right to vote) was extended, granting approximately **10%** of the total population the right to vote, which was a significant increase from previous reforms.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The proposed **All-India Federation** never actually came into existence because the **Princely States** refused to join it, fearing a loss of their internal sovereignty.
 
• The **Government of India Act 1935** served as the primary blueprint for the **Constitution of India** adopted in **1950**. Many features, such as the **federal scheme**, **office of the Governor**, **judiciary**, and **emergency powers**, were borrowed from this Act.
 
• The Act abolished the **Council of India**, which had been established by the **Act of 1858** to assist the **Secretary of State for India**.
 
• It also provided for the establishment of not only a **Federal Public Service Commission** but also **Provincial Public Service Commissions** and **Joint Public Service Commissions** for two or more provinces.

question: Who introduced the Ryotwari System in India?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Thomas Munro**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The **Ryotwari System** was a land revenue system in **British India**, introduced to establish a direct relationship between the government and the cultivators. It was primarily introduced by **Sir Thomas Munro** and **Captain Alexander Read** at the end of the **18th century**.

• **Thomas Munro**, who served as the **Governor of Madras** from **1820 to 1827**, is credited with the formal implementation of this system across the **Madras Presidency** in **1820**. Hence, the correct answer is **Thomas Munro**.

• The system was first trialed by **Captain Alexander Read** in the **Baramahal** region (modern-day **Tamil Nadu**) in **1792** after the **Third Anglo-Mysore War**.

• Under the **Ryotwari** settlement, the **Ryots** (peasants) were recognized as the individual owners of the land. They had the right to sell, mortgage, or transfer the land as long as they paid the fixed revenue to the **East India Company**.

• Unlike the **Zamindari System**, there were no middlemen or intermediaries involved. The revenue was collected directly by **British** officials, and the rates were revised periodically, usually every **20 to 30 years**, based on soil fertility and crop type.

**Additional Information__**

__

• **Lord Cornwallis**: He is famous for introducing the **Permanent Settlement** (also known as the **Zamindari System**) in **Bengal**, **Bihar**, and **Odisha** in **1793**. In this system, **Zamindars** were made hereditary owners of the land, and the revenue amount was fixed permanently.

• **Warren Hastings**: He was the first **Governor-General of Bengal** (**1773–1785**). He introduced the **Ijaradari System** in **1772**, which involved auctioning the right to collect land revenue to the highest bidder for a period of **five years**.

• **Robert Clive**: He served as the **Governor of Bengal** twice and established the **Dual Government** system in **1765** after the **Battle of Buxar**. Under this, the **Nawab** held the **Nizamat** (administrative) powers, while the **British** held the **Diwani** (revenue collection) rights.

• **Mahalwari System**: This was another major land revenue system introduced by **Holt Mackenzie** in **1822**. It was implemented in the **North-Western Provinces**, **Punjab**, and parts of **Central India**, where the unit of revenue assessment was the village or **Mahal**.

**Important Points__**

• **Geographical Coverage**: The **Ryotwari System** covered approximately **51%** of the territory under **British** rule, including the **Madras Presidency**, **Bombay Presidency**, **Assam**, and **Coorg**.

• **Revenue Rates**: The revenue demand was exceptionally high, often reaching **50%** for dry lands and **60%** for irrigated lands. This high demand often led to the exploitation of peasants by **moneylenders** when they could not meet the **British** demands.

• **Economic Impact**: While the system aimed to protect the **Ryots** from **Zamindars**, the rigid collection methods and high taxes resulted in large-scale rural indebtedness and land alienation, as **British** officials were often more oppressive than the former intermediaries.

• **Legal Status**: The **Ryot** was considered the proprietor of the land, but this ownership was conditional. Failure to pay the tax resulted in immediate eviction by the **Government**.

question: The Pravasi Bharatiya Divas marks which Indian leader's return from South Africa?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Mahatma Gandhi**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Pravasi Bharatiya Divas (PBD)** is celebrated in India on **9th January** to mark the contribution of the overseas Indian community to the development of India.

• The date **9th January** was chosen because it was on this day in **1915** that **Mahatma Gandhi**, the greatest **Pravasi**, returned to **India** from **South Africa**. ***Hence, the correct answer is Mahatma Gandhi.***

• The event was first celebrated in **2003**. It was an annual event until **2015**, after which the government decided to celebrate it **biennially** (once every two years).

• The concept of PBD was based on the recommendations of the **High Level Committee (HLC)** on the Indian Diaspora set up by the Government of India under the chairmanship of **Dr. L. M. Singhvi**.

• The other leaders mentioned in the options, such as **Lala Lajpat Rai**, **Sarojini Naidu**, and **Bal Gangadhar Tilak**, were prominent figures in the Indian freedom struggle, but their returns or specific anniversaries are not the basis for this commemorative day. ***Hence, options 1, 2, and 3 are incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Mahatma Gandhi in South Africa:** Gandhi spent approximately **21 years** in **South Africa** (from **1893** to **1914**). It was during this period that he developed his philosophy of **Satyagraha** (non-violent resistance) and fought against racial discrimination. He arrived at **Apollo Bunder** in **Mumbai** on **January 9, 1915**.

• **17th Pravasi Bharatiya Divas:** The **17th PBD Convention** was held from **8th to 10th January 2023** in **Indore, Madhya Pradesh**. The theme for the 2023 convention was **'Diaspora: Reliable partners for India’s progress in Amrit Kaal'**.

• **Pravasi Bharatiya Samman Award (PBSA):** This is the **highest honour** conferred by the **President of India** on **Non-Resident Indians (NRIs)**, **Persons of Indian Origin (PIOs)**, or organizations established by them, to recognize their outstanding achievements and contributions.

• **Nodal Ministry:** The **Ministry of External Affairs (MEA)** of the **Government of India** is the primary body responsible for organizing the PBD conventions and managing the engagement with the Indian diaspora.

• **Regional PBDs:** In addition to the main convention, **Regional Pravasi Bharatiya Divas** events are organized outside India to reach out to those diaspora members who cannot attend the main event in India.

**Important Points__**

• **Lala Lajpat Rai:** Often called **Punjab Kesari**, he was a leader of the **Lal-Bal-Pal** trio and played a major role in the **Swadeshi Movement**. He passed away in **1928** after being injured during a protest against the **Simon Commission**.

• **Sarojini Naidu:** Known as the **Nightingale of India**, she was the first Indian woman to serve as the **President of the Indian National Congress** (1925) and the first woman **Governor** of an Indian state (**United Provinces**). Her birthday, **February 13**, is celebrated as **National Women's Day** in India.

• **Bal Gangadhar Tilak:** A prominent nationalist and teacher, he was one of the first leaders of the **Indian Independence Movement**. He is famous for his quote, **'Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it!'**. He founded the **Home Rule League** in **1916**.

• **Significance of PBD:** The day provides a platform for the **overseas Indian community** to engage with the government and people of their ancestral land, fostering **networking** and **investment** opportunities while celebrating their cultural roots.

• Additionally, he served as the Law and Justice Minister in the inaugural cabinet of Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru. A champion of social justice, Ambedkar inspired the Dalit Buddhist movement after renouncing Hinduism, advocating for the rights and dignity of marginalized communities.
 
• In recognition of his immense contributions to Indian society, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was posthumously conferred with the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian award, in 1990.
 
• His legacy continues to resonate deeply in India's ongoing pursuit of equality and social reform.

subject: GK
question: Why did Mahatma Gandhi call for a campaign against the Rowlatt Act?

options.text: During the non-cooperation movement, thousands of Indians were kept in jail
British censorship of press and permitted detention without trial
Hundreds of people were killed in the Jallianwala Bagh massacre
Sir Sidney Rowlatt was a Britisher

solution:
The correct answer is __**British censorship of press and permitted detention without trial**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Rowlatt Act**, officially known as the **Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act of 1919**, was a legislative act passed by the **Imperial Legislative Council** in **Delhi** on **18th March 1919**.
 
• **Mahatma Gandhi** called for a nationwide campaign against this act because it authorized the **British Government** to imprison people suspected of terrorism for up to **two years** without any trial. This violated the basic principle of **civil liberty** and judicial fairness. ***Hence, the statement regarding detention without trial is correct.***
 
• The act also provided for the **censorship of the press**, allowing the colonial administration to control and suppress the flow of information and nationalist propaganda. ***Hence, the statement regarding censorship of the press is correct.***
 
• The **Non-cooperation movement** (1920-22) happened after the Rowlatt Satyagraha; therefore, the jailing of Indians during that movement was not the reason for Gandhi's initial call against the Rowlatt Act. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• While the **Jallianwala Bagh massacre** (13th April 1919) was a direct consequence of the protests against the Rowlatt Act and the arrest of leaders like **Dr. Saifuddin Kitchlew** and **Dr. Satyapal**, it was not the reason why Gandhi initially called for the campaign. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***
 
• Although **Sir Sidney Rowlatt** was indeed a **British judge** who headed the committee, his nationality was not the primary reason for the protest; rather, it was the draconian nature of the laws he recommended. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **The Rowlatt Committee:** The act was based on the report of the **Sedition Committee** of **1918**, chaired by **Sir Sidney Rowlatt**. The committee was tasked with investigating the **revolutionary conspiracies** of the Indian nationalist movement and suggesting measures to curb them.
 
• **The Black Act:** Gandhi and other Indian leaders referred to the Rowlatt Act as the **Black Act**. The popular slogan associated with the protest was **No Dalil, No Vakil, No Appeal**, meaning there was no right to argument, no right to a lawyer, and no right to appeal against the detention.
 
• **Rowlatt Satyagraha:** Gandhi organized the **Satyagraha Sabha** in **Bombay** to direct the movement. He called for a nationwide **hartal** (strike) on **6th April 1919**, which was observed as a day of **humiliation and prayer** and a protest against the unjust law.
 
• **Resignations:** In protest against the passing of the act, prominent Indian members of the **Imperial Legislative Council**, including **Madan Mohan Malaviya**, **Mazhar-ul-Haq**, and **Mohammed Ali Jinnah**, resigned from their seats.
 
• **Impact on National Movement:** The Rowlatt Satyagraha was the first **all-India struggle** against the British government, although it was largely restricted to cities. It marked the transition of the Indian national movement from an elite-driven struggle to a **mass-based movement** under the leadership of **Mahatma Gandhi**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Punjab Unrest:** The protests were particularly intense in **Punjab**, especially in **Amritsar** and **Lahore**. The government responded with **martial law**, which eventually culminated in the **Jallianwala Bagh Massacre** on **13th April 1919**, where **General Dyer** ordered troops to fire on a peaceful gathering.
 
• **Withdrawal of Satyagraha:** Seeing the violence that erupted following the massacre and the government's brutal repression, **Mahatma Gandhi** withdrew the **Rowlatt Satyagraha** on **18th April 1919**, calling it a **Himalayan Blunder** because the people were not yet fully trained in the methods of **non-violence**.
 
• **Legislative Context:** The act was passed despite the **unanimous opposition** of every single Indian member of the council, highlighting the **autocratic nature** of British rule in India during that period.

question: Who wrote the book "Discovery of India"?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Jawaharlal Nehru**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Jawaharlal Nehru**, the first **Prime Minister of India**, authored the classic book **"The Discovery of India"**.
 
• The book was written during his **imprisonment** between **1942 and 1946** at the **Ahmednagar Fort** in the state of **Maharashtra**.
 
• Nehru was incarcerated by the **British colonial authorities** for his participation in the **Quit India Movement**, which was launched in **August 1942**.
 
• The book provides a comprehensive analysis of **Indian history**, **philosophy**, and **culture**, starting from the **Indus Valley Civilization** and extending to the **British Raj**.
 
• Through this work, Nehru explored the concept of **"Unity in Diversity"**, a phrase he coined to describe the synthesis of various cultures and religions within the **Indian subcontinent**.
 
• The book was published in **1946** and is widely regarded as one of the most definitive works on the cultural and political identity of **India**.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Jawaharlal Nehru__.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Mahatma Gandhi**:
 
 
• Known as the **Father of the Nation**, Gandhi wrote his autobiography titled **"The Story of My Experiments with Truth"**.
 
• He also authored **"Hind Swaraj"** in **1909**, which discusses his views on **Swaraj** (self-rule) and **modern civilization**.
 
• Gandhi led major movements like the **Non-Cooperation Movement (1920)** and the **Dandi March (1930)** based on the principles of **Ahimsa** (non-violence) and **Satyagraha**.
 
 
 
• **B.R. Ambedkar**:
 
 
• Commonly known as the **Father of the Indian Constitution**, he was the **Chairman of the Drafting Committee**.
 
• His significant literary contributions include **"The Annihilation of Caste" (1936)** and **"Who Were the Shudras?" (1946)**.
 
• He served as the first **Law and Justice Minister** of independent **India** and was a staunch advocate for the rights of **Dalits** and the **oppressed classes**.
 
 
 
• **Subhash Chandra Bose**:
 
 
• Popularly known as **Netaji**, he was a radical nationalist whose defiance of **British rule** made him a hero in **India**.
 
• He wrote the book **"The Indian Struggle"**, which covers the **Indian independence movement** from **1920 to 1942**.
 
• Bose is famous for his leadership of the **Indian National Army (INA)** or **Azad Hind Fauj** and his slogan **"Jai Hind"**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Jawaharlal Nehru's Literary Legacy**:
 
 
• Apart from **"The Discovery of India"**, Nehru wrote **"Glimpses of World History"** (a collection of letters to his daughter, **Indira Gandhi**) and his autobiography titled **"Toward Freedom"**.
 
• He served as **Prime Minister** for **17 years**, from **1947 to 1964**, shaping the **modern Indian state** through **Five-Year Plans** and a **non-aligned foreign policy**.
 
 
 
• **Adaptations**:
 
 
• The book was adapted into a famous **53-episode** television series titled **"Bharat Ek Khoj"**, directed by **Shyam Benegal** and aired on **Doordarshan** in **1988**.

question: The result of which of the following movements/satyagrahas was the abolishment of the Tinkathia System under which the farmers were asked to cultivate indigo in 3/20th of their holdings?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Champaran Satyagraha**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Champaran Satyagraha** was a significant movement led by Mahatma Gandhi in 1917.
 
• The main objective of this movement was to address the grievances of the farmers in Champaran, Bihar, who were forced to grow indigo on a portion of their land under the **Tinkathia System**.
 
• The farmers were required to cultivate indigo in 3/20th (approximately 15%) of their holdings, which was highly exploitative and detrimental to their economic interests.
 
• As a result of the Champaran Satyagraha, the British authorities were compelled to abolish the Tinkathia System, providing relief to the farmers.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The **Champaran Satyagraha** marked the first active involvement of Mahatma Gandhi in the Indian freedom struggle and laid the foundation for future non-violent movements.
 
• Gandhi's approach of non-violent resistance and civil disobedience became a cornerstone of the Indian independence movement.
 
• This movement also highlighted the plight of the Indian farmers under British rule and brought national attention to their struggles.

options.text: Signing of the resolution for Poorna Swaraj in Lahore

solution:
The correct answer is __**Signing of the resolution for Poorna Swaraj in Lahore**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **non-cooperation movement** was launched by Mahatma Gandhi in 1920 to resist British rule in India through non-violent means.
 
• The movement included the **boycott of foreign goods**, which aimed at promoting Indian-made products and crippling British economic interests in India.
 
• The **distribution of spinning wheels** was encouraged to promote self-reliance and the use of khadi (hand-spun cloth).
 
• **Picketing at liquor shops** was part of the movement to oppose British-imposed taxes on liquor and to promote temperance.
 
• **Signing of the resolution for Poorna Swaraj in Lahore** is not related to the non-cooperation movement. It was part of a different phase in India's struggle for independence, specifically the Lahore Session of the Indian National Congress in 1929 where the demand for complete independence was formalized.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The non-cooperation movement was a significant phase in the Indian independence struggle, involving millions of Indians who withdrew their cooperation from the British government.
 
• It was characterized by the use of non-violent methods such as non-payment of taxes, surrender of titles, and boycott of British educational institutions and law courts.
 
• The movement was eventually called off by Gandhi in 1922 following the Chauri Chaura incident, where a violent clash led to the death of police officers.
 
• The **Lahore Session** in 1929 was a turning point as it marked the formal adoption of the goal of Poorna Swaraj or complete independence from British rule.

• In December 1929, Jawaharlal Nehru, as the president of the Indian National Congress, formally demanded **complete freedom** from the British Government.
 
• This demand marked a significant shift from the previous demand for dominion status to the more radical goal of complete independence.

• This session is also notable for the declaration of Purna Swaraj (complete independence) as the ultimate goal of the Indian freedom struggle.

• Jawaharlal Nehru's leadership during this period played a crucial role in uniting various factions within the Congress and presenting a united front against the British.
 
• The Lahore session also saw the adoption of the tricolor as the national flag of India.
 
• This period marked the beginning of a series of civil disobedience movements and protests that eventually led to India gaining independence in 1947.
 
• Jawaharlal Nehru later became the first Prime Minister of independent India, serving from 1947 until his death in 1964.

question: Who founded Harijan Sangh and contended that the Shastras did not approve untouchability; and if they did, they should be disregarded?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Mahatma Gandhi**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• **Mahatma Gandhi** founded the **Harijan Sevak Sangh** on **30 September 1932**. This organization was established to eradicate **untouchability** in India and uplift the depressed classes. ***Hence, the statement about the founder is correct.***

• Gandhi strongly contended that the **Shastras** (ancient Hindu scriptures) did not provide any religious sanction for the practice of **untouchability**. He viewed it as a **social evil** that had crept into **Hinduism** over time.

• He famously argued that if any **scripture** were found to support **untouchability**, it should be **disregarded** as it would be contrary to the fundamental principles of **Truth** and **Non-violence** (Ahimsa).

• **Rabindranath Tagore** was a world-renowned poet and philosopher who founded **Visva-Bharati University** in **1921**. While he supported social reforms, he was not the founder of the **Harijan Sevak Sangh**. ***Hence, this option is incorrect.***

• **Gopal Krishna Gokhale** was a moderate political leader and the founder of the **Servants of India Society** in **1905**. He served as a mentor to Gandhi but passed away in **1915**, long before the **Harijan Sangh** was formed. ***Hence, this option is incorrect.***

• **Jyotiba Phule** was a pioneering social reformer from **Maharashtra** who founded the **Satyashodhak Samaj** in **1873**. Although he was a champion for the rights of the lower castes, he was not associated with the **Harijan Sevak Sangh** founded in the **20th century**. ***Hence, this option is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**

__

• **Harijan Sevak Sangh**: Originally named the **All India Anti-Untouchability League**, it was later renamed by Gandhi. The headquarters of the organization is located at **Kingsway Camp** in **Delhi**.

• **Leadership**: The first president of the **Harijan Sevak Sangh** was the prominent industrialist **Ghanshyam Das Birla**, and the first secretary was **Amritlal Thakkar**, popularly known as **Thakkar Bapa**.

• **Satyashodhak Samaj**: Founded by **Jyotiba Phule** in **Pune**, this society aimed to liberate the **Shudra** and **Untouchable** castes from exploitation by upper castes. Phule also wrote the famous book **Gulamgiri** in **1873**.

• **Servants of India Society**: Established by **Gokhale** in **Pune**, its objective was to train **national missionaries** for the service of India and to promote the true interests of the Indian people through constitutional means.

• **Visva-Bharati**: Located in **Santiniketan**, **West Bengal**, it was declared a **Central University** and an institution of national importance in **1951**. **Tagore** envisioned it as a place where the world makes a home in a single nest.

**Important Points__**

• **Poona Pact (1932)**: The **Harijan Sevak Sangh** was a direct outcome of the **Poona Pact** signed between **Mahatma Gandhi** and **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar**. This pact was reached after Gandhi's fast in **Yerwada Jail** against the **Communal Award** of **Ramsay MacDonald**.

• **Harijan Journal**: To spread his message against **untouchability**, Gandhi started a weekly journal named **Harijan** in **1933**. He also published **Harijan Bandu** in **Gujarati** and **Harijan Sevak** in **Hindi**.

• **Harijan Tour**: Between **November 1933** and **July 1934**, Gandhi undertook a **nationwide tour** known as the **Harijan Tour**, covering about **20,000 kilometers** to collect funds (**Harijan Fund**) and mobilize public opinion against the practice of **untouchability**.
</ul

question: In which year was the All India Kisan Sabha founded in Lucknow with Swami Sahajanand Saraswati as the president?
solution:
The correct answer is __**1936.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__​**

__
 
• The All India Kisan Sabha was formed in 1936 at Lucknow.
 
• All India Kisan Sabha is also known as ‘Akhil Bhartiya Kisan Sabha.’
 
• Swami Sahajanand Saraswati was the President of the Sabha.
 
• The secretary of All India Kisan Sabha was NG Ranga.
 
• The motives of the All India Kisan Sabha were:
 
 
• To abolish the Zamindari system,
 
• To reduce land revenue,
 
• To institutionalize credit.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The Kisan Sabha movement was started in Bihar under the leadership of Sahajanand Saraswati.
 
• It was formed in 1929 by the Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha (BPKS) in order to mobilize peasants and vocalize their grievances against the zamindari attacks on their occupancy rights and thus sparking the farmers' movements in India.
 
• Gradually the peasant movement intensified and spread across the rest of India.
 
• The formation of the Congress Socialist Party (CSP) in 1934 helped the Communists to work together with the INC, however temporarily, then in April 1935, noted peasant leaders N. G. Ranga and E. M. S. Namboodiripad, then secretary and joint secretary respectively of South Indian Federation of Peasants and Agricultural Labour suggested the formation of an all-India farmers body.
 
• Soon all these radical developments culminated in the formation of the All India Kisan Sabha (AIKS) at the Lucknow session of the Indian National Congress on 11 April 1936 with **Swami Sahajanand** Saraswati elected as its first President.
 
• It involved people such as Ranga, Namboodiripad, Karyanand Sharma, Yamuna Karjee, Yadunandan (Jadunandan) Sharma, Rahul Sankrityayan, P. Sundarayya, Ram Manohar Lohia, Jayaprakash Narayan, Acharya Narendra Dev and Bankim Mukherjee.
 
• The Kisan Manifesto released in August 1936, demanded the abolition of the zamindari system and cancellation of rural debts, and in October 1937, it adopted the red flag as its banner.
 
• Soon, its leaders became increasingly** distant from Congress **and repeatedly came into confrontation with Congress governments, in Bihar and United Province.

• He was one of the founding members of the Indian National Congress.

• He served as the third President of the Indian National Congress from 1887 to 1888.
 
• He addressed the Congress as President held at **Madras** in 1887.
 
• **He said,** "This Congress is composed of the representatives, not of any one class or community of India, but of all the different communities of India".
 
• He became a Barrister in April 1867.
 
• He was the first Indian to be admitted to the High Court of Bombay as a barrister.
 
• In 1902, he became the first Indian to serve as Chief Justice in Bombay.
 
• The first Muslim politician to build a secular political awareness was Badruddin Tyabji.

• He was popularly famous as a great champion of compulsory primary education for the first time in India.
 
• He publicly demanded the introduction of “Compulsory Primary Education” in India. 
 
• He was also the founder of the **Servants of India Society.**
 
 
 
• **Dadabhai Naoroji**
 
 
• Dadabhai Naroji presided over Congress three times.
 
• He was the Congress president during the 1886, 1893, and 1906 sessions. 
 
• He had also been the founder-editor of the journal Rast Goftar in Bombay in 1851.
 
• He founded the London Zoroastrian Association in 1861.
 
• He was also a founding member of the East India Association and London Indian Society.

__
 
• Dadabhai Naoroji was a prominent Indian political leader who was elected President of the Indian National Congress (INC) during the Calcutta Session in 1886.
 
• His presidency marked a significant period in the Indian freedom struggle, emphasizing the need for greater autonomy and self-governance.
 
• Dadabhai Naoroji is often referred to as the "**Grand Old Man of India**" for his contributions to Indian politics and his role in the independence movement.
 
• Under his leadership, the Congress session focused on issues like the economic exploitation of India by the British and the need for political reforms.
 
• He was the first Indian to be elected to the **House of Commons in the UK**, furthering the cause of Indian independence on an international platform.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Indian National Congress (INC)**

 
 
• Founded in 1885, the INC was the first modern nationalist movement to emerge in the British Empire in Asia and Africa.
 
• The INC played a pivotal role in the Indian independence movement.
 
• It was instrumental in shaping the political discourse in India, advocating for self-rule and civil rights.
 
 
 
• **Dadabhai Naoroji**
 
 
• Born on September 4, 1825, in Bombay (now Mumbai), he was a scholar, trader, and politician.
 
• He was a co-founder of the London Indian Society and the East India Association.
 
• His book "Poverty and Un-British Rule in India" highlighted the economic drain of India by the British.
 
 
 
• **Drain Theory**
 
 
• Proposed by Dadabhai Naoroji, it suggested that a significant portion of India's wealth was being transferred to Britain, leading to widespread poverty in India.
 
• The theory emphasized the economic exploitation of India under British rule.
 
 
 
• **Congress Sessions**
 
 
• The annual sessions of the INC were significant events where leaders discussed strategies and policies for the independence movement.
 
• These sessions were platforms for addressing key issues such as economic policies, social reforms, and political strategies.

• Originating in the districts of **Ludhiana and Amritsar in Punjab, India, in 1849, the Kuka movement, **also known as **Namdharis, **emerged as a religious and political response to the British political establishment of the time.

• The events of the Kuka outbreak of 1872 resulted in severe reprisals, marked by brutality rarely seen in our history. Many Kuka prisoners were tragically killed by cannons, while their leader, Baba Ram Singh, was exiled to Rangoon.

__
 
• **Rabindranath Tagore** renounced his knighthood in protest against the **Jallianwala Bagh massacre**.
 
• The Jallianwala Bagh massacre occurred on **13th April 1919**, when British troops under **General Dyer** opened fire on a peaceful gathering, causing numerous casualties.
 
• Tagore's decision to renounce his knighthood was a significant act of defiance against British colonial rule and highlighted his commitment to Indian nationalism.
 
• Rabindranath Tagore was a renowned poet, writer, and philosopher, and he was the first non-European to win the **Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913**.
 
• Tagore's actions inspired many others in the Indian independence movement to resist British rule through non-violent means.

• The **Jallianwala Bagh massacre** is one of the most tragic events in Indian history and played a crucial role in galvanizing the Indian independence movement.
 
• Rabindranath Tagore's protest was not only a personal act of defiance but also a symbolic gesture that underscored the need for India's self-determination and freedom from colonial oppression.
 
• Tagore's literary works, including his poetry, songs, and essays, continue to inspire generations and are celebrated worldwide for their profound impact on literature and human thought.
 
• In addition to his literary achievements, Tagore also founded the **Visva-Bharati University in Santiniketan**, which became a center for cultural and educational exchange.

• According to him, **all humankind belonged to the same caste. **
 
• **"Oru jati, oru matam, oru daivam manushyanu” (One caste, one religion, one god for humankind) is one of his famous statements. **
 
• The **Sri Narayana Dharma Paripalana (SNDP)** **movement**, among the Ezhavas of Kerala, is an example of a conflict between the depressed classes and the upper non-Brahmana castes.
 
• **The Ezhavas were a caste of toddy-tappers in Kerala.** They were like the Nadars of Tamil Nadu and the Idigas of Karnataka.

• His **Satnam Panth (“Path of the True Name”)** succeeded in providing a religious and social identity for large numbers of Chattisgarhi Chamars.
 
• Ghasidas is remembered for having thrown images of Hindu gods onto a rubbish heap.
 
• He preached a code of ethical and dietary self-restraint and social equality.
 
 
 
• **Swami Dayanand Saraswati **

question: From which district did the peasant revolt against moneylenders and grain traders in the Deccan started in 1875?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Poona.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• **In 1875, peasants in the Bombay Presidency rose in rebellion against the agrarian crisis that faced them.**
 
• **The uprising began at Supa village in the district of Poona.**
 
• The movement** continued for 2 months and spread to over 30 villages.**
 
• The movement also **got support from the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha co-founded by M G Ranade.**
 
• Accordingly,** the Deccan Riots Commission was set up which presented a report to the British Parliament in 1878.**
 
• **In 1879, the Agriculturists Relief Act **was passed which ensured that the farmers could not be arrested and imprisoned if they were unable to pay their debts.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__ **

 
• **Reasons for revolt:**

 
 
• **​In the Bombay Deccan region**, the **British introduced the Ryotwari settlement** as the system of land revenue.
 
• Under this system,** the revenue of land was fixed on a yearly basis.**
 
• In the Ryotwari system, the agreement was between the government and the ryot (cultivator) directly.
 
• The revenue was fixed according to the soil type and the paying capacity of the farmer.
 
• However, the revenues were so high that farmers found it extremely difficult to pay their dues.
 
• Any failure in the rains would deteriorate the situation.
 
• To pay their revenues farmers generally took loans from moneylenders.
 
• Once the loans were taken, **the farmers found it impossible to repay them** since the** interest rates were steep.**
 
• **Peasant indebtedness **became a serious problem in rural areas.
 
• This infuriated the farmers because they were completely dependent on the moneylenders, who were insensitive to their plight.

• Ram Mohan Roy published** Sambad Kaumudi,** a** Bengali weekly newspaper,** from **Kolkata **in the first part of the nineteenth century.
 
• It was a well-known** pro-Reformist periodical** that actively advocated for the **Sati Pratha's removal.**
 
• **Raja Rammohan Roy,** known as the** Father of the Indian Renaissance**, was a multifaceted social, religious, and educational reformer who is known for opposing customs such as **Sati, child marriage, and social divisions**, as well as **advocating education.**

• It contained an **'Appeal to the Bengali Public'** in which it proclaimed that the primary object of its publication was to promote the **'public good'.**
 
• **Governor-General Bentinck, **largely instigated by Ram Mohan Roy, responded to the growing public outcry by **outlawing Sati in 1829.**
 
• In 1822, Roy published the journal Mirat-ul-Akbar in Persian.
 
• Roy set up the** Vedanta College** to spread his teachings of Hindu monotheism. His step was also aimed at promoting subjects like **Mathematics, Geography, and Latin** which were necessary to help the Indians keep pace with the rest of the world.
 
• **Gopal Krishna Gokhale** called Roy the **‘Father of Modern India’.**

question: Who is the author of the famous book "Gitanjali"?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Rabindranath Tagore**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Rabindranath Tagore** is the author of the world-famous collection of poems titled **Gitanjali**, which was originally published in **Bengali** in **1910**. ***Hence, this statement is correct.***

• The collection gained international recognition after its **English** translation, titled **Gitanjali: Song Offerings**, was published in **1912**. This work led to **Tagore** becoming the **first non-European** to win the **Nobel Prize in Literature** in **1913**.

• **C. Rajagopalachari** was a prominent **Indian** statesman and writer, but he is not the author of **Gitanjali**. He is better known for his retellings of the **Ramayana** and **Mahabharata**. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***

• **R. K. Narayan** was one of the most celebrated **Indian** novelists writing in **English**, famous for his works set in the fictional town of **Malgudi**, but he did not write **Gitanjali**. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***

• **Sarojini Naidu**, known as the **Nightingale of India**, was a distinguished poet and freedom fighter, but she is not the author of this specific collection. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Rabindranath Tagore** (**1861–1941**): Often referred to as **Gurudev**, he was a polymath who reshaped **Bengali** literature and music. He founded the **Visva-Bharati University** in **Santiniketan**, **West Bengal**, in **1921**. He is the only person to have composed the **national anthems** of two countries: **Jana Gana Mana** for **India** and **Amar Sonar Bangla** for **Bangladesh**.

• **C. Rajagopalachari** (**1878–1972**): He was the **last Governor-General of India** and one of the first recipients of the **Bharat Ratna** in **1954**. He was a founder of the **Swatantra Party** and a prolific writer in **Tamil** and **English**.

• **R. K. Narayan** (**1906–2001**): His notable works include **Swami and Friends**, **The Bachelor of Arts**, and **The Guide**. He was awarded the **Sahitya Akademi Award** in **1958** and the **Padma Vibhushan** in **2000**.

• **Sarojini Naidu** (**1879–1949**): She was the **first Indian woman** to become the **President** of the **Indian National Congress** in **1925** at the **Kanpur** session. She also served as the **first woman Governor** of an **Indian** state (**United Provinces**, now **Uttar Pradesh**) after **Independence** in **1947**.

**Important Points__**

• The **English** version of **Gitanjali** contains **103** poems, which are prose translations of his own **Bengali** poems. The introduction to this version was written by the famous **Irish** poet **W.B. Yeats**.

• The word **Gitanjali** is a compound of **'git'** (song) and **'anjali'** (offering), literally meaning **'Song Offerings'**. The themes of the book revolve around **spirituality**, **devotion**, **nature**, and **humanism**.

• **Tagore** was awarded a **Knighthood** by **King George V** in **1915**, but he **renounced** it in **1919** as a protest against the **Jallianwala Bagh Massacre** in **Amritsar**.

• The **Nobel Prize** citation praised his **profoundly sensitive, fresh and beautiful verse**, which made his poetic thought a part of the literature of the West.

solution:
The correct answer is __**Heraka**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Rani Gaidinliu **is associated with the **Heraka movement**.
 
• **Gaidinliu **was a **Naga political and spiritual leader** who spearheaded an uprising against British colonial control in India.
 
 
• At 13, she became associated with freedom fighter and religious leader, **Haipou Jadonang**, and became his lieutenant in his social, religious and political movements.
 
 
• **Jadonang**, who was also a Rongmei, **started the ‘Heraka movement’**, based on ancestral Naga religion, and envisioned an independent Naga kingdom (or Naga-Raja).
 
 
 
• The British authorities sentenced 16-year-old Gaidinliu to life in jail after his capture in 1932.
 
• She was released from prison during her early years in 1947, following India's independence.
 
• The first Prime Minister of India, **Jawaharlal Nehru**, **called her** the **“Daughter of the Hills”** and bestowed upon her the **title **of **"Rani"** (meaning "Queen"), and she became well-known locally as **Rani Gaidinliu**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Heraka ****movement**: 

 
 
• ​In the **1920s**, a socio-religious movement known as Heraka emerged in the **Zeliangrong region**, one of the major indigenous Naga communities living in the **tri-junction of Assam, Manipur **and **Nagaland** in India.
 
• **Haipou ****Jadonang formed it** in order to oppose both the British government's imposed reforms and the influx of Christian missionaries.
 
• He, however, was detained by the British in 1931 and killed for defying colonial authority.
 
• **Gaidinliu joined** the movement to make sure it didn't fade away.
 
• She **told **the Zeliangrong **people not to pay taxes**, in an overt act of defiance against British control.
 
• The local Nagas gave her donations as well; many of them also volunteered with her.
 
 
 
• **Meira Paibi**: This was a** women's movement** launched **in Manipur **in **2004 **to fight **against drug abuse and alcoholism**.
 
• **Nupi Lan**: This was a** women's uprising in Manipur** in **1932 **against British colonial rule.
 
• **Nisha Bandh**: This was a movement started in **1990 **by **Medha Patkar **in India to protest **against the construction of large dams** and the displacement of indigenous people.
