subject: GK
question: Which of the following oceans is the third-largest ocean in the world?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Indian Ocean**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Indian Ocean** is the **third-largest ocean** in the world, covering an area of approximately **70.56 million square kilometers**.
 
• It is smaller than the **Pacific Ocean** (the largest) and the **Atlantic Ocean** (the second-largest) but larger than the **Arctic Ocean**.
 
• The Indian Ocean is bounded by **Asia to the north**, **Africa to the west**, **Australia to the east**, and the **Southern Ocean to the south**.
 
• It is the only ocean named after a country, highlighting the historical significance of the **Indian subcontinent** in trade, navigation, and exploration.
 
• The Indian Ocean is known for its **monsoon winds**, which have significantly influenced maritime trade routes for centuries.
 
• It is an essential pathway for global trade, connecting **Europe**, **Africa**, and **Asia**, and is critical for transporting oil from the Middle East to other parts of the world.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Indian Ocean Features:**

 
 
• The Indian Ocean has some unique geographical features, including the **Mid-Indian Ridge**, a tectonic plate boundary, and the **Java Trench**, one of the deepest points in the ocean.
 
• It is home to several critical **island nations** such as the **Maldives**, **Sri Lanka**, and **Seychelles**, which rely heavily on the ocean for tourism and fishing.
 
 
 
• **Other Oceans for Comparison:**
 
 
• **Pacific Ocean**: The largest ocean in the world, covering approximately **168 million square kilometers**. It is known for its vast size and depth, including the **Mariana Trench**, the deepest point on Earth.
 
• **Atlantic Ocean**: The second-largest ocean, covering about **85 million square kilometers**. It is a major trade route connecting the Americas, Europe, and Africa.
 
• **Arctic Ocean**: The smallest ocean, covering around **14.06 million square kilometers**. It is located around the North Pole and is mostly covered by ice.
 
 
 
• **Importance of the Indian Ocean:**
 
 
• The Indian Ocean is vital for global **maritime trade**, accounting for a significant portion of the world's oil transportation.
 
• It plays a critical role in regulating the Earth's climate through the **Indian Ocean Dipole** and its interaction with monsoon systems.
 
• The ocean supports a rich diversity of marine life, including **coral reefs**, **fish species**, and **whales**, making it a hub for biodiversity.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Historical Significance:**

 
 
• The Indian Ocean has been a critical region for ancient trade routes, connecting civilizations such as the **Indus Valley**, **Mesopotamia**, and **Egypt**.
 
• It was a vital part of the **Silk Road** and later the **Spice Trade**, facilitating cultural and economic exchanges between Asia, Africa, and Europe.
 
 
 
• **Economic Importance:**
 
 
• The Indian Ocean contains crucial **marine resources**, including oil and natural gas reserves, making it a strategic region for energy production.
 
• It supports millions of livelihoods through **fishing**, **aquaculture**, and **tourism**.

subject: GK
question: What is the primary reason for tides on Earth?

options.text: Gravitational pull of the Moon and Sun

solution:
The correct answer is __**Gravitational pull of the Moon and Sun**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Tides are caused by gravitational forces:** The primary reason for tides on Earth is the **gravitational pull exerted by the Moon and the Sun**. The Moon's gravitational pull has a stronger influence due to its proximity to Earth.
 
• The gravitational force of the Moon creates a bulge in the oceans on the side facing the Moon, known as the **direct tide**. Simultaneously, another bulge occurs on the opposite side due to inertia, forming the **opposite tide**.
 
• The Sun, though farther away, also contributes to tides. Its gravitational pull interacts with the Moon's pull, creating **spring tides** (strongest tides) and **neap tides** (weakest tides) depending on their alignment.
 
• **High tides and low tides:** Tides result in alternating high and low water levels, which occur twice daily. These fluctuations depend on the rotation of Earth and the relative positions of the Moon and Sun.
 
• The gravitational pull of the Moon and Sun works in tandem with Earth's rotation to create **cyclical tidal patterns**. This is crucial for understanding the movement of water bodies.
 
• Hence, the statement that tides are primarily caused by the gravitational pull of the Moon and Sun is *correct.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Types of Tides:**

 
 
• **Spring Tides:** These occur when the Earth, Moon, and Sun are in alignment during the full moon and new moon phases. The combined gravitational forces result in higher high tides and lower low tides.
 
• **Neap Tides:** These occur when the Moon and Sun are at right angles to each other during the first and third quarter phases of the Moon. The gravitational forces partly cancel each other out, resulting in weaker tides.
 
 
 
• **Role of the Moon:**
 
 
• The Moon's proximity to Earth makes its gravitational influence the dominant factor in the formation of tides. It creates a tidal bulge on the side closest to the Moon.
 
• The opposite side of Earth also experiences a tidal bulge due to centrifugal forces resulting from Earth's rotation.
 
 
 
• **Role of the Sun:**
 
 
• The Sun's gravitational pull is weaker than the Moon's because it is much farther from Earth. However, it still plays a significant role in amplifying or diminishing tides depending on its alignment with the Moon.
 
• When the Sun and Moon align, their combined gravitational forces create spring tides. Conversely, during perpendicular alignment, neap tides are formed.
 
 
 
• **Global Impact:**
 
 
• Tides affect coastal ecosystems, navigation, and fishing industries. They also play a role in maintaining the balance of marine environments.
 
• The study of tides is essential for understanding Earth's gravitational interactions with celestial bodies.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Tidal Energy:**

 
 
• **Tidal energy** is harnessed from tidal movements and is considered a renewable energy source. This energy is generated using tidal turbines or barrages.
 
• Examples of tidal energy projects include the **La Rance tidal power station in France**, one of the earliest tidal power plants.
 
 
 
• **Scientific Studies:**
 
 
• The study of tides contributes to understanding Earth's **gravitational interactions** with the Moon and Sun, as well as the effects of Earth's rotation.
 
• Tidal patterns are critical for predicting **natural phenomena** such as tsunamis and coastal flooding.

question: What does "Green Revolution" mean in Indian agriculture?

options.text: Extraordinary increase in food grain production

solution:
The correct answer is __**Extraordinary increase in food grain production**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The Green Revolution **signifies a significant advancement in agricultural practices aimed at enhancing production through the integration of modern tools and techniques.
 
• It marks a pivotal period in which agricultural systems transitioned into industrialized models, owing to the adoption of innovative methods such as the **utilization of high-yielding variety seeds, tractors, irrigation systems, pesticides, and fertilizers.**
 
• Prior to 1967, governmental efforts primarily focused on expanding agricultural land to meet growing food demands. However, the exponential rise in population outpaced food production, necessitating urgent measures to boost yields.
 
• This urgency culminated in the implementation of the Green Revolution, which revolutionized agricultural productivity and played a crucial role in addressing food scarcity challenges.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Prime Minister Narendra Modi** has given approval for the implementation of the **Umbrella Scheme Green Revolution – 'Krishonnati Yojana' **in the agriculture sector, covering a three-year period from 2017 to 2020.
 
• This initiative includes 11 schemes aimed at fostering holistic and scientific development in the agriculture and allied sectors.
 
• The central share allocated for this scheme amounts to Rs. 33,269.976 crore. The overarching objective of the Green Revolution - Krishonnati Yojana is to enhance farmer income by boosting productivity, production, and improving returns on agricultural produce.
 
• It seeks to fortify production infrastructure, lower production costs, and facilitate the marketing of agricultural and allied products.

question: In which of the following years did the first Amendment Act of the Constitution of India come into force?
solution:
The correct answer is __**1951.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **1951 Constitution (First Amendment) Act **amended the **Fundamental Rights clauses **of the Indian Constitution in a number of ways. 
 
• It offered ways to** impose restrictions** on the **right to free speech and expression** and **supported laws **that** outlawed zamindari.**
 
• It was made clear that the** right to equalit**y does not exclude the passing of laws that give **"particular regard"** to society's **most vulnerable groups.**
 
• This Amendment established a precedent for **rewriting the Constitution** to** override judicial decisions** that** prevented the government** from
 
• carrying out its alleged obligations to **specific policies and programs.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] Additional Information__

 
• A** constitution** is a collection of **guiding ideas or accepted precedents **that serve as the** foundation** for a polity, organization, etc.
 
• The** Indian Constitution **is credited to** Dr. Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar** as its **father.**
 
• On** 26 November 1949, **it was approved by the** Indian Constituent Assembly**, and on **26 January 1950**, it came into force.
 
• The** Government of India Act of 1935** was superseded by the constitution as the** primary law of the land,** transforming the **Dominion of India** into the **Republic of India.**

question: Which of the following food items can be used as natural food preservatives?
solution:
The correct answer is **__Garlic, lemon, sugar and vinegar__**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Garlic, lemon, sugar, and vinegar **are renowned for their multifaceted roles in** food preservation**.
 
• **Garlic's allicin content, lemon's citric acid, sugar's ability to reduce water activity, and vinegar's acetic acid** create a formidable arsenal against microbial growth.
 
• Their combined effect extends **beyond mere preservation, enhancing flavors and textures **while safeguarding against spoilage.
 
• From pickling to marinating, these natural agents infuse foods with both preservation and culinary prowess. Yet, their historical significance transcends mere utility, reflecting a profound understanding of nature's bounty and the artistry of culinary tradition.
 
• As guardians of flavor and longevity, they bridge the gap between past wisdom and contemporary culinary innovation, ensuring that the legacy of natural food preservation endures with every tangy bite and savory morsel.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Natural food preservatives**, derived from sources like plants, minerals, and microorganisms, play a vital role in extending the shelf life of food products while maintaining their quality and safety.
 
• **Salt,** a time-honored preservative, works by drawing out moisture, inhibiting bacterial growth, and preserving meats, fish, and vegetables.
 
• Similarly, **sugar**, in forms such as sucrose, honey, or molasses, reduces water activity, impeding microbial proliferation in jams, jellies, and preserves.
 
• **Vinegar,** rich in acetic acid, creates an acidic environment hostile to bacteria and molds, making it indispensable in pickling and salad dressings.
 
• **Citric acid,** abundant in citrus fruits, acts as a preservative by preventing microbial growth in canned goods and beverages.
 
• Meanwhile, **rosemary extract**, rich in natural antioxidants, serves as a preservative while imparting flavor and maintaining product integrity.
 
• These natural preservatives not only ensure food safety but also reflect a commitment to harnessing nature's bounty for sustainable food preservation practices.

question: Which of the following methods works primarily by inhibiting microbial growth through low moisture?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Dehydration**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Dehydration** is a food preservation technique that works primarily by removing **moisture** from food items. This significantly inhibits the growth of microorganisms such as **bacteria, molds, and yeasts**, which require moisture to thrive.
 
• The process involves removing water content through methods like **air drying, freeze-drying, or sun drying**. Without water, the microbes cannot reproduce, thus preventing spoilage.
 
• Dehydration is widely used to preserve fruits, vegetables, meats, and other food items. Examples include dried fruits like raisins, dried herbs, and jerky.
 
• Compared to other methods, dehydration is a highly effective way to extend the shelf life of food items without significantly altering their nutritional content or flavor.
 
• Dehydrated foods are lightweight and easy to store, making them ideal for purposes like **long-term storage, travel, and emergency preparedness.**
 
• While dehydration inhibits microbial growth, it does not necessarily kill all microorganisms. Proper storage in a **dry and airtight environment** is essential to maintain the efficacy of this preservation method.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Features of Dehydration:**

 
 
• **Dehydration** is one of the oldest food preservation methods, used for centuries across various cultures to preserve seasonal produce and meats.
 
• It removes **80-90% of water content**, creating an environment unsuitable for microbial growth. However, the process retains most nutrients, making it preferable for healthy food storage.
 
 
 
• **Applications:**
 
 
• Dehydrated foods are used in **space missions, hiking, camping**, and survival kits due to their lightweight and long shelf life.
 
• **Industries** such as pharmaceuticals and cosmetics also use dehydration to preserve materials, such as herbal powders and extracts.
 
 
 
• **Other Food Preservation Methods:**
 
 
• **Refrigeration:** Works by slowing microbial growth due to low temperatures. However, it does not inhibit moisture content.
 
• **Canning:** Preserves food by sealing it in airtight containers and heating it to destroy microbes. It does not rely on moisture removal.
 
• **Pasteurization:** Involves heating liquids to kill pathogens but does not remove moisture.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Advantages of Dehydration:**

 
 
• **Cost-effective:** Dehydration is relatively inexpensive compared to other food preservation techniques.
 
• **Environmentally friendly:** Dehydrated foods reduce waste and packaging requirements.
 
 
 
• **Limitations of Dehydration:**
 
 
• While dehydration removes moisture, it does not destroy all pathogens. Proper storage conditions are essential.
 
• Some foods may lose texture or flavor during the dehydration process.

question: ______ is used in buildings and in manufacturing processes to prevent heat loss or heat gain.

__
 
• **Insulation **is a general term used to describe material that creates barriers to the transmission of electricity, heat, moisture, shock, or sound between insulated surfaces of adjacent bodies. These materials could be insulating heat, cold, electricity, sound, or radiation.
 
• **To reduce heat loss or gain, insulation** is utilised in buildings and manufacturing processes.
 
• Although its major goal is to save money, it also allows for more precise temperature management and worker protection.
 
• It reduces rusting caused by moisture on cold surfaces. These materials are porous and have a lot of latent air cells.
 
• The building industry uses thermal insulation to decrease heat loss or gain through the home envelope (external walls, windows, roofs, foundation, etc.).
 
• Thermal insulation provides thermal comfort inside homes by maintaining a comfortable temperature.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The flow of a fluid (liquid or gas) between locations of differing temperatures is known as **convection**.
 
• Heat energy is transferred through collisions between surrounding atoms or molecules in** the process of conduction**. 
 
• **Solidification, commonly known as freezing**, is a phase transition in which a liquid becomes a solid when its temperature is decreased below its freezing point.

solution:
The correct answer is __**D Gukesh**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• **D Gukesh**, full name **Dommaraju Gukesh**, became the **youngest undisputed World Chess Champion in history** in **2024** by defeating the reigning champion, **Ding Liren**.
 
• At the time of his victory, **D Gukesh** was only **18 years old**, making him the youngest player ever to achieve this feat. This surpassed the previous record set by **Garry Kasparov** in **1985**, who won the World Chess Championship at the age of **22**.
 
• The victory of **D Gukesh** was celebrated worldwide as a landmark achievement, and it further established **India** as a prominent force in the world of chess.
 
• **Gukesh** is part of a new wave of Indian chess prodigies, alongside other young talents such as **R Praggnanandhaa** and **Nihal Sarin**, showcasing the immense growth of chess in **India**.

• **D Gukesh** was born on **May 29, 2006**, in **Chennai, India**. He is considered one of the brightest stars in Indian chess.
 
• He became the **second-youngest Grandmaster in history** at the age of **12 years, 7 months, and 17 days** in **2019**.
 
• Gukesh’s rise in the chess world has been meteoric. He has won multiple international and national tournaments, proving his extraordinary talent and dedication.
 
 
 
• **World Chess Championship:**
 
 
• The **World Chess Championship** is the most prestigious title in the game of chess. It has been held since **1886** and has a rich history of legendary champions such as **Garry Kasparov**, **Magnus Carlsen**, and **Viswanathan Anand**.
 
• The championship involves a series of qualifying tournaments and matches where the best players in the world compete for the title.
 
 
 
• **Other Options Explained:**
 
 
• **Magnus Carlsen:** The Norwegian chess legend was the World Chess Champion from **2013** to **2023**. He chose not to defend his title in **2024**.
 
• **Viswanathan Anand:** The Indian chess icon was the World Chess Champion from **2007** to **2013**. He is regarded as the pioneer of Indian chess.
 
• **R Praggnanandhaa:** Another Indian chess prodigy, he gained international recognition for defeating **Magnus Carlsen** in multiple games. However, he has not yet won the World Chess Championship.
 
 

**Important Points__**

 
• **Chess in India:**

 
 
• India has emerged as a global chess powerhouse, with numerous young players achieving significant milestones in recent years.
 
• The **All India Chess Federation (AICF)** has played a crucial role in promoting the game through tournaments, training programs, and scholarships.
 
 
 
• **Future of Chess:**
 
 
• The success of players like **D Gukesh** and **R Praggnanandhaa** inspires a new generation of chess enthusiasts in **India**.
 
• The advancements in chess training, including the use of **AI-based tools** and computer analysis, have revolutionized the game and provided young players with unprecedented opportunities to excel.

question: Which of the following statements about Kho-Kho rules is correct?

options.text: A chaser may change direction only within free zones outside the poles.
A runner is not out even if they step outside the playing area while escaping.
The chasing team has all nine players sitting in the central lane during attack.
Early kho is when the active chaser taps the runner after calling 'kho'.

solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 1**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
__ 
 
• **A chaser may change direction only within free zones outside the poles:** This is a correct statement. In Kho-Kho, the chaser is allowed to change direction in the free zone near the poles, which ensures smooth gameplay and prevents obstruction in the central lane. This rule maintains the integrity of the game and allows the chasers to strategize effectively. 
 
• **A runner is not out even if they step outside the playing area while escaping:** This statement is incorrect. In Kho-Kho, runners stepping outside the designated playing area are considered out as they are violating the boundaries of the game. The rule ensures fair play and prevents runners from gaining an unfair advantage. 
 
• **The chasing team has all nine players sitting in the central lane during attack:** This statement is incorrect. While the chasing team has players sitting in the central lane, not all nine players are actively chasing at the same time. Only one active chaser pursues the runners, while the others wait for their turn. 
 
• **Early kho is when the active chaser taps the runner after calling 'kho':** This statement is incorrect. An early 'kho' refers to a scenario where the active chaser gives a ‘kho’ prematurely, violating the rules of the game. Tapping the runner after calling 'kho' signifies a legitimate chase and does not relate to an early kho. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
__ 
 
• **Kho-Kho Overview:** 
 
 
• Kho-Kho is a traditional Indian sport that emphasizes speed, agility, and teamwork. 
 
• The game is played by two teams, each consisting of 12 players, but only 9 players are allowed to play actively during an innings. 
 
• It originated in Maharashtra, India, and has gained international recognition through tournaments and events. 
 
 
 
• **Free Zones:** 
 
 
• The free zones are areas near the poles where chasers can change direction. 
 
• These zones are crucial for tactical gameplay and ensure smooth transitions for the chasing team. 
 
 
 
• **Basic Rules of Kho-Kho:** 
 
 
• The game is divided into two innings, with each team taking turns as chasers and runners. 
 
• The primary objective of the chasing team is to tag all runners within the given time frame. 
 
• Runners aim to avoid being tagged by the chasers while staying within the designated playing area. 
 
 
 
• **International Recognition:** 
 
 
• Kho-Kho is governed by the Kho-Kho Federation of India (KKFI) and has expanded its reach globally. 
 
• The sport has been included in events such as the Asian Games and South Asian Games, showcasing its popularity. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 
 
• **Chasing Strategies:** 
 
 
• Chasers must utilize the free zones effectively to change directions and strategize their chase. 
 
• Communication among chasers is vital to ensure a coordinated effort in tagging runners. 
 
 
 
• **Runner's Techniques:** 
 
 
• Runners must maintain agility and avoid predictable movements to evade chasers. 
 
• Staying within the boundaries is essential to avoid being declared out. 
 
 
 
• **Role of Referee:** 
 
 
• The referee ensures adherence to rules and resolves disputes during the game. 
 
• Key decisions, such as declaring runners out or identifying violations, are made by the referee.

question: Which of the following situations will result in a point awarded to the defending team in Kabaddi?

options.text: The raider tags two defenders and crosses the midliners
The raider fails to chant "Kabaddi" during the raid
The raider touches the bonus line without being tackled
The defending team crosses the lobby before contact

solution:
The correct answer is __**The raider fails to chant "Kabaddi" during the raid**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In the sport of **Kabaddi**, the **"Cant"** is the continuous clear chanting of the approved word **"Kabaddi"** by the **raider** in a single breath. If the raider fails to maintain this chant or loses their breath during the **raid**, they are declared **out**, and the **defending team** is awarded **1 point**. *Hence, statement B is correct.*
 
• When a **raider** successfully tags or touches **two defenders** and safely returns to their own half by crossing the **midline**, the **raiding team** is awarded **2 points** (one for each defender touched), and those defenders must leave the mat. *Hence, statement A is incorrect.*
 
• Touching the **bonus line** is a specific scoring maneuver. If a **raider** crosses the **bonus line** with one foot while the other foot is in the air, and there are **6 or 7 defenders** present on the mat, the **raiding team** receives **1 point**. This does not result in a point for the defense. *Hence, statement C is incorrect.*
 
• The **lobby** area (the yellow strips on the sides) only becomes **"active"** once a touch has been made between the **raider** and a **defender**. If a defender steps into the **lobby** without any contact being initiated, they are considered **"out of bounds,"** and a point is awarded to the **raiding team**. *Hence, statement D is incorrect.*
 
• According to the **International Kabaddi Federation (IKF)** rules, a **raid** is unsuccessful if the raider is tackled, goes out of bounds, or commits a **technical foul** like losing the **cant**. In all these cases, the **defending team** earns a point and revives one of their own players.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Court Dimensions and Player Count:** A standard **Kabaddi** court for **men** measures **13 meters by 10 meters**, while for **women** and **juniors**, it is **12 meters by 8 meters**. Each team consists of **12 players**, but only **7 players** are allowed on the **mat** at any given time during the match.
 
• **Super Tackle:** This is a unique scoring rule where if the **defending team** has **3 or fewer defenders** on the mat and they successfully tackle the **raider**, they are awarded **2 points** instead of the usual 1. This is a crucial strategy in modern leagues like the **Pro Kabaddi League (PKL)**, which began in **2014**.
 
• **Lobby Rule:** The **lobby** is the **1-meter wide** strip on both sides of the court. It is considered part of the playing area only during a **struggle** (after a touch). If a player enters it without a touch, they are **eliminated** from the current round.
 
• **Duration of Match:** A professional match typically lasts for **40 minutes**, divided into two halves of **20 minutes** each, with a **5-minute break** in between. In the **Asian Games**, where **Kabaddi** has been a regular feature since **1990**, these timing rules are strictly followed.
 
• **Types of Kabaddi:** There are two main styles: the **Standard Style** (played on a rectangular mat) and the **Circle Style** (played on a circular field, popular in **Punjab**). The **Pro Kabaddi League** and **World Cup** follow the **Standard Style**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Do-or-Die Raid:** If a team performs **two consecutive empty raids** (raids where no points are scored or lost), the **third raid** is designated as a **"Do-or-Die" raid**. In this raid, the **raider** must score a point (by touch or bonus), or they will be declared **out**, even if they are not tackled.
 
• **Raid Time Limit:** Every **raid** has a maximum duration of **30 seconds**. If the **raider** fails to return to their half within this **30-second** window, they are ruled **out**, and the **defending team** receives a point.
 
• **All-Out (Lona):** When a team manages to eliminate all **7 players** of the opposing team, they score an **"All-Out,"** which awards **2 bonus points** in addition to the points earned for the individual touches. All eliminated players of the opposing team are then **revived**.
 
• **Technical Points:** Points can also be awarded for **coaching violations**, **wrong substitutions**, or if a defender pulls the **raider's hair** or clothes. These are called **technical points** and do not result in the **revival** of a player.
</ul

question:
Consider the following statements under FIDE chess rules:**
1. A pawn may be promoted to a queen upon reaching the 8th rank, even if the original queen is still on the board.

2. Castling is allowed only if neither the king nor rook has moved, and the king doesn't pass through or into check.

Which of the above statement is/are Correct**?
solution:
The correct answer is __**1 and 2 both are Correct**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• According to the **FIDE Laws of Chess**, specifically **Article 3.7.5.1**, when a **pawn** reaches the **rank** furthest from its starting position (the **8th rank** for **White** and the **1st rank** for **Black**), it must be exchanged as part of the same move for a **new queen, rook, bishop, or knight** of the same color.
 
• The rules explicitly state that the choice of the piece is not restricted to pieces that have been previously captured. This means a player can theoretically have up to **nine queens** on the board at the same time if all eight **pawns** are promoted and the original **queen** remains. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• **Castling** is a unique move in **chess** involving the **king** and either of the original **rooks**. Under **FIDE Article 3.8.2**, castling is only legal if neither the **king** nor the **rook** involved has moved previously in the game.
 
• Furthermore, the **king** cannot castle if it is currently in **check**, if the square it must pass through is under attack by an opponent’s piece, or if the square it lands on would result in the **king** being in **check**. This ensures the **king** never 'jumps' over or into danger during the maneuver. ***Hence, statement 2 is correct.***
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is 1 and 2 both are Correct.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **FIDE (International Chess Federation):** Founded on **July 20, 1924**, in **Paris, France**, **FIDE** is the international organization that connects various national chess federations and acts as the governing body of international chess competition. Its **headquarters** are located in **Lausanne, Switzerland**.
 
• **Promotion Mechanics:** The **promotion** of a **pawn** is immediate. As soon as the **pawn** touches the **promotion square**, the player must replace it with the chosen piece. The new piece's powers are active instantly, meaning a promoted **queen** could deliver a **check** or **checkmate** on the very same move.
 
• **Castling Variations:** There are two types of **castling**: **Kingside castling** (also known as **short castling**) and **Queenside castling** (also known as **long castling**). In **kingside**, the **king** moves two squares toward the **h-file**, and in **queenside**, it moves two squares toward the **c-file**.
 
• **En Passant:** This is another special **pawn** capture rule. If a **pawn** moves two squares forward from its **starting rank** and lands directly adjacent to an opponent's **pawn**, the opponent may capture it as if it had only moved one square. This move is only legal on the **immediate next turn**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Check and Checkmate:** A **king** is in **check** when it is under attack by at least one enemy piece. A **checkmate** occurs when the **king** is in **check** and there is no legal move to escape the attack, resulting in an immediate **win** for the attacking player.
 
• **Stalemate:** This occurs when the player whose turn it is has no **legal moves** and their **king** is **not in check**. Under **FIDE** rules, a **stalemate** results in an immediate **draw**.
 
• **Touch-Move Rule:** In competitive play, if a player touches one of their own pieces, they must move it if a **legal move** exists. If they touch an opponent's piece, they must capture it if legal.
 
• **Draw Conditions:** Aside from **stalemate**, a game can end in a **draw** through **mutual agreement**, **threefold repetition** of a position, the **50-move rule** (no capture or pawn move in 50 consecutive moves), or **insufficient material** to force a **checkmate**.

He achieved this milestone at the **1972 Heidelberg Paralympics** in the **50m Freestyle Swimming** event. He set a **world record** at the time with a finish of **37.33 seconds**. He was the first Paralympian to be honored with the **Padma Bhushan** in **2022**. *Hence, match B-1 is correct.*

Beyond her athletic career, she has been a prominent advocate for disability rights and served as the **President of the Paralympic Committee of India (PCI)**. *Hence, match C-3 is correct.*

question:
Read the below statements marked as Assertion (A) and Reason (R). Mark the correct options:
Assertion (A): Jeremy Bujakowski was the first Indian to compete at the Winter Olympics, participating in the 1964 and 1968 Games.
Reason (R): India did not participate in the Winter Olympics for 20 years after Bujakowski's era.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

solution:
The correct answer is __**Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Assertion (A)** states that **Jeremy Bujakowski** was the first Indian to compete at the **Winter Olympics**, participating in the **1964** and **1968 Games**. This statement is **correct**. **Jeremy Bujakowski**, an alpine skier, made his debut at the **1964 Winter Olympics** in **Innsbruck, Austria**, where he was the sole representative for India. He returned to compete in the **1968 Winter Olympics** held in **Grenoble, France**.

• **Reason (R)** mentions that **India** did not participate in the **Winter Olympics** for **20 years** after **Bujakowski's era**. This statement is also **correct**. Following the **1968 Games**, India did not send any athletes to the Winter Games in **1972 (Sapporo)**, **1976 (Innsbruck)**, **1980 (Lake Placid)**, and **1984 (Sarajevo)**. India only returned to the competition at the **1988 Calgary Games**, marking a exactly **20-year hiatus**.

• While both statements are factually accurate, the **Reason (R)** describes a period of absence that occurred **after** the events mentioned in the **Assertion (A)**. The lack of participation for **20 years** does not provide a causal explanation or logical reason as to why **Jeremy Bujakowski** was the first participant or why he competed in those specific years. **Hence, R is not the correct explanation of A.**

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Jeremy Bujakowski** was of **Polish descent** but represented **India** after his family settled there. In the **1964 Innsbruck Games**, he competed in the **Men's Downhill** event but was unable to finish due to an injury. In **1968**, he competed in **Downhill**, **Slalom**, and **Giant Slalom**, achieving his best finish of **53rd** in the **Downhill** category.

• The **1988 Calgary Winter Olympics** marked India's return to the global stage with a three-member contingent. **Shailaja Kumar** became the **first Indian woman** to compete in the **Winter Olympics** during this edition, participating in **Alpine Skiing** alongside **Gul Dev** and **Kishor Rahtna Rai**.

• **Shiva Keshavan** is perhaps the most famous Indian Winter Olympian, having represented the country in **six consecutive Winter Olympics** from **1998 (Nagano)** to **2018 (Pyeongchang)**. He competed in the **Luge** event and holds the record for being the **youngest person** to ever qualify for the Olympics in Luge at the **age of 16**.

• The **Winter Olympics** are held every **four years** and include sports such as **Skiing**, **Ice Hockey**, **Figure Skating**, and **Luge**. The first-ever **Winter Olympic Games** were held in **1924** in **Chamonix, France**.

• In recent years, India's participation has remained small but consistent. At the **2022 Beijing Winter Olympics**, **Arif Khan** was the only Indian athlete to qualify, competing in both **Slalom** and **Giant Slalom** events.

**Important Points__**

• **First Indian Winter Olympian:** **Jeremy Bujakowski** (**1964**).

• **First Indian Female Winter Olympian:** **Shailaja Kumar** (**1988**).

• **Longest Gap in Participation:** **20 years** (**1968 to 1988**).

• **Most Appearances:** **Shiva Keshavan** with **6 appearances**.

• **Governing Body:** The **Indian Olympic Association (IOA)** manages India's representation, while the **Winter Games Federation of India** oversees the development of winter sports in the country, primarily centered in regions like **Gulmarg** and **Auli**.
</ul

question: In which year did India win its first Olympic gold medal in hockey?
solution:
The correct answer is __**1928**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• India won its first-ever **Olympic gold medal** in hockey at the **1928 Amsterdam Olympics**. This victory marked the beginning of an era of unprecedented dominance for India in the sport of field hockey on the global stage.

• The Indian team was led by captain **Jaipal Singh Munda**, who was a prominent **Adivasi** leader and scholar. Under his leadership, the team displayed exceptional skill and coordination throughout the tournament.

• The legendary **Major Dhyan Chand**, often referred to as the **Wizard of Hockey**, emerged as the star performer of the **1928 Games**. He was the top scorer of the tournament, netting a total of **14 goals** in just five matches.

• In the final match held on **May 26, 1928**, India faced the host nation, the **Netherlands**. India secured a convincing **3-0** victory to claim the gold medal. Remarkably, the Indian team did not concede a single goal throughout the entire **1928 Olympic** tournament.

• The other options provided are significant but do not represent the first win: **1932** (Los Angeles) was India's second gold medal; **1948** (London) was the first gold medal won by India as an **independent nation**; and **1952** (Helsinki) was India's fifth consecutive gold medal.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Dominance in Olympics**: Following the **1928** win, India went on to win a record **six consecutive gold medals** in Olympic hockey from **1928 to 1956**. This remains one of the most impressive winning streaks in any team sport in Olympic history.

• **1932 Los Angeles Olympics**: India defended its title with a massive **24-1** victory over the **United States** in the final. This match remains famous for the highest number of goals scored in an international hockey match.

• **1936 Berlin Olympics**: India won its third consecutive gold by defeating **Germany** **8-1** in the final. This tournament solidified **Major Dhyan Chand's** reputation as the greatest hockey player of all time.

• **1948 London Olympics**: This was a historic moment as India defeated **Great Britain** **4-0** in the final at **Wembley Stadium**. It was the first time the **Indian National Anthem** was played and the **Tricolour** was hoisted at the Olympics after independence.

• **1980 Moscow Olympics**: India won its **eighth gold medal** in hockey at the **Moscow Games**, captained by **Vasudevan Baskaran**. This was the last gold medal for India in hockey for several decades.

• **Recent Achievements**: After a gap of **41 years**, the Indian men's hockey team won a **bronze medal** at the **Tokyo 2020 Olympics** (held in **2021**) and followed it up with another **bronze medal** at the **Paris 2024 Olympics**.

**Important Points__**

• **Indian Hockey Federation (IHF)**: The governing body for hockey in India was formed in **1925** in **Gwalior**. It was the first non-European hockey federation to be admitted to the **International Hockey Federation (FIH)**.

• **National Sports Day**: In honor of **Major Dhyan Chand's** contributions to the sport, his birthday, **August 29**, is celebrated as **National Sports Day** in India every year.

• **Balbir Singh Sr.**: Another legendary figure in Indian hockey, he was part of the gold-winning teams in **1948**, **1952**, and **1956**. He holds the record for the most goals scored by an individual in an Olympic men's hockey final, scoring **5 goals** against the **Netherlands** in **1952**.

• **Total Olympic Medals**: As of **2024**, India has won a total of **13 Olympic medals** in hockey, consisting of **8 gold**, **1 silver**, and **4 bronze** medals.
</ul

question: Which Indian sprinter was stripped of her silver medal at the 2006 Asian Games due to a failed drug test?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Santhi Soundarajan**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Santhi Soundarajan** is an Indian middle-distance runner who famously won the **silver medal** in the **women's 800m** race at the **2006 Asian Games** held in **Doha, Qatar**.

• She was stripped of her medal after she failed a **gender verification test** shortly after the event. The **Olympic Council of Asia (OCA)** disqualified her, stating that she did not possess the sexual characteristics of a woman. While the question mentions a **failed drug test**, it is widely recognized in sports history that her disqualification at the **2006 Asian Games** was due to this controversial medical eligibility test.

• **P. T. Usha** (Option 1) is one of India's greatest athletes, known as the **Payyoli Express**. She won multiple gold medals at the **1986 Seoul Asian Games** and retired long before the **2006** incident, making this option incorrect.

• **Dutee Chand** (Option 3) is another prominent Indian sprinter who faced a ban due to **hyperandrogenism** regulations in **2014**. However, she successfully challenged the ruling at the **Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS)** and was not the athlete stripped of a medal in **2006**.

• **K. M. Beenamol** (Option 4) is a celebrated Olympian and **Padma Shri** recipient who won gold in the **800m** at the **2002 Busan Asian Games**. She was not involved in any medal-stripping controversy during the **2006** games.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Santhi Soundarajan** was born in **1981** in **Kathakkurichi**, **Tamil Nadu**. She grew up in extreme poverty and used sports as a means to support her family.

• Throughout her career, she won **11 international medals** for **India** and around **50 national medals**. Her disqualification in **2006** led to a significant decline in her mental health and financial stability, at one point forcing her to work in a **brick kiln** to survive.

• In **2016**, following years of advocacy, the **Tamil Nadu government** and the **Sports Development Authority of Tamil Nadu (SDAT)** appointed her as a permanent **athletics coach**, recognizing her contributions to the sport.

• Her case remains a landmark in the discussion of **human rights** and **gender ethics** in international sports, alongside athletes like **Caster Semenya**. It highlighted the psychological trauma caused by **sex verification** policies implemented by bodies like **World Athletics** (formerly **IAAF**).

**Important Points__**

• The **Olympic Council of Asia (OCA)** is the governing body for all sports in **Asia** and is responsible for organizing the **Asian Games** every **four years**.

• **Gender verification** tests were once mandatory at major sporting events but were largely abolished in the late **1990s**, only to be reintroduced on a case-by-case basis if an athlete's eligibility was questioned.

• The **2006 Doha Asian Games** saw **India** finish with a total of **53 medals**, including **10 gold**, **17 silver**, and **26 bronze**, excluding the stripped medal of **Santhi Soundarajan**.

• Current regulations by **World Athletics** focus on **testosterone** levels in female athletes with **Differences of Sexual Development (DSD)**, requiring them to medically reduce their levels to compete in certain track events.
</ul

__ 
 
• **Gold medals** are awarded to athletes who achieve **first place** in their respective events at the Olympics, symbolizing the highest level of achievement in sports. 
 
• The tradition of awarding medals in the Olympics began in the **1904 Summer Olympics**, held in St. Louis, USA, where gold, silver, and bronze medals were introduced as awards. 
 
• Gold medals are made primarily of **silver** and are coated with a thin layer of pure gold. As per the **International Olympic Committee (IOC)**, the gold coating must be at least **6 grams**.

• A silver medal is awarded to the athlete or team that secures **second place** in their event at the Olympics. 
 
• It is made primarily of **pure silver**, signifying the second-highest achievement in sports. 
 
• The tradition of silver medals dates back to the **1896 Summer Olympics**, where winners were awarded silver medals instead of gold. 
 
 
• **Bronze Medal:** 
 
• A bronze medal is awarded to the athlete or team that finishes in **third place** in their event. 
 
• It is made of a combination of **copper and tin**, representing the third tier of excellence in sports. 
 
• Bronze medals were introduced in the **1904 Olympics**, along with gold and silver medals. 
 
 
• **Historical Facts:** 
 
• The first modern Olympics were held in **1896** in Athens, Greece, and featured no gold medals; winners received silver medals and olive branches. 
 
• The composition and design of medals are determined by the **host nation** and approved by the **International Olympic Committee**. 
 
• The **Tokyo 2020 Olympics** introduced medals made from recycled electronics to promote sustainability. 
 
 
• **Cultural Significance:** 
 
• Gold medals symbolize **victory, prestige, and excellence** and are often associated with great personal and national pride. 
 
• Winning a gold medal is considered the pinnacle of an athlete’s career and can inspire future generations to pursue sports.

• **Eligibility for Medals:** Athletes participate in various sports disciplines to compete for gold, silver, and bronze medals, which are awarded based on performance rankings. 
 
• **Medal Design:** The design of Olympic medals reflects the **cultural heritage** and identity of the host country. For example, the medals for the **Rio 2016 Olympics** featured elements of Brazilian culture. 
 
• **Medal Composition:** Gold medals contain a minimum of **92.5% silver** and are plated with at least **6 grams of gold**, ensuring durability and aesthetic appeal.

question: What is the name given to the points scored in a basketball game?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Point**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• In the sport of **Basketball**, the scoring system is based on the accumulation of **Points**. A team wins the game by scoring more points than their opponent within the designated playing time. ***Hence, the correct answer is Point.***

• A **Field Goal** is the most common way to score and is worth **2 points** if the ball is thrown from within the **Three-point arc**.

• A **Three-pointer** is awarded when a player successfully shoots the ball into the basket from beyond the **Three-point line**, which is a semi-circular arc on the court. This shot grants the team **3 points**.

• A **Free Throw** is an uncontested scoring opportunity awarded to a player after certain types of fouls are committed by the opposing team. Each successful free throw is worth **1 point**.

• The other options provided are incorrect for basketball: **Goal** is the scoring unit for sports like **Football (Soccer)**, **Hockey**, and **Handball**; **Run** is the scoring unit used in **Cricket** and **Baseball**; and **Touchdown** is the primary scoring method in **American Football**, worth **6 points**.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Basketball** was invented by **Dr. James Naismith**, a Canadian physical education instructor, in **December 1891** in **Springfield, Massachusetts**, **USA**.

• The **National Basketball Association (NBA)**, which is the premier professional basketball league in the **United States** and **Canada**, officially adopted the **Three-point line** during the **1979-1980 season**.

• The **International Basketball Federation (FIBA)** is the world governing body for the sport. It was founded in **1932** and is responsible for organizing international competitions like the **FIBA Basketball World Cup** and the **Olympic Basketball Tournament**.

• The standard height of the **Basketball Rim** (the hoop) is exactly **10 feet** (or **3.05 meters**) above the floor, a measurement that has remained constant since the game's inception.

• The **Shot Clock** was introduced to the **NBA** in **1954** (set at **24 seconds**) to prevent teams from stalling and to increase the number of scoring opportunities, thereby making the game more exciting for spectators.

**Important Points__**

• The record for the most **Points** scored by a single player in an **NBA** game is **100**, set by **Wilt Chamberlain** of the **Philadelphia Warriors** on **March 2, 1962**.

• In modern basketball, **LeBron James** holds the record for the highest **All-time leading scorer** in **NBA** history, surpassing the long-standing record of **Kareem Abdul-Jabbar** in **2023**.

• Basketball games cannot end in a draw. If the score is tied at the end of regulation time, the teams play **Overtime** periods (usually **5 minutes** in the **NBA** and **FIBA**) until a winner is decided.

• The **Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame**, located in **Springfield**, serves as the primary library and museum dedicated to the history and great players of the sport.
</ul

question: How many players are there in a standard Kabaddi team on the field?
solution:
The correct answer is __**7**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In a standard match of Kabaddi, each team consists of **7 players** who are present on the field at the start of the game.
 
• While **7 players** actively participate on the mat, a complete team squad usually comprises **12 players**, with the remaining **5 players** serving as **substitutes**.
 
• The primary objective of the game involves a **"raider"** entering the opponent's half to touch as many **defenders** as possible and returning to their own half within a **30-second** raid clock while chanting "Kabaddi".
 
• For **senior men** and **junior boys**, the match is played over a duration of **40 minutes**, which is split into two halves of **20 minutes** each, separated by a **5-minute** interval.
 
• For **senior women** and **junior girls**, the match duration is **30 minutes**, consisting of two halves of **15 minutes** each.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Court Dimensions**: In **Standard Style Kabaddi**, the rectangular mat for men measures **13 meters by 10 meters**, whereas for women, it measures **12 meters by 8 meters**.
 
• **Lobby and Bonus Line**: The **Lobby** is a **1-meter** wide strip on both sides of the court that becomes active during a struggle. The **Bonus Line** is located **1 meter** inside the **Baulk Line**; a raider earns an extra point by crossing it when the defending team has **6 or 7 players** on the mat.
 
• **Scoring System**: Teams earn **1 point** for every opponent touched or tackled out. If a team manages to get the entire opposition out, they earn an **"All Out" (Lona)**, which grants **2 additional points**.
 
• **International Governing Body**: The **International Kabaddi Federation (IKF)** is the global authority for the sport, founded in **2004**. In India, the sport is governed by the **Amateur Kabaddi Federation of India (AKFI)**.
 
• **Major Tournaments**: Kabaddi has been a regular part of the **Asian Games** since **1990**. The **Pro Kabaddi League (PKL)**, launched in **2014**, has significantly increased the sport's popularity in **India**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Do-or-Die Raid**: After two consecutive **empty raids** (raids where no points are scored), the third raid is a **Do-or-Die raid**. If the raider fails to score a point, they are declared **out**.
 
• **Super Tackle**: If a defending team has **3 or fewer players** on the field and successfully tackles a raider, it is called a **Super Tackle**, and the team is awarded **2 points** instead of 1.
 
• **Revival**: When a defender is touched or a raider is tackled, they must leave the field. They can be **revived** only when their team earns a point by getting an opponent out, following the sequence in which they were eliminated.
 
• **Circle Style Kabaddi**: This variation is played on a **circular pitch** with a radius of **11 meters** and is particularly popular in the state of **Punjab**. Unlike the standard style, it does not involve **lobbies** or **bonus lines**.

question: Which organization in India is responsible for testing athletes for doping violations?
solution:
The correct answer is __**NADA**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• **National Anti-Doping Agency (NADA):** It is the organization responsible for testing athletes in India for **doping violations**. This includes conducting tests, promoting education, and ensuring compliance with anti-doping rules.
 
• It was established by the **Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports**, Government of India, in **2005**, as an independent body to enforce anti-doping measures in sports.
 
• NADA ensures the implementation of the **World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) Code** within India and works to maintain fairness in sports. *Hence, NADA is the correct organization.*
 
• **Functions:** Its primary functions include sample collection, analysis, education, and awareness programs to prevent doping, and enforcing penalties for violations.
 
• NADA collaborates with sports bodies, national federations, and athletes to ensure a doping-free environment. It also conducts **random and competition-specific testing** to identify doping violations.
 
• **Structure:** NADA operates under the guidance of the **Anti-Doping Disciplinary Panel** and the **Anti-Doping Appeal Panel**, which handle cases of violations and appeals respectively.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is NADA.***

**Additional Information__**

__
 
• **About NADA:**

 
 
• **Headquarters:** NADA is headquartered in **New Delhi, India**.
 
• **Mission:** To promote **clean sports** and ensure that Indian athletes compete in a doping-free environment.
 
• **Collaboration:** NADA works in collaboration with the **World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA)** to implement global standards and practices in India.
 
 
 
• **About Other Options:**
 
 
• **Indian Olympic Association (IOA):** The IOA is responsible for the management of India's participation in the **Olympic Games** and other international sports competitions. It is not involved in anti-doping measures.
 
• **All India Football Federation (AIFF):** AIFF is the governing body for **football in India**. It governs the sport's development and organization at the national level but is not responsible for anti-doping activities.
 
• **Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI):** The BCCI governs **cricket in India**. Although it works on ensuring fair play in cricket, anti-doping testing in cricket is under NADA's jurisdiction.
 
 
 
• **Anti-Doping Rules:**
 
 
• India follows the **WADA Code**, which provides a framework for anti-doping policies, rules, and regulations.
 
• NADA ensures compliance with the WADA Code and conducts **awareness programs** to educate athletes about banned substances and anti-doping norms.
 
 

**Important Points__**

 
• **WADA Code:**

 
 
• The **World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA)** Code is a set of rules and policies aimed at ensuring a harmonized approach to anti-doping efforts worldwide.
 
• NADA adopts and enforces the WADA Code to maintain global standards in anti-doping measures within India.
 
 
 
• **Key Anti-Doping Activities in India:**
 
 
• **Testing:** NADA conducts both **in-competition** and **out-of-competition testing** to identify and penalize doping violations.
 
• **Education:** It organizes workshops, seminars, and online modules to educate athletes and coaches about the risks of doping and banned substances.
 
• **Enforcement:** NADA imposes penalties on athletes and support personnel found guilty of doping violations. This can include **suspensions** or disqualifications.

__

• The **raider** must continuously chant the word "**Kabaddi**" throughout the duration of the attack without inhaling; this rhythmic chanting is technically referred to as the **cant**.
 
• In professional formats like the **Pro Kabaddi League (PKL)**, which was launched in **2014**, each **raid** is restricted to a maximum time limit of **30 seconds**.
 
• The objective of a **raid** is to tag or touch one or more members of the defending team and return safely to the home half. Successfully doing so earns the attacking team **touch points**, while failure to return results in the **raider** being declared "out."
 
• **Kabaddi** is a contact sport with deep roots in **ancient India**, particularly in the state of **Tamil Nadu**. It gained massive international exposure after its introduction as a competitive sport in the **1990 Asian Games** held in **Beijing**.
 
• The sport is governed globally by the **International Kabaddi Federation (IKF)** and in India by the **Amateur Kabaddi Federation of India (AKFI)**, which was established in **1972**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• Key terminologies include **Offside**, **Dribbling**, **Free Kick**, **Yellow Card**, **Corner Kick**, and **VAR (Video Assistant Referee)**.
 
• The **FIFA World Cup**, held every **four years**, is the most prestigious tournament in this sport.

• India has won a record **eight Olympic gold medals** in men's hockey, with legends like **Major Dhyan Chand** contributing to its golden era.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

question: In chess, what is the term for a move that allows a player to move their king and a rook?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Castling**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Castling** is a special move in the game of chess that involves both the **king** and one of the **rooks**.
 
• It is the only move in chess that allows a player to move two pieces simultaneously: the king and a rook. This move is performed under specific conditions. *Hence, the correct answer is Castling.*
 
• Castling is considered a strategic move aimed at providing safety to the king and connecting the rooks for better coordination.
 
• This move can only happen if neither the king nor the rook involved has moved previously in the game, the squares between them are unoccupied, the king is not currently in check, and the squares the king passes over are not under attack. *Hence, statement 1 is correct.*
 
• Castling is performed by moving the king two squares toward the rook and then placing the rook on the square immediately next to the king, on the opposite side.
 
• **Castling** can be done on either the **kingside** (short castling) or the **queenside** (long castling), depending on the rook chosen for the move. This is determined by the player's strategy and the game's state.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Castling.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Conditions for Castling:**

 
 
• Neither the **king** nor the **rook** involved in castling must have moved prior to the move.
 
• The squares between the king and the rook must be **unoccupied**.
 
• The **king** cannot be in check, pass through a square that is attacked, or end up in a square that is under attack.
 
 
 
• **Types of Castling:**
 
 
• **Kingside Castling:** The king moves two squares toward the rook on its starting side, and the rook moves to the square on the other side of the king.
 
• **Queenside Castling:** The king moves two squares toward the rook on the opposite side of the board, and the rook moves to the square on the other side of the king.
 
 
 
• **Strategic Importance:**
 
 
• Castling is used to **protect the king** by placing it behind a wall of pawns and to bring the rook into active play by positioning it closer to the center of the board.
 
• It enhances the player's ability to connect the rooks and control the **center of the board**, which is crucial for a strong chess strategy.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Explanation of Incorrect Options:**

 
 
• **Check:** This refers to a situation where the king is under direct attack by an opponent's piece. It is unrelated to castling.
 
• **Checkmate:** This occurs when the king is in check and there is no legal move to escape the threat. It does not involve the movement of both the king and the rook simultaneously.
 
• **Pawn Promotion:** This refers to a pawn reaching the opponent's back rank and being promoted to any other piece (except a king). It is unrelated to castling.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context:**
 
 
• **Origin:** Castling is a relatively modern addition to chess, introduced in the 16th century to make the game more dynamic and strategic.

question: What is "doping" in sports ?

options.text: The use of advanced training techniques to enhance performance.
The consumption of nutritional supplements to improve health
The use of banned substances or methods to unfairly enhance athletic performance.
The practice of psychological conditioning for athletes.

solution:
The correct answer is __**The use of banned substances or methods to unfairly enhance athletic performance.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Doping in sports** refers to the use of **banned substances** or methods by athletes to gain an **unfair advantage** over competitors. The substances used can enhance performance by increasing strength, endurance, or recovery speed.
 
• The practice is considered unethical and is **strictly prohibited** by various sports organizations, including the **World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA).**
 
• Doping can involve the use of **performance-enhancing drugs** (PEDs) such as anabolic steroids, erythropoietin (EPO), or human growth hormones. These substances can boost muscle mass, oxygen delivery, or overall stamina. *Hence, this aligns with the given correct answer.*
 
• Methods like **blood doping** (injecting oxygenated blood into the body) or the use of masking agents to hide drug use also constitute doping. These practices are banned as they violate the principles of **fair play**.
 
• Athletes caught doping may face **severe consequences**, including suspension, disqualification, or permanent bans from their sport. *Thus, the definition of doping matches the correct option provided.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Categories of banned substances:**

 
 
• **Anabolic agents:** These include anabolic steroids that promote muscle growth. Examples are **testosterone** and nandrolone.
 
• **Stimulants:** Substances like amphetamines or cocaine that enhance alertness and reduce fatigue.
 
• **Hormones:** These include erythropoietin (EPO), human growth hormone (HGH), and insulin, which are used to improve oxygen delivery or muscle repair.
 
 
 
• **Anti-doping regulations and organizations:**
 
 
• The **World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA)**, established in **1999**, is a global organization that oversees anti-doping efforts. It publishes an annual **Prohibited List** of substances and methods.
 
• National Anti-Doping Organizations (NADOs) in individual countries ensure compliance with global anti-doping standards. For instance, **NADA** (National Anti-Doping Agency) operates in **India**.
 
 
 
• **Impact of doping:**
 
 
• Doping undermines the spirit of sportsmanship by providing an unfair advantage to athletes who use banned substances or methods.
 
• It can have **serious health consequences**, including cardiovascular issues, liver damage, hormonal imbalances, and even death in extreme cases.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Examples of high-profile doping cases:**

 
 
• **Lance Armstrong:** The cyclist was stripped of his **seven Tour de France titles** after admitting to using performance-enhancing drugs.
 
• **Maria Sharapova:** The tennis player received a **two-year ban** after testing positive for meldonium, a banned substance, in **2016**.
 
 
 
• **Efforts to combat doping:**
 
 
• Regular testing of athletes is conducted during and outside competition to detect banned substances.
 
• Educational programs are run by organizations like WADA and national bodies to inform athletes about the **risks and consequences of doping**.
 
• Advances in technology, such as biological passports, help track long-term changes in an athlete’s physiology to detect doping.

• **The Duckworth-Lewis (D/L) method, **also referred to as the **Duckworth–Lewis–Stern (DLS) method**, made its** debut in international cricket** during a match between **Zimbabwe and England in 1997.**
 
• Subsequently, the **International Cricket Council (ICC) **formally embraced the D/L method in 1999.
 
• This method is a mathematical formula designed to determine revised targets for cricket matches disrupted by rain.
 
• It takes into account both the number of overs and wickets remaining as key resources and adjusts the target accordingly based on their availability.
 
• Renowned for its fairness and objectivity, the D/L method relies on historical data and is relatively straightforward to calculate, even without the aid of a computer.
 
• Its adaptability makes it a valuable tool for ensuring equitable outcomes in rain-affected cricket matches.

• **The Duckworth-Lewis (D/L) method** was originally formulated by** two English statisticians, Frank Duckworth and Tony Lewis.**
 
• In 2015, the method was updated by Australian academic Steve Stern. This method is employed in all international and domestic limited-overs cricket matches, including Twenty20 matches.
 
• It serves as a standardized mechanism for calculating revised targets in matches affected by weather interruptions, ensuring fairness and objectivity in such situations.

• **Statement 2: Tin Height**: 
 
 
• The **tin** is a **48 cm high strip** located at the front wall of a squash court. 
 
• Its purpose is similar to that of a tennis net, acting as a lower boundary for valid shots.

solution:
The correct answer is __**Knight**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Knight** is the specific chess piece that moves in an **'L' shape**. This movement is defined as moving **two squares** in a straight line (either vertically or horizontally) and then **one square** perpendicular to that line. ***Hence, the Knight is the correct answer.***

• A unique characteristic of the **Knight** is its ability to **jump over** other pieces. No other piece on the board, including the **Queen** or **Rook**, can move past a square occupied by another piece. This makes the Knight exceptionally valuable in **closed positions** where the board is crowded with pawns.

• The **Rook** moves in straight lines along **ranks** (rows) and **files** (columns) for any number of unoccupied squares. It cannot move diagonally or in an 'L' shape, and it is blocked by other pieces. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***

• The **Bishop** moves any number of squares in a **diagonal** direction. Each player starts with two Bishops, one restricted to **light squares** and the other to **dark squares** throughout the entire match. They cannot move in an 'L' shape. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***

• The **Queen** is the most powerful piece on the board, combining the movements of the **Rook** and the **Bishop**. While it can move any number of squares vertically, horizontally, or diagonally, it lacks the **'L' shape** jumping capability of the Knight. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Chessboard Layout**: The game is played on a square board divided into an **8x8 grid** containing **64 squares**. The squares alternate between **light** and **dark** colors, and the board is positioned so that each player has a light square on their bottom-right corner.

• **Historical Origins**: Chess is widely believed to have originated in **India** during the **Gupta Empire** around the **6th century AD**. The earliest known form was **Chaturanga**, which featured pieces representing the four divisions of the military: infantry, cavalry, elephants, and chariots.

• **Piece Valuation**: In standard chess theory, pieces are assigned numerical values to help players evaluate positions. A **Pawn** is worth **1 point**, **Knights** and **Bishops** are worth **3 points** each, **Rooks** are worth **5 points**, and the **Queen** is worth **9 points**.

• **FIDE**: The **International Chess Federation** (Fédération Internationale des Échecs) is the global body that governs chess. Founded in **1924** in **Paris**, **France**, it organizes the **World Chess Championship** and awards titles like **Grandmaster**.

• **World Champions**: The first official **World Chess Championship** was held in **1886**, won by **Wilhelm Steinitz**. Since then, the title has been held by legendary players such as **Bobby Fischer**, **Garry Kasparov**, and **Magnus Carlsen**.

**Important Points__**

• **Special Moves**: **Castling** is a unique move where the **King** and a **Rook** move simultaneously to improve safety. **En Passant** is a special pawn capture rule, and **Promotion** allows a pawn to become a **Queen**, **Rook**, **Bishop**, or **Knight** upon reaching the **8th rank**.

• **Check and Checkmate**: A **Check** occurs when the **King** is under direct attack. **Checkmate** happens when the King is in check and there is no legal way to remove the threat, resulting in an immediate victory for the attacking player.

• **Stalemate**: This is a situation where the player whose turn it is has no legal moves and their **King** is not in check. A **Stalemate** results in an immediate **draw**, regardless of the material advantage on the board.

• **Tactical Patterns**: Common tactics include the **Fork** (attacking two pieces at once, often performed by a **Knight**), the **Pin** (restricting a piece's movement because moving it would expose a more valuable piece), and the **Skewer** (an attack on a valuable piece that forces it to move, exposing a piece behind it).

question: In basketball, a player must release the ball within how many seconds when attempting a free throw?
solution:
The correct answer is __**10 seconds**__.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• According to the **Official Basketball Rules** established by **FIBA** (International Basketball Federation) and the **NBA** (National Basketball Association), a player must release the ball within **10 seconds** when attempting a **free throw**.
 
• The **10-second count** begins as soon as the **official** or **referee** places the ball at the **disposal** of the shooter at the **free-throw line**.
 
• If the player fails to release the ball within this **time limit**, a **violation** is called. This results in the **cancellation** of the shot (if it goes in) and the ball being awarded to the **opposing team** for a **throw-in** from the **sideline**, provided no further free throws are pending.
 
• This rule is designed to maintain the **pace of the game** and prevent players from using the **free-throw line** as an opportunity for excessive **rest** or **stalling**.
 
• The option of **5 seconds** is incorrect for free throws; however, it is a critical **numerical value** used for **inbounding** the ball or when a player is **closely guarded** in the frontcourt.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **24-Second Shot Clock**: Introduced in **1954** by **Danny Biasone**, this rule requires a team to attempt a **field goal** that touches the **rim** within **24 seconds** of gaining **possession**.
 
• **8-Second Rule**: Once a team gains possession in their **backcourt**, they must advance the ball into the **frontcourt** within **8 seconds**. Failure to do so results in a **turnover**.
 
• **3-Second Rule**: An **offensive player** is prohibited from remaining in the **opposing team's restricted area** (the **paint** or **key**) for more than **3 consecutive seconds** while their team has the ball.
 
• **5-Second Closely Guarded Rule**: In **international basketball** and **college basketball**, a player who is **closely guarded** (within **one meter**) must pass, shoot, or dribble the ball within **5 seconds**.
 
• **Scoring**: Unlike **field goals** which are worth **2 or 3 points**, each successful **free throw** adds exactly **1 point** to the team's total score.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Court Dimensions**: The **free-throw line** is located at a distance of **15 feet** (approximately **4.57 meters**) from the plane of the **backboard**.
 
• **Invention of the Game**: Basketball was invented by **Dr. James Naismith** in **December 1891** in **Springfield, Massachusetts**, **USA**. The **free throw** was officially introduced in **1894**.
 
• **Penalty/Bonus Situation**: When a team exceeds the limit of **4 team fouls** in a **quarter** (in the **NBA**), the opposing team enters the **bonus** and receives **two free throws** for every subsequent non-shooting foul.
 
• **Lane Alignment**: During a **free throw** attempt, a maximum of **five players** (three defensive and two offensive) may occupy the **lane spaces** to compete for a **rebound** if the shot is missed.
