question: Who wrote the book "Mein Kampf"?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Adolf Hitler**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Mein Kampf**, which translates to **'My Struggle'**, is an autobiographical manifesto written by the **Nazi Party** leader **Adolf Hitler**. It outlines his political ideology and future plans for **Germany**.

• The book was written while **Hitler** was imprisoned in **Landsberg Prison** in **1924**. He was serving a sentence for **high treason** following the failed **Beer Hall Putsch** (also known as the **Munich Putsch**) of **November 1923**.

• The work was published in two volumes: the first in **1925** and the second in **1926**. It was edited by **Hitler's** deputy, **Rudolf Hess**, who also took dictation for parts of the book while they were both in prison. ***Hence, Option 1 is correct.***

• The book was originally titled 'Four and a Half Years of Struggle against Lies, Stupidity and Cowardice', but the title was shortened to **Mein Kampf** by his publisher, **Max Amann**.

• In the book, **Hitler** details his childhood, his years in **Vienna**, and his experiences during **World War I**, while articulating his **anti-Semitic** and **nationalist** views.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Joseph Goebbels** (Option 2): He served as the **Reich Minister of Propaganda** of **Nazi Germany** from **1933 to 1945**. He was one of **Adolf Hitler's** closest and most devoted acolytes, known for his skills in public speaking and his deep-seated **anti-Semitism**.

• **Heinrich Himmler** (Option 3): He was the **Reichsführer of the Schutzstaffel (SS)** and a leading member of the **Nazi Party**. **Himmler** was one of the most powerful men in **Nazi Germany** and a main architect of the **Holocaust**.

• **Rudolf Hess** (Option 4): He was a prominent politician in **Nazi Germany** and served as **Deputy Führer** to **Adolf Hitler** from **1933 to 1941**. While he assisted in the creation of **Mein Kampf**, he is not the primary author.

• **Ideological Themes**: The book promotes the concept of **Lebensraum** (living space), asserting that **Germany** needed to expand its territory to the east, particularly into **Russia**, to sustain the **Aryan race**.

• **Impact**: After **Hitler** became **Chancellor of Germany** in **1933**, the book became a massive bestseller. It was considered the **'Bible of National Socialism'** and was frequently given as a gift to newlywed couples and soldiers.

**Important Points__**

• **Copyright History**: After **World War II** and **Hitler's** death in **1945**, the copyright of **Mein Kampf** was transferred to the state of **Bavaria**. The **Bavarian government** refused to allow any new editions to be printed in **Germany** to prevent the spread of **Nazi** ideology.

• **Public Domain**: The copyright expired on **December 31, 2015**, exactly **70 years** after the author's death. This led to the publication of a heavily **annotated edition** by the **Institute of Contemporary History** in **Munich** in **2016**, intended for academic and historical study.

• **Social Darwinism**: The book is heavily influenced by **Social Darwinism**, portraying human history as a perpetual struggle between races, with the **Aryan race** at the top of the hierarchy.

• **Global Reach**: Despite its controversial nature, the book has been translated into numerous languages and remains a subject of intense historical analysis to understand the roots of the **Third Reich** and the **Second World War**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Dzongkha**, a **Sino-Tibetan language**, holds the distinction of being the official and national **language of Bhutan**. It employs the **Tibetan script **for its written form.
 
• The term** "dzongkha" **translates to "the language of the fortress," derived from "dzong" meaning "fortress" and "kha" meaning "language."
 
• As of 2013, Dzongkha boasted **171,080 native speakers** and approximately 640,000 speakers overall.
 
• Belonging to the South Tibetic language group, Dzongkha shares close linguistic ties and partial intelligibility with Sikkimese, as well as with other Bhutanese languages such as Chocha Ngacha, Brokpa, Brokkat, and Lakha.
 
• While it maintains a more distant relationship with Standard Tibetan, spoken Dzongkha and Tibetan exhibit mutual intelligibility ranging from 50 to 80 percent.

• **Bhutan**, officially known as the **Kingdom of Bhutan,** is a landlocked country located in South Asia, nestled in the **Eastern Himalayas **between China to the north and India to the south.
 
• It encompasses a population of over 727,145 people and spans a territory of 38,394 square kilometers.
 
• Bhutan ranks 133rd globally in terms of land area and 160th in terms of population. As a constitutional monarchy, Bhutan is governed by a king, known as the Druk Gyalpo, who serves as the head of state, while a prime minister leads the government. Vajrayana Buddhism holds the status of the state religion, with the Je Khenpo serving as the spiritual leader.
 
• Both Bhutan and its neighboring region of Tibet have witnessed the propagation of Buddhism, originating from the Indian subcontinent during the era of Gautama Buddha.

question: Which is the deepest point of Earth's oceans with a depth of 11,022 metres?
solution:
The correct answer is the __**Pacific Ocean's Mariana Trench**__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The Mariana Trench, which is the deepest point on earth, is located in the Pacific Ocean.
 
• It is situated in the western Pacific Ocean, to the east of the Mariana Islands.
 
• The Mariana Trench is approximately 2,550 km long and 69 km wide, with a depth of 10,994 meters at its deepest point, known as the Challenger Deep.
 
• The trench is formed by the collision of the Pacific Plate and the Philippine Plate, which creates a subduction zone and leads to the formation of the deepest part of the ocean floor.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Atlantic Ocean -

 
 
• This is incorrect because the Atlantic Ocean, while vast and home to significant depths, does not contain the deepest point on Earth.
 
• Its deepest point is the Milwaukee Deep (Puerto Rico Trench), which is approximately 8,376 meters (27,480 feet) deep, far shallower compared to the Mariana Trench.
 
 
 
• Indian Ocean -
 
 
• This option is not correct. The Indian Ocean's deepest point is the Java Trench (also known as the Sunda Trench), with a maximum depth of about 7,725 meters (25,344 feet), making it much shallower than the Mariana Trench.
 
 
 
• Arctic Ocean -
 
 
• This is also incorrect. The Arctic Ocean's deepest point is the Molloy Deep in the Fram Strait, with a depth of about 5,550 meters (18,209 feet).
 
• While fascinating for its own ecological and geographical characteristics, it does not compare to the depth of the Mariana Trench.
 
 

Thus, the Mariana Trench's extreme depth and unique ecosystem have made it a subject of much scientific research and interest, emphasizing its significance located in the Pacific Ocean.

question: Atmospheric temperature does NOT depend on _________.

The correct answer is __**salinity of oceans.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Atmospheric temperature **is primarily influenced by air temperature, solar radiation, altitude, latitude, and distance from the sea.
 
• While salinity can affect ocean currents and water temperature, it does not directly impact atmospheric temperature.
 
• Variations in salinity can **influence local weather patterns **but do** not have a direct relationship with atmospheric temperature.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Distance from Sea:**

 
 
• Areas closer to the sea tend to have milder temperatures due to the **moderating effect of water,** which heats up and cools down more slowly than land.
 
• Coastal regions often experience less temperature variation compared to inland areas, which can lead to **higher or lower temperatures** depending on their distance from the ocean.
 
 
 
• **Latitude:**
 
 
• Latitude significantly** affects atmospheric temperature**, with equatorial regions generally experiencing warmer temperatures and polar regions being colder.
 
• The angle of sunlight varies with latitude, **influencing the amount of solar energy** received by different parts of the Earth.
 
 
 
• **Altitude:**
 
 
• As altitude increases,** atmospheric temperature typically decreases due to the thinning of the atmosphere **and reduced air pressure.
 
• Higher elevations tend to have cooler temperatures, regardless of latitude or proximity to the sea.

question: Identify a factor that does NOT determine the temperature of ocean waters.

options.text: Unequal distribution of land and water

solution:
The correct answer is __**Longitude**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Longitude** does not determine the temperature of ocean waters.
 
• The temperature of ocean waters is influenced by factors such as **unequal distribution of land and water, latitude, and ocean currents**.
 
• **Latitude** **affects temperature** as it determines the angle of the sun's rays and length of daylight.
 
• **Ocean currents** can** carry warm or cold water** across different parts of the ocean, affecting local temperatures.
 
• **Unequal distribution of land and water** influences the temperature due to different heat capacities of land and water bodies.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Latitude** is a geographical coordinate that specifies the **north–south position** of a point on the Earth's surface.
 
• **Longitude** is a geographical coordinate that specifies the **east–west position** of a point on the Earth's surface but does not influence temperature.
 
• **Ocean currents** are continuous, directed movements of seawater generated by forces such as wind, temperature differences, and salinity gradients.
 
• The **unequal distribution of land and water** leads to varying heating and cooling rates, affecting the climate and temperature of adjacent ocean waters.

question: What is the name of the cold phase of the ENSO climate pattern that describes the unusual cooling of the surface waters of the region?
solution:
The correct answer is __**La Nina**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **La Nina** is the cold phase of the ENSO (El Niño-Southern Oscillation) climate pattern.
 
• It describes the unusual cooling of the surface waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean.
 
• La Nina events typically bring about a variety of weather changes, including increased rainfall in some regions and drought in others.
 
• This phenomenon is the opposite of El Niño, which is the warm phase of the ENSO climate pattern.
 
• La Nina can influence global weather patterns and has significant impacts on agriculture, water supply, and hurricane activity.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The ENSO cycle includes both El Niño and La Nina phases, as well as periods of neutral conditions.
 
• La Nina events are characterized by stronger-than-average trade winds, which push warm water towards the western Pacific, allowing cold water to upwell in the eastern Pacific.
 
• The cooling effect of La Nina can last for several months and typically occurs every 2 to 7 years.
 
• La Nina can also influence the Atlantic hurricane season, often leading to more active hurricane periods.
 
• Scientists monitor the ENSO cycle using various tools, including satellite observations and ocean buoys, to predict and understand its impacts.

question: Ozone layer in the atmosphere shields the surface of the Earth from which radiation from the Sun?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Ultraviolet (UV) light.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• **Ozone layer**

 
 
• It is a layer of ozone molecules found in the **stratosphere** (the second layer of the atmosphere).
 
• Ozone is a molecule made up of three oxygen atoms, often referenced as **O3**.
 
• The ozone layer is typically thicker over the poles than over the equator.
 
• The ozone layer exists in the stratosphere, a layer 10 to 50 km above the Earth’s surface.
 
• **The presence of ozone in the stratosphere prevents about 99.5 percent of the sun’s harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiations from reaching the earth’s surface**.
 
• Thus, protecting humans and other animals from its effect.
 
 
 
• **Harmful effects of UV Radiations**
 
 
• They lead to aging of the skin, cataracts, sunburn, skin cancer, the killing of many phytoplanktons, damage to fish productivity, etc.
 
• It has also been reported that plant proteins get easily affected by UV radiation which leads to the harmful mutation of cells.
 
• It also increases the evaporation of surface water through the stomata of the leaves and decreases the moisture content of the soil.
 
 
 
• **Ozone Layer Depletion**
 
 
• The reasons for ozone depletion are a wide range of industrial and consumer applications, mainly refrigerators, air conditioners (hydrochlorofluorocarbons (HCFCs), chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs)), and fire extinguishers.
 
• Ozone depletion is greatest at the South Pole (Antarctica).
 
• This severe depletion creates the so-called** “ozone hole”**.
 
• The Negative Effects of the ozone hole are certain types of skin cancers, eye cataracts, and immune deficiency disorders.
 
• The international community established **the Montreal Protocol on ozone-depleting substances in 1987,** to address the destruction of the ozone layer.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Ultraviolet Light**

 
 
• UV light from the sun has shorter wavelengths than visible light so it is not visible to the naked eye.
 
• UV radiation’s full spectrum is sourced from the sun 
 
• It can be classified into** UV-A, UV-B, and UV-C** rays according to their wavelength
 
 
 
• **Classification of UV rays**

 
 

 
 
**Types of UV Radiations**

 
 
 
**Characteristics**

 
 
 

 
 
UV-C

 
 
 
 
• Short-wavelength
 
• Most harmful but are completely absorbed by the Earth’s atmosphere.
 
• These rays do not reach the Earth’s surface.
 
 
 
 

 
 
UV-B

 
 
 
 
• Medium Wavelength
 
• Enhances skin aging and significantly promotes the development of skin cancer.
 
• Exposure to UV-B rays can cause DNA and cellular damage in living organisms.
 
• Most solar UVB is filtered by the atmosphere.
 
 
 
 

 
 
UV-A

 
 
 
 
• Relatively long-wavelength.
 
• Accounts for approximately 95% of the UV radiation reaching the Earth's surface.
 
• Enhances the development of skin cancers.

question: Which branch of geology focuses on the study of fossils and ancient life forms?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Palaeontology**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Palaeontology** is the branch of geology dedicated to the study of **fossils** and **ancient life forms**. It involves examining the remains of plants, animals, and other organisms that lived millions of years ago.
 
• The primary focus of palaeontology is to understand the **evolutionary history** of life on Earth by studying fossils.
 
• Fossils provide valuable information about the past, including the structure, behavior, and interactions of ancient organisms, as well as the environmental conditions in which they lived.
 
• Palaeontology plays a significant role in determining the **age of rocks**, correlating rock layers across regions, and reconstructing past ecosystems.
 
• Modern palaeontological studies use advanced techniques like **radiometric dating** to determine the age of fossils and molecular methods to analyze ancient DNA.
 
• Examples of famous fossils studied in palaeontology include the **Archaeopteryx** (a transitional fossil between dinosaurs and birds) and the **Tyrannosaurus rex**.
 
• Palaeontology is interdisciplinary, combining elements of biology, geology, and environmental science to provide a comprehensive understanding of Earth's biological past.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Other Branches of Geology:**

 
 
• **Petrology:** The study of the origin, composition, and structure of rocks. It involves examining igneous, metamorphic, and sedimentary rocks to understand geological processes.
 
• **Mineralogy:** The study of minerals, their chemical composition, properties, and crystal structures. It helps in identifying and classifying minerals found in the Earth's crust.
 
• **Geochronology:** The science of determining the age of rocks, fossils, and sediments using dating methods such as radiometric dating.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Palaeontology:**
 
 
• Reconstruction of Earth's **geological history** and environmental changes over time.
 
• Understanding the process of **evolution** and the development of life forms.
 
• Providing insights into mass extinction events, such as the extinction of the dinosaurs.
 
• Helping in the exploration of **oil and gas** reserves by identifying fossilized microorganisms in rock layers.
 
 
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• The word "palaeontology" is derived from the Greek words **"palaios" (ancient)**, **"ontos" (being)**, and **"logos" (study)**.
 
• Fossils can be classified into two main types: **body fossils** (remains of an organism's body) and **trace fossils** (evidence of an organism's activities, such as footprints or burrows).
 
• Famous palaeontologists include **Mary Anning**, who discovered important Jurassic fossils, and **Charles Darwin**, whose work on evolution was influenced by fossil studies.

question: In 1962, who published 'The History of Ocean Basins', which outlined the theory of how tectonic plates could move, later called 'sea floor spreading'?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Harry Hammond Hess**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Harry Hammond Hess** published 'The History of Ocean Basins' in 1962.
 
• His work outlined the theory of how tectonic plates could move, which later came to be known as 'sea floor spreading'.
 
• Hess's theory was crucial in providing a mechanism for Alfred Wegener's earlier hypothesis of continental drift.
 
• This theory helped to explain the formation of mid-ocean ridges and the symmetrical pattern of magnetic stripes on the ocean floor.
 
• Sea floor spreading is a key component of the broader theory of plate tectonics, which describes the movement of the Earth's lithosphere.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Alfred Wegener** proposed the theory of continental drift in 1912, suggesting that continents had once been joined together and had since drifted apart.
 
• **Louis Bauer** was an American geophysicist known for his work in geomagnetism but did not contribute to the theory of sea floor spreading.
 
• **George Edward Backus** was an American geophysicist known for his work in geophysical inverse theory and geomagnetism, but not related to sea floor spreading.
 
• The concept of plate tectonics has revolutionized our understanding of Earth's geological processes, including the formation of mountains, earthquakes, and volcanic activity.

question: What is the name of the process of gases being outpoured from the interior of the solid earth?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Degassing**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• This started the evolution of the present atmosphere.
 
• The early atmosphere largely contained water vapour, nitrogen, carbon dioxide, methane, ammonia and very little of free oxygen.

• The **summer solstice**, also known as **estival solstice or midsummer.**
 
• It occurs **when one of the Earth's poles has its maximum tilt toward the Sun**. It **happens twice yearly**, once in each hemisphere **(Northern and Southern).**
 
• For that hemisphere, the **summer solstice is when the Sun reaches its highest position in the sky and is the day with the longest period of daylight.**
 
• Within the **Arctic circle (for the northern hemisphere) or Antarctic circle (for the southern hemisphere), there is continuous daylight around the summer solstice**.
 
• On the summer solstice, **Earth's maximum axial tilt toward the Sun is 23.44°. Likewise, the Sun's declination from the celestial equator is 23.44°.**
 
• The** summer solstice** occurs **during summer**. This is the **June solstice in the Northern Hemisphere and the December solstice in the Southern Hemisphere.**

question: The Chagos Archipelago is a disputed territory between ________.
solution:
The correct answer is __**United Kingdom and Mauritius**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The **Chagos Archipelago** is a group of **seven atolls** comprising more than **60 individual tropical islands** in the **Indian Ocean**, located about **500 kilometres** south of the **Maldives** archipelago.

• The sovereignty of the **Chagos Archipelago** has been a long-standing point of contention between the **United Kingdom** and **Mauritius** since the **1960s**.

• The dispute began in **1965**, when the **United Kingdom** decided to excise the **Chagos Archipelago** from the colony of **Mauritius** to create the **British Indian Ocean Territory (BIOT)**, just three years before **Mauritius** gained independence in **1968**.

• **Mauritius** has consistently maintained that the detachment of the islands was a violation of **United Nations Resolution 1514**, which prohibits the disruption of the territorial integrity of colonies prior to their independence.

• In a landmark development in **October 2024**, the **United Kingdom** and **Mauritius** reached a political agreement where the **UK** agreed to transfer sovereignty of the **Chagos Archipelago** to **Mauritius**, effectively resolving the decades-old dispute.

**Additional Information__**

__

• **Diego Garcia**: This is the largest island in the **Chagos Archipelago** and is home to a strategically vital **United Kingdom-United States military base**. The base plays a critical role in **regional security** and global military operations in the **Indo-Pacific** and **Middle East**.

• **Expulsion of Chagossians**: Between **1967** and **1973**, the **United Kingdom** government forcibly removed the entire native population, known as the **Chagossians** or **Ilois**, to **Mauritius** and the **Seychelles** to facilitate the construction of the military base on **Diego Garcia**.

• **ICJ Advisory Opinion (2019)**: The **International Court of Justice (ICJ)** in **The Hague** issued an advisory opinion in **February 2019**, stating that the process of decolonization of **Mauritius** was not lawfully completed and that the **United Kingdom** is under an obligation to end its administration of the **Chagos Archipelago** as rapidly as possible.

• **UN General Assembly Resolution**: Following the **ICJ** ruling, the **United Nations General Assembly** passed a resolution in **May 2019** with an overwhelming majority, demanding that the **UK** withdraw its colonial administration from the islands within **six months**.

• **ITLOS Ruling**: In **2021**, the **International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS)** also ruled that the **United Kingdom** has no sovereignty over the **Chagos Archipelago** and criticized its failure to return the territory to **Mauritius**.

**Important Points__**

• **The 2024 Treaty Details**: Under the historic **2024 agreement**, while **Mauritius** will now hold sovereignty over the entire archipelago, the **United Kingdom** will be authorized to exercise the sovereign rights of **Mauritius** in respect of **Diego Garcia** for an initial period of **99 years**.

• **Resettlement Rights**: The agreement includes a **trust fund** and financial support to enable **Mauritius** to implement a programme of resettlement for the **Chagossian** people on islands other than **Diego Garcia**.

• **Strategic Importance**: The resolution of this dispute is seen as a major step in securing the long-term future of the **Diego Garcia** base while upholding **international law** and completing the **decolonization** process in the **Indian Ocean**.

• **Environmental Protection**: The **Chagos Archipelago** is home to some of the world's cleanest **coral reefs** and diverse marine life; the new agreement ensures continued **environmental cooperation** between the two nations.
</ul

question: Chabahar Port is located in which country?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Iran**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Chabahar Port** is a strategic maritime facility located in the **Sistan and Baluchestan Province** on the **southeastern coast** of **Iran**. It is situated on the **Gulf of Oman** and serves as the country's only **oceanic port**, providing direct access to the **Indian Ocean**.

• The port consists of two separate terminals: **Shahid Beheshti** and **Shahid Kalantari**. The development of the **Shahid Beheshti** terminal has seen significant involvement from **India** to enhance regional connectivity.

• The location is of vital **geopolitical importance** because it allows **India** to bypass **Pakistan** and establish a direct trade link with **Afghanistan** and the **Central Asian Republics**.

• In **May 2016**, a trilateral agreement was signed between **India**, **Iran**, and **Afghanistan** to develop the port as a **transit hub**. This was aimed at reducing **Afghanistan's** dependence on **Pakistan** for sea access.

• The port is managed and operated through a partnership involving **India Ports Global Limited (IPGL)** and the **Port and Maritime Organization of Iran**. In **May 2024**, **India** and **Iran** signed a long-term **10-year contract** for the operation of the **Shahid Beheshti** terminal.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Strategic Rivalry**: **Chabahar Port** is located about **170 kilometers** west of the **Gwadar Port** in **Pakistan**, which is being developed by **China** as part of the **China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC)**. This proximity makes **Chabahar** a counter-strategy for **India** in the **Arabian Sea**.

• **INSTC Integration**: The port is a key node in the **International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC)**, a **7,200-kilometer** long multi-mode network of ship, rail, and road routes for moving freight between **India**, **Iran**, **Azerbaijan**, **Russia**, **Central Asia**, and **Europe**.

• **Economic Impact**: The port facilitates the movement of goods such as **iron ore**, **sugar**, and **rice** from **India**, while **Iran** exports **oil**, **fertilizers**, and **petrochemicals**. It significantly reduces **transportation costs** and **time** by nearly **30 percent** to **40 percent** compared to the **Suez Canal** route.

• **Humanitarian Role**: **India** utilized the **Chabahar Port** to ship **75,000 tonnes** of **wheat** as humanitarian aid to **Afghanistan** in **2020** and has also used it to supply **pesticides** to **Iran** to fight locust infestations.

• **Connectivity Infrastructure**: To complement the port, **India** helped build the **Zaranj-Delaram Highway** in **Afghanistan**, which connects the **Iranian border** to the **Garland Highway**, linking major Afghan cities like **Kabul**, **Kandahar**, and **Herat**.

**Important Points__**

• **Free Trade Zone**: The **Chabahar Free Trade-Industrial Zone (CFZ)** was established to attract **foreign direct investment (FDI)** and promote industrial development, particularly in sectors like **petrochemicals** and **steel**.

• **Exemption from Sanctions**: Due to its importance for the **reconstruction of Afghanistan**, the development of **Chabahar Port** was previously granted a **carve-out** or exemption from certain **United States** sanctions imposed on **Iran**.

• **Distance**: The distance between **Kandla Port** in **Gujarat**, **India**, and **Chabahar Port** is approximately **550 nautical miles**, making it a relatively short and efficient maritime route.

• **Regional Security**: The port enhances **maritime security** in the **Indian Ocean Region (IOR)** and allows **India** to monitor naval activities in the **Gulf of Oman** and the **Strait of Hormuz**.
</ul

question: McMahon Line is the boundary line between India and ________.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The McMahon Line is the boundary line between India and **China**.
 
• It was established as part of the Simla Convention signed in 1914 between British India and Tibet, which was not recognized by China at that time.
 
• The line is named after Sir Henry McMahon, who was the chief negotiator from the British side.
 
• The McMahon Line runs through the eastern sector of the India-China border, which is disputed by China.
 
• It is a major point of contention in the border disputes between India and China, leading to several conflicts, including the 1962 Sino-Indian War.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The Simla Convention was an attempt to settle the boundaries between British India and Tibet, and to establish Tibet as an autonomous region under Chinese suzerainty.
 
• China did not accept the Simla Convention, arguing that Tibet was not a sovereign entity and hence had no authority to sign treaties.
 
• The McMahon Line has been a flashpoint in India-China relations, with both countries strengthening their military presence along the border.
 
• Despite the disputes, the McMahon Line is currently the de facto border in the eastern sector between India and China.
 
• Efforts have been made through diplomatic channels to resolve the boundary issues, but a final settlement has not yet been reached.

subject: GK
question: What is the term for the movement of tectonic plates causing earthquakes?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Plate tectonics**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Plate tectonics** is the scientific theory that describes the large-scale motion of the seven large plates and the movements of a larger number of smaller plates of Earth's **lithosphere**.
 
• Earthquakes occur when these tectonic plates interact at their boundaries. The friction between the plates causes **stress** to build up; when this stress is suddenly released, it sends **seismic waves** through the Earth's crust, resulting in an earthquake.
 
• **Erosion** is a geological process in which earthen materials are worn away and transported by natural forces such as wind or water, which does not cause tectonic earthquakes.
 
• **Sedimentation** is the tendency for particles in suspension to settle out of the fluid in which they are entrained and come to rest against a barrier, a process unrelated to plate movement.
 
• **Convection** (specifically mantle convection) is the slow creeping motion of Earth's solid silicate mantle caused by convection currents carrying heat from the interior to the surface. While it is the **driving force** behind plate movement, the movement itself and the resulting earthquakes are categorized under the theory of **Plate tectonics**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The theory of plate tectonics built upon the concept of **Continental Drift**, an idea first proposed by scientist **Alfred Wegener** in 1912.
 
• There are three primary types of plate boundaries: **Divergent** (moving apart), **Convergent** (moving together), and **Transform** (sliding past each other).
 
• Most of the world's earthquakes and volcanic eruptions occur along the **Pacific Ring of Fire**, which is a direct result of plate tectonics and the movement of several major and minor tectonic plates.
 
• The point inside the Earth where the earthquake starts is called the **Hypocenter** (or focus), and the point directly above it on the surface is the **Epicenter**.

subject: GK
question: Which region of the world has the highest elderly dependency ratio?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Europe**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The **elderly dependency ratio** is a demographic measure that represents the number of elderly people (typically those aged **65 years and older**) per **100 individuals** of working age (usually **15 to 64 years**). It indicates the potential burden on the working population to support the non-working elderly population.

• **Europe** is the region with the highest elderly dependency ratio in the world. This is a result of the region being in the advanced stages of the **Demographic Transition Model**, characterized by **low birth rates** and **high life expectancy**.

• According to data from the **United Nations Population Division**, European countries such as **Italy**, **Germany**, **Greece**, and **Portugal** have some of the highest proportions of elderly citizens globally. In these nations, the number of retirees is growing faster than the number of new workers entering the labor force.

• In contrast, **Africa** has the lowest elderly dependency ratio. This is because the continent has a very young population structure with high **fertility rates**, meaning the proportion of people over **65** is relatively small compared to the large youth and working-age population.

• While **Asia** (specifically countries like **Japan** and **South Korea**) and **South America** are seeing rapid increases in their elderly populations, the continental average for **Europe** remains the highest due to decades of sustained low fertility and medical advancements that have increased **longevity**.

**Additional Information__**

__

• The **Demographic Transition Model (DTM)** describes the transition from high birth and death rates to low birth and death rates as a country develops. Most European nations are in **Stage 4** or **Stage 5**, where the population begins to age significantly or even decline.

• A high elderly dependency ratio poses significant **economic challenges**, including increased pressure on **pension systems**, higher **healthcare costs** for geriatric care, and a potential shortage of labor in the **productive sectors** of the economy.

• **Japan**, although located in **Asia**, is the individual country with the highest elderly dependency ratio in the world, with over **28%** of its population aged **65 or older** as of recent **World Bank** data.

• To mitigate the effects of an aging population, many countries in **Europe** are implementing policies such as **increasing the retirement age**, encouraging **skilled immigration**, and providing **pro-natalist incentives** to boost birth rates.

• The **World Population Prospects 2022** report highlights that the global population is aging at an unprecedented rate. By the **year 2050**, the number of persons aged **65 years or over** globally is projected to be more than twice the number of children under age **5**.

**Important Points__**

• The **Old-Age Dependency Ratio (OADR)** is specifically used by **economists** and **policymakers** to calculate the **sustainability** of **social security** benefits. A ratio of **1:3**, for example, means there are three working-age people for every one elderly person.

• **Sub-Saharan Africa** remains the 'youngest' region, where the **child dependency ratio** (0-14 years) is the primary demographic concern rather than the elderly ratio.

• **Silver Economy** is a term used to describe the economic opportunities and markets that emerge from the needs of the aging population, particularly in sectors like **biotechnology**, **home-care services**, and **leisure**.

• The **United Nations** designates **October 1st** as the **International Day of Older Persons** to raise awareness about the opportunities and challenges of aging in the **21st century**.
</ul

question: Which BRICS country is the largest producer of gold among the group?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Russia**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• Among the options provided, **Russia** is the largest producer of gold. As of **2022** and **2023**, **Russia** produced approximately **310 to 330 tonnes** of gold annually, making it the second-largest producer in the world, trailing only **China**.

• **South Africa**, which historically dominated global gold production for over a century, has seen its output fall significantly due to the depletion of shallow reserves and the high cost of deep-level mining. It currently produces around **100 tonnes** per year, ranking well below **Russia**.

• **Brazil** is a notable producer in the **South American** region, with an annual output of roughly **80 to 90 tonnes**. Most of its production comes from the **Amazon** basin and the state of **Minas Gerais**.

• **India** has very minimal domestic gold production, contributing less than **2 tonnes** annually. The majority of **India** gold is produced by **Hutti Gold Mines Limited** in **Karnataka**. Consequently, **India** relies heavily on imports to satisfy its massive domestic demand.

• While **China** is a member of the **BRICS** group and is the largest gold producer globally (producing over **370 tonnes**), it was not included in the given options, making **Russia** the correct choice among the four countries listed.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **BRICS Expansion**: The **BRICS** bloc, originally consisting of **Brazil**, **Russia**, **India**, **China**, and **South Africa**, expanded in **January 2024** to include **Egypt**, **Ethiopia**, **Iran**, and the **United Arab Emirates**, further increasing the group influence over global mineral resources.

• **Major Mining Companies**: **Russia** gold industry is led by **Polyus**, which is one of the world largest gold mining companies by reserves. Their flagship operation, the **Olimpiada** mine located in the **Krasnoyarsk** region, is a major contributor to the national output.

• **Witwatersrand Basin**: Located in **South Africa**, this geological formation has historically produced nearly **40%** of all the gold ever mined on **Earth**. However, mines here now reach depths of over **4 kilometers**, making them some of the deepest and most expensive to operate in the world.

• **Central Bank Reserves**: **Russia** has been one of the most active buyers of gold globally. The **Central Bank of Russia** holds over **2,300 tonnes** of gold as part of its international reserves to diversify away from the **US Dollar** and **Euro**.

• **Global Ranking**: On a global scale, the top three gold-producing nations are typically **China**, **Russia**, and **Australia**. These three countries combined account for a significant portion of the total global mine production, which is estimated at **3,600 tonnes** annually.

**Important Points__**

• **Kolar Gold Fields (KGF)**: Located in **Karnataka**, **India**, these mines were once the pride of the **British Raj** and independent **India**. They were closed in **2001** due to environmental issues and the diminishing grade of ore, which made extraction economically unviable.

While economically important, these activities frequently cause significant environmental damage, including **mercury** contamination in **Amazonian** rivers.

• **World Gold Council (WGC)**: Headquartered in **London**, the **WGC** is the market development organization for the gold industry. It provides critical data on **demand-supply** balances, **investment** trends, and **Central Bank** holdings for countries like **Russia** and **India**.

• **Economic Impact**: For **Russia** and **South Africa**, gold exports are a vital source of **foreign exchange earnings**. In contrast, for **India**, gold is a major **import** item that significantly impacts the **Current Account Deficit (CAD)**.

subject: GK
question: What characterizes Stage II of demographic transition?

options.text: Birth and death rates are equa
Death rate declines, birth rate remains high
Birth rate falls below death rate

solution:
The correct answer is __**Death rate declines, birth rate remains high**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Stage II of the Demographic Transition:** This stage is characterized by a significant **decline in the death rate** while the **birth rate remains high**. This leads to a rapid increase in the population.
 
• The decline in the death rate is primarily due to **improvements in healthcare, sanitation, and nutrition**. For example, advancements in medical technology and widespread vaccination programs reduce mortality rates significantly.
 
• The birth rate remains consistently high during this stage due to **cultural and societal norms**, lack of awareness about family planning, and the reliance on large families for economic support. *Hence, this option is correct.*
 
• **Population Growth:** The result of this disparity between high birth rates and declining death rates is a **sharp increase in population**. This is often referred to as a "population explosion."
 
• In this stage, countries experience a **demographic momentum**, where population growth accelerates before stabilizing in subsequent stages.
 
• **Historical Examples:** Countries like **India and many African nations** went through Stage II during the mid-20th century when modern medical practices and public health measures were introduced.
 
• *Thus, the characteristic feature of Stage II is the significant decline in the death rate while the birth rate remains high, leading to rapid population growth.*

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] Additional Information____ __**

__
 
• **Demographic Transition Model:**

 
 
• **Demographic transition** is a model that describes the transition of a country’s population from high birth and death rates to low birth and death rates as it develops economically and socially.
 
• The model has **four stages**:
 
 
• **Stage I:** High birth and death rates, leading to a stable and low population.
 
• **Stage II:** Decline in death rates, while birth rates remain high, causing rapid population growth.
 
• **Stage III:** Decline in birth rates, leading to a slowdown in population growth.
 
• **Stage IV:** Low birth and death rates, resulting in a stable or declining population.
 
 
 
 
 
• **Key Factors Influencing Stage II:**
 
 
• The decline in death rates is driven by factors such as **improved medical care, better sanitation, and increased food production.**
 
• High birth rates persist due to **cultural, social, and economic factors**, including the need for labor in agricultural economies and lack of family planning awareness.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Countries in Stage II:**
 
 
• **Historical Examples:** During the 19th century, countries like **England** and **Germany** entered Stage II due to the Industrial Revolution.
 
• **Contemporary Examples:** Many **developing countries**, including parts of Africa and South Asia, are currently in Stage II.
 
 

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] Important Points____ __**

 
• **Stage I vs. Stage II:**

 
 
• **Stage I:** High birth and death rates result in a stable population. Examples include pre-industrial societies.
 
• **Stage II:** Decline in death rates due to medical and public health improvements, while birth rates remain high, leading to population growth.
 
 
 
• **Transition to Stage III:**
 
 
• With urbanization, education, and family planning, birth rates begin to decline in Stage III, slowing population growth.
 
• **Example:** Developed countries like the **USA and Japan** transitioned to Stage III by the mid-20th century.

subject: GK
question: Which of the following best explains the origin of eskers in glaciated landscapes?

options.text: Ridges carved by ice cutting bedrock
Sinuous ridges from subglacial meltwater deposition
Hills shaped by ice pushing sediments

solution:
The correct answer is __**Sinuous ridges from subglacial meltwater deposition**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Eskers** are prominent **fluvio-glacial landforms** characterized by long, narrow, and **sinuous ridges** of **stratified drift**, primarily consisting of **sand and gravel**.
 
• The origin of these structures is attributed to **meltwater streams** flowing through **subglacial tunnels** (beneath the ice) or **englacial channels** (within the ice) under high hydrostatic pressure.
 
• As the **glacier** becomes stagnant and begins to melt, the velocity of the internal stream decreases, causing the **deposition of sediments** along the floor of the ice tunnel.
 
• Once the surrounding **glacial ice** completely disappears, the accumulated sediment is left behind as a **continuous ridge** that winds across the landscape, often reaching heights of several meters and lengths of many kilometers.
 
• Unlike landforms created directly by ice, the materials in an **esker** are **sorted and layered** because they were transported and deposited by **flowing water**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Glacial Till and Moraines**:

 
 
• **Moraines** are ridges formed from **till**, which is **unsorted sediment** deposited directly by the ice rather than meltwater.
 
• **Terminal moraines** mark the furthest reach of a glacier, while **lateral moraines** form along the sides of the **glacial valley**.
 
 
 
• **Drumlins**:
 
 
• These are **oval-shaped or teardrop-shaped hills** formed by the **streamlining** of till or **sediment deformation** under the weight of a moving glacier.
 
• The **steep side** of a drumlin faces the direction from which the **ice advanced**, while the tapered tail points in the direction of **ice flow**.
 
 
 
• **Erosional Landforms**:
 
 
• Landforms like **U-shaped valleys**, **fjords**, and **cirques** are created by the **erosive action** of ice cutting into the **bedrock**, contrasting with the **depositional nature** of eskers.

• **Density of population** refers to the number of people living per unit area of **land**.
 
• This metric is important for understanding how populated an area is and can influence planning and resource allocation.
 
• It is **calculated by dividing the total population by the total land area**.
 
• **Higher population density** can indicate **urbanization**, while **lower population density **may be indicative of **rural areas**.

• Regions with high population density may face challenges like **overcrowding, pollution, and strain on resources**.
 
• Conversely, areas with low population density might struggle with **underdevelopment and lack of services**.
 
• Understanding population density helps governments and organizations to plan for **infrastructure, healthcare, education, and other essential services**.
 
• Population density varies widely across different parts of the world and can be influenced by factors such as **geography, climate, and economic opportunities**.

question: Which BRICS country is known for hosting the Amazon Rainforest?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Brazil**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Brazil** is the **BRICS** member nation that hosts the majority of the **Amazon Rainforest**, with approximately **60%** of the forest located within its national borders. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***

• The **Amazon Rainforest** is a vast **tropical biome** situated in **South America**, making it impossible for **Russia**, which is located in the **Northern Hemisphere** across **Europe** and **Asia**, to host it. **Russia** is instead known for the **Taiga**. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***

• **India**, located in **South Asia**, possesses its own unique tropical forests such as those in the **Western Ghats** and the **Andaman and Nicobar Islands**, but it does not share any territory with the **Amazon basin**. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***

• **South Africa** is situated at the southern tip of the **African continent** and is known for its **savanna**, **Karoo**, and **Mediterranean** climates, which are geographically distinct from the **equatorial rainforest** of the Amazon. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

• The **Amazon** is often called the **'Lungs of the Planet'** due to its role in **carbon sequestration** and **oxygen production**, and **Brazil** plays a central role in its **environmental governance**.

**Additional Information__**
__

• The **Amazon Rainforest** spans across **nine countries** in total, including **Peru** (13%), **Colombia** (10%), and smaller portions in **Venezuela**, **Ecuador**, **Bolivia**, **Guyana**, **Suriname**, and **French Guiana**.

• It is home to the **Amazon River**, which is the largest river by **discharge volume** of water in the world and the **second longest** river after the **Nile**.

• The **BRICS** acronym was originally coined by **Goldman Sachs** economist **Jim O'Neill** in **2001** to describe the fast-growing economies of **Brazil, Russia, India, and China**.

• The group held its first formal summit in **2009**, and **South Africa** joined the bloc in **2010**, changing the acronym to **BRICS**.

• The **Amazon** contains over **390 billion individual trees** divided into **16,000 species**, representing **10%** of the world's known **biodiversity**.

**Important Points__**

• **Deforestation** in the **Brazilian Amazon** is a major global concern, primarily driven by **cattle ranching**, **soybean farming**, and **illegal logging**.

• **Brazil** uses advanced **satellite technology**, such as the **PRODES** and **DETER** systems managed by the **National Institute for Space Research (INPE)**, to monitor forest loss.

• The **Amazon Cooperation Treaty Organization (ACTO)** is an international body aimed at the **sustainable development** of the **Amazon Basin**, with its headquarters in **Brasilia**.

• In **August 2023**, **Brazil** hosted the **Amazon Summit** in the city of **Belem** to coordinate protection efforts among the eight rainforest nations.

• As of **January 1, 2024**, the **BRICS** bloc expanded to include new members like **Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, and the United Arab Emirates**, though **Brazil** remains the primary representative of the **Amazonian** region within the group.
</ul

question: What type of climate occurs along the west coast of continents in subtropical latitudes between 30° - 40° latitudes, covering Central California, Central Chile along the coast in South East and South Western Australia?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Mediterranean climate**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The Mediterranean climate** occurs along the western coasts of continents within **subtropical latitudes**, typically ranging between** 30° and 40° latitudes.**
 
• This climate is evident in regions such as **Central California, Central Chile, and the coastal areas of South-Eastern and South-Western Australia.**
 
• In this climate zone, winters are generally mild and summers are warm, with significant temperature variations among different regions.
 
• Rainfall is irregular, with the majority occurring during the winter months.
 
• Common vegetation in Mediterranean climates includes oaks, olives, citrus fruits, and junipers.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Subtropical steppes** are situated in the transitional areas between dry and humid climates, receiving slightly more precipitation than subtropical deserts. This amount is adequate to support sparse grasslands.
 
• **A humid subtropical climate** is characterized by hot, humid summers and cool to mild winters, falling within the temperate category.
 
• **The marine west coast climate** is typically found midway between the tropics and the Arctic or Antarctic regions, typically between 35 and 60 degrees north latitude.

solution:

• Mean temperatures vary from **20°C (68 °F)** in the south to **24°C (75 °F) **in the north. Interestingly, the coldest periods in the South Western Ghats coincide with the wettest seasons.
 
• The Western Ghats, also known as the Sahyadri mountain range, span an area of 160,000 km² along a 1,600 km stretch parallel to the western coast of the Indian peninsula.
 
• This range crosses through the states of Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu.
 
• Recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the 36 biodiversity hotspots globally, it's often referred to as the Great Escarpment of India.
 
• The Western Ghats harbor a significant portion of the country's flora and fauna, with many species endemic to this region.

question: Which of the following rivers originates from Sihawa Mountain?
solution:
The correct answer is__** Mahanadi.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Mahanadi:**

 
 
• ​It originates from the Sihawa Mountain in the Dhamtari district of Chhattisgarh.
 
• The river originates from an extension of the Eastern Ghats.
 
• It flows in Odisha where it joins the Bay of Bengal.
 
• Other names of Mahanadi are Kanaknandini, Chitrapalal, Mahasweta, Nilotpala etc.
 
• Hirakud Dam is built on the Mahanadi.
 
• It is the largest earthen dam in the world.​
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__ **

__
 
• **Narmada:**

 
 
• ​The Narmada river originates from Amarkantak in the Anuppur district of Madhya Pradesh state in India.
 
• This River is also known as the Reva, and in ancient times it was also called Narbada (Nerbudda).
 
• The River Narmada is well known as the "Life Line of Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh state".
 
• The total number of tributaries of the Narmada river is 41.
 
 
 
• Indus River:
 
 
• The river originates at Lake Mansarovar in Tibet (China).
 
• It drains Tibet (China), India and Pakistan.
 
• At last, the river falls into the Arabian Sea near Karachi (Pakistan).
 
• The length of the Indus is 3,180 km.
 
• **Rigvedic name of Indus is Sindhu.**
 
 
 
• Tributaries:__
 __
 
• ​__Left Bank: Zanskar, Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej.
 
• Right bank: Shyok, Gilgit, Hunza, Kabul, Swat, Kurram.
 
 
 
• Brahmaputra:
 __
 
• It originates under the name of Siang or Dihang, from the Angsi glacier__ of the Kailash range near the Mansarovar lake.
 
• It enters India west of Sadiya town in Arunachal Pradesh. 
 
 
 
• Tributaries: Dibang, Lohit, Siang, Burhi Dihing, Tista, and Dhansari.
 __
 
• It is known as Tsangpo in Tibet and Yarlung Zangbo in China. 
 
• The river crosses Assam below Dhubri and enters Bangladesh where the river is known as Jamuna and it flows for 337 km.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• Most of the major rivers of the Peninsula, such as the Mahanadi, the Godavari, the Krishna, and the Kaveri flow eastwards and drain into the Bay of Bengal.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ad249e3a445616f45713394acb4d8fc52bb4b89ed2a0fc9f38c505a67e6f7f4a.png] 

71:T1e

question: Which of the following rivers originates in Maharashtra?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Godavari**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** 

__
 
• The Godavari River rises from Trimbakeshwar in the Nashik district of Maharashtra.
 
• It is the oldest River in India.
 
• It is also known as the Ganga of South India.
 
• It is the second-longest river in India.
 
• Dams on the Godavari river are - Polavaram Dam (Andhra Pradesh), Pochampad Dam (Telangana).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__** 

__
 
• Tributaries of Godavari river are - 

 
 
• Indravati (Chattisgarh)
 
• Painganga.
 
• Venganga.
 
• Pranhita
 
 
 
• Cities that lie along the Godavari river are -
 
 
• Nasik, Nanded (Maharashtra).
 
• Bhadrachalam ( Andhra Pradesh).
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/6a964872f2447684d0758dfe7fe644bc5755a2e862edb380bb041fdd9f5e50fc.png] 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__** 

 
• Sources of some important Rivers of India -

 
 
• Brahmaputra - Kailash Mansarover Lake
 
• Indus - Kailash Mansarover Lake
 
• Jhelum - Seshnag Lake
 
• Chenab - Bara-la-cha Pass
 
• Ravi - Rohtang Pass
 
• Sutluj - Kailash Mountain
 
• Ganga - Gangotri
 
• Narmada - Maikal Hills
